exp.16:24:
This proverb says that a foolish son, that is, one who acts without good sense and rejects the right path, causes grief and sorrow to his father, and bitterness to the mother who bore him. The word "grief" here speaks of sorrow and frustration, not only of mild annoyance.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, although students of the Bible do not always agree on who wrote each section. Here the theme is the contrast between the wise person and the fool: the verse before speaks of the fool whose eyes wander without direction, and the verse after of prudence. It is a general observation about life, not a promise for every case.

For today: if you are a parent of someone who suffers because of their decisions, do not burden yourself with guilt without reason; pray, love, and keep guiding. If you are a child, remember that your decisions affect the hearts of those who love you.
exp.21:15:
This proverb says that whoever takes advantage of the poor to gain more, or whoever gives gifts to the rich to win their favor, will end up in poverty. "Oppressing" means treating those who have little harshly and unjustly. The word "increase" means becoming richer. Some understand that both actions are ways of seeking unjust gain, and that God does not allow that to prosper.

Here the wise Solomon speaks, or the tradition of wise teachers that the book gathers, like a father instructing his son. The verses nearby speak of temptation, foolishness and correction. Then comes the invitation to listen to the wise. The proverb warns that money gained dishonestly is not secure.

For today: check whether your work or your business treats the weakest fairly, such as employees, customers or neighbors. Paying what is right and not seeking favors from the powerful gives you a clear conscience and trust in God.
exp.21:8:
The one with a generous eye, that is, a bountiful and compassionate outlook, will be blessed. The reason is that this person shared his bread with the one in need. The word "poor" in the verse refers to someone who lacks the basics. In Hebrew, the expression for a good eye usually points to generosity.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom; this section is attributed to Solomon. Here teaching is given in brief sayings. The verses before it speak of the inequality between rich and poor and of reaping what is sown. This verse shows a good sowing: generosity. The Bible does not present it as a business deal, but as a truth about how the compassionate person lives. The blessing can take different forms.

Today we can look for a concrete need close to us, such as a neighbor or a classmate who is hungry, and share something of what we have, without expecting anything in return.
exp.16:23:
The explanation says that the person with understanding has wisdom always before them: they seek it, keep it in view, and hold it as their aim. The fool, by contrast, who looks down on wisdom, has a scattered gaze and wanders in dreams of distant things, "to the ends of the earth," that is, to the farthest limit of the world. The word "ends" in the verse above means the same thing: the far edge or limit.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, many attributed to Solomon, given as a father's counsel to his children. Here two kinds of people are contrasted, as happens throughout the chapter. The verses nearby speak of joy, justice, and the grief that a foolish son causes. Some understand the "face" as the focused attitude of someone who thinks well.

Today we can ask ourselves what occupies our attention. Before chasing distant things, it is good to ask God for wisdom and to apply it in the simple decisions of each day.
exp.22:29:
This verse answers the questions before it: the woe, the strife, the complaints and the wounds belong to those who stay a long time drinking wine and to those who keep going out looking for the "mistura." This old word refers to wine mixed with spices or other things to make it stronger or more flavorful. It does not speak of an occasional drink, but of lingering for a long time and seeking more and more.

The speaker is a wise person, probably a father teaching his son, as in much of Proverbs. He uses questions to get attention and then gives the answer. His purpose is to warn that excessive drinking seems pleasant at first, but in the end it brings suffering and trouble.

For today: if you notice that you find it hard to stop, that you are always looking for something stronger, or that drinking is bringing you conflict, do not wait until it hurts more. Talk with someone you trust and ask for help in time.
exp.6:5:
Here the teacher tells what he saw. He says he was looking out from the window of his house, through the lattice, which is a kind of grille or wooden screen that lets you see outside without being easily seen.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son. Earlier he asked the son to treat wisdom like a very close sister so that it would protect him from the strange and seductive woman. Now he begins an account, like a scene he observed, to show how a young man without judgment falls. Some think it is a true story and others a parable; the text does not make this clear.

For today: learn to watch closely the lives of others, their successes and their falls, and let that teach you to guard your own steps before temptation arrives.
exp.16:21:
It says that a joyful heart does good, like a medicine for both body and spirit. On the other hand, a sad, downcast spirit dries up the bones, meaning it drains a person of strength and life. The phrase "a good disposition" can also be understood as "good medicine" or "healing"; translations vary a little.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Its purpose is to teach how to live well through practical observations. Nearby verses speak of foolishness, a father's sorrow, and wickedness. Here it shows how the state of the heart affects the whole person. It does not promise that joy will cure every illness.

Take care of your heart: thank God for the good in each day, seek friendships that encourage you, and do not carry sadness alone. If discouragement is deep or lasting, asking for help from someone you trust or from a professional is also wise.
exp.14:8:
This verse says that the way of life of the wicked person is detestable to God, but He loves the one who pursues righteousness. "Abomination" means something God rejects deeply. The "wicked" are those who live without regard for God. The phrase "pursues righteousness" means going after what is right, with effort and perseverance.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom teachings, traditionally associated with Solomon, though the book gathers several voices. Here the teacher gives counsel to his hearers. The previous verse already contrasted the sacrifice of the wicked with the prayer of the upright. Afterward it speaks of accepting correction, since a path is judged by its direction, not only by outward religion.

For today: it is not enough to carry out religious duties. Ask yourself what direction your daily life is taking, and seek righteousness in the small things: being honest, accepting correction, and treating others well.
exp.13:15:
This verse compares the wise person with the fool. The wise person fears, that is, has a healthy respect for danger and for God, and for that reason turns away from evil. The fool, on the other hand, rushes headlong, throwing himself into things suddenly and without thinking, and he is also overconfident, feeling sure of himself even while he walks straight into error.

It is a proverb of Solomon, as the book presents it, directed especially at young people who need to learn how to live well. Just before, it speaks of the simple person who believes everything he hears, and just after, of the one who gets angry quickly. The whole passage shows that wisdom involves caution, reflection, and self-control.

For today: before making an important decision or responding in anger, pause and pray. Ask yourself whether that path brings you closer to what is good or farther from it. Having the humility to doubt yourself and to seek advice can spare you from many harms.
exp.4:6:
The verse says that the children should listen closely and not turn away from the words their father teaches them. The phrase "hear me" is the same as "listen to me." "The words of my mouth" means "what I tell you," that is, his teachings. "Depart not" means "do not stray from them or abandon them."

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his children. He has just warned them about the "strange woman," whose ways lead to death. That is why he asks for their attention: what follows is advice meant to protect them, and he will next tell them to keep far away from that danger. Scholars understand this warning in a literal sense, and some also read it as a symbol of any seduction that draws a person away from God.

For today: choose one or two people you trust, such as a pastor, a mature family member, or a faithful friend, and let them counsel you before temptation arrives. Listening in time prevents wounds that are very costly to heal later.
exp.9:15:
What it says: The labor of the righteous, that is, of the person who lives according to God, leads to life. It is something that brings well-being and good fruit. On the other hand, the gain of the wicked, the one who lives without the fear of God, ends in sin. "Fruit" here means what is obtained or produced, and "unto sin" suggests that what they gain pushes them toward more wrongdoing or results in harm.

Context: This is a proverb from the section attributed to Solomon. A teacher of wisdom instructs young people that daily decisions and effort have consequences. The neighboring verses contrast the wise with the foolish and speak of accepting correction. The proverbs describe general tendencies, not automatic promises.

For today: Ask yourself how you use your work and your money. Seek to earn honestly and use what you have to bless others, so that what you do brings life to your family and your community.
exp.27:21:
The explanation says that the man with an "evil eye" runs desperately after riches, and does not realize that poverty is going to come upon him. The text says that this man "hastes," which means he hurries. The "evil eye" was a Hebrew expression for the person who is envious, stingy and ambitious, who looks at possessions with greed.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, compiled by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). They are counsel of wisdom for daily life. The previous verse already warned that whoever hastes to get rich "will not be without guilt." Thus the text contrasts the faithful man with the one who seeks gain at any cost.

Today it invites us to distrust shortcuts to making money and envy of what others have. Before an investment that seems easy or a debt taken on to keep up appearances, ask yourself: am I being honest and patient? God blesses faithful work and contentment.
exp.3:13:
This verse is a clear warning: do not step onto the path of the wicked or walk in the way of evil people. "Path" is a narrow trail or track, and "wicked" refers to people who live without respect for God. The words "enter not" and "go not" speak of not even beginning to walk with them.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son, as throughout this chapter. Earlier he told him to hold fast to his counsel because it is life. Here he explains why that path must be avoided: the wicked do not rest until they have done harm, and they lose sleep if they fail to bring someone down. The danger is real and it spreads.

For today: think about which friendships, settings, or habits pull you toward what is wrong, and step away from them in time. It is better not to take the first step than to have to correct your direction later. Seek out companions who encourage you to do good.
exp.2:30:
It says we should not envy the unjust person, that is, someone who takes advantage of others or acts with malice. We should also not choose or imitate any of his ways, that is, his way of living. Envy means wanting what another person has, and here choosing means preferring or deciding to follow.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, and in this passage a wise father speaks to his son, traditionally associated with Solomon. The verses before it speak of not harming a neighbor or quarreling without reason. The verses that follow give the reason: God rejects the wicked, but blesses and is near to the upright.

Today we can feel envy when someone prospers by cheating or taking advantage of others. Instead of admiring or copying him, let us remember that his success is not the best way. Let us choose honesty, even when it costs us, trusting that God cares for the righteous.
exp.11:20:
This verse says that no harm will come to the righteous, while the wicked will be filled with troubles.

This is a proverb of wisdom, largely attributed to Solomon. A wise father teaches his son how life works under the fear of God. The verses nearby speak of truth and lies, and this one contrasts the path of the righteous with that of the wicked. Proverbs describe general tendencies, not absolute promises: the Bible itself shows righteous people who suffered, such as Job. Many understand that the righteous will not be destroyed by evil, because God sustains them.

For today: seek to live with honesty even when it costs you, trusting that God cares for you. Then, when trials come, you will not face them alone or with a guilty conscience.
exp.30:10:
Her husband's heart trusts in her completely, so he lacks nothing of real value. The word "spoil" means plunder or gain, like what is taken in war. The idea is that he does not need to seek wealth through unjust or risky paths, because she brings stability and well-being to the home.

These words come from the end of Proverbs, where what the mother of King Lemuel taught him is recorded (31:1). She advises him toward justice and then describes a woman of noble character. The poem shows wisdom lived out in everyday life. Many scholars see an ideal portrait rather than a required list for every woman.

For today: trust is built through steady faithfulness and honesty in small things. In marriage, family, or work, keep your word and be people of integrity, so that others can rest in you.
exp.13:4:
This verse contrasts two kinds of witnesses. The faithful witness is trustworthy: he does not lie, because his words match what he saw or heard. The false witness, on the other hand, has a habit of telling lies. The verse speaks of the character of the person, not only of a single moment.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though not all scholars agree in every case. Here no character speaks within a scene; a teacher is giving instruction. The theme of speech already appears in the nearby verses: the mouth of the fool and the lips of the wise. In the ancient world, testimony in a trial could decide a person's fate.

For today: before you repeat something, ask yourself whether you really know it. Be a person whose word can be believed, even when telling the truth is costly.
exp.26:1:
It says that it is better for another person to praise us than for us to praise ourselves. The words "stranger" and "another man" refer to someone who is not part of our family or close circle; that is why their praise sounds more sincere. The two words for "mouth" and "lips" repeat the same idea, as is common in Hebrew poetry.

This proverb belongs to a collection of wisdom that tradition attributes to Solomon, and which, according to Proverbs 25:1, was copied out by the men of Hezekiah. A wisdom teacher speaks like a father to a son. The verse before it warns against boasting about tomorrow, so the theme is humility: we do not know as much as we think, and bragging leaves us looking foolish.

For today: instead of showing off your achievements at work or on social media, do your task well and let your works speak. If someone recognizes you, thank them simply.
exp.16:26:
The explanation says that the wise person does not talk too much. "He that hath knowledge spareth his words" means that such a person controls their speech and measures their words. "A man of understanding is of an excellent spirit" refers to someone with a calm temperament, who is not carried away by impulse. According to the verse, the person who has understanding knows when to be silent.

These words come from the book of Proverbs, which tradition attributes largely to Solomon, although the book gathers sayings from several authors. They are brief counsel for living with good sense. Here the context contrasts the fool, who causes anger and bitterness, with the wise person, who restrains himself. The following verse completes the idea: even the fool seems wise if he keeps silent.

Today: before responding in an argument, at work, or on social media, pause and take a breath. Ask yourself whether what you are about to say helps or hurts. Keeping silent at the right time often prevents conflict and shows your maturity.
exp.28:2:
The explanation says that the young man who loves wisdom, that is, who seeks to live with good judgment and in the fear of God, brings joy to his father. On the other hand, the one who keeps company with prostitutes wastes his possessions. "Possessions" here means wealth or property, and the phrase "brings joy to his father" is the older way of putting it.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though this chapter was copied by the men of Hezekiah (Prov. 25:1). Here a father instructs his son. The neighboring verses speak of righteous and wicked leaders and of decisions that build up or tear down. This saying contrasts two paths of life.

Today we can ask ourselves what decisions we are making with our money, our bodies, and our friendships. Asking God for wisdom and listening to sound counsel protects the family and its resources, and brings joy to those who love us.
exp.14:27:
The explanation says that the righteous person, that is, the one who lives uprightly before God, does not speak without thinking. Before answering, they weigh what they are going to say. The wicked, those who live turned away from God, let evil things pour out of their mouths without restraint, like someone spilling a liquid carelessly. The verse's contrast is between studying an answer and pouring out evil.

This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon, although the book gathers sayings from several authors. It is wisdom expressed through contrast, very common in this book. The nearby verses speak of thoughts and words that are clean or evil, and of how God relates to the righteous and to the wicked.

For today: before answering in an argument, in a text message, or on social media, pause briefly. Breathe, pray silently, and ask whether what you are about to say is true, kind, and helpful.
exp.21:17:
It is pleasant and good to keep the words of the wise deep within oneself (the inner part, the heart). Moreover, those words should be ready on the lips, that is, become part of what we say. "Pleasant" is the thing that delights, and "fitted" can be understood as well prepared and firm, so that they are at hand.

The speaker is the teacher of wisdom in Proverbs, like a father instructing his son. This section (22:17-24:22) is a collection of wise sayings. The verse before it invites us to listen, and the next one explains the purpose: that trust be placed in the LORD. Some scholars see a connection with Egyptian wisdom texts, but this is debated.

For today: it is not enough to read the Bible; keep one verse in your heart each week, repeat it, and use it to encourage or advise someone with your words.
exp.18:27:
The explanation says that a wicked person who gives false testimony does not take justice seriously. He mocks judgment, that is, the courts and what is right. Moreover, the ungodly speak without restraint and even "gulp down" wrongdoing with their mouths, as if they enjoyed evil. The word "iniquity" means injustice or wickedness, and "devours" here can be understood as "swallows" or "drinks," since the Hebrew allows it, so some versions translate it differently.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. It is a father teaching his son to distinguish between the way of the wise and the way of the fool. The following verse announces that God has prepared judgment for scoffers, so mockery does not go without consequences.

Today: let us speak with truth, especially when lying would suit us. And let us not take lightly what is just, whether at work, in the family, or in the church. Let us ask God for an honest mouth.
exp.30:18:
She puts her hands to the spinning. The spindle is a small stick that turns to twist the thread, and the distaff is the staff that holds the wool or flax she is about to spin. In other words, she works diligently to make cloth.

The passage is part of the advice that the mother of King Lemuel taught him (31:1). It describes a wise and hardworking woman. Her work is not only for herself: with what she spins, she clothes her family and helps the needy, as the following verses say. Many believe it is an ideal portrait, not a required list for everyone.

For today: value daily work, even when it seems small or repetitive. Do it with dedication, as for God, and think about whom you can bless with what you do.
exp.7:18:
Here Wisdom says that what she gives is worth more than fine gold and the best quality silver. "Fruit" and "revenue" refer to what is gained as profit: the benefits of living wisely. "Choice" means select, of the first quality.

In Proverbs 8, Wisdom speaks, presented as a person who calls people to listen to her. It follows her saying that she loves those who seek her and that honor and justice are with her. Many understand this as a poetic way of speaking about the wisdom of God. Some Christians also see here a foreshadowing of Christ, though this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: before deciding something important, such as a job, a business, or a relationship, ask yourself what is wisest and most just, not only what will bring the most money. Ask God for direction each morning, and you will see that wisdom yields gains that money cannot buy.
exp.9:7:
This proverb compares two kinds of people. The "wise in heart" is the one who has a teachable and humble heart, and so he accepts commandments, that is, instructions and correction. The "prating fool" is the foolish person who talks a great deal and listens little. The word "fool" here does not speak of sickness, but of a lack of wisdom. "Shall fall" means that he will stumble and suffer the consequences of his own words.

The book of Proverbs gathers wise teachings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here the teacher contrasts the righteous with the wicked, as in the verses around it. The idea is to show that the attitude of the heart becomes evident in how we live and how we speak.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I accept advice or correction with humility, whether it comes from the Bible or from someone who loves me? Before answering defensively or talking too much, it is wise to stop, listen, and think.
exp.10:10:
The explanation says that when upright people bless, that is, when they live and speak in a way that does good to others, the whole city grows and prospers. By contrast, the words of the wicked will end up overturning the city, that is, destroying it or turning it upside down. The word "upright" means people who are whole and honest.

Proverbs is a collection of teachings on wisdom; tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon, though other sections have other authors. Here the teacher speaks like a father to his children. The verses nearby speak of the power of the mouth: the one who slanders does harm, the gossip reveals secrets, and the prudent person keeps silent.

For today: our words build up or tear down communities. Make sure what you say in your family, at work, in your church, or on social media is true, encouraging, and useful, and avoid gossip.
exp.29:10:
There is a generation of people who curse their father and do not bless their mother. "Curse" here means to speak badly of someone, to despise them, or to dishonor them. "Bless" means to speak well of someone, to give thanks, and to honor them. The verse describes people with no respect for those who gave them life.

These words are part of the sayings of Agur, son of Jakeh, in Proverbs 30. We know very little about him. After his prayer asking for neither poverty nor riches, Agur lists several kinds of people who show a crooked heart: those who show no respect to their parents, those who think themselves clean when they are not, and the proud. The verse is an observation about an evil he sees in his surroundings.

For today: honor your parents with concrete words. Thank them, speak to them with respect, and avoid criticizing them with contempt, even if they are not perfect. If they have already passed away, honor their memory by speaking well of them.
exp.17:2:
This verse says that wickedness does not arrive alone. Wherever the wicked person appears, that is, someone who lives without the fear of God, contempt and shame come along too. "Contempt" is mockery or scorn toward others. A "reproach-giver" is someone who shames or humiliates. "Disgrace" is a public offense or insult.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, though some sections have other authors. Here the wise teacher instructs through contrasts: the fool and the wicked seek their own pleasure and do not want to listen. The verse shows the fruit of that path: scorn and insults that harm everyone around. Some also read it as a warning that this path ends in shame for the one who follows it.

Today we can examine our words and attitudes. Before we mock or look down on someone, let us ask what kind of atmosphere we are creating. Let us ask God for a humble heart that builds up rather than humiliates.
exp.10:9:
It says that when things go well for good and upright people, the whole community rejoices. And when the wicked fall or are brought down, people celebrate. The phrase about the wicked being brought down means they die or are overthrown, and the part about people celebrating speaks of shouts of joy and relief.

This proverb belongs to the sayings attributed to Solomon, a teacher of wisdom who shows his people how to live well. The verses around it speak of how each person's mouth and conduct affect the city. Here we see that wickedness harms everyone, and righteousness brings common well-being. It is not about rejoicing in another's misfortune, but about feeling relief when injustice comes to an end.

For today: work to be a person of integrity in your job, your family, and your neighborhood, because your honesty can bless many more people than you imagine.
exp.28:6:
This verse says that the righteous person takes an interest in the cause of the poor, that is, in their rights and their situation, and takes it into account. The wicked, on the other hand, the one who lives without respecting God, does not understand that wisdom and does not give it any importance. The word "cause" refers to their case or their need, especially when they are treated unjustly.

Proverbs gathers teachings from the wise men of Israel, and tradition associates much of it with Solomon. Here the context contrasts two paths: that of the righteous, who sings and rejoices, and that of the wicked, who falls into his own traps. Caring for the poor is presented as part of the wisdom that comes from God.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we are ignoring. You can listen attentively to someone in need, help them in concrete ways, or defend their dignity when others look down on them.
exp.5:6:
This verse speaks of the ant, saying that it has no leader to direct it, no ruler to command it, and no master to watch over it. In other words, no one forces it to work.

The one speaking is a wise father advising his son in the book of Proverbs. Just before this passage, he warns against careless co-signers of debts, and here he rebukes laziness. He uses the ant as an example, a small creature that works without anyone pressing it. Thus the lazy person has no excuse, for even an insect acts with good sense and foresight.

For today: do not wait for someone to watch over you or push you to do what you know you should do. Ask God to help you build self-discipline in your work, your studies, and your responsibilities. Begin today with one small task you have been putting off.
exp.30:8:
It says to speak up boldly and judge with justice, defending the rights of the poor and the needy. The word "needy" here refers to someone who lacks what is necessary to live. The phrase "judge righteously" means: decide with uprightness, without favoritism.

These are words that the mother of King Lemuel taught him (Proverbs 31:1). She warns him against wine and the abuse of power, because a drunken ruler forgets the law and harms the afflicted. Then she asks him to use his voice for those who cannot speak. After that the poem about the capable wife begins.

For today: use your voice, your work, or your influence to help someone who has no one to defend them, such as a mistreated neighbor or an ignored coworker. Speak with truth and without partiality.
exp.17:11:
It says that pride of heart comes before ruin, and that humility comes before honor. The word "destruction" here refers to a fall or collapse. The phrase "the heart is haughty" means the person thinks they are superior. Being brought low means humbling oneself, lowering oneself, not necessarily being humiliated by force.

It is a proverb from Israel's wisdom tradition, traditionally attributed to Solomon. It teaches through brief contrasts. The verses before it compare two places of refuge: trusting in God or trusting in one's own riches. This verse shows that arrogance leads to a fall, while humility opens the way to true honor.

Today we can practice humility by acknowledging our mistakes without excuses. If you receive praise or success, give thanks to God and to those who helped you. When someone corrects you, listen calmly before defending yourself. In this way you guard your heart against pride.
exp.3:19:
It says that a father asks his son to truly pay attention. Paying attention means listening carefully, and the picture of bending the ear is the image of coming close in order to hear better. His sayings, his words of counsel and instruction, are what the son is asked to take in.

The one speaking is a father, or a teacher of wisdom, who speaks to his son. Earlier he described two paths: the way of the righteous, which is like the growing light of dawn, and the way of the wicked, which is darkness where a person stumbles without knowing what they are tripping over. Now he invites his son to choose the path of light by listening to the teaching that will guide him.

Today we can set aside time without distractions to read the Bible and listen to wise people. Putting our phones away for a few minutes can help us listen calmly and put into practice what we learn.
exp.14:7:
It says that God rejects the offerings of someone who lives in wickedness, but he delights when the upright pray. The word "sacrifice" referred to the offering brought to the temple. The wicked are those who live without respect for God. "Abomination" means something He detests. The upright are those who try to live with honesty. "Delight" means joy.

This proverb belongs to the wisdom teachings attributed to Solomon, addressed mainly to young people. It contrasts two ways of life: that of the righteous and that of the wicked. What matters is not only the ritual, but the heart. Other passages in the Bible say something similar, such as 1 Samuel 15:22 and Isaiah 1:11-17.

Today it reminds us that God is not impressed by religious appearances. Before making an offering, singing, or praying, it is good to examine how we live: whether we are honest, whether we ask forgiveness, and whether we treat others well. A simple and sincere prayer pleases him greatly.
exp.13:31:
The wicked person is brought down by his own wickedness. "Ungodly" describes someone who lives without reverence for God, and "will be cast out" means he will be pushed down or thrown off, like someone who falls with no way back up. By contrast, the righteous, the one who lives in line with God, has hope even when his death comes.

These are proverbs of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon. A wise father teaches contrasts between two paths: that of the fool and that of the righteous. Earlier he speaks of a calm heart, envy, and how we treat the poor. Afterward he speaks of wisdom and of righteousness that exalts a nation. Some scholars see here a hope beyond death; others, a general trust in God. The text does not spell this out.

For today: live with integrity even when no one sees you, and trust God with your decisions and with your future. The peace of the righteous does not depend on having everything under control.
exp.2:0:
The explanation says that a wise father or teacher speaks to his son and asks him for two things: not to forget his teaching, which is his instruction, and that his heart keep his commandments. Here, to keep means to care for and preserve, not only to remember. In the Bible, the heart represents the deepest part of a person: thoughts, desires, and decisions.

Proverbs 3 is part of a series of advice from a father to his son. Tradition attributes the book to Solomon, although some scholars think it gathers wisdom from several hands. The verses that follow give the reason: obedience brings a long and peaceful life. These are general principles of wisdom, not automatic promises.

For today: choose one teaching from the Bible that you need, repeat it each morning this week, and ask God to help you put it into practice, not just to remember it.
exp.15:14:
It says that when the king is content and looks on with favor, there is life and well-being for those who depend on him. His "favour" is his goodwill or kindness, and it is compared to the "latter rain," the spring rain that in Israel ripened the crops before the harvest. It is an image of relief and abundance.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, a teacher of wisdom who teaches with brief sayings. The verse before it speaks of the king's wrath as a messenger of death; this one shows the opposite side. It shows how human power can bring either life or harm, and so it is wise to act with prudence and uprightness.

For today: try to be a person who gives encouragement and not fear with whatever authority you have, at home or at work. And remember that the favor of God, the true King, is even better than that of any person.
exp.11:13:
This verse says that a person will be filled with good things because of what comes out of their mouth, that is, through their words. It also says that they will receive the reward of what they did with their hands, meaning their work and their actions.

This is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. A wise father teaches his son how life works under God's care. The verses around it contrast the righteous and the wicked, and the wise and the foolish. Here the emphasis is that words and actions have consequences. It is a general principle, not a promise that always comes true right away.

Today we can be careful about what we say and work with honesty. Before speaking, ask yourself whether your words help, encourage, or tell the truth. Sow with your lips and your hands what you hope to reap.
exp.18:28:
It says that God, or life itself under his justice, has punishments ready for those who mock what is sacred and what is right. The words "prepared in advance" and "ready beforehand" are simply how the verse's idea of readiness is put: the punishments are already set. The "mockers" are those who scoff with contempt. The "fools" are the foolish people who reject wisdom. The "stripes" speak of painful and harsh correction.

The book of Proverbs gathers wise teaching, attributed largely to Solomon. Here a teacher speaks like a father to his son. The verse before it warns against the corrupt witness who mocks justice. This verse completes the thought: despising justice does not go without consequences. It is a general principle of wisdom, not a promise for every case.

For today: guard your heart against mockery. When you laugh at what is good, at the truth, or at correction, ask for humility. Receiving advice in time spares you greater pain later.
exp.15:27:
It says that a froward man, that is, a person with a twisted and malicious heart, stirs up quarrels and divisions. It also says that a whisperer separates close friends. "Strife" means constant quarreling or argument. A "whisperer" is someone who goes around repeating things about others, sometimes exaggerating or making things up, and so breaks trust.

This verse is part of Proverbs, sayings of wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon. Here the wise teacher warns young people about people who do harm with their words. The verses around it describe the wicked person as someone who digs up evil, has words like fire, and deceives his neighbor.

For today: before repeating something about someone, ask yourself whether it is true, whether it is necessary, and whether it helps. If not, it is better to keep quiet. And if someone brings you gossip, do not spread it; invite them to speak directly with the person involved.
exp.13:2:
In the mouth of the foolish is a rod of pride: that is, in the mouth of the person who does not want to learn or to listen to God, there is a rod of pride. A rod is a stick used for striking. His proud words end up hurting, and very often they turn back against himself. But the lips of the wise shall preserve them, that is, they protect those who speak with wisdom.

Context: It is a proverb within the collection attributed to Solomon. The nearby verses contrast the wise with the fool, and the upright with the perverse. The teacher wants to show that words reveal the heart and have consequences. Some interpreters see a rod that punishes the fool; others see one that wounds others.

For today: Before you answer in anger or boast, pause and pray. Speaking with humility and calm can protect you from conflicts and unnecessary harm.
exp.15:25:
This proverb says that the person who works is, in reality, working for his own benefit, because his hunger drives him to do it.

The book of Proverbs gathers practical wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, to teach people how to live uprightly. This verse appears among warnings about words and deceptive ways. Some read it as an observation about the need that motivates effort; others, as a call to diligent work that bears its own fruit. The text does not fully explain it.

For today: do not despise your daily needs, for God can use them to drive you to work with steadiness. Do your labor with honesty and gratitude, knowing that honest effort benefits your household and you.
exp.11:24:
This verse says that worry and deep distress in a person's heart weigh them down and leave them without spirit. But a kind word, spoken with care, brings back their joy. Rewording the source's note on its old phrase: the word for that heavy anxiety means worry that weighs heavily on the mind. The word for being brought low means left bowed down or downcast.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though the book has several compilers. Here the wise man speaks like a teacher advising his people. The verses around this one deal with words, work, and character, so this proverb shows the power that our words have.

Today, think of someone close to you who is troubled. Before giving long advice, offer a few sincere words of encouragement, such as "I am with you" or "I am praying for you." And if you are the one who is suffering, let others encourage you and tell them what you feel.
exp.14:29:
This verse says that a bright look, or a face full of joy, brings gladness to the heart. And that good news, or a good reputation, strengthens the body, as if it made the bones full of vigor and health. Some understand "the light of the eyes" as seeing something good or receiving a kind look; others, as the joy of someone whose eyes are radiant. The original text allows both ideas.

It belongs to the proverbs of Solomon, which are counsel for wise living in daily life. Here it speaks of how what we see and what we hear affects our spirits and even our health. The nearby verses speak of listening to correction and living uprightly.

For today: be someone who encourages. Give a smile and a good and true word. And take care of your own name by living with honesty, for that brings peace and strength to you and to others.
exp.6:1:
It tells us that we should obey the commandments of the wise father so that we may have a full life. "Keep" means to care for and practice, not merely to remember. "Live" speaks of a good life, not just of existing. "The apple of thine eye" refers to the pupil, the most delicate part of the eye, which we protect by instinct. The teaching should be guarded with that same care.

It is spoken by a father, or teacher of wisdom, who gives counsel to his son. In Proverbs 7 he warns against the temptation of adultery and folly. He wants wisdom to be close, as something personal and dear, and not as a distant rule.

For today: choose a biblical principle you need and review it each morning. Ask God to help you live it out in your decisions, especially when you are tempted to take the easy path.
exp.21:7:
The explanation says that whoever sows wickedness, injustice, or harm to others will reap the same. Some understand this to mean that his power to do harm will end; others understand it to mean that God brings his violence to an end.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, addressed to someone learning how to live well. It comes right after a passage about the rich dominating the poor. In this way it warns that abuse does not last forever and has consequences.

For today: before you respond with harshness, deceit, or contempt, remember that what you sow in your home, your work, or your friendships grows. Choose to sow truth, respect, and kindness, and trust that God is just.
exp.11:8:
It is better to be little valued by others, yet have someone to help you and food on the table, than to pride yourself on being important and not have even bread. "Despised" means treated with little esteem. "Pride themselves" means boasting or thinking oneself superior. The word "servant" can also be understood as someone who works for himself, and translators have read it in both ways.

The book of Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, attributed largely to Solomon, meant to teach people how to live with prudence. This verse stands among sayings that contrast the righteous with the wicked and praise honest work. The teaching is that appearance is worth less than a stable and responsible life.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we spend our energy on appearing successful or on meeting what we need with humility and work. It is better to live simply and without debts incurred to show off than to pretend to have what we do not have.
exp.27:25:
The explanation says that whoever trusts only in their own thoughts, feelings, or instincts acts foolishly. By contrast, whoever lives guided by wisdom will be kept safe. A "fool" is someone who does not think straight and does not take God into account. "Will be kept safe" here means will be delivered from danger and harm.

This is a proverb attributed to Solomon, or gathered from the time of his reign. The verses nearby speak of pride and of trusting in the Lord. This verse reinforces that point: the heart, left without guidance, can deceive us. In the Bible, the heart is the center of thoughts and desires, and wisdom begins with the fear of God.

Today, before an important decision, do not rely only on what you feel. Pray, seek what the Scripture says, and ask for counsel from wise and mature people.
exp.7:10:
What it says: Wisdom is worth more than the most expensive jewels. The "precious stones" are gems of great value, and "desire" refers to everything a person might long for. According to the verse, none of those things can be set beside wisdom, because there is no comparison.

Context: In Proverbs 8, wisdom speaks as if it were a person calling out to people in the streets and at the city gates. Earlier, it asked them to receive its instruction before silver and gold. Now it explains the reason: its words are right and lead to a good life. Later it will say that it walks alongside the fear of the LORD.

For today: Before making an important decision about money, work or family, stop and ask God for direction and seek wise counsel. A good decision is often worth more than a quick gain.
exp.25:21:
The explanation of this verse says that what the gossip tells sounds smooth and pleasant, almost like a delicacy. But those words sink deep into the person who hears them. The verse speaks of wounds that go down into the innermost parts of the body, that is, into the deepest part of a person.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed in large part to Solomon, and its purpose is to teach people how to live with prudence. Here, the verses around it speak of quarrels that flare up or die down, like a fire that needs fuel. The gossip is that fuel that feeds discord.

For today: when someone tells you something bad about another person, do not receive it gladly or repeat it. You can kindly say, "Let's talk about that with him or her instead." In this way you guard your own heart and the peace of others.
exp.9:29:
The explanation says that the righteous person, the one who lives uprightly before God, will never be shaken or uprooted from their place. By contrast, the wicked, those who live in evil, will not remain on the earth.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, which a father or teacher gives to teach young people. The nearby verses contrast the hope of the righteous with that of the wicked. The earth recalls God's promise to Israel that they would dwell safely in it. The proverbs describe a general principle, not a guarantee for every individual case.

For today: Make faithfulness to God your foundation. Pressures and setbacks can shake you, but whoever relies on God and lives with integrity has a security that no crisis can take away.
exp.7:19:
Here the passage says that wisdom leads people along the way of what is righteous, that is, along the right path. The word "path" here means a narrow track or trail. "Judgment" refers to what is upright and well decided, not to punishment. "In the midst of" suggests that she walks down the center of those trails, without turning aside.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented as a person who calls out to people in Proverbs 8. The passage comes after she has spoken of her riches and her fruit, which are worth more than gold. Now it makes clear that her value lies not only in what she gives but in how she leads: by righteousness and sound judgment. Some Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, while others understand it as the wisdom of God personified.

For today: before deciding something important, ask yourself not only "what is good for me?" but "what is just and right?" Ask God for wisdom and choose the honest path, even if it is slower.
exp.29:24:
The ants are described as a people that is not very strong, yet during the summer they gather food for later. "People" here means a colony or group. The phrase about preparing food means that they gather and store what is needed before the hard times arrive.

This verse is part of the words of Agur, son of Jakeh, found in Proverbs 30. He uses four small creatures as examples. He says that although they are among the smallest things on the earth, they teach more wisdom than many who consider themselves wise. The ant is one of them. Very little is known about who Agur was, and it is best not to claim more than the text itself says.

For today: you do not need to be strong or important to act wisely. We can learn to prepare ourselves with steady effort, saving a little, organizing our time, and caring for our spiritual life before the difficult days come.
exp.29:9:
Do not speak badly of a servant or employee to his master. The word "accuse" here means slandering someone or speaking against them in order to get them into trouble. The phrase "lest he curse you" means the servant might curse you in return, and "be found guilty" indicates that you could fall into wrongdoing or suffer the consequences of having acted badly.

This verse is part of the words of Agur, son of Jakeh, in Proverbs 30. Shortly before, he asks God for honesty and a simple life, without extremes. Then he speaks of proud and disrespectful people. Some understand that the proverb warns against meddling in other people's affairs or harming someone who is weak; the text does not explain more.

For today: before reporting or criticizing someone with less power, such as an employee, check your motive. If there is a real problem, speak with truth and justice, not with gossip or a desire to harm.
exp.10:30:
It says that the righteous will receive their reward here on earth, that is, in this life. "Shall be recompensed" means that they will receive what corresponds to their actions. So if even the righteous, who sometimes fail, receive consequences, how much more will the wicked (the one who lives without reverence for God) and the sinner (the one who practices evil) receive them. Some translators understand "recompensed" as reward and others as correction; both readings are possible.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon. It is wisdom in the form of brief sayings, teaching that life has moral consequences. The verses before it speak of the foolish person who harms his house and of the righteous person who bears fruit and wins souls. This saying closes that idea: our actions have results.

Today, before making a decision, ask yourself what fruit it will leave behind. Live with honesty and trust that God sees everything, without failing to ask Him for forgiveness and help when you fall short.
exp.5:5:
This verse invites the lazy person to look at the ant. "Go" means "go on" or "go and watch," and "sluggard" is the person who avoids work. Looking at her "ways" means observing how she acts and how she lives. By doing so, the person can learn to be wise.

Proverbs are advice from a wise father to his son; tradition attributes it to Solomon. Before this verse, it warns against getting into debt and against laziness, and it calls for acting with urgency, like the roe that flees from the hunter. Here it uses a simple example from nature to teach diligence.

For today: choose a task you have been putting off, whether at work, in your studies, or around the home, and make progress on it today without anyone having to demand it of you. Daily consistency, even in small things, prepares a more stable future.
exp.23:15:
This verse says that a righteous person may fall many times, and yet gets up again. "Seven times" is not an exact number, but a way of saying "many times." "Gets up again" means "rises up again." By contrast, the wicked fall into evil and do not recover, because their fall ends in ruin.

The book of Proverbs collects teachings of wisdom, and in this passage a teacher speaks to a young man. The verses before it warn the wicked not to attack the house of the righteous. The verses that follow ask us not to rejoice when an enemy falls. So the verse encourages the righteous and warns the one who harms them.

For today: if you fail or suffer a blow, do not stay on the ground. Ask God for help, acknowledge your mistake if there was one, and take the next step to get up.
exp.17:10:
This verse says that the rich man trusts in his wealth as if it were a fortified city, a high wall that protects him. The word "conceit" means that this security lies mostly in his own mind: he feels safe, even though his riches cannot truly protect him.

It is a proverb from Hebrew wisdom literature, traditionally associated with Solomon, although the book gathers sayings from different collections. Just before it, verse 10 says that the name of the Lord is a strong tower for the righteous. The two verses are set in contrast: a real security versus one that only seems secure.

Today we can ask ourselves where our heart rests when there is fear or uncertainty. Saving and working responsibly is good, but money should not be our final refuge. We can pray and trust God first, and use what we have with gratitude and generosity.
exp.7:22:
The verse says that the one speaking existed from everlasting, from the beginning, before the earth was. The phrase "I had the principality" is an old expression; other versions translate it as "I was established" or "I was formed," and the Hebrew word can be understood in several ways.

Here Wisdom speaks, presented as a person. In chapter 8 she invites young people to seek her and explains why she deserves to be heard: she was with God before all creation. Christians have debated its meaning. Many see a poetic personification of God's wisdom; others see a pointer to Christ, the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Both readings have been held throughout history.

For today: if God's wisdom comes before all that was created, it is worth more than any modern advice. Before deciding something important, take a moment to ask God for direction and seek counsel in his Word.
exp.10:8:
It says that a false person, one who appears good but is not, can harm others with his words. By contrast, the righteous are saved through wisdom. Here "hypocrite" can be understood as someone without God or false; "neighbor" means the neighbor or people nearby; and "harms" means that he destroys or damages.

This is a proverb, traditionally attributed to Solomon, that teaches through contrasts between the righteous and the wicked. The nearby verses speak of how wickedness ends badly and of how a city prospers or is ruined according to the conduct of its people. Here the focus is on the power of words to destroy or to protect.

For today: before speaking, think about whether your words build up or wound. Avoid gossip, lies, and false flattery. Ask God for wisdom to discern whom you listen to and to speak with truth and love.
exp.18:3:
It says that wealth attracts many people who want to be friends, but the poor man is abandoned even by the one he believed to be his friend. The words "gather" and "draw" are the ordinary meaning here, and the phrase about being left alone means that people leave him by himself.

This is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. It does not approve of this behavior; it only describes how life is. The verses nearby speak of foolishness, lying, and self-interest, and verse 6 goes on to speak of friendships that seek the one who gives. It notes a painful reality so that we may be wise.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I love my friends for what they have, or for who they are? Reach out to someone who is going through hardship: call them, visit them, and offer your company. In this way we show a sincere friendship.
exp.7:4:
This verse is a call. The "simple" are the naive, inexperienced people who believe everything without examining it. "Discretion" is the ability to think with prudence. The "fools" are those who despise counsel. "Understanding" is good judgment. Wisdom invites both groups to learn to think and live with sound sense.

Here Wisdom speaks, presented as a woman who raises her voice. She does so at the gates of the city, where people gathered, did business, and settled public affairs. Her message is for everyone, not only for the wise. The verses that follow say that her words are upright and true.

For today: before making an important decision, pause, pray, and seek counsel in the Bible and from mature people. Do not let yourself be carried along by haste or emotion alone.
exp.12:8:
The light of the righteous rejoices and keeps shining with joy, and it stays steady. By contrast, the lamp of the wicked goes out, meaning their life ends without hope or future. The verse uses the image of a lamp going out to describe this.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, attributed in large part to Solomon. Here a teacher of wisdom speaks to his hearers, especially young people. The verses around it speak of riches, pride, and counsel. The proverb contrasts what seems like success with what truly lasts. It is a general principle, not a promise for every case.

For today: do not be discouraged if you see the wicked doing well for a time. Try to live with honesty and truth, trusting that such a life gives a light that endures.
exp.28:17:
Here the explanation says that when a people has no "profecía," that is, a word from God to guide it, it falls into disorder and goes out of control. By contrast, whoever keeps God's law is "bienaventurado," that is, happy and blessed.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book, although these chapters were gathered later, in the time of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). The neighboring verses speak of wickedness growing, of discipline in the home, and of the need for correction. Everything points to the idea that, without moral and spiritual guidance, society and the family fall into disorder.

For today: do not let your life run without direction. Set aside a fixed time each week, or each day, to read the Bible and to obey something concrete that you learn from it. In this way your home and your community will have a course to follow.
exp.18:23:
The explanation says the lazy man puts his hand into his bosom, that is, inside his clothing, between his chest and his garment. There it stays, still. He is so idle that, even with food in front of him, he doesn't bother to bring it to his mouth. It is an exaggeration that uses humor to show how far laziness can go.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, which tradition associates with Solomon, though the book gathers sayings from several authors. It is the wisdom of a father or teacher instructing young people. Here it sits among verses that speak of fearing God and living with integrity. It teaches that a wise life includes responsibility and effort.

For today: do not put off the small things you can already do. Take one concrete step today in your work, your studies, or your home, and entrust the outcome to God.
exp.3:14:
It says we should flee from the path of the wicked. The text insists with four commands in a row: leave it, do not pass by it, turn away from it, and keep going. It is not enough to avoid entering; one must stay far away.

Here a father speaks, who in Proverbs 4 passes on to his children the teaching he received from his own father. He warns them that the way of wickedness is attractive but dangerous. The following verses describe the wicked as people who cannot rest unless they do harm, which shows how evil enslaves.

For today: if you know which places, friendships, or habits push you toward doing wrong, do not go near them to test whether you can resist. Make a concrete decision to stay away, and ask God for strength to keep it.
exp.26:0:
This verse tells us not to boast about what we will do tomorrow, because no one knows what will happen. "Boasting" means speaking with pride, as if everything were under our own control. The phrase "what a day may bring forth" in the verse above is the same idea: no one can say what the coming day will bring.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here the teacher speaks like a father advising his son. The verses that follow also speak against pride: it is better for someone else to praise you than for your own mouth to do so. Some see a connection with what James 4:13-15 says, though those are different texts.

Today we can make plans responsibly, but with humility. Before speaking with confidence about the future, we can say in prayer: "Lord, if you will, I will do this." In this way we rest in God, who does know tomorrow.
exp.16:15:
It says that money is of no use to a fool who wants to buy wisdom if he has no understanding. The word "price" here means money or payment; a "fool" is someone who refuses to be corrected; "understanding" in this verse refers to a heart willing to learn. The problem is not a lack of resources but a lack of sincere desire.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, attributed largely to Solomon, directed mostly to young people. The verses nearby speak of quarrels, justice, and friendship. This saying fits as a warning: wisdom is not a commodity but is received with a humble heart. Interpreters also read it as an irony about someone who has opportunities but does not make use of them.

For today: do not trust that more money, courses, or books will make you wise. Ask God for a humble heart willing to learn, and put into practice what you already know (James 1:5).
exp.6:21:
He goes after her at once, without thinking, like an ox walking to the slaughter without knowing what awaits it. He also compares him to a fool who walks into the stocks to receive punishment. The second comparison is difficult in Hebrew, and some translations read it differently.

A wise father is speaking to his son. He has just described how an unfaithful woman, using soft words, persuades a young man who lacks judgment, taking advantage of the fact that her husband is away on a journey. The father does not tell this to entertain, but to warn of the danger.

For today: temptation rarely looks like danger; it usually looks like something pleasant. Do not wait until you feel trapped to react. Decide in advance which places, conversations and habits you will avoid, and ask God for wisdom to flee in time.
exp.22:7:
He says that whoever accepts the food of a stingy and deceitful man will end up regretting it. "You will vomit" is a strong image: the bite you enjoyed will sit badly with you. Also, "you will lose your pleasant words," meaning your compliments and your kindness will have been spent in vain. "A man with an evil eye" means someone envious or greedy.

It is part of the wisdom sayings in Proverbs, where a teacher advises a young man, like a father to his son. It warns against the one who invites you to eat but, deep down, counts every bite and does not have his heart with you. An invitation can hide ulterior motives.

For today: before accepting favors or gifts from someone, look carefully at their motives. Do not let comfort or the desire to please bind you to people with a double heart. Seek out sincere and generous relationships.
exp.25:26:
Whoever digs a pit for someone else will fall into it, and whoever rolls a stone onto another will find that the stone comes back upon them. The phrase "rolling the stone" means rolling it, probably uphill, in order to drop it onto someone else.

This is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of this section (Proverbs 25:1). It speaks of hidden wickedness: people who smile and speak sweetly but harbor hatred and plan harm. The wise teacher is showing that the evil plotted against others often comes back on the one who planned it. Many read this as a general truth about life, not as a promise that always happens right away.

Today it invites us not to repay with deceit or revenge. If someone has hurt you, avoid planning their downfall through gossip or traps. Leave justice in God's hands and seek to do what is right, even when it costs you.
exp.21:5:
It says we should train up a child from an early age in "his way," that is, in his path or course of life. The promise is that when he is old, he will not depart from that path. "Way" here does not mean a profession, but the road along which his life travels.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book. It is wisdom in the form of a short saying, not an absolute guarantee for every case. Proverbs describe what usually happens. Around it they speak of humility, of crooked paths, and of reaping what is sown, so child-rearing appears as a seed that bears fruit over the years. Some understand "his way" also as each child's own manner; others, as the right path of God.

Today we can dedicate constant time to teaching children, by example and by words, to love God, to be honest, and to treat others well. And to pray for them with patience.
exp.5:3:
It says not to let yourself be carried away by sleep or by weariness. The "eyelids" are the skin that closes the eyes, and "drowsiness" is that sleepiness that makes you want to rest. In other words: do not fall asleep until you have resolved what is urgent.

A wise father speaks to his son in the book of Proverbs. Before this, he warns that he has bound himself to a debt or a promise in favor of another person, and now he is trapped by his own words. For this reason he asks him to act immediately: to humble himself, to speak with his neighbor and free himself, like the gazelle that escapes from the hunter.

For today: if you made a promise or took on a debt that you cannot keep, do not put it off. Speak soon and with humility, ask for help, and look for a solution. Acting in time keeps a small problem from growing.
exp.11:6:
It says that God will overthrow the wicked, and they will be no more, but the family of the righteous will remain firm. "Overthrown" is an old word meaning to turn over, knock down, or turn upside down. "Wicked" refers to those who live without respect for God. "House" can refer to the family, to descendants, and to everything that has been built in one's life.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed in the book to Solomon. A wise father teaches his children through contrasts: the righteous think with uprightness, while the wicked deceive and even lie in wait to do harm. It is a general truth about how things usually turn out, not a promise for every case. Other passages in the Bible acknowledge that sometimes the righteous suffer.

For today: do not be discouraged if you see the wicked seem to prosper. Build your home with honesty, truthful words, and trust in God, even if the result takes a long time to appear.
exp.18:1:
It is not good for a person to be without knowledge, and whoever hurries with his feet goes wrong. "Soul" here refers to the person himself, and "knowledge" means understanding or insight. The one who "hurries with his feet" is someone who acts in haste, without thinking. Going wrong means missing the way and straying off course.

This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, attributed in large part to Solomon, although it is not known with certainty who gathered this section. It is wise counsel for anyone who wants to live well. The verse before it praises integrity above crooked wealth, and the verse after it shows how foolishness damages a life and even leads a person to blame God.

For today: before deciding something important, such as a purchase, a commitment, or an angry reply, stop, pray, ask for advice, and seek information. Going slowly and staying well informed prevents many mistakes.
exp.13:33:
This proverb says that when a people lives with justice, that is, with uprightness, honesty and respect for others, it becomes honored and strong. By contrast, sin brings shame. The word "reproach" means disgrace or humiliation.

It is a proverb from the collection attributed to Solomon, the wise king of Israel. The verses around it speak of the wicked who fall, of the wise and the foolish, and of how a king treats his servants. It is a general teaching about how moral conduct affects life in community. Proverbs describe tendencies, not automatic promises.

For today: justice begins in small things. Be honest in your work, pay what is fair, and treat your neighbor well. In this way you contribute, from your own place, to the good of your community and your country.
exp.30:22:
He is respected and recognized at "the gates," which was the entrance of the city. There the "elders of the land," that is, the leaders and judges of the place, sat to handle public matters and settle cases. "Known in the gates" means he has a good reputation.

These words are part of the poem in Proverbs 31:10-31, which describes the woman of noble character. It is presented as teaching that the mother of King Lemuel gave him (31:1). Here the poem shows that her work, wisdom and care for the home benefit the whole family, and also help her husband be valued in the community. Scholars debate whether this describes a single woman or is an ideal.

Today, we can support those we love with generosity and faithfulness, knowing that our quiet character at home can bear fruit in the witness of the whole family.
exp.13:34:
The explanation says that the king takes pleasure in the servant who acts with understanding, that is, with good judgment and wisdom. But he is angry with the one who brings shame on him, meaning the one who acts foolishly or disgracefully. The word "favour" means goodwill or kindness. The word "servant" here refers to someone who serves the king as an official, not a pastor of a church.

This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, which teaches wisdom for life. It comes right after verses saying that righteousness exalts a nation and sin brings reproach to it. In this way, the verse shows that the conduct of those who serve a leader affects the honor of everyone.

For today: wherever you work or serve, seek to act with wisdom, honesty and good sense. Your way of working reflects the one you represent, and as a believer, it also reflects the Lord.
exp.30:19:
She opens her hand and stretches it out to help the poor and the needy. Repeating the image of the hand (she stretches out, she reaches forth) shows real and steady generosity, not just a good wish.

Proverbs 31:10-31 is a poem about the woman of noble character. It begins by saying these are "the words of King Lemuel, which his mother taught him"; there are several views about who Lemuel was. The verse sits between her work with the spindle and the distaff and her care for her family. In this way it shows that her labor also serves to give to others.

For today: if you have some time or income, set aside a part of it to help a specific person, such as a neighbor, a relative, or a trustworthy cause. Helping steadily is worth more than helping only when there is something left over.
exp.22:4:
This verse asks whether it is worth fixing your gaze on riches, when in truth they are nothing. They have no substance and no lasting value. It says that money grows wings for itself, like an eagle, and flies away.

Here a wise father instructs his son, as in much of Proverbs. Before and after this verse, he warns against craving the table of a powerful man or of someone who is envious. Those delicacies seem tempting, but they deceive, because the one who invites you may not be doing so sincerely.

For today: do not live obsessed with gaining more. Work with honesty, but guard your heart, and place your security in God and in what cannot be lost, such as your family, your character, and your faith.
exp.14:16:
This proverb compares two meals. One is simple: "legumbres," that is, vegetables and grains, the food of ordinary people. The other is a feast: "buey engordado," choice and expensive meat. The teaching is that a humble table with love is worth more than a lavish table where there is "odio," that is, resentment and hostility.

Proverbs gathers practical wisdom from Israel, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here it is not a prophet speaking to a particular event, but a teacher of wisdom instructing someone who wants to live well. The verses nearby deal with the same theme: better a little with the fear of the LORD than much with trouble, and the one who is slow to anger calms quarrels.

For today: take care of the atmosphere of your table more than the menu. Before a family meal, set aside a pending argument and offer a kind word.
exp.10:16:
This verse says that the merciful person, the one who treats others with kindness and compassion, ends up doing good to himself. The cruel person, by contrast, does harm to himself. The phrase about tormenting one's own flesh means that he hurts himself, perhaps in his body, his peace, or his whole life. Someone merciful is one who feels compassion and acts to help.

This is in the book of Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings, attributed largely to Solomon. Here the voice of wisdom speaks, teaching how to live well. The nearby verses compare opposite paths: the righteous and the wicked, what bears fruit and what leads to ruin.

For today: practice one concrete act of kindness this week, such as forgiving someone, helping a neighbor, or responding with calm. In doing so, you not only bless others but also take care of your own heart.
exp.7:3:
It says that someone calls out loudly to all people, without exception. "Oh men" and "sons of men" are ways of saying "people, human beings." The old "á" is the "a" of today: "a vosotros clamo" means "I cry out to you." The voice is not reserved for a few, but is directed to everyone.

The one speaking is Wisdom, who in Proverbs 8 appears as a woman who goes out into the street. She stands on the hills, the roads, the crossroads, and the gates of the city, which are the places where the most people pass. In this way she invites everyone to listen and to live uprightly. Some see here a foreshadowing of Christ, whom the New Testament calls the wisdom of God; that reading is a Christian interpretation, not something the text says directly.

For today: God's wisdom is not hidden, nor is it only for experts. Today you can seek it with humility in the Bible, in prayer, and in sensible counsel, and stay attentive to its voice in the midst of everyday life.
exp.21:27:
This verse says we should not move or remove the boundary marker, that is, the stone or sign that marked the limit of a piece of land. "Crossing over" here means going from one place to another, that is, shifting that mark. "Boundary" means the limit or edge of a property. "Ancient" refers to something set long ago, by one's forebears.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, many attributed to Solomon, although scholars debate how this section was put together. In Israel, land was a family inheritance given by God, and boundary markers protected each household. The law of Moses also forbids moving these boundaries (Deuteronomy 19:14). The verses nearby speak of justice, debts, and honest work.

For today: respect what does not belong to you and fair agreements. Avoid taking advantage of others through deception, abuse, or small schemes involving money, property, or work. Act with integrity, even when no one is watching.
exp.13:12:
This verse says that a person can be laughing on the outside and still carry sadness on the inside. It also says that joy can end in heaviness, and by that it means deep anguish or grief. In other words, laughter does not always show what the heart truly feels, and moments of happiness do not always last.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom. Much of it is traditionally attributed to Solomon, though the book gathers several collections. Here the teacher speaks like a father giving instruction. The verses around it contrast the path that seems good with the one that ends badly, and the one who is deceived with the one who thinks carefully about his steps. Some read this verse as a warning about shallow happiness.

Today we can be more attentive to those who seem happy but suffer in silence. Ask someone kindly how they are really doing, and listen without rushing. And seek a joy that is more solid, like the one that grows from trust in God.
exp.9:8:
He who lives with integrity, that is, with honesty and consistency between what he thinks, says, and does, can walk securely. Whoever twists his ways, that is, bends them through deceit or wickedness, will sooner or later be broken, that is, knocked down or undone. "But" is the word that connects the two halves of the verse.

This verse is in Proverbs, a book of wisdom attributed largely to Solomon. Here a teacher of wisdom speaks, like a father advising his children. The verses nearby compare the righteous with the wicked and the wise with the foolish. For that reason this proverb describes two paths of life. It is understood as a general rule, not as a promise that always comes true immediately.

Today you can practice integrity in small things: keeping your word, not lying, and not pretending to be something you are not. Someone who lives without duplicity does not have to guard secrets or fear being found out, and so rests with a clear conscience.
exp.29:2:
He says that Agur does not regard himself as wise. He admits that he has not learned wisdom and that he does not know well "the knowledge of the Holy One," that is, the knowledge of God, the Holy One. The word "knowledge" here means knowing and understanding, not modern science.

Agur, son of Jakeh, speaks, and we know almost nothing else about him. Some think he speaks with genuine humility; others think he says it with irony. What follows are questions about who created the heavens, the winds, and the earth. His point is that no one can grasp God with their own mind. He ends by saying that God's word is pure, meaning clean and trustworthy.

Today we can approach God with humility. Instead of boasting about what we know, we can recognize our limits and trust what He has said in His Word. Ask yourself: am I willing to learn from God today?
exp.10:25:
The explanation says that people curse the one who keeps grain for himself instead of selling it. By contrast, they bless the one who sells it. Here "withholdeth" means holding back or hoarding, and "but" introduces the contrast; "blessing upon the head" is a way of saying that the seller receives the favor and praise of others.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, though not all scholars agree on every detail. This verse belongs to sayings about generosity: whoever gives freely receives more, and whoever refreshes others will be satisfied. Here it is applied to trade. Holding back food to raise prices in a time of scarcity harms the community, while selling it fairly helps it.

For today: if you have something others need, such as work, a product, or knowledge, do not use it to take advantage of their need. Offer it honestly and at fair prices, and let your business be a blessing to your community.
exp.10:2:
This verse says that the honesty of upright people guides them along a good path. By contrast, the wickedness of those who live in sin ends up destroying them. "Integrity" means living with a sincere and consistent heart. "Guide" means to lead or direct. "Perverseness" is the tendency to deceive and do wrong. "Transgressors" here refers to those who betray, that is, the faithless and deceitful.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, attributed in large part to Solomon. Here it speaks like a father or teacher instructing young people. The nearby verses speak of honest weights, humility, and justice. All of them contrast two paths: that of uprightness and that of deception.
