For today: be honest even when no one sees you, at work, with money, and in your words. Integrity does not always bring quick gains, but it gives you a firm direction and a peaceful conscience. Ask God to help you be consistent.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that if someone seeks wisdom with all their heart, they will come to understand what the fear of the Lord means, that is, respecting and honoring God with reverence. It also says they will find the knowledge of God, meaning to truly know Him.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. The verses before it ask the son to seek wisdom the way one seeks silver or hidden treasure. The verse that follows makes clear that wisdom is not invented by people: God himself gives it.

For today: set aside a fixed time each day to read the Bible and pray, asking God for understanding. Seek steadily, like someone digging for a treasure, and trust that God answers those who seek Him sincerely.
exp.3:6:
The explanation says that the most important thing, the first priority, is to seek wisdom. One must go after it with effort, the way someone buys something valuable. In other words: even if you have to give up everything you have, do not stop seeking wisdom.

Here a father speaks to his son, and he remembers that he too learned from his own father. It is a family teaching in the book of Proverbs, which is largely attributed to Solomon. He wants the young man not to abandon wisdom, because wisdom will guard him and he will honor it.

For today: before deciding about money, work, or relationships, ask God for wisdom and seek counsel in his Word. Set aside a fixed time each day to read it.
exp.24:10:
This proverb compares a well-spoken word to an apple of gold set in an ornament of silver. It is something beautiful and valuable. The phrase "fitly spoken" means spoken at the right moment and in the right way. Some translators understand "apples" as fruit or as an ornament; it is not known with certainty what object the author had in mind.

Proverbs 25 begins a collection of sayings of Solomon, copied by men of King Hezekiah. The verses nearby speak about caring for our words: dealing with conflicts directly, keeping secrets, receiving correction, and being a faithful messenger. Thus the proverb shows that speaking well is an art that gives value to others.

For today: before you speak, think about whether it is the right moment, the right tone, and the right way. Sometimes a kind word spoken at the right time encourages more than many explanations.
exp.27:9:
He says that whoever leads upright people down a wrong path, that is, whoever deceives them or pushes them toward doing evil, will end up falling into his own trap. The "pit" is a deep hole or trench. By contrast, the upright (those who are whole-hearted and live honestly before God) will receive something good as their inheritance.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, and here it speaks like a father instructing his children. The verses nearby speak of justice, of wealth gained wrongfully, and of obedience to God. This proverb shows that the harm one prepares for others often turns back against oneself.

For today: take care of your influence. If you advise, teach, or lead, seek to encourage others toward what is good, never toward what is harmful. And trust that living with integrity is worthwhile, even when it isn't immediately seen.
exp.16:9:
The explanation says that a wise person learns a great deal from just one correction. The word for "benefits" means that it is useful to them and bears fruit. The one who "understands" is the person who has discernment and is willing to learn. The fool, by contrast, rejects wisdom, and not even a hundred blows will make him change.

It is a proverb from Israel's wisdom tradition, largely attributed to Solomon. Its purpose is to teach living with prudence. The nearby verses speak of friendship, of rebellion, and of how dangerous a stubborn fool can be. In this way the text contrasts two attitudes toward correction: humility and obstinacy.

Today we can ask God for a teachable heart. When someone corrects you with respect, before defending yourself, ask yourself calmly: "What can I learn from this?" That attitude protects your relationships and helps you grow.
exp.20:16:
This proverb says that a person who lives always seeking pleasure and amusement will end up in need. The word "pleasure" in the verse means enjoyment or fun. The proverb is not condemning joy itself, but making pleasure the thing a person loves most. The verse's phrase about wine and oil refers to costly luxuries, a symbol of indulgence. It means that such a person will not manage to prosper.

The book of Proverbs is attributed largely to Solomon, and it speaks like a teacher advising young people. Here it stands among verses that contrast the righteous with the one who goes astray. The message fits that idea: a life without self-control leads to ruin. Like every proverb, it describes what usually happens, not a promise that holds in every case.

Today we can examine where we spend our money and our time. Setting limits on our desires, saving first, and enjoying things in moderation helps us live with freedom and gratitude, without letting pleasure rule us.
exp.15:19:
The explanation says that the person who gives attention to the matter and understands it will find something good, and that whoever puts their trust in God (Jehovah) is happy. "Blessed" means happy, favored. "The word" can be understood as a matter or counsel, or as the word of God; scholars interpret it both ways.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, to guide young people in daily life. This verse comes after a warning against pride and a praise of humility. Thus, listening with humility and trusting in God are presented as the path opposite to the pride that leads to a fall.

Before making an important decision, take a few minutes to listen: read the Bible, ask advice from someone wise, and pray. Then trust God with the outcome, without letting pride or fear make the decision for you.
exp.23:22:
This verse says that these are further teachings that come from the wise. It then states that it is not good to "have respect of persons in judgment." That is, one should not favor someone because of their position, their money, their fame, or their friendship when deciding a case. The word "judgment" here means deciding with justice.

These words open a short section of sayings from the wise within the book of Proverbs. The one speaking is a teacher of wisdom who instructs a young man. The verses before this one speak of fearing God and avoiding the unstable. The verses that follow say that calling the wicked righteous brings rejection, while correcting him brings blessing.

For today: when you have to give an opinion, grade something, or make a decision, whether at work, at church, or at home, do it with truth and without favoritism, even when that costs you discomfort.
exp.22:2:
This verse says we should not crave the fine food of a powerful man. "Crave" means to desire with excessive eagerness, and "delicacies" are choice, luxurious foods. The Bible calls that food "deceitful food" because it looks like a gift but may hide a hidden purpose.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs. He warns him that when he sits down at the table of a ruler or important person, he should be careful and keep himself in check. Many understand that such a feast may be a way of winning favor or of testing the one who eats. The text does not explain this fully, so there are several ways to understand it.

Today we can apply it this way: when someone offers us invitations, gifts, or advantages, let us ask ourselves what they want from us and what is expected of us in return. Mastering our desires helps us keep our freedom and integrity.
exp.15:20:
This verse says that the person wise in heart, that is, the one who has good judgment and an inner disposition to learn, will be recognized as understanding. It also says that kind words help teaching grow, meaning that it is explained and received better.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although not all scholars agree on every section. The verses nearby speak of humility, of trusting the Lord, and of how the wise person's mouth reflects his heart. Here what is inside and what is outside come together.

For today: before correcting or teaching someone, take care with your tone. Truth spoken with kindness often opens doors that harshness closes.
exp.27:24:
The explanation says that a proud and greedy person stirs up quarrels and divisions around them. In contrast, whoever puts their trust in God will prosper, grow, and be well. That prosperity is not limited to money; it speaks of a life that is well grounded.

These are wisdom proverbs attributed to Solomon, although this chapter was gathered together later, according to Proverbs 25:1. Here two paths are contrasted: trusting in oneself or trusting in God. The next verse reinforces this by calling foolish the one who trusts in his own heart.

For today: the next time a discussion stirs up your pride, stop and pray before you respond. Give God your need to be right. Trusting Him lets you speak calmly and seek peace.
exp.6:13:
She says she had promised to offer peace offerings and that today she has fulfilled her promises (vows). Peace offerings were offerings of thanksgiving to God.

The woman speaking in Proverbs 7 has just embraced and kissed the young man who lacks experience. According to the law of Moses, much of the meat from this offering was eaten by the family, and sometimes on the same day. For this reason many understand that she is inviting him to a feast in her house. She uses religious language to seem pious and to win his trust, although her purpose is to deceive him.

For today: do not confuse spiritual words with a faithful life before God. Look at the actions, and do not let yourself be persuaded by someone who uses religion to justify what God forbids.
exp.5:7:
This verse says that the ant stores up food in the summer and gathers what she needs at harvest time. "Gathers" means "collects" or "brings together," and "harvest" is the time of cutting the grain. "Provision" means food or sustenance. The ant works while there is supply, thinking of what will come later.

Here the teacher of wisdom in Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon, advises a young person the way a father advises his son. Before this, he holds up the ant as an example because she works without anyone ordering her to. Afterward, he rebukes the lazy person who keeps sleeping and looking for rest. The contrast is clear: the ant acts with foresight, while the sluggard stays still.

For today: make use of good times to prepare yourself. You can save a little, study, put your responsibilities in order, or care for your spiritual life, without waiting for someone to pressure you. Doing this with steadiness is a form of wisdom and good stewardship.
exp.28:16:
This verse says that if a father or mother corrects their son with love, they will afterward receive peace and joy. "Correct" means to guide, teach, and set limits. "Rest" is peace, freedom from the anxiety that comes with a child who has no direction. "Delight" is deep gladness. The verse's wording was given in an older form of the language and is now written in its present-day form.

Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and this part is traditionally attributed to King Solomon, although chapter 29 belongs to sayings that were collected later, in the time of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). The verse before it speaks of the rod and of the indulged child who shames his mother. These are general proverbs about what usually happens, not absolute promises.

Today: correcting does not mean shouting or humiliating. It means teaching with consistency, patience, and affection. Choose a clear standard for your home, explain it calmly, and be consistent in upholding it.
exp.10:21:
It says that a beautiful woman who lacks good judgment is like a gold ring placed in the snout of a pig: something valuable and lovely in a place where it does not belong. The image is strong and almost shocking, on purpose.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the title of the book, within a section that contrasts the righteous and the wicked. The verses nearby speak of what pleases God: an upright heart and a blameless way. The proverb teaches that outward beauty, without wisdom or character, loses its worth. Although it speaks of a woman, the principle applies to anyone.

For today: let us not measure people, or ourselves, only by appearance. Let us cultivate prudence, kindness, and the fear of God, which give a worth that lasts longer than the outward image.
exp.17:6:
This verse says that the words of a fool end up ruining him. "Ruin" here refers to destruction or downfall. "Snares" are traps, like the ones used to catch animals. In other words, the fool speaks without thinking, and his own mouth destroys him and catches him. In the Bible, a "fool" is not someone with little intelligence, but someone who looks down on wisdom and believes he needs no advice.

Context: This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, although this chapter does not explicitly say who wrote it. It is wisdom in the form of short sayings meant to teach people how to live well. The verses around it speak of quarrels, gossip, and laziness, and show the harm that careless words cause.

For today: Before responding in anger or sharing a piece of gossip, pause and ask yourself whether those words build up or tear down. Asking God to guard your mouth can spare you many problems.
exp.23:23:
Whoever tells a wicked person, "You are righteous," will be rejected by the people. The words "they will curse him" and "they will abhor him" mean that people will despise him and look on him with disgust, and not just one community but many nations. In today's language: calling what is evil good brings rejection from many people.

These words are part of the sayings of the wise (Proverbs 24:23), a collection of short pieces of advice. The wise man is speaking here about justice in judgment. Just before, he warns that it is not good to show favor to people based on who they are. Then he says that those who rebuke the guilty will be well regarded and will receive a blessing. So the theme is being honest when you judge.

For today: do not flatter or excuse what is wrong out of convenience, fear, or friendship. If you have to give an opinion or make a decision, do it with truth and with love, even when it costs you.
exp.30:7:
It tells us to speak up for those who cannot defend themselves. "The dumb" refers to someone who has no voice and no one to listen to them. "Children of death" is an old expression, understood to mean helpless people at risk of being destroyed or condemned; some think of the most vulnerable members of society. "Cause" refers to a case brought before judges.

These are words that the mother of King Lemuel taught him, according to the opening of the chapter. She prepares him to rule with justice. Before that, she warns that rulers must not lose their judgment through drink, and then she asks him to use his voice to defend the poor and needy. The text does not make clear exactly whom she meant by those at risk of destruction.

Today we can use our voice, time, or influence on behalf of someone who is overlooked: accompanying a neighbor without resources through a bureaucratic process, reporting an abuse, or supporting someone who suffers injustice.
exp.9:28:
The explanation says that God's way, that is, his manner of acting and of guiding life, is like a stronghold for the one who is "upright," a word that here means whole, of sincere heart, though not without errors. But that same way is "destruction," that is, ruin and terror, for those who practice wickedness.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book. It stands in a series of contrasts between the righteous and the wicked. The message is that the same way of God produces opposite effects depending on our attitude toward him. Some scholars understand "the way of the Lord" as his way of governing the world; others, as the conduct he requires.

For today: when obeying God costs you, remember that his way sustains you. Today you can choose one honest decision, even a small one, and lean on God to keep it.
exp.30:9:
It says that a woman of strength is very hard to find, and that she is worth far more than precious stones. The word "strength" here is the Hebrew "jáyil," which can mean brave, capable, or of firm character, not only physical strength. "Far surpasses" means her worth exceeds that of rubies by a great deal. Her "price" is her value.

These words are advice that the mother of King Lemuel gave to her son (Proverbs 31:1). Before this, she asked him to defend the poor and those who have no voice. This verse begins a poem that describes a woman of solid character. Many see it as an ideal portrait of wisdom put into practice, not a checklist to be perfectly fulfilled.

For today: value people for their character, honesty, and faithfulness, more than for appearance or money, and cultivate those virtues in yourself.
exp.14:24:
This proverb says that God will tear down and leave in ruins the house of the proud, but he will protect the widow. "Destroy" means to wipe out completely. The proud are the arrogant, those who think themselves superior. The border is the boundary of a property, the line that marks what belongs to someone. God keeps firm what the widow has.

The wise author of Proverbs says this, teaching his people how to live. Widows were very vulnerable, and the powerful could take their lands away. Around this verse, the text speaks of good words, clean thoughts, and of rejecting bribes and greed.

For today: do not abuse your position or your money against those who have less. Care for the vulnerable with humility, and trust that God sees them and defends them.
exp.2:27:
This passage says we should not make our neighbor wait with excuses like "come back tomorrow" when we already have what they need and can give it to them today. The word "neighbor" here refers to the person close to you, and the old-fashioned spelling "á" is written today as "a", as in "to" or "toward".

This proverb is part of the teachings of a wise father to his son, found in the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon. It comes after a call to trust in God and a statement that good should not be withheld from those who deserve it. It then warns against harming or quarreling without cause with one's neighbor. The whole passage speaks of treating others with justice and honesty.

Today this can be applied this way: if you owe a payment, a favor, or help, and you can give it now, do it without delay. Fulfilling your obligation on time is a concrete way of loving and respecting the person who needs you.
exp.18:13:
This verse says that parents can leave their children a house and money as an inheritance, but a prudent wife, that is, one who is wise and has good judgment, is a gift that comes from God. God's name is the Lord. "But" is the word that connects the two parts of the verse.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and this part is attributed to Solomon. Just before, it describes a quarrelsome wife as a constant dripping. Here there is a contrast: material things can be inherited and planned, but a good marriage does not depend only on human effort. Some read this as a general truth, not as a promise for every case.

For today: value wise people and those of good character more than possessions. If you are married, thank God for your spouse and take care of them. If you are looking for a partner, ask God for wisdom and look at character, not only at outward things.
exp.3:23:
This verse asks us to put far away from us speech that is crooked and deceptive. The words "perversity of the mouth" refer to words that are false, twisted, or harmful. "Iniquity of lips" speaks of the same thing: the unjust words that come out when we talk. The idea is to remove such speech and keep it far from us, not merely to avoid it now and then.

The one speaking in Proverbs 4 is a father teaching his son, and he says he received this wisdom from his own father. Just before this, he asks his son to guard the heart, because life flows from it. This verse continues that line: what we say reflects what is within. Then the counsel moves to the eyes and the feet, that is, to living uprightly in everything.

For today: before you speak, or before you write a message, ask yourself a simple question: "Is it true, is it right, and does it help?" If not, it is better to keep silent or to say it another way.
exp.14:15:
It says that it is better to have little while living in reverence and honor toward God than to have great riches accompanied by unrest. The phrase "fear of the Lord" does not mean fear, but reverence and trust toward God. Trouble means anguish, confusion, or problems. Treasure refers to many possessions kept in store.

This proverb belongs to a collection of wise sayings attributed to Solomon (Proverbs 10:1). It addresses the person who seeks to live well. The nearby verses speak of a contented heart and of love in the home, and so they compare what truly gives peace with what only seems to give it. It is not a condemnation of wealth, but a warning that wealth is not enough to give tranquility.

Today you might ask yourself: "Am I trading my peace for more gain?" Before accepting a job or making a purchase, consider whether it brings you closer to God and your family or pushes you further away.
exp.30:29:
It says that charm and physical beauty are neither reliable nor lasting. "Deceitful" means it can look like more than it is worth, and "vain" means fleeting, without lasting value. "Fears the Lord" does not mean being afraid, but respecting and honoring God with reverence. That woman is the one who deserves true praise.

These words close Proverbs 31, which presents the virtuous woman. The passage begins by saying these are the words of King Lemuel, which he learned from his mother. Here the portrait is summed up: her children and her husband praise her for her character, her work, and her wisdom. Many understand this poem as an ideal, not as a required checklist for every woman.

For today: value people, and yourself, more for their faith, honesty, and service than for their appearance. Cultivate each day a heart that honors God, because that leaves a lasting mark.
exp.18:7:
This verse says that the one who gets wisdom does good for himself. "Getteth wisdom" means gaining good judgment, and "loveth his own soul" means caring for his own life. "Keepeth understanding" means holding on to it and putting it into practice. The promise is that this person "shall find good," that is, things will go well for him in life.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, though other texts have other authors. Here the teacher speaks to a young man. The verses around it speak of self-interested friendships, of poverty, and of lies. Against that, this proverb shows that wisdom is a treasure that does not depend on what others think.

For today: before making an important decision, stop to ask for counsel and to pray. Then do what you have learned, not just listen to it. In this way you care for your own life.
exp.1:20:
This verse says that upright people, meaning those who live with honesty and do what is right, will live at peace in the land. "Perfect" does not mean free from mistakes, but whole, with a sincere and complete heart. "Remain" means they will stay, enjoying stability.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as in all of chapter 2 of Proverbs. He asks him to seek wisdom so that he walks the path of the good. The next verse contrasts this with the fate of the wicked. For the people of Israel, "the land" was the inheritance promised by God; some also understand it as an image of blessing and security in general.

For today: choose to be honest in small things, at work, in the family, and in your words. A whole life gives firm roots, even when everything around you is shifting.
exp.22:9:
It says not to move the old boundary marker, the stone that marked the limit of a piece of land, nor to go and take the soil from orphans.

These words are part of the sayings of the wise in Proverbs, where a teacher advises a young man. In that time orphans had no one to defend them, and it was easy to take advantage of them by moving the boundaries. The following verse gives the reason: God himself is their defender and will take up the case against anyone who strips them of what is theirs.

Today we can apply this by being honest about what is not ours, especially when someone cannot defend themselves. Avoid taking advantage of whatever advantage you have, whether in business, inheritances, or dealings with vulnerable people.
exp.6:8:
This verse says that the young man was walking at dusk, when the day was fading and deep night was coming on. "Darkness" is the idea here, and the verse describes how it grew dark. The scene is full of shadows, and no one could see it clearly.

It is a wise father who speaks, recounting in Proverbs 7 what he observed from his window. He wants to warn his son about the temptation of adultery. Notice that the young man is lacking in understanding: he is not a wicked man, but a careless one who draws near a dangerous place. The darkness sets the mood for what comes after.

For today: bad steps almost always begin with small carelessness, such as going where we should not go or at improper hours. Ask God for wisdom, and step away in time from places and situations where you know you are weak.
exp.0:29:
They would not listen to the counsel of wisdom, and they looked down on every time she corrected them. "Looked down on" means treating something as if it had no value. "Correction" is a rebuke meant to teach and to make us turn from our wrong direction.

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a woman who raises her voice in the streets (Proverbs 1:20-33). The verses before this one explain that she called out and no one paid attention. Now she describes why the consequence came: they rejected her counsel and her correction, and did not choose to fear the LORD, that is, to revere him and live according to his will.

Today we can ask ourselves how we react when someone wise corrects us. Even when it hurts, it is worth listening with humility, praying, and considering whether there is something we should change. Accepting correction in time can spare us a great deal of pain later.
exp.5:18:
This verse completes a list of things that God hates. It speaks of two kinds of conduct: the false witness, who lies when he should tell the truth, and the one who stirs up strife, that is, who provokes quarrels and divisions. Here "brethren" may refer to the family, to the people of God, or to the community in general.

It belongs to the teachings of a wise father to his son, in the book of Proverbs. Earlier, Proverbs 6:16 says there are six things that God hates, and seven are an abomination to him. This verse is the seventh. The list warns about attitudes that harm others and destroy trust. Then the father asks his son to keep his teachings.

Today we can take care with our words. Before you comment on something about someone, ask yourself whether it is true and whether it will help peace. If not, it is better to keep silent or to speak with love.
exp.7:28:
It says that when God created the world, he set a limit for the sea and commanded the waters not to cross it. "Statute" and "commandment" mean a firm order or law. It also says that God "established the foundations of the earth," like someone laying secure bases for a house.

The speaker is Wisdom, who in Proverbs 8 appears as a figure who speaks to people. She says she was present alongside God when everything was created. Many Christians see here a pointer to Christ, though others understand her only as a poetic way of speaking about God's wisdom. Its purpose is to invite us to listen to her.

For today: if God set limits on the sea with such order, we can also trust that he cares for our lives. Before deciding something important, let us ask him for wisdom and live within his good limits.
exp.1:21:
It says that wicked people, those who live without regard for God, will be cut off from the earth. The "transgressors" are those who betray or break trust, who act with deceit and fail to do what is right. To be "rooted out" means to be pulled up by the roots, like a plant that can no longer live in that place.

Here a father, or teacher of wisdom, is advising his son. Throughout the chapter he explains that wisdom protects him from the evil way. The verse before says that the upright will dwell in the land; this verse shows the contrast. In Israel, the land was a symbol of God's blessing. It is poetic language about the final destiny of each path.

For today: before deciding something, ask where that path leads, not just what benefit it gives you today. Choose honesty, even when it costs you, and trust that God cares for those who follow him.
exp.6:7:
He says the young man lacking understanding was walking along the street, near the corner where the woman mentioned later lived, and that he was heading toward her house. Note the old-fashioned wording: the verse names her as "her," the woman who appears in the verses that follow. The text says he went the way to her house, meaning her house.

The speaker is a wise man, who presents himself as a father looking out from his window and telling what he saw. It is a scene meant to teach young people. He wants to warn them how temptation toward adultery arrives, step by step, without a person noticing.

For today: it is not enough to say that one will not fall into temptation; we must also watch where we walk. If we know where we are weak, let us avoid going near those places or situations, and ask God for wisdom to decide in time.
exp.3:9:
The explanation says that a son should listen carefully and accept his father's words. The word "sayings" in the verse means teachings or advice. The promise is that if he receives them, he will have a long life. Proverbs usually speak of a general tendency: living wisely tends to protect life. It is not a guarantee for every case.

Here a father speaks, perhaps Solomon, remembering what he learned from his own father. It is family advice. Before this verse, wisdom is presented as something valuable that honors the one who embraces it. Afterward, the father says that he has already guided him along straight and safe paths.

Today, choose a trusted person who is wise in the faith, such as a father, a mother, or a pastor. Ask them for advice and listen without becoming defensive. Then, put that advice into practice this week.
exp.30:16:
She prepared herself with strength for her work, the explanation says. The phrase "girded her loins" is an old image: people gathered up and tied their long robes at the waist so they could move about freely. "Strengthened her arms" means she made her arms strong and ready for the task. In other words, she got ready with spirit and energy.

These words are part of the closing poem of Proverbs 31, which describes the woman of noble character. The chapter says these are words that the mother of King Lemuel taught him (31:1). Many understand that she shows him what kind of character to seek and value. The poem is not a simple list of chores but a portrait of wisdom, diligence, and the fear of the Lord.

For today: face your responsibilities with spirit and order, without waiting until you feel strong. Ask God for energy, take care of your rest, and work steadily at what He has entrusted to you.
exp.17:23:
It says that whoever wants friends must be a true friend, with affection and loyalty. It also says there is a friend who is closer and more devoted than a brother by blood. This first sentence can be translated in other ways. Some Bibles say that a person with many friends may come to harm, but that there is a friend more faithful than a brother.

It is a proverb of wisdom, and tradition attributes it to Solomon. Its purpose is to teach how to live well. The verses around it speak of marriage, of words, and of how we treat others. This proverb adds that friendship requires giving of yourself, not just keeping company.

Today, instead of counting how many friends you have, take care of the few who are closest to you. Call someone, listen to them, keep the promises you make, and stand with them in their hard moments.
exp.22:13:
He says that the father who corrects his son with the rod (a stick, a symbol of discipline) protects him from a bad fate. The word "hell" here translates the Hebrew "Seol," which usually means the grave or the world of the dead. So "deliver his soul" can be understood as saving his life from a path that leads to ruin.

It speaks like a wise teacher, like a father advising his son. The neighboring verses call for paying attention to instruction and express the wish that the son become wise so as to gladden the heart of the one who raises him. Some understand the rod literally and others as an image of firm correction.

For today: correct with love, patience, and consistency, seeking the good of the one who is learning. Discipline should never be an outlet for anger or cause harm.
exp.13:21:
This verse asks whether those who plan evil do not go astray. The expected answer is yes. By contrast, those who plan or intend good will receive mercy and truth.

Proverbs gathers wisdom aimed mostly at young people, and tradition largely attributes it to Solomon. Here, just after speaking of how the poor are treated, the verse contrasts two paths: plotting harm or seeking the good of one's neighbor. Some understand that good includes helping those in need, though the text does not say this directly.

Today, before you react to an offense or a need, ask yourself what good you could plan. Thinking ahead about how to help, forgive, or speak the truth makes your decisions bear fruit and draws you closer to God.
exp.28:24:
This verse says that being afraid of what people will think or do traps us, like an animal caught in a snare. By contrast, whoever places their trust in God (Jehovah) will be safe. The word "snare" refers to a trap, and the phrase "will be safe" means they will be protected, lifted up and secure.

It is a proverb from the wisdom tradition of Israel. Tradition links it with Solomon, though the book had several editors. Its purpose is to teach how to live well. The verses nearby speak of pride, of accomplices who stay silent out of fear, and of those who seek the favor of the powerful. Everything points to the conclusion that human approval is not what determines our lives: judgment comes from God.

Today, when you feel pressure to please others or to keep quiet about the truth out of fear, stop and pray. Ask yourself: "Whom am I trying to please?" Ask God for the courage to act with honesty and with respect.
exp.21:1:
The rich and the poor cross paths in life: they share streets, markets, and cities. Although their circumstances are very different, both were made by the Lord, that is, God. The phrase "meet together" can also be understood as "have this in common." Words from older wording: "á" is "a," and "Jehová" is the name of God.

This is a proverb attributed to Solomon, within a collection of sayings of wisdom for daily life. It comes right after affirming that a good name is worth more than riches. Thus the verse reminds us that money does not define a person's worth, because both have the same Creator.

Today we can treat with the same respect the boss and the one who cleans the office, the neighbor with resources and the one who barely survives. Before judging someone by what they have or do not have, let us remember that God made them and values them.
exp.14:6:
The lips of the wise spread knowledge like seed scattered in different directions. The explanation of the word "scatter" is rewritten below. This verse says that wise people speak in a way that gives out knowledge and good judgment, like someone sowing seed. To scatter means to spread something widely in many directions. In contrast, the heart of the foolish does not do the same, because it has no wisdom to give. In the Bible, the heart is the center of a person's thoughts and decisions.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here the teacher contrasts the wise person with the fool, something that repeats throughout the chapter. Earlier he spoke of accepting correction, and afterward he speaks of what pleases God. This shows that what we say comes from what is within us.

For today: before you speak, guard what fills your heart. Read the Bible, listen to advice, and accept correction. In this way your words can encourage and guide others.
exp.1:3:
It says we should seek wisdom with the same eagerness that someone seeks silver. "Examine closely" means to look over carefully, digging until you find something. The phrase about hidden riches speaks of treasure kept out of sight. It is part of a long sentence that begins in verse 1 and runs through verse 5: if you do this, then that will follow.

The book of Proverbs presents here a wise father or teacher speaking to his son. Tradition attributes it to Solomon, though the text of this chapter does not say so explicitly. He teaches that wisdom does not come by chance but requires attention, prayer, and effort. The goal, according to the verses that follow, is to know God and to honor him.

For today: set aside a fixed time each day to read the Bible calmly, ask questions, and ask God to teach you. Just as people work for money, wisdom is worth working for.
exp.1:17:
This verse says that the house of that woman sinks down toward death, and that her paths, that is, her ways, lead toward the dead. The word "dead" refers to those who are already in the place of the departed. It is a way of saying that following her ends in ruin.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son. He warns him against the woman who flatters with her words, who abandoned her husband and forgot the covenant with God. Some see her as a real woman who seduces, and others as an image of foolishness in general.

For today: do not let yourself be carried away by what sounds sweet but draws you away from God and from your commitments. Before following a path, ask yourself where it ends, and take care of your promises and your friendships.
exp.7:29:
This verse says that Wisdom was beside God while He set everything in order. She was his joy every day, and she rejoiced in his presence always. The phrase "I was his delight" means that she gave God great pleasure; the word "solace" means joy and rest. Some other translations render the same word as "architect" or "master workman," since the Hebrew term has several possible meanings.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented as a person who calls out to the young. Here she describes being with God from the beginning of creation. Many Christians see in her an image that points to Christ, though others understand her only as a poetic way of speaking about the wisdom of God. Her purpose is to invite the reader to listen.

For today: if God's wisdom is so ancient and good, it is worth seeking before you decide. Before an important step, pray and consult the Bible calmly.
exp.26:10:
What it says: A father asks his son to be wise. When the son lives wisely, the father is glad. In addition, the son then has an answer for anyone who criticizes or insults him. The word that means to insult or speak badly of someone is set aside here; the sense is simply to insult or speak ill of another person.

Context: The speaker is a father or wise teacher, as in much of Proverbs, which is largely attributed to Solomon. A wise son is the best defense of his family: if he lives well, criticism loses its force. The nearby verses speak of friendship, counsel, and prudence.

For today: Living with integrity, working honestly, and treating others well is the best answer to criticism. If you are a son or daughter, your good character gives joy to your parents. If you are a father or mother, teach by your example.
exp.3:16:
He says that the wicked live on wrongdoing the way someone lives on food and drink. The "bread of wickedness" and the "wine of violence" are figures of speech: their daily sustenance is evil, and what they gain through violence or deceit. This can be understood in two ways: that they feed on what they obtain by doing harm, or that doing wrong is as routine for them as eating.

A wise father speaks to his son in the book of Proverbs. He warns him not to follow the path of the wicked (verses 14 to 16). This verse explains why: wrongdoing has become a habit and a necessity for them. Then the father contrasts that path with that of the righteous, which is like the light of dawn.

Today we can take care with whom we associate and which things we accept as normal. If a job, a friendship, or a gain depends on deceiving or harming others, it is wise to step away in time. God invites us to a path of light.
exp.28:3:
This verse says that a ruler who acts with justice and uprightness gives stability and firmness to his country. By contrast, "the man who receives gifts" is someone who lives off receiving presents, that is, bribes, and by that practice ends up ruining the nation. Here the word "judgment" means justice, and "gifts" are presents given to buy favors. Some scholars also understand the phrase as someone who burdens the people with excessive taxes.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed for the most part to Solomon, and it was gathered to teach how to live well. The verses around it contrast the righteous with the wicked and show how the character of those who lead affects the whole people. Here the point is that justice holds a society up and corruption weakens it.

For today: if you have any authority, in your home, your work, or your church, decide with honesty and not for favors or advantages. Also pray for those who govern, that they may seek justice.
exp.12:20:
Evil goes after sinners, like someone who follows closely until they catch up with them. But good is what comes back to the righteous, since God repays them with good.

The phrase "shall be repayed" means they will receive a good reward. The words "á" and "mas" are old forms of "to" and "but" and are no longer used this way.

These words come from the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, though other parts have other authors. It is wisdom in the form of teaching: it speaks of how the two ways of living tend to end. The verses nearby speak of friendships and of what is inherited. It is not a mechanical promise, for other biblical texts recognize that sometimes the righteous suffer.

For today: choose your decisions and your friendships thinking about where they lead in the long run. Do good even when the fruit is not seen soon, and trust that God is just.
exp.26:3:
It says that anger is cruel and fury is like a flood that sweeps everything away, but that envy is even more dangerous. The question "who can stand before envy?" means that almost no one can resist it. Your verse uses the word "outrageous" for anger, which here means violent and overwhelming; in the King James wording, anger is described as "outrageous," meaning it rushes forward with destructive force.

This is part of the Proverbs of Solomon, sayings of wisdom given by a teacher to shape character. Just before, it speaks of the fool and his anger, which weighs more than stone and sand. Afterward it speaks of sincere relationships. Anger erupts and is noticed, but envy tends to hide and lasts longer.

For today: if you feel bothered by another person's success, do not ignore it. Bring it before God in prayer, give thanks for something specific in your life, and bless that person with sincere words. In this way envy loses its strength before it damages your relationships.
exp.8:11:
This verse says that wisdom or mockery has personal consequences. If someone chooses to be wise, the benefit is for themselves. If someone chooses to be a scoffer (someone who ridicules and rejects correction), they will bear the result alone. The idea of bearing the result refers to suffering the consequences.

In Proverbs 9, Wisdom appears as a woman who invites everyone to her table to learn how to live well. Then the foolish woman speaks, offering the opposite path. This verse closes Wisdom's invitation: each person must decide. Some scholars see here a warning, and others an exhortation to listen. In both cases, the decision is personal.

Today, we can ask ourselves whether we receive correction from others well or whether we respond with pride. Accepting sincere advice, even when it hurts, helps us grow. Let us ask God for a humble heart, willing to learn.
exp.1:2:
This verse says we should earnestly ask for understanding and discernment. "Criest after" means calling out loudly, with sincere desire. "Liftest up thy voice" means raising your voice to ask. Put simply, it is not enough to wish to understand; we must seek it with our whole heart.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs. This verse is part of a series of conditions: receiving the words, listening carefully, inclining the heart, and crying out. Then comes the promise: to understand the fear of the Lord and to find the knowledge of God.

For today: before making an important decision, take some time to pray and ask God for wisdom. Then seek his guidance in the Bible and in the advice of wise people, without rushing.
exp.24:6:
This verse says that it is better for someone in authority to invite you to move up to a place of honor than to be sent to a lower place and be shamed in front of an important person. "Prince" here refers to a ruler or noble. "Humbled" means being brought down publicly.

It is part of the proverbs of Solomon, collected by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah (Proverbs 25:1). These are words of wisdom for someone who appears before the king. The verses before it warn against boasting and taking the place of the great. Jesus taught something similar about choosing the last place at a banquet (Luke 14:7-11).

For today: do not seek to stand out or take the first place. At work, in church, or in the family, serve with humility and let others recognize your worth. It is healthier to be invited to come up than to suffer shame for having put yourself forward.
exp.23:10:
It says we should not stand by doing nothing when someone is in danger of unjust death. To "rescue" means to save or deliver. A "slaughter place" is where people are killed, like a slaughterhouse. Here the 1909 version expresses the idea as a condition: if you refuse to help, that is, if you hold back from rescuing them. The next verse makes clear that God takes this seriously.

It is part of the wisdom sayings that a wise father or teacher gives to his son, in keeping with the style of the book. The verses around it speak of being lazy in the difficult day and of making excuses such as "we did not know." Some understand it to refer to victims of injustice or violence; others extend it to any serious danger. The text gives no specific historical details.

For today: do not look the other way in the face of abuse or injustice. According to your abilities, speak up, accompany, help, or support those who work to protect the vulnerable.
exp.15:7:
This proverb says that it is better to have a little, obtained in a fair way, than to have a great deal of gain gotten through injustice. The phrase "great revenues" means large amounts of income. The phrase "without right" means without justice, that is, dishonestly or unfairly.

This verse is in the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although the book gathers wisdom from several authors. It is spoken by a teacher of wisdom who gives advice to his hearers. The nearby verses speak of the fear of the LORD and of ways that please him, so the proverb shows that righteousness is worth more than wealth.

Today we can apply it to work and money. Before accepting a gain, ask yourself whether you obtained it honestly. A modest wage, earned with integrity, brings peace and a good conscience, something that unjust money cannot buy.
exp.21:6:
It says that someone who has a lot of money usually has power over the poor. It also says that whoever borrows becomes subject to the one who lent to them. The word "rules" means that they will dominate or be in charge. Note that "borrower" in the verse refers to the one who takes a loan. Someone who serves is one who must obey or attend to another.

This verse is in the collection of proverbs attributed to Solomon. It is a teaching of wisdom, not a command. It describes how life works: debt creates dependence. Around it, the text speaks of dangerous paths, of raising children, and of being generous to the needy. Some believe it warns against going into debt; others believe it also calls the rich not to abuse their position.

For today: before taking out a loan or buying on credit, think about whether you truly need it and whether you will be able to repay it. Try to live with a clear budget and, if you have more, help others generously without taking advantage of anyone.
exp.15:24:
This verse says that sometimes a path looks right, and the person is sure it is the good one, but in the end it leads to ruin. The word "end" means the final outcome, where the road finally goes. "Paths of death" speaks of destruction, not only of dying physically.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. The teachers of Israel taught young people with short sayings like this one. Here we see a contrast: first the wise person is described, who guards his words, and then the wicked person, who digs out evil. It is repeated almost word for word in Proverbs 14:12.

For today: before an important decision, do not rely only on what "feels good." Pray, open the Bible, and ask advice from mature and wise people. Good intentions are not always enough; we need humility to let ourselves be corrected.
exp.10:12:
This verse compares two kinds of people. The one who goes around spreading gossip, carrying tales from place to place and repeating what should not be repeated, "reveals secrets," that is, discloses what was meant to be kept private. The one with a faithful spirit, by contrast, is someone who can be trusted, who knows how to keep to himself what has been entrusted to him, and so "conceals the matter."

It is part of the book of Proverbs, a collection of sayings of wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon. Here the context speaks of how words affect the community: the mouth of the wicked overturns the city, and the prudent person knows when to keep silent. Keeping silence is presented as a sign of good sense.

For today: before you repeat something someone has confided in you, ask yourself whether it is yours to share. Be a person who is safe to talk to, someone others can open up to without fear. If keeping a secret would cause harm to someone, seek wise counsel.
exp.13:1:
It says that the way a person lives shows what they really think of God. Whoever walks in uprightness, that is, whoever lives with honesty and justice, fears Jehovah: they respect him and take him seriously. On the other hand, the one who is perverse in his ways, that is, the one who walks crookedly and turns aside on purpose, despises him: they do not value God.

This verse is in Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings. Tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon, although not all the sayings are his. Its purpose is to teach how to live wisely. The nearby verses contrast the wise with the foolish: the wise woman builds up, while the foolish one tears down, and the words of the fool bring trouble.

For today: examine whether your daily decisions, such as what you say, do, or promise, reflect respect for God. Ask him to help you be honest, even when no one sees you.
exp.14:25:
This verse says that God detests the thoughts of the wicked person, but he delights in the words of the pure, that is, of those who are clean-hearted and sincere. "Abomination" means something deeply hated. "Expressions" are the words someone speaks, and "pure" means sincere, without wickedness or deceit. Some versions translate the second part as "pleasant words," and so there are small differences in translation.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon. Here the wise man teaches a young person through contrasts: the proud and the humble, the greedy and the just. In this verse we see that God looks at hidden thoughts and not only at the words that are heard.

For today: before you speak, examine what you are thinking. Ask God to cleanse your heart, so that your words come out sincere, kind, and without any intention of harming anyone.
exp.27:6:
This proverb compares two kinds of sons. The wise son is the one who keeps the law, that is, God's instruction and commandments. The one who keeps company with gluttons, people who live without restraint in eating, drinking, and excess, brings shame on his father. The phrase "brings shame on his father" means that he causes dishonor.

This book gathers wisdom attributed mainly to Solomon, and here it speaks like a father advising his son. The nearby verses contrast those who seek the LORD and live with integrity with those who despise the law. Some understand "gluttons" in a broad sense, as wasteful and disorderly people.

Today we can ask ourselves what friendships are shaping us. Choose companions who encourage you to live with self-control and to honor God, and guard your home with your decisions.
exp.5:19:
It says that a son must take care of and obey what his father commands him, and not abandon what his mother teaches him. "Keep" means to preserve, protect, and put into practice. "Forsake not" means not to abandon or forget. Both the father and the mother appear with authority in the upbringing of children.

The book of Proverbs presents the voice of a wise father who instructs his son (tradition links him to King Solomon). Earlier, seven things that God hates were mentioned: wicked thoughts, lies, and division among brothers. Now the teacher offers the opposite path: holding fast to the teaching received at home, which protects from those evils. The verses that follow ask that it be carried in the heart.

For today: think of a good piece of advice you received from your parents or from someone who taught you the faith, and decide to put it into practice this week. If you are a father or mother, teach both with words and with your example.
exp.23:12:
It says that eating honey is good and pleasant. The phrase "honeycomb" is the wax structure where bees store honey, and the word for "taste" refers to the sense of taste. The accent mark on the word "á" comes from old spelling; today it is written "a". The father or teacher invites his son to enjoy something sweet and healthy.

The speaker is a teacher of wisdom, like a father advising his son, in a book of proverbs that tradition links to Solomon and other wise men. Just before, he speaks of helping those who cannot defend themselves. Just after, he compares honey to wisdom: just as honey sweetens the taste, wisdom does good to the soul and gives hope.

Just as you enjoy something sweet, seek God's wisdom gladly, not as a burden. Set aside a moment each day to read the Bible and ask God to guide you, and you will see how it strengthens and encourages you.
exp.9:22:
It is like a game to a fool to do wrong (the "abominación," that is, something God detests, is like a joke or a source of laughter to him). It does not weigh on him or worry him. By contrast, the man "entendido," that is, the sensible one, knows that such things are serious and lives with wisdom. Some versions translate the final phrase as saying that wisdom is the joy of the person of understanding; the Hebrew text allows that reading.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings attributed largely to Solomon, aimed at shaping character. This verse stands among contrasts: the righteous and the foolish, God's blessing and the path of the wicked. Here it is shown that the fool does not see the weight of his actions, and the verses that follow speak of the consequences.

For today: if we notice that we laugh at, or grow used to, what God calls evil, it is a warning sign. Let us ask God for a sensitive heart and seek his wisdom in the Bible and in wise counsel.
exp.5:8:
This verse speaks directly to a lazy person and asks two questions: how long will he keep sleeping, and when will he get up? A "lazy person" is someone who avoids work out of laziness. The "sleep" here refers to excessive rest, not normal sleep.

The text is part of a wise father's advice to his son in Proverbs. Shortly before, he holds up the ant as an example, which prepares its food in time without anyone to command it. Afterward, the writer warns that poverty will arrive suddenly, like a traveler or a man with a weapon. It is a call to wake up, not a mockery.

For today: think of a task you have put off, such as a payment, a study session, or unfinished work. Give it a small first step today, without waiting until you feel like it.
exp.16:25:
This verse says that it is not right to punish or declare guilty a person who is righteous, and it is also not right to strike or mistreat rulers who act with integrity and uprightness.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, although this particular saying falls within a section of short proverbs without a single unifying thread. Here the wise teacher speaks about justice: punishing the innocent or attacking someone who does good is an injustice that goes against the order God desires. Some scholars see here a warning to judges and to the people alike.

Today we can take care with our words and our judgments. Before criticizing, accusing, or spreading gossip about someone, ask yourself whether it is true and whether it is fair. And if someone in authority does their job well, acknowledge it and respect them.
exp.4:7:
This verse advises keeping well away from "her," the woman described in this chapter as a seducer or adulteress. It says that one must not only avoid sin but also not come near "the door of her house," that is, not even pass close by. The word "thy" is an older form of "your," and "nigh" is an older word for "near."

A wise father speaks to his children. He asks them to listen to his words and not turn away from them. His aim is to protect them from losing their honor, their years, and the fruit of their labor, as the following verses say. Scholars understand that "the strange woman" may refer to a real woman and also, in a broader sense, to any temptation that seduces and destroys.

For today: do not trust your willpower if you can avoid the danger. If something tempts you, such as an improper relationship, a conversation, or a website, create distance with concrete decisions, for example by deleting contacts or changing your route.
exp.27:17:
Whoever lives with integrity, that is, with honesty and uprightness, will be kept safe from danger or disaster. On the other hand, whoever walks crooked paths, that is, doing wrong and deceiving others, will sooner or later fall. The phrase "will fall" is understood to mean falling into one of his crooked paths, like someone who stumbles into a pit. Being "safe" here speaks of being secure or protected, not necessarily of eternal salvation.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the title of the book, gathered among God's people to give practical wisdom. The verses nearby speak of unjust rulers, violence, laziness, and the desire to get rich quickly. The common theme is that an honest life brings stability and dishonesty brings ruin. Proverbs describe what usually happens; they are not absolute promises.

Today you can choose honesty in small things: paying what is fair, not cheating at work, and keeping your word. Doing this with trust in God gives you peace and firmness.
exp.25:23:
This proverb says that a person who hates another can appear to be the opposite through their words. The phrase "appears in the lips" means that they show themselves as different from what they really are. "The one who hates" is the person who feels hatred. Inside, within themselves, they hold deceit, that is, lies and bad intentions.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed mainly to Solomon, and this section is a collection of sayings meant to shape character. Here the wise teacher warns about pretense. The verses nearby speak of smooth words that hide an evil heart, like a coating of cheap silver over a clay vessel. The lesson is not to trust only pleasant words.

For today: pay attention to a person's actions and consistency, not only their flattery. And examine your own heart: ask God that what you say with your mouth may be true on the inside too.
exp.5:11:
This verse describes a wicked person, someone whose character is twisted, and whose way of speaking is full of evil. "Depraved" means corrupted, someone who has lost their moral direction. "Crooked speech" means that their words are deceitful, false, or harmful. The original Hebrew suggests a mouth that is "twisted," one that does not say things straight.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom teachings, attributed largely to Solomon, addressed to a young person so that they might learn to live well. Before this, the text warns against laziness; after it, the passage describes this man with deceptive gestures and a heart that plans evil and stirs up quarrels. Some see it as a warning about how to recognize people who cause harm.

For today: take care with your words. Before you speak, ask yourself whether what you say is true, sincere, and builds others up. Ask God to cleanse your heart, for out of it comes what we say.
exp.10:1:
It says that pride and disgrace go together: wherever pride appears, shame soon follows. By contrast, wisdom accompanies the humble. "Pride" means arrogance, thinking oneself superior to others and to God. "Disgrace" means the loss of a good name, public shame.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though the book has several authors. Here the teacher instructs young people on how to live well before God. The verse before speaks of the honest scale; the following verses speak of integrity. The whole passage contrasts the upright character with the deceitful one.

For today: when you are corrected at work, at home, or at church, listen before you defend yourself. Ask yourself: what can I learn from this? Recognizing a mistake in time prevents greater harm and opens the door to wisdom.
exp.20:8:
It says it is better to live in a very small space, even in a corner of the roof or terrace, than to share a large house with a quarrelsome woman, that is, a woman who fights and argues all the time. The sentence about the old word that named a poor, narrow room, almost an attic, is removed: it explains a word that does not appear in the verse above, and the point of the verse stands without it. The meaning is that peace is worth more than comfort.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, and here it is presented as practical advice from a teacher to his listeners. This proverb appears almost word for word in Proverbs 25:24. It sits among sayings about justice and the heart of the wicked. For that reason it is understood that an atmosphere of strife also wears down the soul, no matter how much wealth one has.

For today: peace at home is worth more than a big house. This applies to everyone, men and women alike. Ask God to help you speak with gentleness and to settle disagreements with calm and respect.
exp.15:3:
The verse says that God made all things with a purpose that has to do with Himself ("for himself", that is, for His own ends). Even the wicked, the one who lives turned away from God, is seen within that plan, since his life does not escape the "day of evil", that is, the time of judgment or of consequences. Scholars understand this in several ways. Some see that God governs even wickedness, and others see that every course of conduct will reach its just outcome.

The book of Proverbs gathers the wisdom of Solomon and other sages to teach people to live in the fear of God. This chapter contrasts our own opinion with God's judgment, which weighs the spirits, and then warns against pride.

For today: do not feel at peace just because your way seems right to you. Place your plans in God's hands, trust that He governs all things, and live with humility.
exp.6:3:
This verse invites us to treat wisdom as a sister, and understanding as a very close relative. "Kinswoman" means a family member, someone you can fully trust. The phrase "Say unto wisdom" means speaking to wisdom and giving it that name. The idea is to have a close, warm, everyday relationship with wisdom.

The one speaking is a father instructing his son, as in the whole opening of Proverbs. He has just asked his son to keep his commands and carry them in his heart. He then explains the purpose: that wisdom will protect him from the immoral woman and her smooth, deceitful words. Closeness to wisdom serves as a defense.

For today: make wisdom a regular companion. Read the Bible often, ask advice from sensible people, and think before you decide. That way, when temptation comes, you will already have a familiar voice to guide you.
exp.13:0:
This proverb compares two women. The wise one builds up her house, that is, she constructs it and strengthens it. The foolish one, with her own hands, tears it down, that is, she destroys it. The word "house" can mean the home, the family, and also what a person looks after and manages. The difference lies in daily decisions.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although not all scholars agree on every section. It is wisdom in the form of a brief contrast. The verses that follow keep the same style: they speak of the one who fears God and of the fool, showing that biblical wisdom springs from reverence for God and shows itself in deeds and words.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are building in our home: with kind words, patience, order and prayer, or with criticism, neglect and anger. Men and women alike can choose today one small habit that strengthens our family.
exp.14:20:
Folly brings joy to the one who lacks wisdom, meaning that acting without thinking, mocking what is serious, or living without direction delights and gladdens such a person. But the person of understanding will walk uprightly, that is, correct the way they live and keep to a straight path. The phrase "lacks wisdom" simply means that the person has poor judgment.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book, within a collection of wise sayings that a father teaches his children. The nearby verses contrast the wise with the fool, and the diligent with the upright. Here it is shown that what gives someone joy reveals how mature their heart is.

For today: ask yourself what things truly give you pleasure. If you enjoy what does not do you good, ask God for wisdom and listen to sincere counsel to correct your course.
exp.9:30:
The person who is just, that is, the one who lives uprightly before God, speaks with wisdom, like a tree that bears fruit. By contrast, the froward tongue, the one that deceives or does harm, shall be cut out, like a dry branch that is pulled off. The word "bringeth forth" means to bear fruit, and "froward" means twisted or malicious.

This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon in this section. It is a wise teacher instructing young people. The verses nearby contrast the just person, who remains steady, with the wicked, who has no secure future. Here the contrast is applied to words: what we say reveals and affects the course of our life.

Before speaking, ask yourself: "Will what I am about to say build up or tear down?" Strive for words that, at home, at work, or online, encourage, speak truth, and give good counsel, and set aside mockery, lies, and gossip.
exp.15:29:
He shuts his eyes as he schemes evil, and presses his lips together while he plots harm. "Crooked things" are twisted deeds, the opposite of what is straight and right. "Moving his lips" most likely describes the gesture of someone who is planning or has already settled on doing harm; "brings to pass" means he carries it out. Evil does not happen by accident: first it is thought over, then it is decided.

These are proverbs of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, and they are addressed to anyone who wants to learn to live well. The verses before this one speak of the wicked person who stirs up quarrels, the gossip who separates friends, and the one who deceives with flattery. This verse completes the picture by showing the gesture of someone who plots harm. Some scholars understand the gesture in other ways, but the central idea is clear.

For today: take care with what you think in secret, because that is where what you later do begins. Before you speak or act, ask God to help you think uprightly and to seek peace.
exp.9:14:
The explanation says that money gives the rich person a sense of security, like a city with walls. By contrast, poverty leaves the poor person weak and fearful. The word "destruction" here means ruin, collapse, or fear that drains a person's strength. The proverb describes a reality without saying whether it is good or bad.

It is a proverb attributed to Solomon, within a collection of short sayings meant to teach people how to live wisely. The surrounding verses speak of prudence and of the righteous. Some believe this verse simply observes how life works; others see a subtle warning, since other proverbs say that trusting in riches is fragile (Proverbs 11:28).

Today we can be generous and attentive toward those who live in need, because their burden is real. And if we have more, it is wise to remember that money protects only in part; our true security is in God.
exp.2:19:
It says that God, by his knowledge, caused the depths of the waters to break open, and that dew falls from the sky onto the earth. The word "knowledge" here means understanding or wisdom. The "depths" are the deep waters beneath the earth, and "drop down" means to fall gently, like drops.

The speaker is a wise father, traditionally identified with Solomon, who is advising his son. He is speaking of wisdom as something precious, and he says that God used it when creating the world. If God made everything with wisdom, it is worth that his son seek it and hold on to it. Scholars understand in various ways how this wisdom relates to creation, but the central idea is clear.

For today: when you see the dew, the rain, or nature, remember that God cares for the world with order and wisdom. Trust that he can also guide your daily decisions, and ask him for that wisdom each morning.
exp.15:2:
It says we should entrust our work and our actions to God. "Entrust" means putting something into another's hands with confidence. "Works" are what we do, and "established" means made firm and stable. So when a person places what they do into God's hands, their plans and thoughts become secure.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, traditionally associated with Solomon, although the book has several authors. Here the wise teacher instructs his reader. The surrounding verses show that people make plans and feel sure they are right, but God is the one who examines the heart and has the final word. That is why entrusting our works is an act of humility.

For today: before you begin an important task or decision, pray and tell God what you intend to do. Ask him for direction, and then work with honesty, trusting that he can order your path.
exp.5:13:
This verse describes a person whose heart is twisted. "Frowardness" means wickedness or crooked thinking, and the verse uses the word "mischief" for the harmful plans such a person keeps making. That person plots evil all the time, not just now and then, and he soweth discord, that is, he stirs up quarrels and strife among people.

It is part of a wise father's teaching to his son in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Here he warns about the wicked man who deceives with gestures and signs. Then he says his ruin will come suddenly, and this sets up the list of seven things that the Lord hates.

For today: check what you think about in secret, because that is where words and quarrels come from. Before you comment on something or pass along a rumor, ask yourself whether it helps peace or breaks it. Ask God for a clean heart.
exp.17:3:
The words of a person can be like deep waters: there is much within them, and you cannot see to the bottom at a glance. And the source of wisdom is like a brook that bubbles up and runs without stopping. "Overflowing" means it spills over and keeps flowing; it never dries up.

This is a proverb, attributed largely to Solomon. It comes after a verse about the fool, who only wants to talk about what he thinks, and before another verse about righteousness. Scholars disagree about whether the "deep waters" are something good or whether they speak of how hard it is to know the heart; here, given the contrast with the brook, it seems to be a positive image.

Today, before you speak, ask yourself where your words come from. Seek wisdom in the Bible and in prayer, so that what you say is fresh and gives life to others.
exp.23:25:
This verse says that whoever gives a straight answer, meaning an honest and upright one, will receive a gesture of appreciation. The phrase about kissing the lips is a way of saying that such a person will be esteemed and respected. Other versions understand it as a frank and correct reply, which is valued as a sign of sincere friendship.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings from the wise men of Israel to guide everyday life. Here, the wise man contrasts the one who calls the wicked person upright, and is therefore rejected, with the one who rebukes with truth and receives blessing. Kissing the lips could be a sign of affection or loyalty, although scholars do not explain it in only one way.

Today, when someone asks for your opinion, tell the truth with respect, even if it is not the most comfortable thing to do. An honest word, spoken with love, builds trust and can be a true gift.
exp.11:25:
The righteous person has the advantage over his neighbour, that is, he goes a step ahead of those who surround him. By contrast, the way of the wicked leads them astray and makes them lose their direction. Note that the Hebrew of the first clause is difficult, and some versions say that the righteous person is a guide to his neighbour, or that he chooses his friends well. In any case, the contrast is clear.

This is a proverb, a short saying of wisdom. This section of the book is attributed to Solomon. It is addressed to anyone who wants to learn how to live well, and the nearby verses speak of diligence, good words, and the path that leads to life.

For today: take care with your decisions and your companions. Living with integrity gives you direction and can also help others not to lose their way. Ask yourself: where is this path taking me?
exp.24:7:
The explanation says that one should not rush to bring a problem to a dispute, that is, to a quarrel or a lawsuit. The word for "rush" means to hurry, and the other party is your neighbor. The danger is that, in the end, you may not know what to do if the other person leaves you confused or put to shame, because his side turned out stronger than you thought.

This is a proverb of Solomon, copied by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah (Proverbs 25:1). It is wisdom for daily life. Before it, the passage speaks of humility before the king, and after it, it advises settling the matter in private. So the verse teaches prudence: not acting on impulse or out of pride.

For today: when someone offends you, do not react at once with accusations, angry messages, or posts on social media. Take a breath, pray, check the facts, and first seek to speak with the person alone. Many times it can be resolved in peace and without greater hurt.
exp.9:5:
It says that God's blessings come upon the life of the righteous person, like a crown on their head. By contrast, the mouth of the wicked is covered with violence. "Wicked" refers to those who live without respect for God. The phrase "covers the mouth" can be understood in two ways: that their violence hides their true intentions, or that the violence they cause ends up silencing them and reaching them themselves.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, according to the heading of the chapter. It is wisdom in the form of contrasts: the diligent and the lazy, the righteous and the wicked. The proverbs describe what usually happens; they are not automatic promises for every case.

For today: seek to live with integrity and speak with kindness. Before responding with anger or hurtful words, take a breath and choose words that build up. In this way your life becomes a place where blessing can grow.
exp.7:11:
The explanation says that wisdom dwells alongside discretion, that is, prudence and good judgment. Also, "I find out the knowledge of witty inventions" means that wisdom finds knowledge and sound ideas to give good direction. Some translations express it as "I find out knowledge and discretion." The nuances of the original Hebrew are discussed, but the general idea is clear.

In Proverbs 8, wisdom speaks as if it were a person calling out to people in the streets. It invites everyone to prefer its teaching over silver or gold. Here it presents its qualities: it is prudent, sensible, and gives good counsel. Afterward it will say that it hates evil and that strength is found in it.

For today: before making an important decision, stop and think, ask God for direction, and seek the counsel of wise people. Acting with prudence, and not on impulse, is one way of living out this wisdom.
exp.19:13:
The explanation says that the buyer, while bargaining, speaks badly of what he wants to buy: "It is naught, it is naught," that is, "it is worthless, it is bad." But when he walks away with his purchase, he boasts and congratulates himself on the bargain he got. The word "gone his way" means "leaving" or "walking away."

This is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon, that observes everyday life in the marketplace. It does not give a command, but describes a common custom: haggling with exaggerations to lower the price. Its neighboring verses are about laziness, prudence, and securing debts, all about honest dealing and common sense in business. The author shows, with some irony, that people do not always tell the truth when it suits them.

For today: we can negotiate firmly, but without lying or belittling what belongs to others. Let our "yes" be yes and our "no" be no. We should also be wary of our own exaggerations.
exp.3:24:
