This verse invites us to look ahead with uprightness and without being distracted. The word "eyelids" refers to the folds that cover the eyes, and the phrase "straight before thee" means in a straight line, without veering off. It is an image of focus: the gaze fixed on what is right.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom. In this chapter a father speaks to his son and teaches him to guard his heart, his mouth, and now his eyes. Afterward he speaks of the feet and the path. In this way the passage moves through the whole body as an invitation to live with integrity and without detours.

For today: what we look at shapes what we desire and what we do. You can decide what you allow yourself to see or consume on your phone, on social media, or on television. Ask yourself what brings you closer to what is good and what distracts you from what God has placed before you. And keep your eyes on your goal with steady perseverance.
exp.20:22:
This proverb says that whoever watches what they say avoids many troubles. "Keeping the mouth and the tongue" means thinking before speaking, and "keeps his soul from troubles" means that protecting one's speech protects one's life from the distress, quarrels, and pain that careless words can cause.

It is a proverb of wisdom attributed to Solomon, although this section of the book was gathered and passed down over time. It is addressed to anyone who seeks to live with prudence. The verses nearby contrast the wise person with the proud one who speaks with arrogance and mockery, which is why care in speech appears as a sign of humility.

Before you respond in anger, in an argument, or on social media, pause and take a breath. Ask yourself: is this true, is it necessary, and does it help? If it does not, it is better to stay silent or wait. In this way you spare yourself conflicts and regrets.
exp.6:19:
He says that the woman's husband has taken a bag of money with him and will not return until the appointed day. The phrase is usually understood to mean the full moon or a fixed date, although some scholars have doubts about its exact meaning. The bag of money suggests a long business trip.

The speaker is the seductive woman of Proverbs 7, addressing a young man who lacks judgment. She wants to reassure him and take away his fear of being found out. She gives him details to make him believe there will be no consequences. What follows shows that it is a trap: he follows her like an ox going to the slaughter.

For today: be wary of phrases that say "no one will ever know." When a temptation promises that there will be no consequences, remember that God sees everything. Flee in time and seek wise counsel before acting.
exp.18:0:
It is better to be a poor person who walks in integrity than someone who speaks with deceit and acts like a fool. "Integrity" here means honesty and uprightness; "crooked lips" are twisted or lying words; "fool" means someone who thinks he is wise but is not.

This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, attributed largely to Solomon, though the book gathers sayings from several hands. It is wisdom given to shape character. The verses that follow speak of lacking knowledge, of reckless haste, and of how foolishness leads a person to blame God. In this way, the proverb compares two paths: the straight one, though humble, and the crooked one.

For today: do not measure your worth by what you have, but by how you live. Before you speak or make a deal, ask yourself whether what you are saying is true. Choose an honest and peaceful life over a gain obtained through lies.
exp.12:21:
The explanation says that a good person leaves an inheritance to their grandchildren, that is, something that lasts longer than their own life. It also says that what the sinner accumulates ends up in the hands of the righteous. The word "wealth" means goods or riches, and "heirs" refers to what is left to the next generation.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, which a father or teacher shares to teach how to live well. It comes after speaking of friendships and of how evil and good have consequences. It is a general rule, not a promise that is fulfilled the same way in every case. Scholars discuss whether the inheritance is only material or also moral and spiritual.

For today: think about what you are sowing in your family. Besides money, leave a good example, honesty, prayer and faith. That too is an inheritance that passes from generation to generation.
exp.13:24:
This verse compares two kinds of witnesses. The true witness "saves lives," that is, by his honesty he rescues people and protects them from injustice. The deceitful witness, by contrast, deceives on purpose, and all he knows how to say is lies. "Souls" here means people, their lives.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, which a father or teacher passes on to the young. This verse appears among sayings about words, work, and the fear of the Lord. The writer was surely thinking of the courts, where a testimony could decide whether someone lived or died. Interpreters also see here a general warning about the power of words.

For today: always tell the truth when you are asked about others, even when it is uncomfortable. An honest word can defend an innocent person; a lie can do enormous harm.
exp.24:15:
This proverb asks whether you have found honey, and advises you to eat only as much as you need. If you eat too much, you will become overfull and end up throwing it up.

The Proverbs in this chapter are sayings of wisdom attributed to Solomon, copied out by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah (Proverbs 25:1). Here the teacher speaks like a father instructing his child. Honey was a valuable pleasure, and the counsel is one of moderation. The verse that follows applies the same idea to visiting a neighbor's house too often.

Even good things become harmful when they have no limit. You can apply this to rest, to food, to screens, to money, or even to the company of others. Ask God for self-control, and learn to say "that is enough" in time, so that you enjoy his gifts with gratitude.
exp.27:11:
It says that when the righteous are doing well and rejoice, everyone notices, and there is great honor or splendor in society. But when the wicked rise to power, people go into hiding. The phrase "a man is sought" is usually understood this way: people are hunted down to be persecuted or abused, so they keep themselves out of sight. Other translations say "a man is hidden."

This is a proverb attributed to Solomon, part of a collection of wise sayings meant to teach people how to live uprightly. Here it contrasts two kinds of rule or climate: one just, where there is freedom and joy, and another unjust, where fear reigns. The nearby verses speak of falling into the wrong path and of confessing sin.

For today: value and support what is right in your family, your work, and your community. Pray for those in authority, and seek to be someone who brings security and joy to others, not fear.
exp.18:22:
Respecting God with reverence and love, it says, leads to a full life. The person who lives this way rests, satisfied and at peace. The phrase "shall abide satisfied" may sound unusual; it means they will stay content and at ease. The phrase "he shall not be visited with evil" sounds old-fashioned; it means that evil will not reach him as the master of his life. It does not promise that he will never suffer, but that he lives under God's care.

Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon. Here the wise man speaks like a father to his son. The verse before it says that many human plans pass away, but God's purpose endures. Therefore, living in the fear of God is the safest course. The proverbs describe what usually happens; they are not absolute guarantees.

Today you can bring your worries to God and decide to act with respect toward Him: be honest, ask for His guidance before you act, and trust that He cares for your life. That brings rest to the heart.
exp.19:4:
What a person thinks and plans inside is like water hidden in a deep well: it cannot be seen at a glance. "Counsel" here means purpose, intention or thought. But someone who has understanding, that is, who is wise and attentive, knows how to draw that water out, that is, to discover what is truly in another person's heart. "Draw it out" means to bring it up into the light.

Proverbs is a collection of sayings about wisdom. Much of it is traditionally attributed to Solomon, although some scholars think it was gathered together by several editors. The verses around this one speak about how to live with good sense: avoiding quarrels, not being lazy, being faithful. This proverb fits in because it speaks of the wisdom needed to understand people.

For today: before judging or responding, listen patiently and ask good questions. Often what someone feels is not said right away. And ask God for wisdom to know your own heart as well.
exp.3:0:
Proverbs 4:1 says that children should hear a father's teaching and give careful attention, so that they may gain understanding, that is, good judgment and common sense.

The speaker is a father instructing his children, within the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon. In the verses that follow, he says that he too was a son and received teaching from his own father. In this way one sees a chain of wisdom passed from one generation to the next. His purpose is to guide young people toward a wise life.

For today: listen humbly to the advice of trusted older people, whether parents, grandparents, or teachers of the faith. Before deciding something important, ask for their opinion and reflect calmly.
exp.8:0:
The explanation says that wisdom is portrayed as a person who builds a large, sturdy house. "Hewn out" means that she carved or shaped her seven pillars with care. The number seven often represents fullness or perfection, though it is not known for certain what those pillars exactly symbolize; there are several interpretations.

In Proverbs 1 through 9, a wise father speaks to his son and presents wisdom as a woman who invites. Here she prepares a banquet and sends her servant women to call people in (in the verses that follow). Opposite her is the foolish woman of the same chapter, who also invites, but toward death. Many Christians see in this a reflection of Christ, the wisdom of God, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: wisdom is built with patience and dedication. Set aside time each day to read the Bible and pray, and seek counsel from wise people, so that your decisions have firm foundations.
exp.26:7:
The explanation says that a person who leaves their place is like a bird that abandons its nest. "Their place" can mean their home, their family, their work, or the responsibility God gave them. A bird without its nest is left exposed, without protection and without a safe direction.

These words are part of the Proverbs of Solomon, gathered to give practical wisdom for everyday life. The verses nearby speak of faithful friendship, sincere counsel, and staying close in difficult times. Some believe this warns against instability or aimless wandering; others think it may also speak of someone who distances themselves from their own people. The text does not make this clear.

Before leaving your place, whether it is a job, a church, or a home, stop to pray and seek counsel from wise people. Some changes are good, but it is not wise to decide on impulse or to flee from what is hard without thinking it through carefully.
exp.12:5:
It says that living with righteousness protects us, and that wickedness ends up bringing down the one who practices it. The phrase about the person of blameless path refers to the person of integrity, who lives with sincerity and not with duplicity, so I'll simply describe it that way here. Overthrow means to tear down or ruin, so the verse's "overthroweth" refers to bringing down or ruining. Ungodliness is living without respect for God.

It is a proverb of wisdom, largely attributed to Solomon, that teaches a young person how to live well. The nearby verses contrast the lazy with the diligent, and the righteous with the wicked. In this way, the author shows that moral choices have consequences. It is a general rule of life, not a promise that is always fulfilled immediately.

For today: choose to be honest even when no one sees you, for example, by paying what is fair or keeping your word. Integrity cares for your conscience and your relationships, and trusts that God sustains the one who walks in uprightness.
exp.20:5:
The verse says that gathering riches through lies is something worthless and senseless. The source's word for "gathering" is replaced here by the verse's own wording: getting treasures means piling up or accumulating wealth. "Vanidad," which here means something empty and fleeting, corresponds to the verse's "vanity," and that is how the sentence should be read. "Desatentada," meaning without care or judgment, is rendered through the verse's "tossed to and fro," which conveys wealth scattered about without stability or sound judgment. The closing phrase speaks of those who, without realizing it, are seeking their own ruin, which matches the verse's "they that seek death."

This verse is in the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, a king who taught practical wisdom. The verses around it speak of pride, the rush to get rich, and the violence of the wicked. The whole passage contrasts the crooked path with the straight one.

Today, before closing a deal or earning money, ask yourself whether you are being completely honest. Gain obtained through deceit becomes a burden. It is better to have less with a clear conscience.
exp.13:26:
It says that respecting and honoring God, which the Bible calls "the fear of the Lord," is like a spring: a source of fresh water that gives life. That life helps a person avoid the snares of death, that is, the traps that lead to harm and ruin.

Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, and here it speaks like a father or teacher advising his children. The previous verse says that in the fear of the Lord there is firm confidence. This one completes it: that fear also gives life and protects. Then the text moves on to speak of rulers and of patience.

For today: before making an important decision, ask yourself whether it honors God. Praying and seeking his guidance helps you avoid traps you may not yet see.
exp.26:23:
It says that money and possessions do not last forever. The question at the end means that not even a crown, that is, a position of power or a high rank, passes safely from generation to generation. Everything material can come to an end.

The one speaking is a wise teacher, traditionally Solomon, who advises like a father. The verses around it call for diligent care of the sheep and the flocks, because from them comes the livelihood. This verse gives the reason: wealth does not sustain itself, and one must work with attention and steadiness. Some understand the crown as royalty, others as any kind of prosperity.

Today we can responsibly care for what God entrusts to us: work, saving, and family. Without setting our heart on money, because it is not secure forever.
exp.14:21:
The verse says that plans fail when no one is consulted. The word "purposes" here means plans or intentions, and "disappointed" means they fall short and come to nothing. In contrast, when there are many counsellors, plans are "established," that is, they become firm and succeed.

This verse is in the book of Proverbs, which gathers wisdom traditionally attributed in large part to Solomon, although the book has several authors or collections. It speaks like a teacher instructing his children. The nearby verses contrast the wise person with the fool: the wise listen and correct their path, while the fool thinks he is sufficient.

For today: before an important decision, such as a job, a business, or a marriage, seek the opinion of wise, mature, and honest people. Listen even to the one who tells you what you do not want to hear, and pray asking God for direction.
exp.26:6:
It says that someone who is already full, even when offered something as rich as a honeycomb, tramples on it or despises it (the word "trampled" means tramples or rejects). By contrast, someone who is very hungry finds even what is bitter to be sweet. What we value depends on how much need we feel.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon in this section of the book (Proverbs 25:1 speaks of proverbs copied by the men of Hezekiah). These are short sayings that teach through images from everyday life. Here, among verses about sincere correction and a friend's advice, it suggests that a heart satisfied with itself rejects what is good, although some read it in a more general way, about appetite and need.

For today: ask God for a hungry and humble heart. If you feel very secure, you may reject a correction that would do you good. Receive sincere advice with gratitude, even when it is bitter.
exp.9:18:
This verse says that when someone talks too much, it is easy for them to end up saying something wrong. By contrast, the one who knows how to hold back and watch what they say acts with wisdom. "Holding back" means restraining or controlling, as one does with a horse. "Lips" refers to the way a person speaks. "Wise" means sensible.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom. Tradition associates it with Solomon, although it also contains other collections. Here the teacher speaks to anyone who seeks to live well. The verses around it contrast the righteous person, whose words are precious and nourish others, with the fool, who speaks without thinking and harms himself.

For today: before offering an opinion, responding in anger, or passing on gossip, pause briefly and ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true, necessary, and kind. Sometimes keeping silent at the right moment prevents hurt and shows wisdom.
exp.3:25:
This verse invites us to think carefully about the direction of our lives. The word "ponder" means to observe and weigh something with close attention. The "path of your feet" is the steps we take each day. And "established" means firm and well directed, not walking blindly. Some translations use other words for this idea, and they all point toward walking with thought and reflection.

Here a father, speaking with the voice of wisdom, is addressing his son. In Proverbs 4 he passes on what he has learned so that his son may live well. Earlier he spoke about guarding the mouth and the gaze. Now he reaches the feet: words, eyes, and steps should all move in one straight direction. Then he asks his son not to turn aside, neither to the right nor to the left.

For today: at the end of the day, take a few minutes to review your decisions and habits. Ask yourself whether they bring you closer to what is good or pull you away from it, and ask God for help to correct your course.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that God used wisdom and understanding to create the world. "Founded the earth" is like laying the foundations of a house, and "established the heavens" means that he made them firm and in good order. The words "cling" and "knowledge" in the nearby verses mean "hold fast" and "knowledge."

Here a father, or teacher, is giving advice to his son. In the verses before this, he praises wisdom as a path of peace and a tree of life. Here he shows that this wisdom is not merely human advice, since God himself used it when creating everything. Therefore, the son should value it and not let it depart from his eyes.

For today: if God made the world with wisdom, he can also guide your life with it. Before deciding something important, stop, pray, and ask him for direction. Then seek his counsel in the Bible.
exp.23:32:
This verse describes a person who gives in to laziness little by little. It says "a little sleep, a little slumber," that is, dozing off or nodding in drowsiness. "A little folding of the hands to sleep" means crossing the arms and doing nothing. Each rest seems small, but it keeps being repeated again and again.

The one speaking is the wise man of Proverbs, who tells what he saw when he passed by the field of a lazy man. That field was full of thorns and nettles, and its stone wall had fallen down. The wise man reflected and drew a lesson from it. He then warns that poverty will come suddenly, like a traveler or like a man armed with a shield. Some understand this as an unavoidable attack; others understand it as a visitor who settles in.

For today: do not put off until later what you can do today. Choose one pending task, such as a job, a study, or a debt, and give it a fixed amount of time today, without postponing it.
exp.10:27:
This verse compares two paths. Whoever puts his trust in wealth will fall, meaning he will fail or collapse, because riches are not a firm foundation. The righteous, by contrast, will flourish as a branch, that is, they will be like fresh, living leaves on a tree, full of life and fruit.

This proverb belongs to the sayings attributed to Solomon, which offer practical wisdom for daily life. Nearby, the proverbs speak of generosity, of greed (the one who hoards the grain while the people are in need), and of conduct within the home. The theme is that trust and character matter more than what a person accumulates.

For today: enjoy and manage well what you have, but do not rest your security on it. Seek God first, live with integrity, and share generously. That gives deeper roots than a bank account.
exp.5:32:
He says that the man who commits adultery will get a "wound," meaning blows, harm or punishment, and also shame. His "dishonour," that is his disgrace, "shall not be wiped away," which means it will not be erased or removed, like something scraped off a surface. The bad reputation will be left behind.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as in all of the book of Proverbs, warning him about adultery. The verses before it speak of what is lost when a man falls into it, and the following verses explain that the wronged husband, full of jealousy, will not accept any payment to forgive. It is a proverb that describes common consequences, not a promise about every case.

For today: guard your faithfulness from the small things. Avoid conversations, relationships or habits that feed unfaithfulness, and if you have already failed, seek forgiveness from God and wise counsel, for He restores, although the consequences sometimes remain.
exp.8:16:
It says that what is forbidden seems richer and more attractive. "Stolen waters" are water taken by theft, and "bread eaten in secret" is food enjoyed in hiding. "Pleasant" here means agreeable, tasty. It is a seductive phrase that promises pleasure without anyone finding out.

The one speaking is the foolish woman, who in Proverbs 9 appears as a contrast to Wisdom. She sits at the door of her house and invites the simple, those who lack understanding. Her words sound tempting, but the next verse reveals the deception: her house leads to death. Many understand her to represent temptation in general, including immorality.

For today: when something attracts you because it is secret or forbidden, stop and ask where it leads. If you need to hide it, that is a good warning sign. Seek a trustworthy person and ask God for wisdom to choose what truly gives life.
exp.23:30:
It says the wise man saw a field and a vineyard left unattended. They were full of thorns and nettles, which are plants that sting and spoil the ground. The word rendered as "face" refers to the surface of the ground. The stone wall that protected the place lay broken down.

The one speaking is the author of Proverbs, presented here as an observer who learns from what he sees. He passes by the land of a lazy man who lacks common sense. The verses that follow say that he looked, considered it, and drew a lesson: laziness brings ruin little by little.

For today: do not neglect the small things. A prayer, a debt, a relationship, or a habit that is left alone "just a little" can end up overgrown with thorns. Choose one thing today that you have stopped caring for and give it some of your time.
exp.5:33:
It says that a wronged husband's jealousy is like a fury that cannot be controlled. When the time for revenge comes, he will show no mercy. The word "fury" means violent anger, and the phrase "the day of vengeance" refers to the moment when that husband acts against the one who wronged him.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, within the counsel of Proverbs 6. He warns that adultery brings serious and lasting consequences. It is not only a hidden sin: it can cause harm, shame, and real danger. The text describes what usually happens; it does not command taking revenge.

For today: guard your faithfulness and that of your relationships. If you feel temptation, step away in time and seek help. And if you are hurt, do not let anger rule you; surrender it to God and seek wisdom.
exp.19:1:
The explanation says that a king's anger is as frightening as the roar of a young lion. Whoever provokes him and makes him furious harms himself, since "sins against his own soul" means he puts his own life at risk. Old words: a "roar" is a loud, deep growl; a "young lion" is a lion cub; "to become furious" is to fill with anger.

This is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. A wise father teaches his son how to live. In that time, a king had the power to decide over people's lives. That is why caution before authority is advised. The nearby verses speak of avoiding quarrels and of not being foolish, so the theme is self-control.

For today: before provoking a boss, an authority, or anyone with power, think about the consequences. Show respect, speak calmly, and do not look for unnecessary conflict. That is not cowardice; it is wisdom.
exp.23:28:
This verse asks us not to take revenge. It says we should not think: "As he did to me, so I will do to him." Nor should we believe it is up to us to give each person exactly what they deserve for what they did. The word "work" here means what someone has done, and "render" is the response or punishment one wants to give back.

These words are part of the proverbs of the wise, which teach us to live with justice and prudence. Shortly before, it speaks of being honest with our neighbor, of not accusing him without cause, and of not flattering him with falsehood. This verse continues that line: personal revenge breaks justice. That is why many understand it as a call to leave judgment in God's hands.

Today, when someone offends you, before answering in kind, stop and pray. Look for a calm response, such as speaking with respect or setting a healthy boundary, without returning evil for evil.
exp.23:1:
This verse explains why we should not envy wicked people. It says their heart "studieth destruction," that is, they plan to do harm and to take what belongs to others. And "their lips talk of mischief" means that their words are full of wrongdoing: deceit, mockery, or unjust schemes.

Proverbs gathers words of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon and to other wise men, to guide those who want to live uprightly. Here the teacher warns his reader not to admire or seek the company of wicked people, because their apparent success hides a crooked heart. Right after this, he contrasts that path with the path of wisdom, which builds up and fills the house with true riches.

For today: before envying someone's success, look at what lies behind their words and plans. Choose friends and examples who speak the truth and act with honesty, and ask God for a wise heart.
exp.13:25:
This proverb says that whoever lives with respect and reverence toward God has a firm confidence, like a secure refuge. "The fear of the Lord" is not a paralyzing dread, but honoring God and taking Him seriously. The phrase about the children means that this security also reaches the family: children find shelter and a future.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom from Solomon and other wise men of Israel, to teach people how to live well. Here the context speaks of contrasts between wise and foolish, truth and lies. The following verse repeats that the fear of the Lord is a "fountain of life." The proverbs express general principles, not absolute promises for every case.

For today: if you want to give stability to your family, start with your own relationship with God. Pray, read the Bible, and make honest decisions before Him. Your children will learn more from your example than from your words.
exp.9:21:
This verse says that true riches come from the blessing of God (the LORD), and that when He gives, He does not mix His gift with pain or worry. The word "makes rich" can refer to material goods, but it can also refer to a full life. The phrase "he addeth no sorrow" means that it does not bring anguish with it.

It is a proverb from Hebrew wisdom literature, traditionally attributed to Solomon. It belongs to a series of contrasts between the righteous and the wicked. The nearby verses speak of wise words, of understanding, and of what each person receives in the end. The proverbs give general principles, not absolute promises for every case.

For today: before pursuing gain at any price, ask yourself whether what you are chasing could be received with peace and a clear conscience. Trust God with your work and be thankful for what He gives you, whether much or little.
exp.2:21:
It says that the wisdom and sound counsel mentioned in the previous verse will be "life" to your soul, that is, they will strengthen it and keep it alive within. They will also be "grace" to your neck, meaning an ornament that adds beauty, like a necklace.

Here a father, or a wise teacher, speaks to his son. In Proverbs 3 he encourages him not to lose sight of wisdom and good judgment. Earlier he spoke of how God created the world with wisdom. Afterward he promises that you will walk with confidence, without stumbling, and sleep without fear.

Today we can apply it this way: before deciding something important, stop and ask God for direction, and seek sound counsel in his Word. That habit brings peace to the heart and also shows in how we treat others.
exp.21:20:
This verse says that the teacher writes these instructions so that the reader may know with firmness what is true and dependable. The word "certainty" means security, something sure. "Words" here means sayings or teachings. "Those who send to you" refers to people who send you to ask questions or look for an answer. In this way you will be able to answer with truth.

The speaker is a wise man who, in this section, teaches his disciple as a father would teach his son. The verses before it say that he wants your trust to be in the LORD. The ones that follow speak of not robbing or oppressing the poor. Some scholars see here the influence of wisdom texts from other cultures, but this is debated.

For today: before you give an opinion or advice, learn well the truth of God's Word. Then, when someone asks you, you will be able to answer with honesty, humility, and firmness, without making things up or exaggerating.
exp.6:24:
This verse is a direct warning. It asks that the heart not turn aside toward the ways of the seductive woman, and that a person not go astray by walking down her paths. Here "turn aside" means "lean toward" or "give in to," and "go astray" means "make a mistake" or "wander off course."

A wise father speaks to his children within a long teaching in the book of Proverbs. He has just described a young man who falls into temptation without noticing the danger, like a bird rushing into a trap. Now he asks for attention, because he wants to save his son from that end.

For today: the heart is guarded before temptation arrives. Avoid the places, conversations, and habits you know weaken you, and seek advice from wise and trustworthy people.
exp.16:16:
A true friend loves at all times, in good moments and in bad, not only when it suits them. And the brother, or the sister, is born, that is, exists, to help when distress arrives, that is, affliction and hardship. Some understand "brother" as a blood relative; others as someone close who acts as one.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon. These are brief sayings meant to teach practical wisdom. Here it is surrounded by verses about righteousness, foolishness, and reckless commitments. This verse highlights what a healthy and loyal relationship is, in contrast to foolishness.

For today: think of someone who is going through a difficult time and reach out to them this week. Call them, listen to them, or help them with something concrete. In this way you practice a constant love that does not depend on circumstances.
exp.9:1:
It says that riches gained through wrongdoing, such as theft, deceit or injustice, are of no use when it really matters. By contrast, living righteously, that is, doing what is right before God and before people, can save someone from death. Here "death" can be understood as ruin, punishment or the loss of life.

This is the beginning of Solomon's sayings in the book of Proverbs. They are short sayings, written with wisdom to teach young people how to live well. The verses around it contrast the righteous with the wicked, and the diligent worker with the lazy person. These are general principles about how things tend to go, not promises for every case.

For today: before you seek money or an advantage, ask yourself whether you are getting it honestly. Gain that is clean brings peace; gain that is crooked weighs on you sooner or later.
exp.13:7:
It says that the true wisdom of the prudent consists in thinking carefully about where their life is going, that is, in paying attention to their steps and to where they lead. By contrast, the folly of fools is "deceit": they deceive themselves, believing they are doing well when they are lost. Here "wisdom" means practical good sense, and "folly" means a lack of good judgment.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed in large part to Solomon, though it is not always known who wrote each saying. It speaks to anyone who wants to learn to live well. The context contrasts the wise person with the fool, who mocks sin and does not listen to advice.

For today: before deciding something important, stop and ask yourself, "Where is this path taking me?" Ask God for direction and listen to the counsel of sensible people.
exp.3:10:
It says that the one speaking has guided his son along the path of wisdom, that is, a way of living with good judgment and the fear of God. It also says he made him walk in "right paths," that is, straight roads, without turning aside or deceiving. Guided means he showed him the way and directed his course.

A wise father speaks here, instructing his son. In Proverbs 4, the writer recalls what he himself learned from his family, and it is often connected with the teaching of Solomon, though the text does not make this clear at this point. His purpose is that the son listen, receive the counsel, and have a good and stable life.

For today: think about who has guided you with wisdom and thank them for it. Then look for a sound piece of advice from the Bible or from a mature person, and put it into practice this week, even if it is hard.
exp.26:16:
This proverb says that when iron is rubbed against iron, it is sharpened and becomes more useful. In the same way, a person helps to improve his friend. The word "sharpeneth" means to make something sharp or give it an edge, and "countenance" here is understood as the whole person, his character and way of thinking.

The Book of Proverbs is a collection of wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, and this chapter is connected with the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). These are brief sayings, without a strict sequence. The verses nearby speak of living together, of difficult people, and of loyalty. For this reason this saying shows the positive side of relationships: good friends help us grow.

Seek sincere friends who encourage you and also correct you with love. And be that kind of friend yourself: talk, listen, and advise with respect, without humiliating anyone.
exp.27:16:
This proverb speaks of someone who carries the guilt of having shed innocent blood. The phrase about doing violence to the blood of a person means that he is burdened by having killed someone. That person "shall flee to the pit": he will live on the run, with a troubled conscience, until he dies. And "let no man stay him" can be understood in two ways: that no one should help him escape justice, or that his flight will end only in the grave.

It is a proverb of Solomon, copied by the scribes of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). It stands among sayings about wicked rulers and righteous people. It contrasts violence with the upright walk of the verse that follows.

For today: violence never brings peace, not even to the one who thinks he has gotten away with it. Seek to resolve conflicts with calm, and ask forgiveness from God and from people when you have caused harm.
exp.23:13:
This verse compares wisdom to the honey of the verse before it: just as honey is sweet to the taste, wisdom is good for the soul. "When thou hast found it" means "when you find it." The "reward" is a good future, and "thy expectation shall not be cut off" means that your hope will not come to an end or be cut short.

Proverbs are the advice of a wise father to his son. Before this, the text warns against ignoring someone who needs help, and reminds us that God weighs hearts and knows our excuses. Afterward, it warns against harming the righteous. Wisdom here means living uprightly before God.

For today: just as you care for your body with good food, nourish your soul every day. Set aside a few minutes to read the Bible and ask God to help you apply it to one concrete decision.
exp.27:10:
It says that a rich person often thinks of himself as very clever, but a poor person with good judgment will search him out, that is, he will examine him and find out whether he truly has wisdom or only an appearance of it. "Understanding" means that he has discernment.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings from the wise men of Israel, and many are attributed to Solomon. Here the wise man contrasts pride with humility. The verses nearby speak of listening to God's law, of the upright, and of confessing sins. So money does not give wisdom; wisdom comes from living honestly and paying attention to God.

For today: do not confuse having more resources, education or success with being right. Listen respectfully to those who think differently, whether rich or poor, and ask God for a humble heart willing to learn.
exp.15:0:
This verse says that people make plans and prepare their thoughts in the heart, but the final answer that comes from the mouth is from God. "Preparations" means plans or arrangements. The phrase "answer of the tongue" can be understood as the right words, or the outcome of what is said or done.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the title of the book, meant to teach wisdom for daily life. It opens a series of sayings about God and our plans. The verses that follow speak of how we may think we are right, but the Lord examines the spirit, and they invite us to commit our works to him. Some read this as meaning that God guides the words; others, that he directs the outcome.

For today: make your plans with diligence, but before you speak or decide something important, pray and ask God for wisdom. He can give you the words and the outcome that suit you best.
exp.18:5:
Many people seek the favor of the prince, that is, of someone with power or authority. Here "intreat" means to ask or plead for a favor. The verse also says that everyone wants to be a friend to the one who gives gifts or help. It is an observation about how people behave when they expect to receive something.

This verse is in Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings, largely attributed to Solomon. Here the teacher neither approves nor condemns but describes reality. The nearby verses speak of how wealth attracts friends and poverty drives them away. In this way it warns that not every friendship is sincere.

Today you might ask yourself whether your friendships are based on affection or on convenience. Try to be a faithful friend, both when someone has much and when someone has nothing. And value those who stand by you in difficult times.
exp.5:10:
This verse says that poverty will come upon the lazy person suddenly and without any way to stop it. The word "traveller" refers to someone who moves forward with steady steps, and the "armed man" is a soldier carrying a weapon. Need and lack arrive like a traveller who does not stop or like a warrior who cannot be resisted. Some scholars understand the "traveller" as a thief or bandit who attacks on the road.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Just before this, the text asks the lazy person how much longer he will sleep. His neglect seems small, a little more sleep, but its results pile up.

For today: do not leave for tomorrow what you can do today. Choose one pending task, such as paying a debt, saving something, or finishing a piece of work, and do it today. Small, repeated neglect ends up weighing heavily.
exp.15:21:
This verse compares understanding to a spring of water that gives life to the one who has it. "Understanding" is the ability to grasp things wisely and act well. The word translated "learning" here means instruction or teaching, and "fools" are people who reject God's wisdom. So the teaching of a fool only produces more folly, even when it sounds learned.

Proverbs gathers wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. It speaks to someone who wants to live well, and the verses nearby speak of trusting the LORD, speaking with gentleness, and having a wise heart. The emphasis is that true wisdom begins with God and shows in how we speak.

For today: before seeking only more information or credentials, ask God for understanding and put into practice what you learn. Also notice whom you listen to, because not every piece of advice that sounds clever gives life.
exp.3:5:
It says that wisdom is like a faithful companion. If a person does not abandon her, she takes care of him; if a person loves her, she keeps him. "Preserving" here means protecting, and "keeping" means keeping safe. Wisdom is presented almost as a person who returns the affection of the one who seeks her.

The speaker is a father, who remembers what his own father taught him, and he addresses his son. He wants the young man to understand that living with wisdom is a path of life and not a burden. That is why he insists that he acquire her and not forget her.

For today: make wisdom a daily habit. Set aside a few minutes to read the Bible and ask God for direction before deciding, and return to her even when it is difficult.
exp.29:4:
The explanation says that every word of God is pure, without lies or stain. "Pure" here means tested and free of impurities, like well-refined metal. It also says that God is a shield, that is, a protection, for those who put their trust in him, that is, those who rely on him and take refuge in him. The phrase "unto them that put their trust in him" is the older way of putting it, meaning "to those who trust in him."

Agur, son of Jakeh, speaks in this chapter. At the beginning he humbly admits that he does not have all wisdom. After asking who governs the heavens, the winds, and the earth, he answers that God is worthy of trust and that his word is sure. Right after, he warns that nothing should be added to it. Some scholars debate who Agur was, since the Bible says very little about him.

Today, when you feel insecure or confused, turn to the Bible before shifting opinions. Read it with humility, trust what God says, and let his truth take care of you.
exp.17:0:
This says: whoever separates himself from the path follows his desire, that is, his whim or the desire of the moment. And "meddles with all business," that is, he gets involved in every matter without being invited. Note: this verse is difficult in Hebrew. Other translations say that the one who separates or isolates himself seeks his own pleasure and rejects all good counsel.

The speaker is the teacher of wisdom in Proverbs, a book of short sayings that tradition largely attributes to Solomon. He wants to warn young people. The following verse shows the idea: the fool has no interest in understanding, only in showing what he thinks. He is described as someone who listens to no one.

For today: before deciding something important, ask counsel from a wise and mature person. If you notice that being corrected bothers you, that is a good sign to stop and listen.
exp.2:11:
It says that God corrects those he loves, just as a father corrects the son he truly wants.

It is the advice of a wise father to his son in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Just before, the son is asked not to despise or grow weary of the Lord's correction. This verse gives the reason: God corrects because he loves. Then the text speaks of the happiness of the one who finds wisdom. The teaching is that accepting correction leads to growth.

For today: when you receive correction, whether from life, from the Bible, or from someone wise, do not react right away with anger. Calmly ask yourself what you can learn, and pray for humility to change.
exp.24:14:
It says that with great patience a ruler who is angry can be calmed or persuaded. "Prince" here is a person with authority. The word "persuaded" means brought around to another view, and the phrase about the tongue is a picture of strength: the gentle overcomes the hardest things.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon, and was later gathered together, according to Proverbs 25:1. It belongs to a series of sayings about treating others with prudence: the faithful messenger, false generosity, and moderation with honey and with visitors. The exact setting of each saying is not known, since they are separate sayings.

For today: when you have to speak with a boss, a relative, or someone in authority who is upset, do not answer with shouting. Wait, listen, and speak calmly. Many times patience opens doors that force does not open.
exp.11:27:
It says that living justly, that is, doing what is right before God and before people, leads to a true and full life. The second part repeats the idea in reverse: on the path of righteousness there is no death. Some understand "no death" as a promise of life without end, and others as meaning that this path does not lead to ruin.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, attributed largely to Solomon. It is wisdom for teaching young people. The verses before it compare the righteous with the wicked and the diligent with the lazy. Here the teaching is summed up: righteousness guides toward life, while evil leads a person to lose the way.

Today we can apply it with a simple decision: choose honesty even when it costs us. For example, telling the truth at work, paying what is fair, or keeping a promise. Doing so does not always bring immediate gain, but it cares for the heart and for relationships, and keeps us walking toward God.
exp.18:8:
What it says: The one who declares something false against another person, especially when giving testimony, will not escape the consequences. "Will be ruined" speaks of downfall or destruction: whoever lives by lies ends badly. "Will not go unpunished" means they will not come away free of guilt.

Context: Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of them to Solomon. This verse is almost the same as verse 5. It comes after speaking of the injustice suffered by the poor, whom even their friends abandon. A false witness could bring down someone with no resources, so the text reminds us that God sees and that lies have consequences.

For today: Be honest in what you say about others, in the family, at work, or on social media. Do not repeat gossip or accusations without being sure. Defending the truth protects the weakest and guards your own heart.
exp.0:5:
The explanation says that proverbs serve to help a person learn to understand the sayings with deeper meaning, and the explanation, which is a clear teaching or interpretation. They also help us grasp the words of the wise and their dark sayings, which are hard or puzzling phrases that are not understood at first glance and call for reflection.

The book opens by stating its purpose. It is traditionally attributed to Solomon, and speaks in the tone of a teacher or father. It aims to form both the simple and the young as well as those who are already wise. Shortly after, in the following verse, it says that wisdom begins with respect and reverence for God.

Today, do not be discouraged if a teaching in the Bible seems difficult. Read it calmly, pray, ask questions, and return to it. Wisdom usually grows with patience and humility.
exp.23:27:
It says we should not accuse our neighbor without reason, that is, without a true basis. A "witness" is someone who testifies in a trial. The second part of the verse is difficult in Hebrew, and some translations read it as a question. Deceive is the key idea in the second half of the verse, and the sense of flattering with words is captured by this same idea of deceiving with the lips.

These words are part of the sayings of the wise (Proverbs 24:23 onward). A teacher of wisdom instructs those who want to live well. The verses nearby speak of upright words and of not taking revenge. The emphasis is on justice and honesty when speaking about others.

For today: before saying something bad about someone, whether in person, at work, or on social media, ask yourself whether it is true and whether it is necessary. And avoid praising with your mouth what you do not feel.
exp.27:23:
Here the explanation says that whoever takes something from his father or mother, and justifies it by saying "it is no transgression," is like a robber. The word "destroyer" speaks of someone who ruins and harms others. "Companion" means that he shares their path and their character. The words "á" and "ó" are the old spellings of "a" and "o."

This is a proverb of wisdom, attributed in this book to Solomon (or to those who gathered his sayings, depending on how one understands it). It speaks in the tone of a father teaching his children. Many believe that in that time robbing one's parents was considered especially serious, because it went against the respect that the law commanded (Exodus 20:12). The worst thing here is not only the theft, but excusing it.

For today: if we take money, time, or belongings from our parents without their permission, or leave them without support when they need it, let us not justify ourselves. Let us acknowledge it, ask forgiveness, and repair the harm. God honors humility and honesty in the family.
exp.21:14:
This verse says that foolishness, that is, silliness or a lack of good judgment, is bound to the heart of the child or young person. It is something natural to them from an early age. The "rod of correction" is discipline, and the proverb says it helps drive that foolishness far away.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, sayings meant to teach wisdom to young people. Around them are warnings against laziness, temptation, and injustice. Some understand the "rod" literally, as physical punishment; others see it as an image of all firm discipline. Christians interpret it in different ways.

Today, if we care for children or young people, we can correct them with love, firmness, and patience, seeking their good and not venting our anger. Correction also includes teaching by example.
exp.22:31:
Wine, although it may seem pleasant at first, in the end does harm, like a serpent that bites. The word "but" is used here to set up that contrast between the pleasant start and the painful finish. The creature mentioned was a dangerous snake, a venomous viper; the original Hebrew term is understood this way, though no one knows for certain what species it refers to.

This is a piece of wisdom advice, like the counsel a father or teacher gives a young person. It is traditionally attributed to the wise men of Israel. Here it warns that wine which catches the eye goes down smoothly, but ends in confusion, poor decisions and loss of control, as the verses that follow describe.

For today: do not let yourself be guided only by what looks appealing right now. Ask yourself where it leads in the end. If something is taking hold of you, set clear limits and ask for help from someone you trust.
exp.15:6:
This verse says that when a person's way of living pleases God, He can cause even that person's enemies to be at peace with them. The word "pleases" here means that God finds them pleasing or approves of them. "Make peace" means that God will bring about peace or calm hostility.

It is a proverb, part of the wisdom attributed to Solomon. The verses nearby speak of pride, which God rejects, and of the fear of the Lord, which turns a person away from evil. Here a general principle is taught, not a promise that always works out the same way. Jesus himself was faithful and still had enemies.

For today: live with integrity and humility, without becoming obsessed with winning every conflict. Often kindness and honesty soften difficult relationships. And if someone remains against you, you can trust that God cares for your path.
exp.22:21:
This verse asks us to listen carefully to our father, who gave us life, and not to look down on our mother when she is old. "Hearken" means "listen"; "begat" means "gave you life"; "be old" means "reach old age"; "despise" means "treat as if she were worth little."

Proverbs 22:17 through 24:22 gathers sayings of the wise, and here the speaker is a teacher addressing his son as a father would. It comes between warnings against excess and the call to buy the truth. This suggests that wisdom is passed down within the family, and that parents' old age deserves honor, not disdain.

For today: listen with respect to the counsel of your parents or other older people, even when you think differently, and care for them in their old age through visits, phone calls, patience, and concrete help.
exp.0:0:
This verse is the title of the book. It says that what follows are the proverbs of Solomon, son of David and king of Israel. A proverb is a short, wise saying that teaches how to live well. Here "of Solomon" can mean that he wrote them or that they were gathered under his name.

The book begins by presenting its main author. Solomon is remembered in the Bible for his wisdom (1 Kings 3 and 4). The verses that follow explain the purpose: to help the reader receive wisdom, good judgment, and justice. Scholars debate whether Solomon wrote the whole book, since other authors, such as Agur and Lemuel, appear later.

Today we can read Proverbs like someone listening to a wise father: with humility and a desire to learn. You could read one proverb each day and ask God to help you put it into practice in your decisions, your work, and your relationships.
exp.29:8:
The explanation says that the author fears two extremes. If he had too much, he might become satisfied, forget God, and say with pride: "Who is the Lord?" If he were very poor, he might steal and so bring dishonor to God's name. "Being full" means being too satisfied; "stealing" means taking what belongs to someone else; "taking God's name in vain" means speaking with contempt about God.

The speaker is Agur, son of Jakeh, in Proverbs 30. Shortly before, he asked God for two things: to keep lies far from him, and to have neither poverty nor riches, but only the bread he needs. This verse gives the reason: both abundance and scarcity can put faith and conduct at risk. His prayer is humble and sincere.

For today: take care of your heart both when you have plenty and when you lack. Give thanks for what you have, ask God for what you need, and pray to keep trusting Him in every situation.
exp.4:9:
This verse warns that if a person gives in to the temptation of another man's wife, others will end up taking advantage of everything that person has gained through hard work.

Here a wise father speaks, instructing his son in the book of Proverbs. He wants to protect him from adultery and its consequences. The verses nearby show that the damage reaches one's honor, the years of one's life, and even old age. Some understand "strangers" in different ways, but the general idea is losing what is one's own.

For today: guard your boundaries. If you know which situations lead you to fall, step away in time, because protecting your faithfulness also protects your family, your work, and your peace.
exp.13:27:
This proverb says that a king feels honored and strong when he rules over many people. If the people decrease, the ruler is left weak. The word "glory" in the verse refers to honor or greatness, and "destruction" means ruin or collapse. Here "prince" refers to a ruler, not only to the son of a king.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, attributed largely to Solomon. This verse speaks about public life: a leader's strength depends on those who follow him. Some read it as a simple political observation; others see a reminder that a ruler must care for his people. The verses around it speak of the fear of God, calm, and self-control.

For today: if you lead in your home, your work, or your church, your true strength lies in the people you look after. Treat them with respect, patience, and service, not as a means to your own prestige.
exp.1:12:
The explanation says that certain people abandon the paths of uprightness, that is, the straight and just ways, to walk in the ways of darkness, meaning dark roads where evil hides. The verse's wording of "paths" is the key image here: it refers to the course of life a person follows. It is a choice: they leave what is good for what is dark.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs, which is traditionally attributed largely to Solomon. In this chapter he explains that wisdom and good counsel protect the young person from wicked men. The verse describes what those men are like, whom the son should avoid.

For today: be careful about who you walk with and what influences you accept. If an environment or friendship gradually pulls you away from what is right, take it seriously. Ask God for wisdom and seek counsel from people of integrity before you decide.
exp.21:22:
It says that God himself will defend the poor and afflicted in judgment. "Will plead their cause" means he will take up their case as their advocate. "Spoil the soul of those that spoiled them" means he will take the life, or what is most precious, from those who took away their goods. The idea is that God repays in the same measure the one who abuses the weak.

It is part of the proverbs of the wise, here attributed to the tradition of Solomon, which teach a young person to live justly. The verse before it forbids robbing the poor or mistreating them in the gate, the place in the city where judgments were made. This phrase gives the reason: no one who is weak is left without a defender, because God sees them.

For today: do not take advantage of someone who cannot defend themselves, such as an employee, a needy neighbor, or someone with little information. Be honest in payments, dealings, and contracts, and trust that God sees what no one else sees.
exp.19:17:
It says that plans are made firm and put in order when a person seeks advice, and that a war should be waged with good strategy. It is not about acting recklessly, but about thinking and preparing well.

The Book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although this particular saying does not say who spoke it. It sits among practical advice about prudence: not trusting too quickly, not gossiping, not deceiving. The verse ties these ideas together: a wise life is a life that is thought through and counseled.

Before making an important decision, such as a job, a loan, or a family conflict, seek the advice of wise and trustworthy people. Listen, make a plan, and pray. This way you avoid mistakes that later cost you dearly.
exp.24:26:
It says that, although honey is sweet and good, eating too much of it no longer does any good. The same goes for seeking honor for oneself: when it becomes an obsession, it stops being honorable. The second part is difficult in the original language, and some versions translate it differently, but the general idea is that every excess, even of good things, ends up doing harm.

It is a proverb of Solomon, copied and gathered by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah (Proverbs 25:1). It is practical wisdom for everyday life. The verses nearby speak of self-control: the next one compares a person who does not control himself to a city without walls.

Today we can enjoy God's gifts with gratitude and moderation. If you desire recognition, ask yourself whether you seek it out of love for others or only to make yourself great. Serving with humility and letting God honor you in his own time guards the heart.
exp.5:29:
It says that people do not look down on a thief who steals to satisfy his hunger, nor do they regard him as worthless. To "look down on" means to hold in low regard. The phrase "to satisfy his soul" means to relieve his hunger, and "to steal" means to take what belongs to another.

The text is part of a wise father's warnings to his son about adultery. Here he makes a comparison: if someone who steals out of hunger must still pay back seven times over (verse 31), then the one who commits adultery has far less excuse. The thief has a real need; the adulterer has only desire. Some interpreters also read the sentence as a question, but the overall meaning is the same.

For today: let us not justify our sins by saying "I could not help it." If even hunger does not erase guilt, a passing whim erases it even less. Let us flee from temptation in time.
exp.26:21:
Though you should grind a fool in a mortar among grain with a pestle, his foolishness would still not leave him. The imagery is strong: even the harshest punishment cannot, by itself, change someone who refuses to learn.

This is found in the Proverbs of Solomon, which were gathered by the men of Hezekiah (Prov. 25:1). It is wisdom in the form of short sayings. In the surrounding text, the point is that trials reveal what is in the heart. Here the fool is not someone who is slow-witted, but someone who rejects correction. It is exaggerated language meant to add emphasis.

For today: do not place your hope in changing others by force. Ask for humility for yourself, receive correction with an open heart, and with others give counsel in love, and pray, trusting that only God transforms the heart.
exp.7:33:
It says that the one who listens to wisdom and stays alert every day, like someone waiting by the entrance of a house, is happy and blessed. The word "blessed" in the verse means happy and favored. The idea of watching carefully means staying attentive and alert. The thresholds, the entryways, are the place where a person stands to wait.

The speaker is wisdom, who in Proverbs 8 appears as a figure calling people to listen to her. After inviting the sons of men to heed her counsel, she says that whoever seeks her steadily will find life and the favor of God. Many believers see here a foreshadowing of Christ, though this is an interpretation, not something the text states directly.

For today: set aside a fixed moment each day, even ten minutes, to read the Bible and pray, humbly expecting God to guide you in your decisions.
exp.25:7:
It says that giving honor to a fool is as absurd as tying a stone into a sling: if the stone is tied fast, it cannot be flung out, and the sling is useless. The word "tie" here means to bind, and a fool is a person who rejects wisdom and correction. Some scholars say the Hebrew of this verse is difficult and has been translated in other ways, but the central idea is the same: something is out of place.

This is the voice of a teacher of wisdom who teaches through comparisons. These proverbs (chapters 25 through 29) were gathered in the time of King Hezekiah, according to Proverbs 25:1. Here the teacher warns about what happens when someone is honored who does not deserve it.

Today, think about who you give a voice, authority, or applause to. Honor those who show humility, honesty, and a desire to learn, not only those who are popular or speak loudly.
exp.15:10:
This verse says that accurate scales and weights belong to God. "A just weight and balance" are instruments that measure truthfully. The weights of the bag were the stones a merchant carried in a bag to weigh money or goods. God considers them his work, meaning he cares that they are correct.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom, and here the voice of the wise teacher speaks. The verses around it speak of kings, justice, and truth. Many understand that if a ruler must be just, so must the trade of his people. It is said that God himself supports honesty in business.

For today: be honest in what you give, charge, and promise. Give the right measure, pay what was agreed, and do not cheat in small things. God also sees what no one else checks.
exp.5:21:
This verse says that the teachings of parents, mentioned just before, stay with us at all times. "When thou goest, it shall lead thee" means: they will guide you as you walk through life. "When thou sleepest, it shall keep thee" means that they protect you even while you rest. "When thou awakest, it shall talk with thee" shows that they will be the first thing on your mind when the day begins.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son in the book of Proverbs. Earlier he asked the son to keep his father's commands and his mother's teaching, binding them to the heart and tying them around the neck. Then he explains that they are like a lamp that gives light and that they protect from temptations such as immorality. His purpose is to guard the young man from harmful paths.

For today: at the start of the day, take a few minutes to remember a good teaching you have received, or to read the Bible, and ask God to guide you in your decisions.
exp.22:17:
It says that there truly is an "end," that is, an outcome or a future, and that the hope of the one who fears God will not be "cut off," meaning it will not be lost or come to nothing. The word "end" can be understood as a final result or as what lies ahead.

The one speaking is a wise father, or a teacher, advising his son. Earlier he told him not to envy sinners, who sometimes seem to prosper, but to live always in the fear of the LORD, that is, in respect and trust toward God. This verse gives the reason: what can be seen today is not the end of the story.

For today: when you feel envious seeing others do well without caring about what is right, remember that God looks at the long run. Keep doing what is just with patience, and trust that your hope in Him will not be left empty.
exp.13:23:
The explanation says that wisdom brings honor and blessing, like a crown for the one who lives it. In contrast, the foolishness of fools only produces more foolishness. "Foolishness" here is an old-fashioned word for silliness or madness, and some understand "riches" as material possessions while others understand it as wisdom itself, and both readings fit the book.

Proverbs is a collection of sayings of wisdom, largely attributed to Solomon, that teaches how to live uprightly. The nearby verses contrast good thinking, fruitful work, and empty talk. Here the result of a wise life is compared with that of a foolish one.

For today: value character more than money. Decide with prudence, work with steadiness, and listen to advice, because these simple choices, repeated each day, shape a life that is worth living.
exp.17:21:
This verse says that whoever finds a wife finds something good, and with it receives the favor or kindness of God. "Found" means discovered, and "obtained" means received, and the word "favor" refers to the kind and generous way God treats someone.

Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, to guide daily life. This saying sits among verses about the power of words and the value of relationships. It is a proverb, that is, a general truth and not a promise for every case. Some read it as praise of marriage, and others emphasize the wisdom of choosing well.

For today: if you are married, value your spouse as a gift from God and express your gratitude with words and deeds. If you are single, look for character and faith, not just appearance.
exp.29:0:
The explanation says that what follows are the words of a man named Agur, son of Jakeh. It calls them a "prophecy," which here can mean a serious message or a teaching received with weight from God. The man speaks to two people, Ithiel and Ucal. The word "unto" is an old form of "to."

About Agur, Jakeh, Ithiel and Ucal we know almost nothing. Scholars interpret them in several ways. Some think they were disciples, and others believe some of the names carry a symbolic meaning. What we do see is that Agur presents himself as a humble teacher, and in the verses that follow he acknowledges that he does not regard himself as wise.

For today: before teaching or advising others, begin with humility. If you recognize that you need to learn from God, your words will carry more honesty and more value for those who listen to you.
exp.12:11:
This verse says that when a person waits a long time for something and it does not come, the heart grows sick with sadness. "Hope deferred" is a wait that stretches on and on. "Torment" here means deep pain or discouragement. But when the longed-for thing finally comes about, it brings life and joy, like a tree of life, a picture of freshness and fullness.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here it does not speak of one specific event, but of a truth about life, placed among sayings about pride, work, the word of God, and wisdom. Some think the "desire" is any good longing; others see it in a more spiritual sense.

Today, if you are waiting for something and you grow weary, do not be ashamed of your pain. Tell God honestly about it, and seek the support of someone you trust while you wait.
exp.16:5:
It says that grandchildren are like a crown for grandparents, that is, a source of pride, joy and honor in old age. It also says that parents are the honor, or the source of dignity, of their children. The crown was a symbol of honor and of a life well lived. There is a blessing that flows in two directions: from children toward their elders, and from parents toward their children.

This text is in Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, and consists of wise counsel for daily life. Around it are warnings about lying, mockery and wickedness. This verse offers a contrast: in place of what destroys relationships, it shows the beauty of a family bound together across generations.

Today we can value our grandparents and elders by listening to them and giving them our time. And if we are parents, we can live with integrity, so that our children can feel honored by us.
exp.26:5:
The verse says that the wounds caused by someone who loves us are faithful and trustworthy, while the kisses of someone who hates us are deceitful. "Faithful" means loyal, dependable. "Abundant" here means plentiful or excessive, according to many translations; the Hebrew term is uncommon and some read it as "deceitful."

This is a proverb from Hebrew wisdom literature, attributed to Solomon in this section of the book. It comes right after saying that "open rebuke is better than hidden love." The teacher compares sincere correction with false affection or with love that is never expressed, and shows which of the two does us more good.

For today: value the people who dare to tell you the truth with respect, even when it hurts. Before you take offense, ask yourself whether they are doing it out of love. And when you must correct someone, do it with humility, seeking their good and not your own release of frustration.
exp.2:3:
This verse promises that whoever lives with mercy and truth will be well regarded by God and by people. "Favor" here means goodwill or esteem, and "good name" means a good reputation or good judgment, that is, being valued as a person of integrity. Other versions render it as "favor and good understanding."

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son, in the style of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon. The verse before it speaks of not letting mercy and truth depart from you. It is then followed by an invitation to trust in God. Proverbs describe what usually happens; they are not absolute promises, since sometimes good people are rejected.

For today: practice kindness and honesty at work and at home, without seeking applause. If someone misunderstands you, trust that God sees your heart.
exp.11:23:
It says that hardworking and steady people will come to hold authority and responsibility, while laziness ends in servitude. The "diligent" are those who work with effort and care. The phrase about ruling means that someone will govern or have dominion. "Negligence" is carelessness or idleness, and the word about tribute means that a person will have to pay or serve others, like someone obliged to work for a master.

This verse is found in Proverbs, a collection of wisdom that tradition attributes largely to Solomon, although not every saying can be dated with certainty. They are counsel from a teacher of wisdom to those who want to live well. Around it there are contrasts between truth and lies, wisdom and foolishness, and this verse adds the contrast between diligence and laziness. It is a general principle, not a promise that always works out the same way.

For today: choose a task you have been putting off and do it steadily this week, offering your effort to God. Small faithful steps often open doors of trust and responsibility.
exp.16:13:
Starting a fight is like opening a floodgate: at first only a little water comes out, but soon no one can stop it. That is why the advice is to drop the dispute in time.

It is a proverb within the collection attributed to Solomon (Proverbs 10 through 22). It is wisdom given in short sayings for anyone who wants to live with good judgment. The verses nearby speak of the fool, of evil repaid for good, and of justice, so the theme is how foolishness and contention harm relationships and homes.

Today: before you answer in anger in a family, work, or social media argument, pause. If you see it growing, step away, lower your voice, or postpone the conversation. Stopping early prevents wounds that later take a long time to heal.
exp.7:27:
This verse says that when God set the heavens firm above, and when he gave strength to the fountains of the deep (the deep waters beneath the earth), wisdom was already there.

The one speaking is Wisdom, who in Proverbs 8 is presented as a person who calls people to listen. She says that she existed before creation and was beside God when everything was put in order. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, though others understand her as God's wisdom personified in a poetic way.

For today: if God ordered the whole universe with wisdom, he can also guide your life. Before making an important decision, ask God for wisdom with humility and seek his Word.
exp.19:9:
This verse says that God is repulsed by cheating in business.

Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, and here it speaks like a teacher advising his people. Before this, it speaks of the king who judges and of how hard it is to say that one has a completely clean heart. Afterward, it says that even a child is known by his actions. In this way, honesty in the marketplace reveals what the heart is like.

For today: be fair in what you charge, pay, promise, and measure. Do not use one standard for others and another for yourself, whether in business or at work.
exp.0:10:
This verse describes the invitation of wicked people: "Come with us." They want to set ambushes to kill, and to lie in wait without cause for the innocent, that is, to spy on and attack someone who has done nothing wrong. Ambushes are traps or hidden plans.

Here a wise father speaks to his son. In the verse before, he warns him not to give in when sinners try to deceive him. This is an example of that temptation: a group that invites you to join their violence with the promise of easy gain, as the verses that follow show.

For today: evil almost always comes as a friendly invitation. Before joining a group or a business, ask yourself whether someone will be hurt. If the answer is yes, say no, even if it costs you a friendship.
exp.8:1:
It says that wisdom prepares a complete banquet for her guests. The verse says "She hath killed her beasts," so the animals she slaughtered for the meal are the ones in view. "Mingled her wine" means that she mixed the wine, probably with water or spices, to leave it ready to drink. "Furnished her table" means that everything was set in order to receive the people.

In Proverbs 9, wisdom is presented as a woman who builds her house and invites everyone. She speaks to call the simple and those who lack understanding. Her invitation contrasts with that of the foolish woman, who appears later in the same chapter. Some scholars see the seven pillars as an image of fullness, although their exact meaning is interpreted in several ways.

For today: wisdom is not imposed, it is offered with generosity. We can accept her invitation by setting aside time each day to read the Bible and pray, and by asking advice from sensible people, instead of deciding everything in a rush.
exp.15:9:
This proverb says that the king speaks with an almost divine authority, as if his words were an inspired decision. The word for "divine sentence" here is not witchcraft but a judgment or decision with special weight. And "his mouth transgresseth not in judgment" means that he must not twist justice or fail in his duty when he judges.

The book of Proverbs gathers the traditional wisdom of Israel, associated with Solomon. Here the sage speaks of the ideal king, and the verses nearby speak of justice, honest scales, and thrones established in righteousness. Some think it describes what the king should be, not what he always is. Real kings did fail.

For today: if you have some authority, at home, at work, or in the church, your words carry weight. Speak with truth, decide with justice, and do not favor anyone out of convenience. And if you have no authority, pray for those who govern.
exp.11:11:
The wicked man desires the gains that evil people gain by trapping others with tricks and deceit. In contrast, the root of the righteous produces fruit: their life, though it uses no tricks, is well rooted and yields something good and lasting.

Some scholars understand the text a little differently, because the original is brief and can be translated in several ways.

These words are part of the Proverbs of Solomon, a collection of wisdom to guide people in everyday life. Here the one who seeks profit by crooked paths is contrasted with the one who lives with integrity, as in the nearby verses about honest work and a sincere mouth.
