For today: do not envy the dishonest shortcuts of others. Put down roots with honesty, steady work, and truth, and trust that God will make fruit grow in its time.
exp.13:3:
This proverb compares two situations. If there are no oxen, the stable stays clean, with no manure and no mess. But without oxen there is also no good harvest. The strength of the ox, which plowed and carried loads, produces an abundance of bread. The word for the stable here can refer to the place where grain was kept or to a feeding trough, and some understand it one way and others another way.

The book of Proverbs gathers practical wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon. Here it does not speak of God directly, but of everyday life. The verses around it contrast the wise person with the fool, and this proverb shows that what is valuable usually also brings work and complications.

For today: if you want fruit in your family, your work, your church, or your service, prepare yourself for some disorder and effort. A life without trouble may be clean, but it is also empty of fruit.
exp.17:4:
This verse says it is not good to show favoritism to the wicked or give them special treatment, especially when that causes a righteous person to lose what is rightly theirs.

The phrase "to accept the person of the wicked" means showing favoritism. The "wicked" are those who live without fear of God. "What is rightly theirs" refers to the justice the righteous person deserves, for example in a court case.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings. Here the verse is attributed to Solomon, although the book has several authors. The verses nearby speak of words, of lawsuits, and of foolishness. It is likely that this saying has in mind judges or people in authority who allow themselves to be swayed by power or money. The Law of Moses also forbade twisting justice (Leviticus 19:15).

Today we can apply it this way: when you must give an opinion, make a decision, or judge something, whether at work, in the family, or in the church, do not let yourself be carried along by influence or sympathy. Seek the truth and defend the one who is in the right.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that wisdom begins when a person acknowledges God with respect and reverence. The phrase "fear of the Lord" does not mean living in terror, but honoring Him, trusting Him, and taking Him seriously. "Fools" are those who refuse to learn. They despise both wisdom and instruction, that is, correction and teaching.

Proverbs is attributed largely to Solomon, and here he speaks like a father instructing his son. The verses before this one say that the wise person listens and keeps growing. This verse works as a motto for the whole book: before learning to live well, one must humbly place oneself before God. Then comes the invitation to listen to one's parents.

For today: before deciding something important, pray and ask yourself whether you are willing to listen to God and to those who correct you with love. A humble attitude is the first step toward learning.
exp.7:34:
The explanation says that whoever finds wisdom finds true life, and also receives God's approval and affection.

In this chapter, Wisdom speaks, presented as a person who calls out to people in the streets and at the city gates. Her purpose is to invite young people to listen to her and not to despise her advice. The next verse shows the contrast: whoever rejects her harms himself. Some Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, although the text is mainly about the wisdom of God.

Today we can seek wisdom every day, like someone waiting beside a doorway. For example, set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible and pray before making important decisions.
exp.22:8:
Speak not in the ears of a fool: that is, do not spend your wise words on someone who refuses to learn or to listen. The phrase "in the ears of" means "in front of" or "so that he hears it." The word "despise" means that he will look down on your words and treat them as worthless. "The wisdom of thy words" refers to how sensible what you say is.

This proverb belongs to the "words of the wise" in Proverbs. It is a piece of wise counsel, like a teacher speaking to a student. Just before it, the text speaks of a stingy host who invites you to eat, but without sincerity. The point here is that some people have closed hearts, and speaking to them too much only brings contempt and wears you out.

For today: before you give advice, notice whether the other person is willing to listen. If they mock or argue without wanting to understand, it is better to keep silent in peace, pray for them, and save your words for someone who will receive them.
exp.7:25:
This verse says that Wisdom already existed before God made the earth. The "open fields" are the wide, open country, and "the first of the dust of the world" refers to the earliest materials of the earth, the substance from which everything began.

In Proverbs 8, Wisdom speaks, presented as a person who invites people to listen to her. Here she explains that she is older than creation and was present when God set it in order. Many Christians see in this an image of Christ, the wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24). Others understand it as divine wisdom personified. Both readings emphasize that she is valuable and trustworthy.

For today: before making an important decision, ask God for wisdom in prayer and seek his guidance in the Bible. The one who created all things knows the best path.
exp.15:23:
The verse says that pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healthy for the body. "Pleasant words" are words spoken with kindness and grace. "Soul" refers to the whole person, including their feelings and their spirit. "Bones" stands for the body and inner strength. So sweet words both lift the spirit and strengthen.

Proverbs is a collection of teachings on wisdom, largely attributed to Solomon. Here the context speaks of the wise person who controls his mouth and teaches with prudence. The wise heart produces words that build others up. It is practical advice for everyday life, given to shape sensible people.

Today, before you answer someone in anger or weariness, pause and look for a kind and truthful phrase. It can be an encouragement, a word of thanks, or a correction spoken with respect. Your words can be medicine for others.
exp.9:3:
The explanation says that the careless and lazy person ends up in poverty, while the diligent person, that is, the one who works with effort and steadiness, generally prospers. "Slack" means lazy or careless. "Maketh rich" does not necessarily speak of being a millionaire, but of having what is needed and something more.

This is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the chapter, addressed to those who seek wisdom for living. It stands among verses that contrast the righteous and the wicked, and next to another that praises the one who gathers the harvest in time. It is a general principle, not an absolute promise: other proverbs recognize that there are poor people because of injustice or because of circumstances beyond their control.

For today: choose a task you have been putting off, at work, in your studies, or at home, and do it today with dedication, as one who serves God.
exp.8:4:
Here Wisdom, presented as a woman who has prepared a banquet, invites everyone to sit at her table. The word for "mingled" means mixed with water or spices, so the wine is already ready to be served. "Come" and "eat" are kind commands, like saying "come and eat."

The one speaking is Wisdom personified. In the verses before, she sent her servants to call out from the highest parts of the city, so that everyone could hear. She invites the simple, inexperienced people without judgment, so that they will leave behind their foolishness and live. This is contrasted with the foolish woman of the same chapter, who also invites, but toward a path of death.

For today: accept God's invitation to learn. Set aside a moment each day to read the Bible with humility, and ask God to correct you and guide you in your decisions.
exp.2:17:
This verse says that wisdom is like a tree of life to those who embrace it. "Lay hold upon" means to take firm hold of it, to grip it. "Happy" means blessed, or content. And "retaineth" means to keep it, not to let it go. So the happy person is the one who holds on to wisdom and does not let it slip away.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as in the whole opening of Proverbs. In this chapter wisdom is presented almost as a person who offers long life, honor and peace. The phrase "tree of life" recalls the garden of Eden, and many understand it to point to a full and blessed life. The verses that follow say that God himself created the world with wisdom.

For today: admiring wisdom is not enough; we must hold on to it. Set aside a few minutes each day to read the Bible, and ask God for direction before you make decisions.
exp.19:22:
This verse says that deception in buying and selling is detestable to God. "Abomination" means something God firmly rejects. The "divers weights" were two sets of weights: a heavier one for buying and a lighter one for selling, so the merchant gained more than he should. The "false balance" is the rigged scale. The verse says it "is not good": it is unjust.

This text is in Proverbs, a collection of wisdom attributed largely to Solomon. Here a teacher of wisdom instructs about everyday life. The verse before it speaks of riches gained in haste and of not taking revenge, but of waiting on God. Everything points toward trusting that God is just and sees our dealings.

Today almost no one uses weights, but we can still deceive: charging too much, giving less than what was promised, lying about a price or about hours worked. Let us ask God to be honest even in small things, because it matters to Him.
exp.23:18:
This verse advises not to get involved with wicked people or to envy what they have. "Fret" here means not to get worked up, upset, or angry because of them; some translations say "do not be irritated because of the wicked." "Malignant" and "impious" refer to people who live with their backs turned to God.

These words are part of the sayings of the wise in Proverbs, where a father or teacher gives advice to his son. The verses next to it explain the reason: the wicked person has no good future, and his light, like a candle, will go out. So his apparent success does not last.

For today: when you see someone doing well through cheating or wrongdoing, do not spend your heart on envy or anger. Instead, do what is right with patience and trust that God sees everything and is just.
exp.17:12:
It says that whoever answers before listening carefully acts foolishly and brings shame on himself. "Folly" means foolishness or a lack of good judgment, and "shame" here is public disgrace or humiliation. Answering in a hurry, without having understood, shows little wisdom.

This verse is in the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although this particular section does not say who wrote it. These are short sayings for living sensibly. Nearby, the book speaks about pride and about seeking knowledge, and the verse that follows praises the ear that seeks to know. Listening is part of wisdom.

For today: in a difficult conversation, at home, at work, or on social media, wait a moment. Listen until the end, ask a question if something was not clear to you, and then respond with calm.
exp.24:16:
It says not to visit your neighbor's house too often. The first sentence, "Detén tu pie," means "don't go over there so much" (rewritten here: "Withdraw thy foot" becomes simply "withdraw your foot," so the phrase is kept as the verse wording). If you become a constant visitor, your neighbor may end up without any desire to see you.

This is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon and gathered in this section by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). The verse before it speaks of honey: eat enough to be satisfied, so that you do not become sickened by it. The neighbor is like that honey. Good things, in excess, wear us out. The proverb teaches moderation in relationships.

For today: value your friends and neighbors by giving them space. Let them know before you visit, notice whether the person is tired or busy, and do not take advantage of their hospitality. In this way you care for affection and mutual respect.
exp.2:32:
This verse says that God places his curse, that is, his disapproval and his judgment, on the house of the one who lives without respecting him. On the other hand, he blesses the dwelling of the righteous, those who live uprightly. "Lord" is the name of God, and "wicked" describes someone who lives without taking God into account.

Proverbs is wisdom that a father passes on to his son. Before this, the wise teacher warns him not to envy the unjust person or imitate his ways, because that person may seem to prosper. This verse shows the full picture: the proverbs describe how God usually acts; they are not automatic promises for every case, and the Bible itself acknowledges that sometimes the righteous suffer.

For today: when you see someone prospering through dishonest means, do not envy them or copy them. Choose to be honest in your work and in your home, and trust that God cares for those who follow him, even though his blessing is not always wealth.
exp.16:4:
It says that mocking the poor is an offense against God, who made them. Words like "mocketh" and "reproacheth" in the verse above carry the sense of the explanation: to mock with contempt, to insult or disgrace someone. "Maker" in the verse is the Creator. It also warns that rejoicing when someone else suffers will not go unpunished; the verse's "calamities" are disasters or tragedies.

This belongs to the book of Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here the teacher speaks like a father to his children. The nearby verses speak of lying, of hearts tested by God, and of family. It teaches that God looks at the heart and that poverty does not take away anyone's worth, because all of us are his handiwork.

Today we can guard our words and jokes about those who have less, and avoid enjoying gossip about other people's falls. Better to offer respect, concrete help, or a sincere prayer for someone who is suffering.
exp.7:9:
It says that instruction is worth more than having money. "Receive" means "accept" or "take in." "Knowledge" here is not modern science, but correct understanding and insight. "Choice gold" refers to gold of the highest quality, the purest. The idea is to choose instruction first and then riches.

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a woman who calls out loudly to the people (Proverbs 8:1-4). She affirms that her words are just, upright, and without deceit. For this reason she asks that they listen to her and prefer her. In the next verse she goes on to say that she is worth more than precious stones.

For today: before making an important decision, such as a job or a business, ask yourself not only how much you will earn, but what is right and what teaching from God guides you. Set aside time to read the Bible and to ask for direction.
exp.5:30:
It says that if the thief is caught, he must pay back seven times what he stole. The phrase "seven times over" is what the verse means by that. He might even have to hand over everything he has in his house. "Substance" means goods or wealth. In other words, theft carries a very high price.

Here a wise father speaks to his son in the book of Proverbs. He compares the thief with adultery. People understand a hungry thief a little, but he must still pay. With adultery there is no excuse, and the consequences are more serious. Some scholars point out that Moses' law did not always require seven times, so the number may be a way of speaking about full and severe repayment.

For today: do not fool yourself into thinking that a bad decision will come cheap. Before giving in to a desire, think about what you could lose: your family, your peace, and your witness. Ask God for self-control.
exp.2:15:
This verse presents wisdom as a person who carries gifts in her hands. In her right hand she brings "length of days," that is, a long life. In her left hand she brings riches and honour, which are possessions and a good reputation.

The speaker is a wise father teaching his son (this is clear throughout the chapter). He wants the young man to value wisdom above silver and gold. It is poetic language: Proverbs gives general principles, not automatic promises. Other passages in the Bible show that sometimes the righteous suffer or have little.

For today: before seeking success or money, ask God for wisdom to decide well. Practice honesty, patience, and good treatment of others at your work and at home. This usually brings stability and a good name, and it is worth more than any quick gain.
exp.4:4:
She says that the path of the "strange" woman (the woman who seduces and leads into unfaithfulness) goes straight toward death. "Her feet go down" shows a descent that does not stop. "Her steps take hold on the grave" means that each step she takes follows her and brings her closer to the tomb.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs. Earlier, verse 3 explains that the words of this woman seem sweet as honey, but the end is bitter. This verse explains why. Some understand the "death" as a real ruin; others understand it also as spiritual death.

For today: do not let yourself be guided by what looks attractive at the start. Before making a decision, ask yourself where it leads. Flee from temptations that promise pleasure but destroy your life and your relationships.
exp.8:17:
He does not realize that she is taking him to the place of the dead. It looks like a feast, but in reality it is a place of death. The phrase "her guests" refers to the people she has invited, and "the depths of the grave" is a poetic way of speaking of Sheol, the place of the dead.

Proverbs 9 presents two invitations: that of Wisdom, which offers life, and that of the foolish woman, which offers hidden pleasure. Here the teacher speaks, warning young people who lack experience. The chapter closes by showing the end of the one who chooses the easy and forbidden path.

For today: before accepting a temptation that looks sweet and secret, ask yourself where it ends. What is hidden usually destroys. Seek the voice of God's wisdom and trustworthy people who can help you decide well.
exp.20:25:
He spends all day long craving more and more, always wanting to have. The righteous person, by contrast, gives generously and does not keep everything for himself. The word "coveteth" means to desire eagerly what one does not have. "Spareth not" means that he does not hold back or hoard; he gives without keeping anything back for himself.

The book of Proverbs is wisdom gathered into short sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. No specific historical moment is given here. The nearby verses speak of the sluggard, whose desire kills him because he does not want to work. So this saying contrasts the greedy sluggard with the diligent righteous person, who has something to share. Some read it this way, although the text does not fully explain it.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we live always wanting more or are thankful for what we have. A good practice is to work honestly and set something aside each week to help someone in need.
exp.2:5:
It says we should acknowledge God, that is, keep him in mind and count on him, in everything we do. If we do, he will make our paths straight, meaning he will make our ways right and guide us. A "way" here means the manner of living and the choices of each day.

The book of Proverbs is traditionally attributed to Solomon, and this chapter sounds like a father advising his son. Earlier he asks him to trust the Lord with all his heart and not lean on his own understanding. Then he warns him not to think himself wise in his own eyes. The counsel aims to protect the young man from deciding alone and without direction.

Before a decision, whether big or small, take a moment to pray and ask God for direction. Then act with humility, open to advice and to changing course.
exp.27:12:
This verse says that whoever hides their sins will not find true success. But whoever acknowledges them before God and stops practicing them will receive mercy, that is, compassion and forgiveness. The word "covereth" means to cover up or conceal. "Prosper" speaks of getting ahead in a good way, and "forsaketh" means turning away from sin and leaving it behind.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom teachings, and this chapter is traditionally attributed to Solomon, although scholars debate how these sayings were gathered. The context speaks of the righteous and the wicked, of humility, and of unjust rulers. The verse shows that true wisdom includes being honest with God and with ourselves.

Today, if there is something you are hiding, bring it before God with honesty. Ask for forgiveness and take a concrete step to change. If the sin affected someone else, seek to be reconciled with that person as well.
exp.10:7:
This verse says that God rescues the righteous person when distress comes upon him, and that the wicked person ends up falling into that same distress. The word "trouble" in the verse means a tight spot, danger, or suffering. The "wicked" is the one who lives without reverence for God. The phrase "cometh in his stead" means that the evil person takes the place of the one who was delivered.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, attributed largely to Solomon. Here the teacher speaks like a father instructing his children. The nearby verses speak of the justice that delivers and of the wickedness that traps. It is a general principle of life, not a promise that the righteous will never suffer. Other passages, such as Job, remind us that there are exceptions.

For today: do what is right even when it costs you, and trust that God cares for you. Do not rejoice when the wicked suffer; rather, pray for them and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.26:12:
It says that if someone has become surety for a stranger, that is, has committed himself to pay another person's debt, his garment should be taken as security. And if he did so for a strange (or foreign) woman, a pledge should be taken from him. "Surety" means he answered for another, and "pledge" is an article kept until the debt is paid. The saying is harsh, and some understand it as an ironic piece of advice.

It is a proverb of Solomon, a father instructing his son. It comes after a request for wisdom and praise for the prudent person who sees danger and steps aside. Here the danger is rash suretyship. Scholars debate whether "the strange woman" refers to an outsider or to a woman of bad reputation; the general sense is the same: vouching for strangers is risky.

Before you sign as a guarantor or lend your name to someone you do not know well, think about the consequences. Helping others is good, but do it with prudence and without putting your family at risk.
exp.13:9:
This verse says that each person knows their own inner pain better than anyone else. "Bitterness" here refers to deep sorrow, and "soul" refers to the innermost part of a person. It also says that a stranger, that is, someone who is not close, cannot fully share in another's joy. There are things in the heart that no one else can fully understand.

This is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Here a teacher speaks who observes life. It stands among a series of sayings about the wise and the foolish, and about the straight path and the deceitful one. It seems to remind us that the inner life is complex and that we should not judge others only by what we see on the outside.

For today: be patient and humble with others, because you do not know what they carry inside. And bring your deepest sorrows and joys to God, for He knows your heart completely.
exp.24:11:
The explanation says that a correction given with wisdom is as valuable as a gold jewel. An earring is a piece of jewelry worn on the ear, and an ornament is a small decorative piece of jewelry. A receptive ear is that of someone who listens and accepts counsel. Thus, a reproof serves as an adornment to the one who knows how to receive it.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, attributed in this section to Solomon, although the text says it was copied by the men of Hezekiah (25:1). It comes after another saying about a word spoken at the right time and before comparisons about the faithful messenger. The whole passage speaks of the value of well-spoken words and of words well received.

Today, when someone corrects you respectfully, try to listen without becoming defensive. Ask yourself: "What can I learn from this?" And when you need to correct someone, do it with humility and at the right moment.
exp.22:10:
This verse says that orphans have a powerful defender. "The Mighty One" is one way of naming God. Here the Bible text uses a word meaning the protective relative who stands up for a family member who has no resources, and so the verse presents God in that role. "He shall plead their cause against you" means that God himself will take up their case in court and stand against anyone who mistreats them.

This is a proverb of wisdom, partly attributed to Solomon, addressed to a young person learning to live justly. The verse before it forbids moving the ancient boundary marker, the stone that marked the edge of a piece of land, and taking the inheritance of orphans. Whoever has no one to protect them is not alone, because God cares for them.

Today, we can deal honestly with those who have less power than we do: not taking advantage of them in business, work, or inheritances, and helping to defend children and the vulnerable.
exp.9:4:
This proverb compares two people. "Summer" is the season of heat when the crops ripen. "Harvest" is the gathering of the crops. "Shameful" means that it brings disgrace. The one who gathers the harvest in its time shows good judgment; the one who falls asleep when he should be working brings shame on himself.

It is a proverb from Israel's wisdom tradition, attributed in large part to Solomon. A wisdom teacher speaks to young people, using the life of the field, which everyone knew. The nearby verses contrast the diligent with the lazy and the righteous with the wicked, showing that wisdom is lived out in everyday life.

For today: there are moments that do not come back, such as a job opportunity, a time to study, or a chance to care for family. Ask God for wisdom and act in time, without putting off until tomorrow what needs to be done today.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that when someone follows wisdom, they walk through life with security and do not fall. "Then" points to the result of what came before. "Safely" means with calm and without fear. "Your foot shall not stumble" is an image: you will not hurt yourself through falls along the way.

The one speaking is a wise father teaching his son, within the book of Proverbs. Earlier he asked him to keep "the law and the counsel," that is, the teaching and good judgment. Then he promises peace when sleeping and protection from fear. This is the language of wisdom: it describes what usually happens, not a guarantee that there will never be problems.

For today: before deciding something important, stop to pray and seek the counsel of the Bible. Obeying step by step gives you more firmness and peace on the way.
exp.18:17:
Correct your son while there is still hope, that is, while he is still in time to learn. Here "chasten" means to discipline and correct. And "let not thy soul spare" means not to let yourself be carried away by anger to the point of harming him. The end of the verse can be understood in other ways, but the general idea is that correction must not become destructive.

This proverb belongs to the wisdom of Israel, attributed in large part to Solomon. It is advice from father to son, and it seeks to shape character. The verses around it speak of anger and of accepting correction.

For today: correct with firmness and in time, but never in anger. If you are very angry, wait, breathe, and speak afterward with calm, so that your son feels your love and not your revenge.
exp.2:33:
It says that God responds according to each person's attitude. To "scorn" means to mock with contempt. Those who mock God and others find that God himself gives them what they deserve. By contrast, "the lowly," that is, those who do not think themselves superior and recognize their need, receive God's favor, the kindness and goodwill of God that they have not earned.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom teachings, attributed largely to Solomon, that speaks like a father to his son. In this chapter, the teacher contrasts two paths: that of the wicked, whom God rejects, and that of the upright, who live near God. This verse sums up that difference. The New Testament quotes it in James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5.

Today, when someone corrects you or argues against you, before mocking or defending yourself, pause and ask yourself: "What can I learn here?" Asking God for a humble heart opens the door to his help.
exp.13:29:
This proverb says that a calm and peaceful heart gives health and life to the body, while envy slowly destroys a person from within. "Flesh" refers to the whole body. The phrase "rottenness of the bones" is a strong image: envy is like a sickness that weakens the deepest part of the person.

Proverbs is a collection of teachings on wisdom, and tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon. Here the text speaks of themes such as self-control, temperament, and fair treatment of others. The verse contrasts the person who has serenity, who is slow to anger, with the one who gives way to inner passions.

For today: when you notice yourself comparing yourself to someone and feeling bitterness, stop and thank God for something specific you do have. Ask him for a peaceful heart, and try to sincerely rejoice in the good of others. That cares for your soul and for your health as well.
exp.8:6:
It says that if someone tries to correct a scorner (a mocking person who laughs at wisdom and rejects all advice), they will receive insults and disgrace in return.

In Proverbs 9, Wisdom invites the simple to her banquet so that they will leave behind their foolishness and live. But the passage also warns that not everyone receives teaching well. The proverb appears between the invitation and the contrast between the wise person and the mocker: the wise person welcomes correction, while the scorner responds with hatred.

For today: before correcting someone, look at their attitude. If there is humility, speak with love and clarity. If there is only mockery and rejection, do not argue endlessly; pray, set a good example, and leave the door open. Jesus also spoke about not throwing what is holy to the dogs (Matthew 7:6), though this is interpreted with care.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that wisdom helps us escape the "strange woman," that is, a woman who belongs to someone else, someone who is not your wife. She "flatters with her words": she uses sweet phrases and flattery to draw you in and deceive you. Rescuing you means saving you or keeping you safe.

The one speaking is a wise father teaching his son. Earlier he spoke of men on crooked paths, and now he warns of another danger: seduction. The verses that follow say this woman abandoned the marriage vow she made and forgot the covenant of her God. Some scholars think it refers to a particular adulterous woman, and others think it also symbolizes any temptation that pulls us away from God.

Today, be wary of smooth words that aim to lead you toward something you know is wrong. Ask God for wisdom, guard your boundaries in friendships and online, and flee quickly from anything that could destroy your faithfulness.
exp.21:28:
Says that whoever works with earnestness and dedication ends up standing out. The word "diligent" in the verse means careful, attentive, and quick to do a task well. The phrase about standing before kings means he will serve important people. The words "mean men" refer to people of low standing or no reputation, so the diligent person will not always remain unnoticed.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon, though this section is related to the "words of the wise." It is a counsel of wisdom, not an absolute promise. The verses before it speak of debts and of respecting property boundaries, that is, of living with honesty and responsibility.

Do your work with excellence, even when no one is watching or when it seems small. Do not do it only to get ahead, but as service to God and to others. Over time, consistency often opens doors, though God decides how and when.
exp.14:32:
It says that revering God with awe and love is the school where one learns to live wisely. The phrase "fear of the Lord" does not mean living frightened, but taking God seriously and trusting Him. "Instruction of wisdom" means teaching or discipline that shapes a person. It also says that before receiving honour, that is, recognition or respect, comes humility.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition attributes largely to Solomon, though it contains other collections as well. Here the sage speaks like a father or teacher. The verses before this one speak of accepting correction. This verse closes that idea: whoever allows themselves to be taught shows that they fear God, and that humble attitude comes before what is good.

For today: the next time someone corrects you, listen first without defending yourself. Ask God for a heart willing to learn, and consider what you can improve.
exp.26:25:
It says that the lambs provide wool for making clothing, and that the goats can be sold to pay for a field. Here "the price of the field" means the money to buy or maintain the land. The following verses add that the goats' milk will feed the family and the servants.

These are proverbs of Solomon, later gathered together in the time of King Hezekiah. The counsel comes after a warning that riches do not last forever. For that reason it encourages people to care diligently for what they have: knowing the state of the flock well and attending to the animals. It was very practical advice for a society of shepherds and farmers.

For today: let us not trust that money will last on its own. Let us faithfully care for our work, our savings, and what God has given us, managing it wisely so that it is enough for the family and to help others.
exp.16:10:
This verse says that a rebellious person is only looking for trouble, that is, problems, conflicts and disobedience. Because of this, someone harsh and without compassion will be sent against them to punish them. "Cruel messenger" can be understood as a messenger sent by the king or as the severe consequences that come on their own. Scholars interpret it in different ways.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although it cannot be said that he wrote every saying. Here the wise person, who learns from a rebuke, is contrasted with the fool, who does not change even after a hundred blows. The rebel, who rejects all correction, ends up facing a harsher discipline.

For today: when someone corrects you with respect, listen with humility before life corrects you more harshly. Ask God for a heart willing to learn.
exp.0:18:
The explanation says that the path of the person who lives given over to greed (an excessive desire to have more, even at the expense of others) ends badly. The word "ways" here means paths or ways of living. The word "takes" means to seize or take away. So greed seizes and destroys the life of the one who clings to it. Some understand "life" as life itself, others as the whole person.

The one speaking is a wise father or teacher warning his son. Earlier he has told him not to be carried along by those who invite him to steal by violence. These men think themselves clever, but they are setting their own trap. This verse closes that warning.

For today: before accepting an easy or doubtful gain, ask yourself what it will really cost you. Practice generosity and honesty, even if you earn less.
exp.3:3:
He taught me and said to me, "Let your heart hold fast to my words; keep my commands and you will live." Here "words" means the teachings, the things he said. "Hold fast" means to keep them firmly, to hold on to them. "Live" speaks of a full and good life, not merely of continuing to breathe.

The one speaking here is Solomon, who remembers what his father taught him when he was young (it is usually understood to be David, although the text does not give the name in this verse). Now Solomon repeats that teaching to his own children. It is advice passed from one generation to the next, born of affection and a desire to protect.

For today: it is not enough to hear good advice; we must keep it in our hearts. Choose one teaching from the Bible this week, review it each day, and look for a way to put it into practice in one specific decision.
exp.22:24:
This verse says that a person's parents can be filled with joy because of them. "Shall be glad" means they will be full of gladness, and "she that bare thee" is the mother, the one who gave you life. It is a wish and almost an invitation: that your way of living be a reason for happiness to those who raised you.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son in the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon, though the book gathers several collections. Before this verse, the father urges his son to buy the truth and wisdom, and says that the father of a righteous son rejoices. Afterward, he asks for his son's heart and warns him against paths that destroy.

For today: think about how your decisions, your honesty, and your character affect your family. Choose one wise decision today, and if your parents are no longer living or the relationship is difficult, seek to honor those who have guided you with gratitude and a good witness.
exp.2:23:
It says that someone who lives with wisdom can lie down without fear and rest peacefully. "When you lie down" means "when you go to bed." "You will lie down" is better rendered as "you will rest," that is, you will rest. "Sweet" here means a restful sleep, without startling awakenings.

This book gathers teachings of wisdom, and in these chapters a father speaks to his son. He asks him to hold on to wisdom and good judgment, and he promises a safer life. The verses that follow explain the basis of that calm: trusting in the LORD, who watches over the way. The proverbs express general principles, not absolute guarantees that there will never be trouble.

For today: before sleeping, hand your worries over to God in prayer. Also think about whether there is something you should put right, such as asking forgiveness or settling a debt, so that you can go to bed with a clear conscience.
exp.23:33:
The explanation says that poverty will come to the lazy person quickly and unavoidably. One who is passing through is someone who keeps moving forward without stopping, and arrives before anyone can stop him. A strong soldier is commonly understood as an armed fighter who attacks with force and cannot be resisted. Some scholars translate this as "an armed man," and other versions understand it that way too.

The one speaking is the wise man of Proverbs. He tells how he passed by the field of a lazy man and saw it full of thorns, with its wall broken down. He reflected on what he saw and drew a lesson: small neglect, repeated day after day, ends in need. That passage is a warning for anyone who leaves everything for later.

For today: look at which responsibility you have been putting off, whether it is your work, your finances, or the care of your family. Take one small, concrete step today, and repeat it with consistency. God blesses faithful effort.
exp.4:18:
It says the husband should find fullness and joy in his own wife. The comparison with the doe and the deer (animals of the field, symbols of tenderness and beauty) shows affection and admiration. The words "delight yourself" are not in the verse, so that sentence is removed. "Let her breasts satisfy you" and "at all times" speak of a constant joy, not a passing one. Some versions render the last phrase as "be ravished" or "be intoxicated" with her love.

Context: a wise father speaks to his son in the book of Proverbs. Shortly before, he has warned against the adulterous woman, and here he presents the alternative: a faithful and passionate marriage. The following verses remind that God sees all the ways of a man.

For today: cultivate affection in your marriage with concrete gestures. Today, for example, tell your spouse something you admire about that person, and avoid comparing them with others or with images you see on screens.
exp.20:27:
A false witness will come to ruin, but a person who listens carefully and reports what they truly heard and saw will keep their word firmly. The phrase "the man who hears" here means someone who gives an account of what they actually perceived. The word "what he declares" simply means what that person says. The end of the verse is difficult in the original, and some translations render it differently, but the general idea is clear: the lie falls and the truth endures.

This verse is found in Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings that tradition largely attributes to Solomon. Here wisdom is taught through contrasts between the wicked and the righteous. Nearby the text speaks of greed, wickedness, and the fact that no one can stand against God. Lying is a form of deception that sooner or later comes to light.

Today: before you tell something, listen well and make sure it is true. Speak honestly, even when it costs you, because truth brings lasting trust.
exp.4:3:
It says that what at first seems sweet ends up being very painful. The word translated "wormwood" refers to a very bitter plant, and it is used as an image of suffering. The phrase "twoedged sword" describes a sword that cuts on both sides, meaning it wounds without remedy. "Her end" refers to the final result of following that woman.

It is a wise father instructing his son, in the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon. He wants the young man to keep good judgment. Before this, he describes the words of the "strange woman" (a woman outside of marriage) as honey and oil: smooth and attractive. Here he warns about how that path ends.

For today: do not let yourself be guided only by what looks pleasant at first. Before making a decision, ask yourself where it leads in the end. When a temptation promises pleasure, think about its consequences and seek wise counsel.
exp.16:3:
This verse says that the wicked person pays attention to lips that speak evil, and that the liar gladly listens to a tongue that speaks ill of others. A wicked doer is one who acts unjustly or with bad intent. A tongue that tears down someone's good name, by criticizing, slandering, or ruining their reputation, is what the verse calls a naughty tongue. The verse shows that it is not only the gossiper who does harm: there is also the one who takes in and feeds on such words.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, which teach wisdom for daily life. Just before this, the text says that God tests the hearts, as fire tests gold. What we gladly listen to shows something of what is inside us.

For today: think about which gossip, news, or criticism you gladly listen to or pass along. If someone begins speaking badly about another person, you can change the subject or simply refuse to go along with it. Ask God for a heart that prefers truth and goodness.
exp.11:21:
God hates lying lips. "Abomination" means something He detests deeply. By contrast, those who "deal truly," that is, who act honestly and keep their word, are his "delight," meaning his joy and pleasure. "Jehovah" is the name of God.

This verse is part of Proverbs, sayings of wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, though not all scholars agree on every detail. A wise father teaches his son how to live well. The surrounding verses contrast the deceitful with the upright, and the foolish with the prudent. Truthfulness appears as part of a character that pleases God.

Today we can take care of our words in small things: not exaggerating, not making excuses with lies, and not promising what we will not keep. Telling the truth with love may cost us something, but it gives us peace and pleases God.
exp.3:7:
This verse tells us to give wisdom a very high place in our lives. Our reader's verse uses "Exalt her," which is the same idea as valuing her and holding her in high regard. If we do this, she will promote us, that is, she will raise us up and give us a good name. The phrase "she shall bring thee to honour" means that she will bring us respect. Embracing her speaks of holding on to her with affection, never letting her go.

In this chapter a father speaks, whom the text identifies with Solomon, who recalls the teachings he himself received and passes them on to his son. He personifies wisdom as someone beloved who cares for and protects. His goal is that the young man choose the good path from an early age.

For today: give wisdom real time. Before deciding something important, pray, read the Bible, and ask advice from mature people in the faith. Valuing wisdom in this way will help you decide better and live with integrity.
exp.9:19:
It says that what a just person says is very valuable, like silver of the finest quality, pure and clean. On the other hand, the understanding of the wicked, that is, their thoughts and way of thinking, is worth almost nothing. The word "choice" means select, of first quality. "But" is what the source uses here for the contrast.

The book of Proverbs gathers short wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, to teach people how to live well before God. In this passage much is said about the power of words. The verses before it warn against lying, slander and talking too much. This verse contrasts what comes out of an upright heart with the emptiness of a heart without God.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself whether your words encourage, teach or heal. Speaking little, with truth and kindness, makes your voice a treasure to those around you.
exp.14:19:
The wise son brings joy to his father, but the foolish man despises his mother. "Despises" means that he does not value or respect her. In the Bible, a "fool" is not someone who lacks intelligence, but someone who lives ignoring God and good advice.

This verse is part of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, a teacher of wisdom speaking to young people. The verses nearby speak of straight paths and fools, and of the importance of listening to advice. Here it shows how a son's wisdom or foolishness affects his family.

Today we can honor our parents or those who have cared for us, with respect, gratitude, and a call or visit, and by listening to their advice even when we do not always agree.
exp.1:16:
She leaves "the guide of her youth," that is, the companion or guide of her younger years, meaning her husband. She also forgets "the covenant of her God," which may refer to the marriage vow made before God or to God's covenant with Israel.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as in the whole book of Proverbs. He wants to warn him against the unfaithful woman who seduces with smooth words. Scholars agree that adultery is in view, though some also see an image of spiritual unfaithfulness. The verse shows that this woman breaks sacred promises, and for that reason her path leads to ruin.

For today: keep your promises, especially those of marriage. Flee from words or situations that invite you to betray your word, and ask God for help to be faithful.
exp.22:0:
It says that when you sit down to eat with an important person or someone in authority ("a certain ruler"), you should pay close attention to what is set before you. The words "sittest" and "consider" are older forms; today we would say "sit" and "consider" in this sense, as the verse reads: "When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee." It is a call to be careful and not to act without thinking.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings. Many are attributed to Solomon, although this passage belongs to a section of sayings from the wise and not everyone agrees on who wrote it. It is addressed to a young person who might be invited to a governor's table. The verses that follow suggest that such an invitation may hide hidden motives, and so it calls for self-control.

Before accepting a favor, an invitation, or an opportunity, ask yourself: "What lies behind this?" Keep calm, do not let desire carry you away, and guard your integrity.
exp.22:26:
This verse compares the immoral woman to a deep ditch and a narrow pit. A "harlot" is a woman who sells her body, and "the stranger" is another man's wife, someone one must not be involved with. The idea is that it is easy to fall and very hard to get out.

A wise father is speaking to his son. He has just pleaded, "Give me your heart, my son," meaning that the son should pay attention and obey. After that appeal, he warns about a danger that destroys life. The verses that follow describe it as a thief lying in wait, and then speak of the sorrows of those who are lost in vices.

For today: what seems attractive can trap us beyond escape. It is wise to set limits before we reach the edge: to guard what we look at, who we are alone with, and what conversations we have. Giving our heart to God protects us.
exp.12:13:
This verse says that the teaching of a wise person is like a spring, a fountain of fresh water that gives life. That instruction helps a person avoid falling into the snares of death, that is, the traps or dangers that lead to ruin. The word "law" here means teaching or instruction, not only rules.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, and it presents itself as advice from parents and teachers to those who want to live well. In the verses nearby, the one who despises the word and goes astray is contrasted with the one who respects the commandment and is rewarded. In this way, the wise person appears as someone who guides others along a safe path.

For today: seek counsel from wise people and from the Bible before deciding, especially in difficult matters. Listening in time can spare you from mistakes that cost dearly.
exp.27:14:
This verse compares a wicked ruler to two dangerous animals: a roaring lion and a hungry bear. It says that this is what the ungodly ruler is like, meaning the leader who has no fear of God, when he rules over a poor people who cannot defend themselves.

Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon; this chapter is usually placed among the sayings collected in the time of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). The verses nearby speak of confessing sin, fearing God, and rejecting greed. In this way, the author shows that power without humility or justice ends up devouring the weak.

For today: if you have some kind of authority, at home, at work, or in the church, use it to care for others and not to take advantage of them. And pray for those who govern, asking that they act with justice and compassion toward the most vulnerable.
exp.2:25:
What it says: This verse promises that God himself will be the security of the one who obeys him. The phrase about keeping your foot from being taken uses the image of a trap or net: God will watch over your steps so that you do not fall into it. The verse uses the image of a trap or net, and the idea is that God will guard you from being caught in it.

Context: Proverbs is a book of wisdom. Here a father or teacher speaks to his son (tradition links the book to Solomon). The verses before it speak of sleeping without fear and of not dreading sudden disasters. This verse gives the reason: peace comes from trusting the Lord, not from the absence of dangers.

For today: When you feel anxious about the future or about problems you cannot control, pray and give that worry to God before you sleep. Then do honestly what is yours to do, and rest knowing that he upholds your steps.
exp.0:11:
Here the wicked keep on talking, and they boast of their cruelty. They say they will swallow their victim "alive," as the grave does (the tomb, the place of the dead), and "whole," as those who fall into a pit do, that is, a deep hole. The idea is that they will leave no trace of him at all.

The speaker is a group of sinners who invite the young man to join their attacks. The father, who is instructing his son, quotes their words to show how terrible their plan is. They want to attack an innocent person for no reason and take what he has. The text does not say who the specific victim is; the scene is a general warning.

For today: be careful with invitations that sound exciting or promise easy gain but harm others. Before you say "yes" to a group, ask yourself who it will hurt. It is better to say "no" in time.
exp.22:3:
This verse warns you not to wear yourself out trying to become rich. The phrase "cease from thine own wisdom" means putting a limit on your own cleverness or human wisdom, that is, not trusting your own ingenuity to accumulate riches. Some modern translations understand it as "have the sense to stop."

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, addressed to a young person to guide his life. This passage continues a warning against letting yourself be drawn in by the feasts of the powerful. The text says that wealth is not secure: it grows wings and flies away like an eagle.

Today we can work with honesty and diligence, but without living enslaved to earning more. A good practice is to set a healthy limit on your working hours and to reserve room for God, family, and rest.
exp.4:11:
This verse describes the lament of someone who, at the end of his road, admits his mistake. He says that he despised counsel and that his heart would not accept rebuke, that is, correction. To hate instruction means he felt a strong rejection of it, and to despise reproof means he treated it as worthless.

The one speaking is a wise father who warns his son in chapters 5 to 7 of Proverbs. Picture how the young man would speak if he followed the path of immorality: he would groan at the end of his life, with his strength spent and his body worn out. It is a warning so that he does not come to that point.

For today: accept correction before it is too late. Choose someone you trust, such as a pastor, a mature relative, or a good friend, and ask them to speak to you frankly. Listening to them with humility today may spare you much pain tomorrow.
exp.30:28:
It says that there are many women who have acted with courage and kindness, but that this woman surpassed them all. The word "surpassed" is the one the verse uses, and it is a generous and sincere praise.

The verse is part of the poem that closes Proverbs (31:10-31), which is attributed to the teachings that the mother of King Lemuel gave him (31:1). Here the husband and the children speak, praising the woman for her work and her character. Some see in her an ideal portrait and others a summary of many virtues. In any case, the following verse makes the central point clear: what is worth most is fearing the Lord.

Today, practice appreciation: tell someone in your home or in your church, with specific words, what good they do and how much you value them.
exp.13:30:
This verse says that whoever mistreats or abuses the poor offends God, who made them. On the other hand, whoever has compassion on the poor and helps them honors God. "Oppresses" means to crush or treat unjustly. "Reproaches" means to insult or show disrespect. "Maker" is the Creator. "Mercy" is compassion that becomes concrete help.

The book of Proverbs is a collection of sayings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here the wise teacher shows that the way we treat others reveals what we think of God. The neighboring verses speak about character: patience, a calm heart, envy, justice, and wisdom. This proverb shows that wisdom is also lived out in how we treat the weakest.

Today we can look with respect on those who have less: paying a fair wage, not taking advantage of someone in need, or sharing with a person or family close to us who is going through a hard time. In this way we honor God through simple deeds.
exp.15:17:
It says that pride, that is, thinking more of oneself than one really is, comes before a disaster. "Destruction" in the verse means ruin or collapse, and "haughty spirit" describes a heart that is arrogant and looks down on others. First the pride swells, and then the fall comes.

This verse is in the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, though the book has several authors and compilers. These are words of wisdom for everyday life. Here, among verses that praise wisdom and humility, pride is warned against as a dangerous path, while trusting in the LORD brings well-being.

For today: when something goes well for you, give thanks and recognize that others helped you. And if someone corrects you, listen before you defend yourself. That simple attitude protects you from falling because you believe you are invincible.
exp.2:20:
This verse is a father's call to his son: not to let go of or lose sight of these things, meaning the wisdom and understanding the passage has been speaking about. The phrase can also be understood as taking care of practical wisdom and good judgment. Here, the teaching is not only about rules but about wise guidance for living well.

The speaker is the teacher of Proverbs, traditionally presented as Solomon, who is advising a young man. Just before this, the text shows that God created the world with wisdom. The idea is that if God made everything with wisdom, then living by wisdom means living in harmony with his work.

Today, you might choose a pending decision and, before acting, stop to pray and seek biblical counsel and the advice of mature people. In this way you keep wisdom in view and not only in memory.
exp.27:19:
The explanation says that the faithful and honest person ("a man of truth" means someone trustworthy, who keeps his word) will receive many blessings. On the other hand, the one who is in a hurry to become rich ("hastens to get rich") will not be left without guilt; that is, he will not come out clean from the consequences of his actions.

It is a proverb attributed to Solomon, part of a collection of short sayings of wisdom. The nearby verses contrast the one who walks with integrity and works his land with the one who pursues easy gain. The text suggests that the rush for riches often leads to unjust shortcuts, as verse 22 shows.

For today: before seeking a quick income or business, ask yourself whether it is honest and whether you could explain it without shame. Prefer steady work and a kept word, even if progress is slow.
exp.16:2:
This verse compares two works of fire. The crucible is the vessel in which silver is melted, and the furnace is the oven where gold is refined. The heat draws out the impurities and leaves the metal pure. In the same way, the Lord tests the hearts, that is, He examines what is genuine in the innermost part of each person.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, attributed in large part to Solomon. Here it speaks of practical wisdom. The nearby verses deal with quarrels at home, with lies, and with mocking the poor. This suggests that God looks at the hidden intentions behind what we do and say.

For today: when a difficulty comes, do not think only about the pain. Ask God to show you what is in your heart and to cleanse it, and live with sincerity, not just with a good appearance.
exp.5:17:
This verse names two of the seven things that God detests: a heart that devises wicked plans, and feet that are swift to run toward evil. The heart that devises evil is the one that carefully schemes and plots harm. Wicked plans are the schemes of a crooked, unjust mind. Swift feet are feet that rush eagerly, without hesitation. The verse speaks both of what a person thinks and of what a person does.

Here the wise teacher instructs his son in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. He lists seven evils, using the pattern of "six things... yes, seven," so that the young man will recognize them and avoid them. Then he encourages him to obey the teaching of his parents.

For today: be careful what you feed your mind. If you begin to dwell on a plan to hurt someone, stop and pray. Ask God for a clean heart and an eagerness to run toward what is good.
exp.18:15:
He says that whoever obeys the commandment takes care of his own life, but whoever looks down on his ways, meaning the way he lives and acts, will end up dying.

"Keep" means to obey and to take care of. "Despise" means to treat something as if it were worth nothing. "Soul" here refers to the person's whole life.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, that gives practical wisdom in short sayings. The verses nearby speak of laziness, of helping the poor, and of correcting children. Some understand "the commandment" as God's law; others, as wise instruction in general. And "his ways" can refer to one's own ways or to God's ways; the text allows both readings.

Today we can ask ourselves which teaching from God we have been setting aside, because it seems small or uncomfortable to us. Choose one, such as being honest, forgiving, or setting aside time to pray, and obey it this week. In this way you take care of your life.
exp.23:14:
This verse is a warning addressed to a wicked person. It tells them not to lie in wait for the home of a righteous person, watching for the moment to attack it, and not to rob them of their belongings. To lie in wait here means to keep watch with bad intentions. The home is the dwelling where the righteous person lives, and the resting place is the place where their possessions are kept. To spoil means to rob by force.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, and here a teacher speaks in the tone of a father to his son. It comes after an invitation to seek wisdom, which is as sweet as honey. Right after this, it says that the righteous person may fall but gets up again, while the wicked person ends up ruined. Many understand that the verse warns the wicked person, and others that it also cautions the young man not to join with such people. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: do not seek to take advantage of someone who lives with integrity, whether through deceit or abuse. Instead, protect and respect others, and trust that God cares for those who follow him.
exp.24:23:
This proverb says that it is better to live in a corner of the roof of the house, in a small and uncomfortable place, than to share a large house with a quarrelsome wife. A "quarrelsome" person is one who argues a great deal and constantly stirs up disputes. The idea is that space and comfort are worth little if there is no peace at home.

This text is part of the proverbs of Solomon, which according to Proverbs 25:1 were copied out by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah. It is wisdom in the form of a short saying, and it speaks to everyday life. The same proverb appears almost word for word in Proverbs 21:9. It stands among sayings about words and behaviors that do harm.

For today: peace in the home is worth more than comfort. This applies to everyone, not only to one gender: watch the way you speak at home, ask forgiveness quickly, and seek to calm conflicts before they grow.
exp.17:18:
It says that a brother who has been offended is harder to win back than a fortified city. And quarrels between brothers are like the bars or locks of a palace fortress: hard to open. Here "hard to win over" means hard to persuade, and "fortress" means a castle or stronghold.

It is a proverb attributed to Solomon, within a collection of wise sayings about everyday life. It comes after verses about quarrels and the need to hear both sides. Many understand "brother" to mean a family member or a close neighbor. The Hebrew text is brief and some translations phrase it differently, but the underlying idea is clear: resentment between those close to us shuts doors.

For today: if you have offended someone close to you, do not wait. Ask for forgiveness soon and with humility, before the hurt becomes a wall. And if you have been offended, try to speak calmly, because words can either open the way or close it.
exp.0:8:
This verse says that the teaching of parents is like a beautiful ornament: like a crown or garland of grace on the head, and like necklaces that adorn the neck. The word "ornament" means something that makes a person look good. Here the beauty is not gold, but character.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, in the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon. He has just asked his son to listen to his father and his mother. Then he will warn him against bad friends who invite others to do harm. Obeying wisdom will protect him and bring him honor.

Today, you can value the wise advice of your parents, grandparents, or mentors as a treasure, not as a burden. Before deciding something important, listen humbly to the one who loves you and guides you well. That attitude will give you a character that others respect.
exp.1:14:
This verse describes the wicked people from the previous verse. Their ways are crooked, meaning they are not straight or honest. Their manner of living is twisted, full of deceit and roundabout dealings. Crooked is the opposite of upright.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as in the whole chapter. He explains that wisdom will deliver him from wicked people, who leave the straight path to walk in darkness and take pleasure in doing evil. The text then adds that this wisdom will also deliver him from the seductive woman who forgets the covenant of her God.

For today: be careful about who you walk with and whom you imitate. Whoever lives with lies and shortcuts ends up entangled. Ask God for wisdom to choose friends and decisions that are upright, even when they cost more.
exp.19:2:
The explanation says that it is an honour for a person to stay away from quarrels and arguments. The fool, by contrast, who does not think or control himself, is always getting drawn into them.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, attributed largely to Solomon, although the book has several authors or compilers. Here the teacher gives practical advice for living well. The verses nearby speak of foolish behaviour that harms life: drinking to excess, provoking the anger of a king, and laziness. Quarrelling fits in as another way of acting without wisdom.

For today: before you answer an insult or join a pointless argument, take a breath and ask yourself whether it is worth it. Staying silent or withdrawing in time is not weakness; it is wisdom and self-control.
exp.0:23:
This verse says that someone called out insistently and no one wanted to answer. "I have stretched out my hand" is a gesture of offering help or inviting someone to come closer. "No one paid attention" means that no one listened. The phrase "because I have called" explains the reason for what follows: the rejection.

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a woman who cries out in the streets (Proverbs 1:20-23). She addresses the simple, those who are carried along without thinking, the scornful, and the foolish. She offers them correction and teaching, but they reject her. The verses that follow show the consequences of ignoring her.

For today: God often speaks to us through his Word, through a sincere piece of advice, or through our conscience. This week, when someone corrects you with love, or when you read something in the Bible that makes you uncomfortable, stop and listen before you defend yourself.
exp.20:10:
This proverb says that the punishment of a scoffer serves as a lesson for others. A "scorner" is someone who mocks what is right and rejects correction. The "simple" is the naive person, who has not yet developed good judgment and can be influenced for good or for ill. By seeing the consequences the scoffer suffers, the simple learns. And the wise, with just a warning, grows in knowledge.

The book of Proverbs is largely attributed to Solomon, although students of the Bible debate how much of it was compiled later. It is wisdom in the form of brief sayings, meant to shape character. Here, among verses about evil and injustice, it shows that correction has a purpose: to teach, not only to punish.

For today: learn from the mistakes of others without waiting to make your own. And when someone corrects you with respect, listen with humility, because that is a sign of wisdom.
exp.29:25:
The explanation says that the conies are a people with little strength, yet they still make their homes in the rocks, where they are safe. The phrase "not strong" means they have no great power. Some scholars point out that the Hebrew animal (shaphan) may be the rock hyrax or badger, not a rabbit like the ones we know, though there is no complete certainty.

Proverbs 30 records the words of Agur, who recognizes himself as humble and limited. Here he teaches with examples of four small creatures that show true wisdom. They stand out not for their size or strength, but for acting with intelligence.

For today: recognize your limits without shame, and look for a secure place to lean on. For the believer, the Bible speaks of God as a rock and a refuge. When you feel weak, do not remain exposed: draw near to God in prayer and seek the support of your community.
exp.30:30:
This verse says that this woman should be given recognition for what she has worked for. "The fruit of her hands" refers to the results of her daily effort. "The gates" were the entrance of the city, where people gathered and public matters were handled. So her own works praise her before everyone.

Chapter 31 ends with a poem describing the woman of noble character. The text says these are words that the mother of King Lemuel taught him. It is not known for certain who Lemuel was, and there are different opinions about this. The poem joins wisdom with everyday life and emphasizes that what is most valuable is fearing God, not outward appearance.

Today we can recognize, with sincere words, the work of those around us, especially the work that goes unnoticed at home, at work, or in the church. A concrete "thank you," spoken at the right time, honors people and reflects the character of God.
exp.15:31:
Proverbs 16:32 says that a patient person is worth more than a powerful warrior. It also says that someone who controls their temper is better than someone who conquers a city. "Slow to anger" means they do not get angry quickly. "Ruleth his spirit" means they govern their own emotions and reactions, like a ruler who is in charge of their own household.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though other parts have other authors. Here the wise writer contrasts the violent and wicked people of the previous verse with the person who has self-control. The verse uses a comparison: military strength is impressive, but mastering oneself is harder and more valuable.

For today: when something bothers you, pause before you respond, take a breath, and pray briefly. Ask God for calm, and then speak with respect. That pause can prevent hurt in your family or at work.
exp.13:11:
There is a way that seems right, correct, and safe to a person, but it ends badly. "But" simply means the contrast that follows. "The end" means the final destination or result. The phrase about the ways of death speaks of ruin, harm, and separation from the good life God wants to give. The problem is not that the way looks ugly, but that it looks good.

This is in the book of Proverbs, which gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although this section does not say who spoke. The verses around it compare the wicked with the upright and show that appearances deceive: even laughter can hide pain. The proverb warns against blindly trusting yourself.

For today: before an important decision, do not rely only on what you feel or think. Pray, open the Bible, and ask advice from wise and trustworthy people. In this way you can discover whether your path is truly right.
exp.22:23:
It says that the father of a righteous person will have great joy. And whoever has a wise child will be glad because of him. "Begetteth" means he was the father of that child. "Righteous" refers to someone who lives in an upright and honest way.

Here a wise father is teaching his son. Earlier he asked him to listen to his parents, not to despise his mother when she grows old, and to buy the truth and wisdom, that is, to value them more than anything else. This verse gives him a reason to live this way: his good conduct brings joy to those who raised him.

For today: think about how your decisions affect your family. Choose one honest or wise action today, and perhaps listen to some advice from your parents or elders. If you are a father or mother, guide with patience and by example.
exp.6:17:
It says that a woman invites a young man to spend the night with her, with the idea of enjoying love until morning. The phrases "Let us get drunk on love" and "Let us delight ourselves in love" are rendered in the verse above as "take our fill of love" and "solace ourselves with loves." Both phrases mean letting oneself be carried away by pleasure, like someone who gets drunk. The second one reinforces the same invitation.

It is the seductive, adulterous woman described in Proverbs 7. A father warns his son about her. She prepares her bed and her room with fine, perfumed things, and assures him that her husband is away on a trip. Her speech sounds attractive, but the text presents it as a trap that leads to ruin.

For today: be wary of anything that promises immediate pleasure without commitment or consequences. Before giving in to a temptation, ask yourself where the path ends. Fleeing in time and guarding your faithfulness, with God's help, protects your life and your relationships.
exp.19:21:
This proverb asks us not to take revenge into our own hands. "Say not, I will recompense evil" means restraining the urge to repay evil with evil. "Wait on the Lord" means trusting and waiting patiently for God. "He shall save you" means that God will rescue you or give you justice in his own way and in his own time.

This verse is in the book of Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, though the book had several compilers. Here a teacher of wisdom speaks to a young man. Around it are warnings about honoring one's parents, unjust gain, and false weights. Everything points toward living with integrity and letting God be the judge.

When someone wrongs you, do not respond with resentment or with gossip to get even. Pray, seek peace if it is possible, act honestly, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.11:10:
The explanation says that whoever works his own land will have bread in abundance. By contrast, whoever chases after empty pursuits lacks understanding, that is, good judgment. "Shall be satisfied" means he will have enough, and "empty pursuits" here is understood as idle people of little worth, or things that are futile and produce nothing.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, offered as advice to those who want to live well. The verses around this one speak of humility, of taking care of what one has, and of the difference between the righteous and the wicked. Here the verse contrasts steady work with wasting time on things that bear no fruit. It is a general principle, not an absolute promise for every case.

Today it can encourage us to be steady in our work or study, and not to spend our energy on shortcuts, easy promises, or friendships that only distract us. Ask yourself: what "land" was entrusted to me to care for today, and what is pulling me away from it?
exp.0:2:
This verse says that the proverbs serve to receive instruction that shapes character.

The book begins by presenting its purpose. It is traditionally attributed to Solomon, son of David, who appears here as a teacher. His aim is that the reader not only receives information but learns to live well. The verses that follow say that this teaching is for the simple and the young, but also for the wise, who keep on learning.

For today: before making an important decision, ask advice from someone wise and ask yourself whether what you intend to do is sensible, just, and honest toward others. Receiving correction with humility is a sign of maturity.
exp.10:18:
This verse compares two paths. Just as living righteously leads to life, the one who pursues evil heads toward his own death. "Pursueth" here means going after something with determination. "Righteousness" is living uprightly, in line with what God approves.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom. Tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although the book mentions other authors or compilers. These sayings teach, above all to young people, how to live well. In this chapter the righteous is contrasted with the wicked: the merciful does good to himself, and the cruel harms himself. The proverbs describe general tendencies, not automatic promises in every case. "Life" and "death" can be understood in several ways: a full life, or the harm that evil brings.

Today we can ask where our small daily decisions are leading us. Choosing honesty, kindness, and truth today, even when it costs us, is walking toward life.
exp.0:12:
This verse says that certain men promise to gain every kind of wealth and fill their houses with stolen goods. "Spoil" refers to goods taken from others by force.

The speaker is a group of sinners who want to lure a young man. In Proverbs 1, a wise father warns his son about these invitations. The wicked tempt him with quick gains, even though getting them harms an innocent person. The verses that follow show that the father asks his son not to go with them.

For today: be wary of any offer of easy money that harms others or asks you to silence your conscience. Before joining a group or a business, ask: "Is this fair? Does someone get hurt?" If the answer is no, walk away in time.
exp.24:5:
It says we should not show off or act self-important before an authority. "Put not forth thyself" means not speaking well of oneself or making a display of oneself. "Stand not in the place of great men" means not taking a place of honor that does not belong to you, as if you were a person of high rank.

These are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, copied and gathered centuries later (Proverbs 25:1). They speak about how to behave at court. The verses that follow give the reason: it is better to be invited to come up than to be humbled in public. Jesus taught something similar about the best seats at a banquet (Luke 14:7-11).

Today we can apply this at work, at church, or at home: do your part well without looking for applause or the best place. Let others recognize your effort, and if honor comes, receive it with gratitude and humility.
exp.21:11:
