This verse says that God watches over and protects true knowledge. "Knowledge" here means knowing, correct understanding. The "transgressors" are treacherous people who turn away from what is right and deceive. "Overthroweth" means that God brings down or undoes their plans and words.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. A wise father teaches a young man how to live. Just before, it speaks of pushing away the scoffer and of loving purity of heart. Afterward, it speaks of the lazy man who makes excuses. In this way, the verse shows that God sees and values the truth, and that lies will not last.

For today: seek the truth with humility and be honest, even when it costs you. Do not rely on deception to get ahead. God sees everything, and He upholds the one who walks in what is right.
exp.15:12:
This verse says that kings take pleasure in people who speak with righteousness and truth. "Delight" means joy or pleasure. "Righteous lips" are honest and upright words. Furthermore, the king values and loves the one who says what is right, even when it is not the most comfortable thing to hear.

These words are part of the proverbs attributed to Solomon, which give wisdom for life. Here the theme is good government. The previous verse says that kings detest wickedness, because the throne is established through justice. The following verses show that the king's favor or anger weighs heavily. For this reason it is wise to speak with wisdom.

For today: try to speak with honesty and respect, including before bosses or authorities. Do not flatter or lie to make a good impression. A sincere word, spoken with kindness, builds trust and reflects the character of God.
exp.19:0:
Wine is said to deceive the person who drinks it, and so is strong drink. The word translated "mocker" means a scoffer: the drink laughs at the person, makes a fool of them, and leads them into foolish behavior. The word for "raging" speaks of something that stirs up quarrels and disorder. And the phrase "whosoever is deceived thereby" means that the one who loses control because of drink shows that they are not wise.

The book of Proverbs gathers wise sayings, many attributed to Solomon, to teach people how to live with prudence. This saying is brief and has no close narrative setting. The verses that follow speak of the anger of a king and of avoiding fights, so the common theme is self-control.

Today it invites us to be honest about what has power over us. If something takes away our control or leads us into quarrels and poor decisions, it is wise to set clear limits, ask for help, and seek wisdom.
exp.12:7:
It says that money can serve to save a person's life, as when a wealthy person pays a ransom. The word "ransom" here means the price paid to free someone. By contrast, the poor man "hears no rebuke," that is, he receives no threats, because no one expects to get anything out of him. Scholars understand this in several ways: some see an advantage in poverty, and others see that the rich man is more exposed to being threatened.

It is a proverb of Solomon, traditionally, given as a lesson of wisdom to young people. It stands among verses that contrast true and apparent riches, righteousness and wickedness. It does not say that money is the most important thing, but describes how things work in life.

Today we can be thankful for what God gives us, whether much or little, and not place our security only in money. If we have resources, let us use them with generosity and wisdom, remembering that what is most valuable, eternal life, cannot be bought with money.
exp.11:2:
It says that no one can achieve a stable and secure life by doing evil. "Wickedness" is living without reverence for God and without justice. To be "established" means to stand firm and secure. By contrast, the righteous are like a tree with deep roots: they "shall not be moved," that is, they will not be uprooted or shaken loose.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon, although the book gathers several collections of wisdom. Here the wise teacher contrasts two paths: that of the person who accepts correction and seeks what is good, and that of the person who follows wicked thoughts. It is a general truth about how life tends to go, not a promise that the righteous will never face trials.

For today: if you are tempted to take a dishonest shortcut to secure your future, remember that what is built that way is fragile. Better to put down roots in honesty, prayer, and obedience to God, even if you advance more slowly.
exp.22:5:
It tells you not to accept or desire the food of a person with an "evil eye." This Hebrew expression is usually understood to mean someone who is stingy, envious, or ill-intentioned. "Delicacies" are fine foods, and "craving" means desiring something eagerly.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon, within a father's advice to his son. The following verses explain the reason: that person invites you to eat, but his heart is not with you. His generosity is false and can bring shame or obligations. Some scholars think it also warns against letting yourself be won over by the luxuries of others.

For today: before accepting a favor, a gift, or an invitation, look closely at the intention of the one offering it. Do not let the desire for comfort or luxury lead you to depend on someone who does not truly value you.
exp.0:1:
It says that proverbs serve two purposes: to understand wisdom and instruction (that is, teaching or guidance), and to know "razones prudentes," which are sensible words or arguments that help a person think and act with good judgment. It is not only about knowing facts, but about learning to live well.

The one speaking is the author of the book, who presents himself as Solomon, son of David. Many scholars accept that much of the book comes from him, though some sections are attributed to other wise men. This verse opens the purpose of the book: to shape the character of young people and of those who still lack experience.

For today: don't assume you already know everything. Spend a few minutes each day reading one proverb, thinking about it, and asking yourself how to apply it to a real decision, such as the way you speak, work, or manage money.
exp.24:4:
It says that if a king wants to rule well, he must remove wicked people from his presence. A "wicked" person is someone who lives without reverence for God and does evil. A throne like that stands firm and secure, and it is held up by righteousness, not by deceit.

These are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, copied and gathered together (Proverbs 25:1). Before this, the text compares silver and its dross: just as impurity is taken out of metal so that it comes out clean, wicked advisers are removed from government. The verses that follow speak of humility before the king.

For today: the people we listen to shape our decisions. Whether at work, in the family, or in the church, seek to surround yourself with honest counselors, and keep away from those who push you to do what is wrong.
exp.24:13:
He says that someone who boasts of being generous, yet gives nothing, is like clouds and wind that promise rain and never bring it. "Boasteth" means showing off or bragging. "Liberality" means generosity. "Vain" means empty, or without fruit. The clouds look fine, but the dry ground is still waiting.

The book of Proverbs gathers sayings of wisdom; this chapter is attributed to Solomon and was copied by the men of Hezekiah (Prov. 25:1). The verses around it speak of words and conduct that bring refreshment or disappointment, like the faithful messenger who brings relief. This proverb adds the contrast: showy promises that are not kept.

Let your deeds back up your words. Before promising help or gifts, think about whether you can truly follow through. And if you do promise, do it simply, without showing off, so that others can trust you.
exp.27:18:
The explanation says that whoever works his land will have bread in abundance, but whoever chases after idle people, or after empty things, will have poverty in abundance. The phrase "will have plenty" means he will have more than enough. The idle refers to people who waste their time without useful work. Some translations render "empty things," and both ideas fit.

Proverbs gathers practical wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, although this chapter belongs to a section said to have been copied by the men of Hezekiah. Here the contrast is between living with integrity and steadiness, or with shortcuts and bad companions. The verses nearby speak of straight paths, of blessing, and of the rush to get rich.

For today: value steady, honest work, even when it is simple. Also review how you spend your time and with whom you share it, because that shapes your future.
exp.7:23:
It says that Wisdom existed before there were oceans and springs. "Depths" are the deep waters of the sea, and "I was brought forth" means she was brought into being or born. "Fountains abounding with water" are the springs from which water flows. It is poetic language meaning that Wisdom was there from before creation.

In Proverbs 8, Wisdom speaks as if she were a person and calls people to listen to her. Here she explains that she comes from God and is older than all that has been created. Many Christians see in this a pointer to Christ, whom the New Testament calls the wisdom of God; others read it only as divine wisdom personified. There is debate over the word "brought forth."

For today: if God's wisdom is as ancient and firm as creation itself, it is worth seeking every day. Before deciding something important, ask God for direction and listen to his Word.
exp.19:12:
It says not to love sleep, meaning not to want to sleep too much or to live in laziness, because that leads to poverty. "Lest you come to poverty" means "so that you do not come to poverty." In contrast, opening your eyes means being awake and active, and the result is that "you will be satisfied with bread," that is, you will have enough food.

This verse is in Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings. Tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon, although not all the sayings can be dated with certainty. Here wisdom speaks like a father advising a young man. The nearby verses speak of a person's deeds and of God, who made the ear and the eye.

For today: take care of your habits of work and rest. Rest is good, but do not use rest to escape your responsibilities. Start a pending task today, with perseverance and with gratitude to God.
exp.9:2:
The explanation says that God will not allow the righteous person to go without what is needed to live. The word meaning to let someone go hungry is replaced here with the verse's own wording: the Lord "will not suffer" the soul of the righteous to famish, and "soul" here refers to the whole person, with their life and their needs. By contrast, wickedness and the ungodly, those who live without respect for God, end in failure; God casts away or rejects their desires, as the verse says he casts away the substance of the wicked.

These words come from the proverbs of Solomon, short sayings of wisdom meant to teach people how to live well. They are general principles, not automatic promises: the Bible also recognizes that sometimes the righteous suffer need. Here the emphasis is that wickedness does not give true security, and that God cares for those who obey him. The context also speaks of working with diligence.

For today: trust that God cares for you, but live with honesty and work with diligence. Avoid gaining money through tricks or deceit, and rest in the knowledge that God knows what you need.
exp.8:12:
The verse presents the "foolish woman," who is a symbolic figure. It says she is clamorous, meaning noisy, boisterous, and never quiet. It also says she is simple (without judgment, easily deceived) and that she knows nothing and does not even recognize it.

In Proverbs 9, the wise teacher sets two women side by side, representing two invitations: Wisdom, who calls to her table calmly, and Folly, who shouts from the door of her house. Both speak to the same listeners. Wisdom offers life; Folly offers easy pleasures that end badly. In this way the writer helps his reader choose.

Today, many loud voices promise joy without effort. Before following one, ask yourself whether it leads you to life or only makes noise. Seek the quiet voice of God's wisdom.
exp.7:24:
This verse says that before God set the foundations of the mountains and before the hills existed, the one speaking was already there. The word "settled" means established on a firm base. The hills are the low rises of the land. "Brought forth" means born or produced, and it can also be understood as "brought into being."

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a person who calls people to listen to her (Proverbs 8). She speaks of her ancient origin to show that her counsel is trustworthy and comes from before creation. Some Christians see in this an image of Christ, the wisdom of God; others understand it only as a poetic way of speaking of divine wisdom. There is discussion about how to interpret the phrase "brought forth."

For today: before deciding something important, ask God for wisdom and seek his Word. If God's wisdom is older than the mountains, it is worth more than our hurry and opinions.
exp.16:17:
It says that a person without good judgment makes a hasty deal: he shakes hands to close an agreement and becomes a guarantor for another, that is, he promises to pay someone else's debt if that person fails. He does it "in the presence of his friend," as if to look good or to show how generous he is. "Striking hands" was a gesture of agreement, like a handshake. "Becoming surety" means standing as a guarantor.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and many are attributed to Solomon, although it is not always known who wrote each saying. Here the teacher warns the young against overconfidence. The verse before speaks of the faithful friend in difficult times; this one reminds us that helping without thinking can also cause harm.

For today: before signing as a guarantor or promising money, think, pray, and consult with your family. Helping is good, but do it with prudence, without pressure and without a desire to appear important.
exp.24:1:
It is the glory of God to conceal a thing, the explanation says, and the honour of kings is to search out a matter. In the verse, "a thing" is the matter or the subject. "Search out" means to examine thoroughly and look for it with effort until one understands. God does not reveal everything all at once, and diligent searching is something worthy.

These proverbs are attributed to Solomon, and the text says that the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, copied them centuries later. For that reason it is understood that they were gathered and carefully preserved. The verses that follow speak of what is beyond reach: the heavens, the earth, and the heart of kings. Some understand the king to represent someone who rules with wisdom; others see a general principle.

For today: do not be discouraged if you do not understand something from the Bible or from life. Search with patience, pray, study, and ask questions. God rewards the one who seeks sincerely.
exp.27:2:
He says that a man who is poor and takes advantage of other poor people is like a heavy rain that destroys everything but leaves no food behind. A flash flood is a storm that causes flooding; instead of watering the crops, it carries away the soil and the harvest. Leaving no food means that it produces no fruit or benefit.

Proverbs is wisdom traditionally attributed to Solomon, although this chapter belongs to a collection that the book says was copied in the time of King Hezekiah. The verses around it speak of the wicked and the righteous, of rulers and of the law. This saying shows how injustice becomes more cruel when someone with little power oppresses someone who has even less. Some scholars understand "poor" as someone with lesser authority; the text does not make this entirely clear.

If today you have some advantage, even a small one, do not use it to profit from someone who is worse off. Use what you have to help, to pay fairly, and to deal with others honestly.
exp.17:7:
This verse says that gossip sounds gentle, almost like a tasty morsel, but it sinks deep into the person who hears it. The word "talebearer" refers to someone who carries comments about others from one person to another. The idea of being "soft" or "smooth" can be understood as pleasant or sweet, and the phrase "innermost parts of the belly" is a way of saying the deepest part of a person. Some translations compare the words to savory bites that one swallows with pleasure.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed in this book to Solomon. It comes after warnings about the foolish person and the harm his mouth causes. The teacher wants to show that gossip attracts because it seems harmless, but it leaves lasting marks on the one who receives it and on relationships.

Today, when someone starts telling you something bad about another person, you can gently stop them: "It would be better to speak to him directly," or change the subject. That way you do not fill yourself with what later poisons your heart.
exp.18:4:
This proverb says that whoever lies before others in order to harm or deceive will not escape the consequences. A "false witness" is someone who testifies to something that is not true, especially in a court of law. The phrases "shall not be unpunished" and "shall not escape" repeat the same idea to make it firm: a lie sooner or later has to be paid for.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon. Here the wise man speaks about how life works in an unjust world. The verses nearby speak of the poor being forgotten and the rich having many friends. In that setting, the poor could easily be victims of false testimony, and this verse reminds us that God sees, and that justice cannot be mocked.

Today we can take care with our words: not exaggerating, not repeating gossip, and not accusing others without being sure. If we have lied and done harm, the best thing is to admit it, ask forgiveness, and make it right.
exp.15:32:
It says that although people cast lots, that is, use stones, sticks, or another object to decide something, the final result comes from God. "The fold" was the fold of the clothing over the chest, where the objects were shaken. "Judgment" here means decision or outcome. Thus, what seems like pure chance, the Bible sees under God's care.

This verse is in Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings, largely attributed to Solomon, to teach living with prudence and the fear of God. The verses before it speak of mastering one's character and walking in righteousness. This one closes the thought: even what we cannot control is in God's hands. Scholars understand it as an affirmation of his sovereignty, not as a recipe for deciding everything by chance.

For today: do what is yours to do with responsibility and effort, and entrust to God what you cannot control. In this way you can rest with more peace before uncertain results.
exp.13:10:
It says that the house of the wicked (the ungodly) will be destroyed, that is, it will be left in ruins. By contrast, the tent, meaning the simple home, of the upright will flourish, grow, and prosper. It is a contrast: a house that is firm and looks strong can fall, and a frail tent can prosper.

It is a wise proverb, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Its purpose is to teach how to live well. The verses nearby speak of mocking sin and of paths that seem good but end badly. Proverbs describe how things usually turn out in the long run; they are not automatic promises for every case.

For today: do not measure success only by what can be seen right now. Choose honesty in your home and your work, even when it costs you. Over time, an upright life gives a safer foundation than quick gains.
exp.0:30:
It says that those who rejected wisdom will have to eat the fruit of their own way, that is, live with the consequences of their choices. "They shall be filled with their own devices" means they will be full, even to the point of being stuffed, with their own ideas and plans. Here "devices" refers to their own plans and ways of thinking.

The speaker is Wisdom, personified as a woman who calls out in the streets (Proverbs 1:20). She warns those who refused her, despised her correction, and did not choose the fear of the Lord. The verse shows that their troubles are not an arbitrary punishment but the natural result of their own choices.

For today: before making an important decision, ask where that path leads and seek wise counsel. Accept correction with humility; it is easier to listen now than to reap later what we have sown.
exp.20:2:
This verse says that doing what is just and right pleases God more than any religious offering or sacrifice. The word "judgment" here means acting with uprightness and fairness, and "more acceptable" means that it pleases him more.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although this chapter does not say so. The verses nearby speak of the king's heart, which God guides, and of God examining hearts. This suggests that God cares about the inner attitude and conduct, not only the ritual. Other biblical texts, such as 1 Samuel 15:22, express a similar idea.

For today: before we think about how much we give or how much we serve in the church, let us ask ourselves whether we are honest at work, fair with others, and whether we pay what we owe. Sincere worship includes living with integrity.
exp.28:19:
The explanation says there is a person who is "hasty in his words," meaning someone who speaks quickly, without thinking or weighing what they say. The verse states that there is more hope for a fool (someone without wisdom) than for someone like this. The word "hasty" here means rash or impulsive, not someone pleasant or carefree.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed mainly to Solomon, although this chapter belongs to a section that, according to Proverbs 25:1, was copied by men of Hezekiah. These are short sayings meant to shape character. Around this verse the text speaks of correction, discipline, and self-control, and the theme of hasty words fits with the warning against anger.

Today we can practice a pause before we answer, especially when we are upset or on social media. Before speaking, let us ask ourselves: is it true, is it necessary, is it kind? A few seconds of silence and prayer can prevent wounds that are later very hard to heal.
exp.0:22:
The explanation says that Wisdom invites people to turn back when they are corrected. "Turn" means to change direction, and "correction" is a rebuke meant for good. She promises to "pour out my spirit," that is, to generously share her way of thinking, and also to make known her words so they can be understood.

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a woman who calls out in the streets and at the gates of the city, where people gathered. She addresses the simple, the scoffers, and the foolish. Her warning comes from care, not anger, since she offers a way out before the consequences arrive. Some see in "my spirit" only the wise inclination of the heart; others see a reflection of God's Spirit.

Today: when someone corrects you with respect, do not become defensive. Listen and ask what you can learn.
exp.3:11:
This verse says that whoever follows the path of wisdom will have freedom and security as they move forward. "Your steps shall not be straitened" means you will not feel trapped or hemmed in, but will have room to walk. And "you shall not stumble" promises steadiness even when you are hurrying along.

The one speaking is a father teaching his son (Proverbs 4:1-4). He reminds the boy that he has already guided him along straight paths and asks him to hold on to his advice. It is family teaching that passes from one generation to the next. This promise is understood as a general principle of wisdom, not as a guarantee that there will never be difficulties.

For today: before important decisions, such as money, work, or friendships, pause to seek wise counsel and to pray. A well-considered path gives us more peace as we move forward.
exp.30:23:
The explanation says that the virtuous woman made cloth, probably of linen, and sold it. It also says she delivered "girdles" to the merchant, that is, sashes or belts tied around the waist. The word that the old text spells differently is now written in its modern form, and a merchant means a trader. Some scholars translate "girdles" as belts; the general sense is the same.

These words are part of the poem about the virtuous woman, which closes the book of Proverbs. They are teachings that the mother of King Lemuel gave to him (Prov. 31:1). The poem describes a hardworking, skillful, and wise woman. Many understand it as an ideal portrait of wisdom put into practice, not as a required list for every woman.

For today: God values work done with care and honesty. Whether at home, in a business, or in a job, we can use our skills to bless others and support our family, without forgetting the wisdom and kindness that should surround them.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that wisdom and understanding serve to deliver us from the evil way, that is, from a way of living that turns away from what is good. It also speaks of being rescued from men who speak twisted things, that is, people who say crooked, deceptive, or harmful things. The word "deliver" means to rescue or protect you.

Proverbs 2 is a teaching from a wise father to his son. In this book, tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although not the whole book is understood in the same way. Here the father warns that if the son receives wisdom into his heart, wisdom will guard him. The verses that follow describe those men who leave the straight path and delight in doing evil.

For today: make sure God's wisdom is your guide before you make decisions. That includes thinking carefully about which voices you listen to and which friendships influence you. Ask God for discernment and seek counsel in his Word.
exp.18:21:
This old word, "desire," means what is wanted or longed for. The proverb says that what is most valuable in a person is their kindness and mercy. That is why it is better to be poor than to be a liar. Some translators understand what a person longs for as being able to be generous, but the central idea is similar.

This text is in a collection of proverbs that tradition attributes to Solomon. These are counsels of wisdom, given as from a father to a son. Here it sits alongside verses about listening to advice and fearing God: true wisdom shows in character.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I prefer to be seen as successful, or to be honest and compassionate? This week, help someone in need and tell the truth even when it costs you. A simple, sincere life is worth more than riches gained through deceit.
exp.22:18:
It says that a father invites his son to listen carefully, to be wise, and to direct his heart toward the good path. "Hear" means "listen," and "guide" can mean "set straight" or "lead." In the Bible, the heart represents thoughts, desires, and decisions.

Proverbs presents the voice of a wise father instructing his son. Earlier, he warns him not to envy sinners and to live in the fear of the LORD, that is, in reverence and trust toward God. Afterward, he warns against excess in drinking and eating. Thus this verse joins both ideas: a wise life begins with caring for the heart.

Today we can ask ourselves: what is guiding my desires? Before deciding who to spend time with or what to pursue, it is wise to pray and to listen to sound counsel, so that the heart does not drift through envy or excess.
exp.5:25:
The verse says that dealings with a whorish woman can leave a man in poverty, reduced to "a piece of bread", that is, to almost nothing. Furthermore, the adulteress "hunts" or traps something far more valuable: the man's "precious life", his whole life and his integrity. Some scholars also understand it to refer to the other man's wife who destroys the life of a married man; the text allows for those readings.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, within the book of Proverbs. He wants to protect him from falling into adultery and immorality. The preceding verses warn him about smooth words and seductive glances, and the following ones use images of fire and coals to show that no one plays with this without getting burned.

For today: sin almost never shows you its price. Guard what you look at, with whom you find yourself alone, and which conversations you feed, and flee quickly before the fire is kindled.
exp.29:27:
It says the spider takes hold with its hands, that is, it holds on with its little legs, and yet it reaches the palaces of kings. The word in the original is uncertain: some translations say "lizard." In either case it is a small, weak creature that reaches a very high place.

This saying comes from Agur, son of Jakeh, in Proverbs 30. He teaches with four small creatures (ants, rock badgers, locusts, and this one) that are wise despite their size. He wants to show that God's wisdom can be seen even in the humblest parts of creation.

For today: do not lose heart if you feel small or have few resources. With perseverance and trust in God, you can reach places that seemed impossible. Take the next step, even if it is small.
exp.5:12:
The explanation says that the wicked person communicates deceptively through the body. "Winketh with his eyes" means making signals with the eyes; "speaketh with his feet" probably refers to gestures or movements with the feet; and "teacheth with his fingers" means pointing or signaling with the hand. Scholars are not sure of the exact detail, but the idea is that he uses subtle signals to deceive or manipulate.

The passage is spoken by a wise father who instructs his son (Proverbs 6). Before this, he speaks about laziness and poverty, and here he describes the wicked man, whose heart plans evil and sows discord. The following verse announces that his ruin will come suddenly.

Today it invites us to guard our honesty, even in what we leave unsaid. We can ask ourselves whether our gestures, glances, or hints aim to hurt, deceive, or divide. Let us strive to speak with clarity and sincerity, and to seek peace.
exp.20:28:
The explanation says that the wicked person "hardens his face," meaning he puts on a brazen expression, stays stubborn and shameless, with no regret or repentance. The upright person, by contrast, "directs his way": he thinks, examines, and guides his conduct with care. Some translators understand that the upright person "considers" or "makes sure of" his path.

This belongs to the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although not all the proverbs can be dated with certainty. They are counsel from a wise teacher who shows two ways of living. The nearby verses speak of falsehood, of offerings made with wickedness, and of how no human plan can overcome God.

For today: instead of defending yourself with pride when you are wrong, stop and review your decisions before God. Ask him for wisdom, admit your mistakes, and correct your course with humility.
exp.4:1:
This verse says that if the son pays attention to wisdom, he will be able to keep good judgment and discretion. It also says that his lips will hold on to knowledge, meaning he will speak with understanding and not with foolishness. Here "knowledge" means practical wisdom for living well, not scientific studies.

A wise father speaks to his son, as he does throughout the beginning of Proverbs. He wants to prepare him before warning him about the adulteress, whose words sound sweet but end in pain. First he invites him to listen carefully, because wisdom protects before temptation arrives.

For today: before you speak or decide, stop for a moment and ask yourself what wise counsel you have received about that matter. Watching what you say and whom you listen to helps you resist attractive words that lead you down the wrong path.
exp.11:5:
The explanation says that the wicked use their words like an ambush to shed blood, that is, to harm or even kill others. By contrast, what the upright say protects them. "Lie in wait" means to watch from hiding in order to attack, and "wicked" refers to those who live without reverence for God.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, who teaches his son. In this chapter it contrasts the righteous with the wicked: their thoughts, their counsel, and their destiny. Here the contrast lies in the power of words to destroy or to rescue. It is not clear whether "shall deliver them" refers to the upright themselves or to innocent victims; both readings are possible.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself whether your words help or wound. Use your voice to defend the truth, clear up a misunderstanding, or protect someone who is being slandered, instead of joining in the gossip.
exp.6:4:
It says that wisdom and understanding serve to protect us from the woman who is not our wife, and from the stranger whose words are smooth: she speaks with flattery and gentle phrases to seduce. The stranger who flatters with her words is the one the verse warns about.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son in Proverbs. He has just asked him to keep his commandments, bind them on his fingers, and write them on his heart. When he calls wisdom a close companion, it speaks of closeness and trust. Right after, the father tells what he saw from his window: a young man without judgment who falls into that trap. It is a warning with a real example.

For today: don't wait until you are tempted to decide what you will do. Fill your mind with the Word of God and set clear limits in your conversations and on your social media, because sweet words can deceive.
exp.30:2:
This verse is advice from a mother to her son, the king. She says he should not give his strength to women, that is, he should not spend his energy, his time, and his life on disordered relationships. Nor should he give his way, that is, his manner of living, to what destroys kings.

The mother speaking is the mother of King Lemuel, who passes on a serious teaching. She speaks to him with affection and urgency, because a king with power can easily fall into excess. The verses that follow connect this with caution regarding wine and with the responsibility to do justice for the afflicted. Exactly who Lemuel was is not known with certainty.

Today, this advice invites us to take care of our strength and our decisions. Each of us can ask: is there something that is consuming me and pulling me away from serving others with justice? Let us ask God for self-control and wisdom.
exp.18:2:
The foolishness of a person ends up leading his life astray. The source's word for this is "foolishness" in the sense of lacking good sense, that is, acting without wisdom or the fear of God. A phrase in the source says his way is made crooked, meaning that he twists it and ruins it. And the source says that his heart grows angry within him, meaning he becomes resentful inside, and instead of admitting his mistake, he blames God.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, attributed largely to Solomon, though some sections have other authors. It speaks like a teacher of wisdom warning his listeners. The verses nearby speak of simplicity, of lack of knowledge, and of those who rush ahead and fail. In this way it teaches that many falls come from our own poor decisions.

Today it invites us to examine ourselves before complaining. When something goes wrong, ask yourself humbly: "Did I have a part in this?" Then pray, ask for direction, and correct what you can, rather than hardening your heart against God.
exp.19:18:
This proverb says that whoever goes around telling other people's secrets is a gossip. "Revealeth secrets" means revealing what has been entrusted to them. "Flattereth with his lips" means that he flatters, speaking sweet and false words. The advice is not to get involved with or join someone like that, because a person who talks too much and flatters too much cannot be trusted.

This book gathers the sayings of wisdom attributed to Solomon, and this section is a collection of short proverbs. The verses nearby speak of deceit, of planning with counsel, and of acting with prudence. Their purpose is to teach how to live well and how to choose companions wisely. There is no specific historical event behind this verse.

For today: if someone tells you gossip about others with great kindness, they will probably do the same to you. Take care with your friendships, and guard carefully what people trust you with.
exp.2:29:
This verse says that we should not start a quarrel or a dispute with someone without reason, especially when that person has done us no harm.

The sentences that explain the source-language words are not part of the reader's verse, so I have rendered the meaning directly: to contend means to argue, fight, or take someone to court, and the second term refers to an offense or an unjust injury.

These words are part of the advice of a wise father to his son in Proverbs 3. The book is traditionally attributed to Solomon, although it also contains other contributions. The neighboring verses speak of treating others well: giving what is owed on time, not plotting evil, and not envying the violent. Together they teach living with justice and simplicity.

Today we can apply this before we complain, criticize, or argue with someone: asking ourselves whether there is truly a just reason. Often pride or anger push us to fight. Seeking peace, speaking calmly, and forgiving protects our relationships and honors God.
exp.16:1:
It says that a wise and well-behaved servant can come to have more authority than the master's son who brings shame on the family. He may even receive a share of the inheritance along with the brothers. "Will rule over" means he will govern or hold authority. "Will divide the inheritance" means he will receive a portion of the family's property.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, a father and teacher who instructs his readers. Here it is not recounting a historical event but describing a reality: in life, character weighs more than position. A proverb is a general truth, not a promise that always works out the same way. The verses around it also speak of peace in the home and of a God who tests the heart.

For today: do not trust in your family name, your job, or your position. Cultivate an honest and responsible character, because that is what truly gives value and trust before God and before others.
exp.26:14:
This verse compares a leak that keeps dripping on a rainy day with a quarrelsome woman, meaning a woman who is always looking for fights and arguing about everything. "Continual dropping" is the steady drip of a leaking roof, and "alike" means the two things resemble each other: both wear a person down and take away peace from the home.

Proverbs gathers the wisdom that Solomon and other wise teachers passed on, mostly in the form of short sayings meant to teach people how to live well. Here an exaggerated image, common in that kind of writing, is used to show how exhausting it is to live with constant conflict. A similar saying appears in Proverbs 19:13. The book also warns against the same fault in men, so the point is the harm of contention, not an attack on women.

Today, let us check whether our words bring peace or wear down the home. Before we complain, let us ask God for calm and speak with respect and patience, whether we are a man or a woman.
exp.3:18:
The explanation says that the life of those who live in wickedness is like walking in deep darkness. They walk without seeing the ground, so they stumble and do not even know what they trip over or why they fall. The word "wicked" refers to people who live without reverence for God.

The one speaking is a wise father who is teaching his son (according to tradition, Solomon). He compares two paths: that of the righteous, which is like the light of dawn and grows brighter, and that of the wicked, which remains in darkness. He wants his son to choose well and, for that reason, immediately asks for his attention.

Today, if a decision or a company leads you to hide or to justify yourself, that is a sign of darkness. Seek the light: read the Bible, ask for wise counsel, and pray before deciding. In this way you will avoid falls you did not see coming.
exp.2:28:
It says not to plan or scheme to harm your neighbor, the person who lives close to you, when that person trusts you and lives at peace beside you. To plan harm means to plot or prepare something bad against someone. A neighbor is the one who is near us, and to be secure with you means that the person feels safe with you.

It is part of the advice of a wise father (traditionally Solomon) to his son in Proverbs 3. Just before, it speaks of giving what is good without delay, and after, of avoiding quarrels without cause and envy. The theme is honesty in daily dealings with others. When someone trusts you, any betrayal becomes more serious.

For today: take care of the trust others place in you. If a neighbor, coworker or family member opens their door to you or tells you something personal, do not use it to take advantage or to harm them. Be a person others can feel safe with.
exp.25:20:
This verse compares two things. Just as charcoal keeps the embers glowing and wood feeds the fire, the quarrelsome man serves to ignite fights. "Quarrelsome" describes someone who looks for disputes, who is always arguing or provoking anger. Wherever he goes, the argument grows.

It is a proverb of Solomon, within a series of sayings about the tongue and conflict. The verse before it says that without wood the fire goes out, and without a gossip the strife ceases. The verses that follow show how the gossip's smooth words wound from within. The teacher of wisdom wants to warn how quarrels are fed.

For today: before repeating a comment, ask yourself whether it puts out the fire or stirs it up. If it helps no one, be silent. You can also step away from conversations that only seek a fight.
exp.25:8:
It says that a saying or lesson in the mouth of a fool is like a thorn stuck into the hand of a drunkard. The word "stuck" here means driven in. Some understand that the drunkard hurts himself without realizing it. Others understand that he waves the thorny branch around and wounds those who stand near him.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon. Here the wise man warns, with strong images, that truth misused does not help. The fool may repeat correct sayings, but he lacks the judgment and character to apply them well.

Today, before you quote a verse or a piece of advice, examine your heart. Use it with humility, not to attack others or to put yourself above them. Ask God for wisdom to apply it first to your own life, and then, with love, to others.
exp.5:16:
This verse names the first three of seven things that God hates: haughty eyes, that is, a proud look that feels superior to others; a lying tongue, which speaks falsehoods; and hands that shed innocent blood, meaning those who kill or harm people who have done no wrong. The word "hates" means that they deeply repel him.

Proverbs is a collection of teachings on wisdom, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon. Here a father or teacher warns his son about conduct that destroys. The passage uses a list pattern of "six and seven," a common poetic device in Hebrew literature, which underlines the last item as especially serious.

For today: honestly examine how you look at and speak about others. Before saying something, ask yourself whether it is true and whether it honors the other person. Ask God for a humble heart that values and respects everyone.
exp.16:22:
It says that a wicked person secretly accepts a bribe in order to bend justice. The word "gift" here means a present or payment. The phrase "out of the bosom" refers to hiding it in the fold of one's clothing, close to the chest, where money was kept. "The ways of judgment" are the paths of justice.

This is a proverb, part of the wise sayings attributed mostly to Solomon. The one speaking is a teacher of wisdom who instructs young people. The verses nearby speak of the fool, of sorrow in the family, and of the cheerful heart. Here the theme is different: corruption carried out in secret, which harms the whole community. Some see a connection with foolishness, since the one who sells himself does not think about the consequences.

Today we can ask ourselves: would I accept a favor or a payment that makes me stay silent or decide wrongly? Let us practice honesty even when no one is watching, and reject every deal that bends what is right.
exp.15:11:
This verse says that for kings it is something detestable to commit wickedness. "Detestable" means something that causes strong disgust, and "wickedness" refers to acting without respect for God or for what is right. The second part says that the throne stands firm because of righteousness.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon. Here it describes how a good ruler should be, according to God's ideal. The verses around it speak of right judgment, honest scales, and sincere lips. It is a general teaching, not necessarily a description of every real king.

If you have authority, even a small amount, in your home, your work, or your church, seek to be just and honest. Power used with wickedness grows weak, but righteousness produces trust and lasting stability.
exp.17:1:
The explanation says that the foolish person takes no pleasure in understanding things or in learning. What they enjoy is talking about what they already think and bringing their own opinions into the open. The phrase about the heart, which in the verse means that the heart reveals itself, means that they like to show what is inside them, their ideas and feelings, without any filter.

This verse is in the book of Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings that tradition attributes in large part to Solomon, although not all scholars agree on every section. The one speaking is a teacher of wisdom who instructs the young. The verses around it contrast the fool, who isolates himself and meddles in everything, with wise words, which are like deep waters.

For today: before giving your opinion, ask and listen more. Ask God for a heart willing to learn, and in a difficult conversation, try first to understand the other person.
exp.22:30:
This verse warns us not to keep staring at wine when it looks red and bright in the cup.

Here a wise man speaks, like a father advising his son. Earlier he described the pains of drunkenness: quarrels, complaints, wounds, and black eyes. Then he says that in the end wine bites like a serpent. The warning focuses on the temptation that begins with a look.

For today: what seems pleasant at first can enslave later. If something tempts you, don't wait to see what happens; move away in time. Ask God for strength and seek the support of trusted people to help you stay firm.
exp.12:15:
The prudent person acts with wisdom, that is, thinks before doing things and acts with care. The fool, on the other hand, is the one who does not want to learn, and he shows his lack of judgment in what he does and says.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although the book brings together several collections. Here the teacher compares two paths. The verses nearby speak of accepting correction and of the consequences of despising advice. The fool, sooner or later, is brought into the open.

For today: before you answer in anger or make an important decision, pause and pray. Ask yourself what God's Word says and what advice wise people would give. In this way your actions will show your trust in God.
exp.21:13:
This verse says that the seductive words of the "strange" woman (the woman who belongs to another, the one who leads to unfaithfulness) are like a very deep pit, from which it is hard to get out. The verse also says that the mouth of such women is a deep pit. A warning is given: whoever has already turned away from God is more exposed to falling into that trap.

It is a proverb of Solomon, addressed as a word of wisdom to young people. There is no story here, only a brief teaching. Many understand that the fall is not a direct punishment in every case, but the consequence of ignoring God and his guidance. The verses nearby speak of foolishness, laziness and correction.

For today: guard your heart before temptation arrives. Flee from conversations, places or online spaces that seduce you, and seek God and wise people who can help you stay firm.
exp.6:16:
Here the woman says she has scented her room with three highly prized fragrances: myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.

She is the seductive woman of Proverbs 7, who goes out to catch a young man lacking judgment. She has already told him she decked her bed with fine linens, and now she uses the pleasant scent to make her invitation more appealing. Fragrances are mentioned in other Bible passages too, but here they serve a deception: she hides sin (adultery) beneath a pleasing and luxurious appearance.

Today we can remember that sin almost always comes well presented, with flattery and comfort. Before we let ourselves be carried away by what attracts us, it is wise to ask what lies behind it and where it leads. Asking God for wisdom and fleeing temptation in time protects us.
exp.1:18:
The explanation says that those who go to "her" (the strange or unfaithful woman the passage speaks of) almost never come back, and do not walk again on the paths that lead to life.

A wise father speaks to his son in Proverbs 2. He warns him against the woman who abandons her husband and forgets the covenant with God. Some see here a literal adultery; others, an image of folly and spiritual unfaithfulness. It is a warning with the tone of an alarm, not a sentence without hope: the following verse invites the reader to choose the way of the good.

Today, think about where the paths that pull you away from God begin: a friendship, a habit, a temptation. Step away in time, ask for wisdom, and surround yourself with people who encourage you to keep to the straight way.
exp.12:23:
The explanation says that a father who does not correct his son does not truly love him well. By contrast, the one who truly loves him hurries to correct him. "Refrains" means to hold back or refuse to use something. "Punishment" here is the rod, that is, discipline. "Diligently" means he does it early, with eagerness, and without leaving it for later.

Proverbs is wisdom that a father teaches his son; tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Around this verse the topics include inheritance, justice, and managing well what one has. Discipline appears as part of a wise life. Some understand the "rod" literally and others as correction in a broad sense.

For today: correcting with love and in good time is a way of caring. Do it calmly, without shouting or violence, and always seek the good of the child.
exp.24:12:
This proverb compares a faithful messenger to the cold of snow in the time of harvest. Harvest is a season of heat and hard work, so something icy would be a great relief. Yet the text says that a trustworthy messenger gives rest and joy to the one who sent him. The explanation's gloss on "refreshment" (meaning relief or renewal) and on "the soul of his master" (meaning his whole person) is not needed for your reader, so it is omitted, and the word "harvest" is already used in the verse itself.

These are proverbs of Solomon, which according to the chapter's heading were copied by the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah. They are brief sayings of practical wisdom. Here the theme is trust: whoever sends someone out needs to be sure that the person will carry out the task well. The verses nearby also speak of timely words and of empty promises. Commentators debate how snow could be found at harvest time, but the central idea is clear.

For today: be someone others can rely on. Do what you are asked, with punctuality and honesty, and you will bring peace of mind to others.
exp.3:2:
It says that the one speaking was a son dearly loved by his father. "Tender" here means gentle, cherished, and cared for with affection. The word "only" means that he was the favorite or especially precious to his mother. In other versions it appears with wording such as "only begotten" or "only," and some think this does not always mean he had no brothers or sisters, but that he was deeply loved.

The speaker is Solomon, who remembers his childhood and how his father David taught him. It is understood that he now teaches his own children in the same way. He wants to show that wisdom is passed from one generation to the next, with love and not only through rules.

For today: if you received good teaching in your home, thank God for it and value it. And if you have children or young people near you, teach them with affection and with your example, so that wisdom is not lost.
exp.24:3:
It says that if the dross is removed from the silver, the silversmith can make a good vessel. The "dross" is the impurity and residue that remain mixed with the metal when it is melted. The "silversmith" is the craftsman who works the metal with fire.

This is a proverb attributed to Solomon, later gathered by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). It stands in a section about kings. The next verse applies the image: if the wicked are removed from the king's presence, his throne is established in righteousness. A government, like silver, becomes useful when what contaminates it is taken away.

For today: ask God to show you what "dross" is in your life, such as a bad habit, a resentment, or a friendship that pulls you away from doing good. Removing it is not easy, but it allows God to use you with greater clarity.
exp.19:5:
Many people claim to be generous and good, and each one announces his own goodness. But finding someone who is truly faithful and dependable is very hard. The phrase "a faithful man" means someone who is loyal and worthy of trust.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed in large part to Solomon. Its aim is to teach us to distinguish between words and deeds. The nearby verses speak of the deep counsel of the heart and of the righteous man who lives with integrity, so the contrast is between outward appearance and character proven over the years.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our goodness shows more in what we say or in what we quietly do. Strive to be faithful in small things, keep your word, and help without seeking applause. Also be wise: do not let yourself be impressed merely by someone who talks a great deal about himself.
exp.20:30:
It says that the soldier prepares his horse for the day of battle, that is, he does everything he can to be ready. But victory does not depend on the horse or on the preparation, but on God. "Prepares" in the verse means getting the horse ready for war. "Safety" here refers to giving victory or delivering from danger.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book, and a text of wisdom. It comes right after saying that no human plan can stand against God. In that time, the horse was a symbol of military strength. The proverb does not despise preparation, but it places God above it.

Prepare yourself responsibly: study, save, plan, work. But do not place your final trust in your own resources. Do your part with effort, and hand the result over to God in prayer, with peace.
exp.29:21:
The explanation says that the earth trembles, or cannot bear it, when a servant becomes king and when a fool (a person without good sense) eats until he is full. The word "filled" in the verse means to be filled or satisfied, and "disturbs" means that it causes disorder.

These words are from the sayings of Agur, son of Jakeh, in Proverbs 30. He uses a list of "three things, yes, four" to point to situations that upset life. He is not mocking the poor; the problem is character. Some understand that the passage speaks of power or abundance that falls into the hands of someone who is not prepared. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: power, money, or success reveal what is in the heart. Ask God for humility and wisdom before receiving more responsibility, and use it to serve, not to dominate.
exp.0:4:
The wise person never stops learning: when they listen, they grow in knowledge. And the one who understands, who already has good judgment, seeks guidance, which here means wise direction for making good decisions. Where the verse says "will hear," the source has the word for listening, and where it says "attain," the source has the word for getting or obtaining.

These words stand at the beginning of the book of Proverbs, which tradition attributes to Solomon (1:1). In the verses nearby the purpose of the book is explained: to give prudence to the simple and to teach people to understand difficult sayings. This verse clarifies that wisdom is not only for beginners; even those who already know a great deal still need to keep listening. Then the text says that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.

For today: practice listening with humility. This week, ask the counsel of a wise and faithful person about a decision, and pray before you answer or defend yourself.
exp.12:19:
This verse says that the people we walk with gradually shape us. Whoever walks with wise people becomes wise. But whoever keeps company with fools, meaning those who reject wisdom and God's correction, will be destroyed, that is, will suffer harm or ruin.

Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and many are attributed to Solomon. Here the teacher, like a father speaking to his son, contrasts two paths. The nearby verses speak of accepting correction, of turning away from evil, and of the consequences of choosing well or badly.

For today: review your friendships and your influences, including what you see and hear. Seek out people who love God and encourage you to grow, and ask God for wisdom to be a good influence for others as well.
exp.14:0:
This proverb says that a gentle answer turns away anger, while a harsh word makes it grow. "Soft" and "gentle" are the words in the verse for the first kind of answer, and "wrath" and "anger" are the words for the second. Grievous words are words that cut or hurt, and "stir up" is like throwing wood onto a fire.

The book of Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here no character speaks in a scene; instead, a teacher of wisdom advises his reader. The verses that follow speak of the tongue of the wise and of the fool, and remind the reader that God sees everything. In this way, the way we speak is presented as something that matters before God.

For today: when someone speaks to you in anger, pause before you answer. Breathe, lower your voice, and respond calmly. It will not always change the other person, but it will keep the argument from blazing up further.
exp.29:14:
The horseleach is a worm that lives by sucking blood, and it has two "daughters" that do nothing but cry out: "Give, give!" Then the verse begins a list of things that are never satisfied: three, and even a fourth, that never say "It is enough." "Satisfied" means filled completely.

These words are in Proverbs 30, attributed to Agur, son of Jakeh. He is not a king but a wise man who recognizes his limits. The verse before speaks of proud and cruel people who devour the poor. That is why many understand the horseleach as a picture of unrestrained greed. Scholars debate exactly who the two "daughters" are, but the central idea is clear.

For today: examine where you feel that enough is never enough. Practice giving thanks and sharing something with someone in need; in this way greed loses its strength.
exp.5:0:
Here the wise teacher speaks to his son about a risk: to stand as guarantor means to commit yourself to paying another person's debt if that person cannot. Striking hands was a gesture of closing a deal, like a handshake. A stranger is someone outside your circle, not someone you can trust. The verse raises the case of a person who has bound himself to someone else's debt.

The speaker is a wise father, in the book of Proverbs, who gives practical advice for living with prudence. The verses that follow show that whoever makes such a commitment becomes trapped by his own word. For that reason he advises acting quickly to free himself. The Bible does not condemn helping others, but it warns against hasty or reckless promises.

For today: before you sign as a guarantor or promise money for someone, think, pray, and consult your family. Measure whether you could truly keep your word. Help with generosity, but with wisdom, and without putting at risk what God has entrusted to your care.
exp.23:24:
It says that those who rebuke the wicked, that is, those who correct him with truth, will be looked upon with favor. "Be pleasant" here means that things will go well for them and they will be accepted. And "a good blessing" means they will receive a good and abundant blessing.

This proverb belongs to a section called "sayings of the wise," which teaches how to judge fairly. Just before, it warns that favoring someone because of who he is, rather than because of what he has done, is not good, and that calling the guilty man righteous brings rejection. Here the contrast is shown: correcting with honesty, even when it costs, ends up being a blessing.

Today, if you have to speak a hard truth at work, in the family, or in the church, do it with respect and without favoritism. It may be uncomfortable at first, but honesty given with love often brings peace and trust.
exp.20:26:
It says that God rejects the offerings and religious acts of wicked people, that is, of those who live in evil without repenting. "Abomination" means something that God detests. And it is all the more so when that offering is brought with a wicked mind, a phrase that can be understood in two ways: with bad intentions (to cover up a sin or to seek some gain), or by someone who keeps living in wickedness.

It is a proverb from the wisdom tradition of Israel, attributed in large part to Solomon. Its purpose is to teach his people that true worship is not merely an outward ritual, but is joined to an upright heart and a just life. The nearby verses speak of laziness, greed, lying, and righteousness.

For today: before you pray, sing, give an offering, or serve in the church, examine your heart. If there is something you need to correct, such as a lie or an injustice, ask forgiveness and make things right. In this way your worship will be sincere.
exp.0:24:
It says that certain people rejected all of wisdom's counsel and would not accept her correction. The word for "set at nought" means they cast it aside and looked down on it. "Reproof" is a correction meant to make someone change course. The phrase about not being willing means they had no desire to receive it.

In Proverbs 1, wisdom speaks like a woman calling out in the streets. She invites the simple and the scornful to listen to her. Earlier she had offered them her spirit and her words, but they ignored her. The verses that follow show the consequences of rejecting her again and again. It is more a warning than a mocking remark.

Today, ask yourself whom you have stopped listening to because of pride. A correction from a family member, a friend, a pastor, or the Bible may hurt, but it can spare you greater trouble. Receive it with humility and pray: "Lord, teach me to listen."
exp.22:14:
Here a father speaks to his son and tells him that, if the son's heart is wise, he himself will be filled with joy. In the Bible, the word "heart" refers to the mind, the will, and the deepest desires. The old spelling of "mine" and the phrase "shall rejoice" in the verse mean the same as the modern words "my heart shall rejoice."

The speaker is a teacher of wisdom, in the manner of a father, instructing a young man. The verses before it speak of correction, and the verses after it call for speaking with uprightness and living in the fear of the LORD. His joy comes from seeing the young man choose a good path. Some understand the voice to be that of Solomon, though the text does not make this clear in this passage.

For today: if you guide children, students, or young people, pray for them and teach them by your example. And if you are young, listen to the advice of those who love you, because your wisdom brings joy to others.
exp.19:10:
Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure, and whether it be right.

This proverb says that even a child or a young person shows what they are like by what they do. Their actions reveal whether their conduct is pure (sincere, without wickedness) and right (honest, upright). A young person is simply someone who is young, and their work means what they do, their way of acting.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, though not all scholars agree on every section. The verses nearby speak of honesty, of false weights, and of the fact that no one can boast of having a perfectly clean heart. In this way the text joins what is inward with what is visible: character shows itself in conduct.

For today: if you are a parent, teacher, or leader, watch with care the actions of young people, not just their words. And if you are young, remember that your daily decisions, even the small ones, are showing who you are. Ask God to cleanse your heart.
exp.29:28:
It says there are three things that walk with grace, and a fourth that also advances with dignified bearing. "Stately stride" means a sure and majestic step. "Walks very well" means walking with dignity. The verse announces the list, which follows after: the lion, the greyhound (a swift and slender dog; the Hebrew term is uncertain), the male goat, and a king.

Agur, son of Jakeh, speaks, a wise man who reflects on creation with numerical sayings. He uses examples of animals and a king to teach us to observe with humility the wisdom God placed in the world. Here the emphasis is on steadiness and firmness.

For today: walk with confidence and firmness in what is right, without arrogance. An upright and serene life, grounded in God, has no need to pretend or to back down under pressure.
exp.21:3:
This verse says that humility and reverence for God bring good rewards: riches, honor, and life. The word "rewards" in the verse refers to a prize or payment that comes from living this way. The phrase "fear of the Lord" does not mean being afraid of God, but a deep respect and a desire to please him.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom for everyday life, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here the teaching is given as a general principle, not as an automatic promise. The verses nearby speak of God having made both the rich and the poor, and of the dangers the wicked face. Some understand the "riches" in a literal way, and others, more broadly, as blessing.

Today we can practice humility by acknowledging our mistakes and asking for advice. If we put God first, we will have a healthier and more stable life, even if it is not always richer in money.
exp.19:14:
This verse says that in the world there is gold and many precious stones, things that people admire and desire. But more valuable than all of that are wise lips, that is, the words that come out of a person with wisdom. A precious jewel is a fine gem or an object of great worth.

The book of Proverbs is largely attributed to Solomon, although not all of the sayings have a certain author. Here wisdom is taught through short comparisons. Just before, it speaks of laziness and of the buyer who criticizes the goods to pay less. Afterward, it speaks of promises and debts. The context shows how words can be deceptive or trustworthy.

Today we can take care with what we say. Before speaking, let us ask: Is this true, helpful, and kind? A wise word, such as honest advice or a timely encouragement, can be worth more than money.
exp.4:20:
It says that everything a person does is in plain view of God. The words "ways" and "paths" in the text refer to the way we live, the choices we make, and the steps we take each day. The word "pondereth" means that God watches closely and weighs what we do. Nothing is hidden from Him.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, in the book of Proverbs, which tradition attributes to Solomon. Earlier he advises him to be faithful to his wife and to enjoy her love. Then he warns that sin traps like cords. This verse is the central reason: faithfulness is not only a private matter, because God sees everything.

For today: before deciding something in secret, ask yourself whether you would do it knowing that God is watching you. Let this not frighten you, but move you to care and trust, for He also sees you in order to guide you.
exp.14:23:
The verse says that for the wise person, the path of life leads upward, and so he turns away from the depths below. The word "hell" in the King James wording translates the Hebrew "Sheol," which in the Old Testament usually means the place of the dead or the grave. A "prudent" person is one who thinks and acts with wisdom.

It is a proverb attributed to Solomon, a father-king teaching young people. It comes after advice about asking for help and speaking at the right time, and before warnings against pride. Some see here only a life protected from an early death; others also see a hope beyond the grave. The Bible does not fully make this clear in this verse.

Today: before deciding something important, ask wise people for advice and pray, so that your steps lead you toward life and not toward ruin.
exp.2:9:
It says that if someone honors God with the first and best of their earnings, their barns will be full of plenty. It also says that their winepresses will overflow with new wine, which is the fresh juice of the grape, still unfermented.

The book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon, is spoken by a wise father, or teacher, to his son. He wants the young man to trust in God and not in himself. Proverbs usually show general principles of life, not automatic promises. The passage then speaks of God's discipline, which reminds us that the life of faith also includes difficult moments.

For today: give God first place in your money, your time and your decisions. Do it with gratitude and trust, not thinking of it as a business deal to make you rich. God cares for those who honor Him, though in His own way.
exp.15:28:
It says that a wicked person deceives his neighbor with sweet and false words, and so leads him down a path that is not good. "Á" is an old spelling of "a".

This is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Here the teacher warns with a group of portraits of wickedness: the one who digs up evil, the one who stirs up quarrels, and the gossip. This verse shows that harm can also come with a friendly face, and not only with shouting. Its purpose is for the young person to learn to recognize those voices and to stay away from them.

For today: do not trust only the one who speaks to you nicely. Before following a piece of advice or an invitation, ask yourself where it would lead you and whether it agrees with what is right. And take care that your own words do not flatter in order to manipulate, but speak the truth with love.
exp.28:13:
This proverb says that a king who judges the poor with truth, that is, with justice and without deceit, will have a stable government. "Judging with truth" means deciding without favoritism or lies. "His throne shall be established for ever" is a way of saying that his authority will remain secure and lasting.

The book of Proverbs collects teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here it speaks about rulers. The verse before it warns that a leader who believes lies surrounds his government with wickedness. This one contrasts with it: the one who defends the weak with honesty stands firm. As a proverb, it expresses a general principle, not an automatic promise in every case.

Today, whether you lead a household, a workplace, or a community, treat with justice those who have less power or resources. Listen, do not lie, and do not favor only the influential. In this way you build lasting trust.
exp.5:2:
If someone has promised to answer for another person's debt and has become trapped by it, the explanation says they must act at once to get out of that situation. The phrase "Go, humble yourself" means going to the other person and asking humbly to be released from the commitment. The phrase about making sure of your friend is understood as persisting until the matter is resolved. The word "neighbor" here refers to the one who received the guarantee, the creditor.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son, within the practical counsel of Proverbs. He warns against becoming a guarantor, that is, backing another person's debt with a pledge of one's word or a handshake. His concern is to protect the son from financial ruin through a hasty commitment.

For today: before you sign as a guarantor or promise money on someone's behalf, think carefully about what you could lose. If you have already made such a commitment and it is drowning you, do not ignore it. Speak humbly and look for a solution soon.
exp.23:9:
It says that if you become slack or give up when the hard day comes, the day of distress or heavy labor, your strength is small. The word "slack" here can be understood as fainting or going limp before difficulty. The Hebrew plays on the idea of distress: the one who collapses in the moment of testing shows that his strength was small.

The book of Proverbs gathers the wisdom of Israel's parents and teachers to shape young people toward the right path. This saying sits in a section of "sayings of the wise." The verses that follow speak of rescuing those being led off to death and of not excusing yourself by saying "we did not know." That is why many read it this way: do not give up when your help and your effort are needed.

For today: when a difficult moment comes, such as a heavy burden or someone who needs you, do not hide or lose heart. Take the first step, even if it is small, and ask God for strength.
exp.9:10:
What it says: The mouth of a righteous person is like a spring of living water, giving life and encouragement to those who hear it. But the mouth of the wicked hides violence. "Well" here means a spring or fountain. The phrase "violence covers" can be understood in two ways: that their words cover up a violent intent, or that the violence they commit ends up falling back on them. Scholars debate which meaning is intended.

Context: This is a proverb of Solomon, within a collection of short sayings that contrast the righteous with the wicked. The nearby verses speak of integrity, of foolish lips, and of the prudent. The theme is the power of words to bless or harm.

For today: Before you speak, ask yourself whether your words will give life, like cool water, or whether they will wound. Today you can encourage someone with a sincere word, a kind piece of advice, or a prayer, instead of responding with anger.
exp.7:32:
It says we should pay attention to counsel, that in this way we will grow in wisdom, and that we should not treat it with contempt. "Attend" means "pay attention." "Despise" means "to hold cheap" or "to give no value to."

The one speaking is Wisdom, who in Proverbs 8 appears as a person who calls out to people. Earlier it said that it delights in the sons of men, and now it invites them like a loving father or a caring teacher. Many Christians see here a pointer to Christ, though others read it as a poetic way of speaking about God's wisdom. Its call leads to life and to the favor of Jehovah.

For today: when someone of good reputation corrects or advises you, do not react defensively. Listen calmly, pray about it, and ask yourself what you can learn.
exp.25:19:
It says that a fire goes out when no more wood is added, and that a quarrel ends when no one keeps carrying tales back and forth. A "gossip" is someone who spreads other people's business to stir up trouble. A "quarrel" means a dispute or argument.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, and this chapter speaks of fools, lazy people, and troublemakers. Just before this, it mentions someone who harms his neighbor and then says, "I was only joking." Afterward, the quarrelsome person is compared to charcoal and wood, and there is a warning that the words of a gossip seem gentle but wound deeply. The purpose is to teach readers to recognize what feeds conflicts.

For today: when someone tells you a piece of gossip, don't repeat it. You can kindly say, "I'd rather not talk about that," or encourage that person to speak directly with the one they have the problem with. In this way you stop being fuel for the fire.
exp.14:11:
This verse says that the scorner, the mocking person, does not love the one who corrects him. Nor does he go to the wise.

Proverbs are sayings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon. Here the context is correction: whoever hates it is lost, and God knows even the most hidden things of the heart. The scorner mocks everything, so he avoids the one who could help him see his mistake. The verses that follow contrast a heart that seeks wisdom with the mouth of the fool.

Today we can ask ourselves how we react when someone corrects us with good intentions. Before becoming defensive, we can pray and consider whether there is some truth in what they say. Seeking wise friends and listening to them, even when it stings a little, helps us grow.
exp.21:26:
This verse asks a warning question: if you have nothing to pay a debt with, why risk having even your bed, where you sleep, taken from you? It refers to someone who puts themselves forward as a guarantor for another person. Taking away your bed means the creditor carries off the most basic thing you have.

Here a teacher of wisdom speaks, whom tradition associates with Solomon, though this section is also connected with the sayings of the wise. He advises a young person, as a father would advise his son. The verses just before this one ask us not to shake hands on deals that guarantee other people's debts. The teaching aims to protect the family from ruin.

For today: before you sign as a guarantor or lend your name to a loan, ask yourself calmly whether you could pay it yourself. If you could not, it is wiser to help in another way.
exp.25:5:
Says that entrusting an errand or a message to a foolish person is as harmful as cutting off one's own feet. "Drinking his harm" means that the one who does it suffers the consequences of his own decision. "Fool" does not refer to someone without schooling, but to the one who despises wisdom and acts without judgment.

The book of Proverbs gathers the teaching of Israel's wise men; this chapter is traditionally attributed to Solomon, though some scholars think it was compiled later. Here the sage speaks of the fool in several verses in a row, with strong and sometimes humorous images. His purpose is to warn us whom to give responsibilities to and how to deal with someone who rejects counsel.
