Before entrusting something important, look at the character of the person, not only at his availability. Ask God for wisdom to choose well whom to trust, and so you will avoid unnecessary losses and pain.
exp.7:6:
It says that the one speaking is Wisdom, and that her words are true. She rejects wickedness: her lips detest it, meaning they loathe it and want nothing to do with it. "Ungodliness" means living and speaking without reverence for God, and also without uprightness.

In this chapter, Wisdom appears as a person who calls out loudly to everyone, and she addresses the naive (people without experience) and the foolish (those who ignore the good path). She invites them to listen because what she will say is excellent and right. Many Christians also see here a sign that points to Christ, although the text speaks directly of the wisdom of God.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself whether what you are saying is true and whether it pleases God. Work to make your words, at home or at work, honest and clean, even when it costs you.
exp.9:20:
It says that the words of a righteous person feed and strengthen many, like a shepherd who gives food to his flock. On the other hand, fools, that is, those who refuse to listen to wisdom, bring ruin on themselves through their lack of understanding. The word "feed" means to give pasture or nourishment; "die" speaks of a ruin that can reach as far as death.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, which teaches his people how to live wisely. The verses nearby speak of the power of words: the tongue of the righteous is like choice silver, and talking too much brings trouble. Here what gives life is contrasted with what leads to ruin.

Today we can ask ourselves: do my words nourish or wear down those who hear me? Before speaking, think about whether you can encourage, give honest counsel, or comfort someone. And ask God for wisdom to listen as well.
exp.20:13:
A gift given in secret calms anger, and a present kept hidden in the bosom (that is, tucked into the folds of one's clothing) soothes strong wrath. "Present" and "gift" both mean a gift, and "soothes" means to calm.

This is a proverb traditionally attributed to Solomon, a wise man who teaches through observations of life. Here it describes what usually happens; it does not necessarily approve of it. Some read it as advice for calming conflicts; others read it as a warning about bribery, because the context speaks of justice and of the wicked. It may carry both meanings.

Today, a kind gesture, such as a sincere gift or a humble apology, can soften an angry heart. But never use gifts to buy favors or to bend justice.
exp.24:27:
It says that a person who cannot control their temper and impulses is as defenseless as a city whose walls have been torn down. A "bridle" is the strap used to guide a horse; a person without a bridle is someone who lets themselves be carried away by anger, pride, or desires, with no restraint.

It is a proverb of Solomon, later copied out by the scribes of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). In that time, walls were a city's main defense; without them, any enemy could get in. The verses before it speak of moderation (too much honey), and this one closes the thought: governing yourself protects your life.

For today: think about the area where you most often lose control, for example anger, spending, or social media. Give it a concrete "wall": pause before you respond, or ask God for help and a friend to walk with you.
exp.7:0:
Here the verse says that wisdom does not hide itself: she calls out loudly, and understanding also raises her voice. The question "Doth not wisdom cry?" is rhetorical; it means "of course she does cry out." Some words in the verse need explaining: "cry" means to shout out or call out with force, and "put forth her voice" means to speak openly.

Here the author of the book speaks, a book traditionally attributed to Solomon, although scholars debate how the book came to be formed. It presents wisdom as a person, a woman who addresses the people. In the earlier chapters there were warnings against folly and temptation; now wisdom makes her invitation in public places, where everyone passes by.

For today: God does not make it hard to find his guidance. Before making an important decision, stop for a moment, pray, and listen. Open the Bible, ask advice from mature people in the faith, and consider the consequences calmly. Wisdom is calling; we must be willing to hear her.
exp.22:28:
This verse asks a series of questions to get the reader's attention. It asks who has pain, sadness, quarrels, complaints, bruises for no reason, and bloodshot eyes. The word "woe" is a cry of pain. "Contentions" means arguments and fights. "Without cause" means for no reason. "Bruises" are the marks left by blows.

The author is a wise father speaking to his son in the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon, though the book gathers several collections. Earlier he warned about immorality; now he warns about excessive wine. The answer comes in the next verse: those who stay a long time drinking.

For today: it is not enough to see the pleasure of the moment; think about what it costs afterward. If something is controlling you, such as alcohol, seek help and talk with someone you trust before it damages your health, your relationships, and your peace.
exp.21:4:
This verse says that the path of the wicked person is full of thorns and traps. The "thorns" speak of pain and obstacles; the "snares" are traps, like those used to catch animals. By contrast, the one who keeps his soul, that is, who takes care of his life and his heart, stays far away from those dangers.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition attributes largely to Solomon, although some scholars think it was compiled by several authors. Here it speaks like a teacher to his students. The nearby verses contrast the prudent person, who sees danger and turns aside, with the naive one, who keeps going and suffers the consequences.

For today: take care of what you let into your heart and your life. If you notice that a friendship, a habit, or a decision is leading you toward deceit or harm, step away in time, before you become trapped.
exp.28:23:
Whoever becomes a partner with a thief harms himself. "Partner" means companion or associate. The phrase "hates his own life" means that, in practice, he damages himself. If he hears a public curse that calls on witnesses to speak up and he stays silent, he becomes an accomplice and bears the guilt.

It is a proverb from Israel's wisdom tradition, attributed to Solomon in this section. It teaches that sin is not only what a person does, but also who he joins himself with and what he keeps quiet about. According to the law (Leviticus 5:1), whoever heard a public call to testify and did not speak carried his own guilt. It stands among warnings about pride and the fear of other people.

For today: do not cover up what is unjust out of fear or misplaced loyalty. If you know of a fraud or an abuse, look for the wise way to tell the truth.
exp.19:20:
It says that an inheritance or wealth gained hastily at the beginning will not in the end be blessed. The words "hastily" and "end" in the verse above are the ones this explanation refers to: "hastily" means quickly and in a rush, and "end" means the final outcome. Some understand this as gains obtained through greed or in unjust ways; the Hebrew allows several shades of meaning.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon in this section of the book. It speaks like a teacher advising young people. The neighboring verses deal with honesty, not taking revenge, and false weights, so the theme is living with integrity and patience.

Today, do not seek to gain quickly at any cost. Prefer honest and steady work, even if progress is slow, and trust that God blesses what is built with uprightness.
exp.21:24:
This verse gives the reason for the warning before it: do not keep company with the hot-tempered man, "lest thou learn his ways." That is, so that you do not pick up his character. The phrase "get a snare" means falling into a trap or net; in this way, a person can end up caught in a tangle that harms his own life, here called "soul."

These words belong to the sayings of the wise within Proverbs, a book of practical teaching traditionally associated with Solomon. The teacher speaks like a father to his son. His purpose is to protect the young man from harmful habits that spread through everyday association.

For today: think about who your closest companions are, including in social media and chats. Over time, frequent contact shapes our reactions. Surround yourself with patient and wise people, and do not stop treating with love someone who struggles with anger, but take care not to adopt his way of responding.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that we should stay away from the path of the stranger woman, so that we do not hand over our honour, that is, our dignity and good name, to other people. "Lest thou give" means "so that you do not give." "Unto the cruel" refers to someone merciless, who does not care for you. The years are the life and strength that a person has.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. He has already warned about the seductive woman, and here he shows the consequences: losing one's reputation, the fruit of one's labour, and one's health, and ending up grieving at the end of life.

For today: guard your integrity by setting clear limits from the start. Avoid the situations, relationships, or habits that lead you to give your life to something that wears you down and gives nothing good back.
exp.3:22:
This verse says that, more than anything else you look after, you should guard your heart, because from it flows life. "Keep thy heart with all diligence" means to watch over and protect it above everything else that needs care. To "keep" is to watch over and guard. "Issues" means what flows out, like water from a spring. In the Bible, the heart is the center of thoughts, desires and decisions.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as in all of chapter 4. Before this, he speaks of not letting his words slip from sight, since they give life. Afterward, he advises guarding the mouth, the lips and the gaze. In this way, the heart is protected in what a person says and looks at.

For today: think about what you let into your mind, such as what you see, hear or repeat. Choose something today that draws you closer to God, such as reading a Bible passage, and set aside something that fills you with anger or discouragement.
exp.30:3:
This verse says that drinking wine or strong drink is not fitting for kings or for rulers.

Here the mother of King Lemuel speaks, giving direct advice to her son. Shortly before, she warns him not to waste his strength on women. Then she gives the reason: a ruler who drinks without restraint may forget the law and pervert justice, harming those who are weakest.

About who Lemuel was, there is no certainty; it is debated whether he was a foreign king or a symbolic name.

For today: if you have some responsibility over other people, at home, at work, or in the church, guard your mind and your habits. Ask God for self-control so that you can decide with clarity and treat everyone with justice.
exp.17:20:
This verse says that words have great power: with them we can bring life, such as encouraging someone, correcting them in love, or telling the truth, or we can bring death, such as wounding, slandering, or destroying. "Power of the tongue" means that the tongue has the strength to accomplish either of these. "They that love it shall eat the fruit thereof" means that each person will receive the consequences of what they speak.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though it also contains other collections. Here the sage teaches, like a father to his children. The verses before this one speak of the fruit of the mouth and of quarrels between brothers, so the theme continues: what we say comes back to us and can either build up or break relationships.

Before responding in a discussion, pause and ask yourself: "Does this build up or tear down?" Today, try to say a sincere word of encouragement to someone.
exp.22:33:
It says that whoever gets drunk will feel like someone lying down in the middle of the sea, rocked by waves with no control, or like someone up on the top of a mast, where everything moves and there is danger of falling. A mast is a tall pole or spar on a ship. The image describes dizziness, instability and risk.

These words are part of the wisdom sayings, where a teacher, speaking with the voice of a father or a sage, warns his student. It comes after the warning about wine, which at the end "bites like a serpent." Some understand the "lying down in the sea" as a body that can no longer keep itself steady. The word "adder" refers to a poisonous snake, though it is not known with certainty which one.

For today: do not let yourself be carried away by what promises fun but takes away your control. If something makes you lose your bearings, ask someone you trust for help and set it aside in time.
exp.12:1:
A person who uses their words well will receive good things, like someone who eats the fruit of their own tree. But the "transgressors," that is, traitors or those who act with deceit and wickedness, will receive suffering. The word "shall eat" in the verse means to take in or receive, and it is used here for what comes back to a person. What we say has consequences.

The book of Proverbs collects teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though the book has several compilers. Here no character speaks in a scene; instead a teacher instructs, probably young people. The nearby verses speak of listening to counsel, guarding the mouth, and working with diligence. The common theme is that daily decisions, including our words, shape our future.

Before speaking, especially when you are upset, ask yourself: "Will this sow something good?" Today you can choose an honest, kind, and helpful word, and trust that God honors what is sown with integrity.
exp.23:19:
It says that the one who lives in wickedness has no good ending and no hopeful future. The word "candle" in the verse is a lamp; it is an image of life, light and prosperity. That the candle "shall be put out" means that the life of the wicked person will come to an end and his apparent success will not last. "Wicked" describes someone who lives without reverence for God.

This is a proverb of wisdom, part of the teaching a father or teacher gives to his child. The verses before it ask the reader not to envy evil people or join them. This verse gives the reason: although they may seem to prosper today, their path does not lead to a good destination. It is a general principle of the Bible, not a promise that applies to every individual case.

For today: when you feel envy toward someone who succeeds by cheating, remember that what shines today can be put out. Choose honesty and trust in God.
exp.4:5:
The paths of the seductive woman the author speaks of are "moveable," that is, unstable and changing, without a firm direction. The phrase "that thou canst not know them" sounds old-fashioned. Many scholars believe the Hebrew is difficult and that other translations understand it this way: she does not think about the path of life, and her steps wander without her noticing.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son. He warns against adultery, whose pleasure seems sweet at first, but ends in bitterness and ruin, as the neighboring verses say.

Today, before following a tempting path, stop and think about where it really leads. What promises excitement but has no direction or commitment often leaves emptiness. Ask God for wisdom and choose decisions that care for your life and your relationships.
exp.27:7:
He who gets rich by charging usury (loans with abusive interest) and excessive profit is, in fact, gathering that money for another: someone who will indeed show compassion to the poor. The word "gathers" in the verse means "collects." Unjust wealth does not stay with the person who piled it up.

Proverbs is wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, and this chapter contrasts the righteous with the wicked. The law of Moses forbade charging abusive interest to a needy brother (Exodus 22:25). The nearby verses speak of integrity, obedience, and how God regards those who despise his law. Some understand that God himself redirects that wealth; the text does not say how this happens.

For today: check whether, in your business, loans, or sales, you take advantage of other people's need. Prefer to gain through justice and to be generous, trusting that God cares for the poor.
exp.27:15:
This proverb compares two kinds of rulers. A "prince" is someone with authority, and "oppressions" are abuses or injustices. The leader who lacks understanding, that is, who lacks wisdom and good judgment, ends up multiplying the abuses. By contrast, the one who hates "covetousness" (the desire to gain more at the expense of others) will live a longer life.

The book of Proverbs is largely attributed to Solomon, although this chapter belongs to a section that, according to the book itself, was later copied by the men of Hezekiah. The verses around it speak of ungodly rulers who oppress the poor. The teacher wants to warn that greed in power destroys, and that justice brings stability.

Today, anyone who has some authority, whether at work, in the church, or at home, can ask: "Do I use my position to serve or to benefit myself?" Asking God for wisdom and practicing generosity protects others and also oneself.
exp.29:19:
This verse compares the adulterous woman to someone who eats, wipes her mouth, and carries on as if nothing happened. "The way" means the path or manner of acting. She treats her sin as something as simple and ordinary as a meal, and says without guilt: "I have done no wickedness."

The speaker is Agur, son of Jakeh, in Proverbs 30. Before this, he spoke of mysterious things that leave no trace, such as the eagle in the air or the ship on the sea. Adultery also hides and seems to leave no sign. Then he speaks of things that disrupt society. Some understand this saying to refer to anyone who hides their sin.

For today: do not get used to excusing your faults or saying "nothing happened." Speak to God with sincerity, ask for forgiveness, and seek to change.
exp.17:9:
It says that the name of the Lord, that is, God himself with all his character and power, is like a strong tower where one takes refuge. The righteous, the one who seeks to live uprightly before God, runs to that tower and is lifted up, that is, set on high, out of reach of danger.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition attributes in large part to Solomon, though other wise men also contributed. Here the contrast is clear: the verse that follows speaks of the rich man who trusts in his wealth as if it were a high wall, but only in his own fancy. God is a real security; riches, an illusion.

When pressure, sickness, or fear comes, do not run first to your savings or your cleverness. Run to God in prayer, remembering who he is, and rest in his care.
exp.25:15:
It says the sluggard thinks himself wiser than seven people who give him good advice. "In his own conceit" means "in his own opinion" or "in his own eyes." The number seven stands here for many, for a whole group of sensible people. Even so, the sluggard does not allow himself to be corrected.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and this part speaks of several kinds of fools. Earlier, the sluggard is described as a door that turns on its hinges without going anywhere, always in his bed. Afterward, other fools are mentioned, such as the one who gets involved in quarrels that are not his. It is attributed to Solomon, although the book brings together different collections. The purpose is to warn against the pride that shuts the ear.

For today: if you notice that you make excuses to avoid acting, ask two or three trusted people for their opinion about one neglected area of your life. Listen to them without defending yourself, and take one concrete step this week.
exp.7:5:
This verse is an invitation to listen. The word "Hear" means "listen." Wisdom says she will speak of excellent things, that is, noble things of great worth, and that her lips will speak right things, meaning just and sincere things, without deceit.

In Proverbs 8, Wisdom appears as a figure who speaks aloud, calling out to everyone, especially to the simple (those who still lack experience and good judgment) and to fools (those who act without thinking). She does not hide herself: she offers clear and trustworthy teaching. The verses that follow say that her mouth speaks truth and rejects wickedness. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, the wisdom of God, though this is an interpretation.

Today, before deciding something important, stop and listen to the wisdom of God in his Word. Ask yourself: is what I am hearing true, just, and good? Also try to speak that way yourself.
exp.5:15:
This verse begins a list of things that God rejects. "Hate" means that they deeply displease him, and "abominate with his whole being" means that they are utterly repugnant to him. The phrase "six... yea, seven" is a way of speaking found in Hebrew poetry: it announces a list and gives emphasis to the last item. It is not necessarily an exact count.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs. Just before this, he described the wicked man who sows discord and suddenly falls to ruin. Now he presents a concrete list of attitudes and actions that God detests: pride, lying, violence, planned wickedness, eagerness to do evil and, at the end, sowing division.

For today: before you speak or act, ask yourself whether what you are doing reflects what God loves. Ask him to help you let go of pride, lying, and everything that divides.
exp.20:12:
This verse says that whoever turns a deaf ear when a poor person asks for help will, one day, also ask for help, and no one will answer. "Stopping the ears" means refusing to listen and to act. A "cry" is an urgent call for help.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, largely attributed to Solomon. These sayings teach how to live justly. Here, the verse stands among sentences that speak of correction, of justice, and of the consequences of wrongdoing. It shows that a lack of compassion is not a small matter. Some understand it as a warning that a person reaps what they sow; others, as a reference to God's judgment.

For today: do not ignore someone near you who needs help. You may not be able to solve everything, but you can listen attentively, help with what you have, or stay with that person until they find support.
exp.2:14:
This verse says that wisdom is worth more than the most expensive jewels. Nothing a person could desire can be compared with it. The word "á" is an old form of "a," and "no se puede comparar" means that wisdom has no equal. (Delete this sentence? No—this sentence explains archaic wording not present in the reader's verse, so it is rewritten below.)

Corrected translation follows:

This verse says that wisdom is worth more than the most expensive jewels. Nothing a person could desire can be compared with it. The verse's wording means that wisdom has no equal.

The book of Proverbs presents a wise father or teacher who speaks to his son to guide him through life. Here he compares wisdom with silver and gold to show that its benefits last longer and are worth more than any material gain. For this reason the previous verse calls the one who finds it "blessed."

For today: before making an important decision, such as a job, a purchase, or a friendship, stop to pray and ask God for direction. Also seek the advice of wise people and read the Bible. Valuing wisdom above money helps you decide better.
exp.4:17:
This verse says that a husband should receive the love of his marriage with gratitude. The "fountain" is an image of the wife and of intimacy with her; "be blessed" means to be blessed and valued. The word "youth" is the key to the phrase "the wife of your youth," which refers to the wife you married when you were young. You are invited to rejoice with her.

The speaker is a wise father advising his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs. He warns against adultery and offers an alternative: to enjoy, faithfully, the love of one's own marriage. The preceding verses use water as a picture of the commitment that should be exclusive.

Today we can care for marriage through concrete acts: giving thanks, setting aside quality time, and choosing faithfulness every day, including in our thoughts and in how we use our phones.
exp.10:6:
The verse says that when a person who lived without God dies, what he was hoping for dies with him. Everything he trusted in, such as his money, his strength or his plans, does not go with him beyond death.

The word "expectation" in this verse means what a person hopes to receive or achieve. A "wicked man" is someone who lives without respect for God.

These words are part of the proverbs attributed to Solomon, which are wise counsel for daily life. The verses around it compare the righteous, who is guided and delivered by his uprightness, with the wicked, who falls because of his own evil. This verse adds that the hope of the wicked ends with him.

For today: check where you have placed your hope. The things of this world come to an end, but trusting in God and living with honesty gives a firmer hope.
exp.3:17:
The explanation says that the life of righteous people is like the light of dawn: it begins soft and faint, but grows little by little until it reaches the full day. "Path" means the way one walks, and "the just" are those who live uprightly before God. The dawn is the first light before the sun rises. "Perfect" here means full, complete.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son. Earlier he warned against the wicked, who cannot sleep unless they have done harm. Then he describes the way of the wicked as darkness, where they stumble without knowing what they strike against. The contrast is clear: growing light against darkness.

For today: do not be discouraged if your spiritual growth seems slow. God guides you step by step. Keep being faithful in small things, such as prayer, honesty, and daily kindness, and in time your path will grow clearer.
exp.12:6:
This proverb speaks of two people who are not what they appear to be. One makes a show of being rich: they boast and pretend to have much, but in truth they own nothing. The other makes a show of being poor: they live simply and without displays, yet they possess great wealth. Some understand this to mean material wealth, and others spiritual wealth; both readings are possible.

The book of Proverbs gathers the wisdom traditionally attributed to Solomon, addressed to those who want to learn how to live well. The verses around it contrast the righteous with the wicked, and this verse shows that appearances deceive and that true value is not always visible on the outside.

For today: do not measure your life or the lives of others by what is displayed. Avoid going into debt or pretending in order to impress, and value character, honesty, and faith, which are riches that no one can take from you.
exp.20:15:
The person who turns away from the path of wisdom, the explanation says, will end up among "the dead." The word "wanders" means to get lost or to stray from the right direction. "Will end up" means that this will be where that person arrives, their final destination. The Hebrew word translated "the dead" (rephaim) can refer to those already in the realm of the dead, the shadows of the afterlife. Some understand it as an early death, and others as complete ruin.

This is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of chapter 10 onward. It is wisdom in the form of advice from a father to his children. Around it, the text speaks of righteousness, wickedness, and the consequences of our choices. It shows that life has two paths, and that each one leads to a different place.

For today: do not move away from wisdom all at once, but drift away little by little. Review your small decisions, such as your friendships, your habits, and what you listen to, and ask God for direction. He gives wisdom to those who ask for it.
exp.10:29:
The explanation says that the life of the righteous bears good fruit, and that this fruit is like a tree of life: it nourishes, heals, and gives hope to others. The phrase "winneth souls" is an older way of saying it; the Hebrew verb can mean "take" or "win" people. Many understand it as drawing people toward good with wisdom; others see it as caring for the lives of others. Both ideas fit.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, largely attributed to Solomon. Here it contrasts the one who trusts in his riches, who falls, with the righteous one, who "flourishes." It then speaks of the righteous receiving their reward on earth. The verse shows that an upright life also benefits those around it.

For today: aim for your honest and kind conduct to be fruit that helps others. Before speaking of your faith, serve, listen, and be people of integrity. In this way your life invites others to draw near to God, without pressure.
exp.20:18:
It is better to live alone in a desert place, dry and without comforts, than to share a house with a quarrelsome and ill-tempered wife. "Quarrelsome" means someone who looks for fights and arguments; the one who "is angry" easily loses her temper. It is a deliberate exaggeration, meant to show how much peace in the home matters.

This proverb belongs to the sayings attributed to Solomon, a teacher of wisdom who instructs with short, striking sentences. The verses around it speak of luxuries misused and of foolishness in contrast with wisdom. The book has a similar proverb in 21:9 and 25:24, and it also warns against the man given to anger (22:24). The counsel is addressed to both sexes in spirit.

For today: take care of the atmosphere in your home. Before you respond in anger, pause, lower your voice, and look for a kind tone. A peaceful home is worth more than winning an argument.
exp.18:9:
It says that a fool, that is, a person who does not want to learn and lives without wisdom, is not suited to a comfortable life full of pleasures. And much less is it fitting for a servant, that is, a household worker, to come to rule over princes, who are the governing leaders. In both cases, something is out of order.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although not all scholars agree on every section. It comes after speaking of understanding and of lies. It teaches that order and honor need wisdom and character, not only comfort or power.

Today we can remember that blessings and responsibilities call for maturity. Before desiring comfort, fame, or authority, let us ask God for wisdom and for a humble yet firm character.
exp.4:0:
The explanation says that a father asks his son to pay attention to what he has learned. Being attentive means listening carefully. The phrase that invites the son to draw near in order to hear well, with humility, is an expression of humble readiness. The explanation of the old-spelling and vocabulary comments does not apply to this reader's verse, so those notes are omitted here. "Understanding" here refers to good discernment for living well.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son, as in much of the book of Proverbs. Tradition attributes the book to Solomon, though it also contains the work of other authors. This call opens a warning about sexual immorality, which the following verses develop. Before giving his advice, the father asks for a heart willing to listen.

Today we can practice truly listening. Before making important decisions, let us seek the counsel of mature and faithful people, and read the Bible with attention, ready to obey what we hear.
exp.9:25:
It says that a lazy worker is a nuisance to the one who sends him, just like vinegar that sets the teeth on edge or smoke that stings the eyes. A "sluggard" is someone idle and careless. "Them that send him" are those who give him a task and expect it to be done. If he cannot be trusted, he causes annoyance and delay.

This is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book. It is brief wisdom, with images from everyday life. Here it stands among verses that contrast the righteous and the wicked. Many understand that laziness is presented as a form of folly, although the verse does not say it in those words.

For today: carry out faithfully what you are entrusted with, whether at work, at home, or in church. If you say you will do it, do it on time and with willingness. In this way you honor God and bless others.
exp.29:32:
Here is what the verse describes: every action has its natural result. If someone churns milk, butter comes out. If someone blows his nose hard, blood comes out. In the same way, whoever stirs up another person's anger ends up causing a quarrel. Here "churning" means beating or pressing, and "strife" means argument or fighting.

Context: This closes chapter 30, which is attributed to Agur, son of Jakeh. It follows warnings about pride and advice to stay silent when one has been thinking wrongly. The book uses everyday images from farm life to teach. The word "wrath" can also be understood as anger or rage; some read it as directed at other people, and others as one's own anger.

For today: Before you insist on a subject that irritates someone, ask yourself what harvest you are preparing. A harsh word or a repeated jab rarely brings peace. Better to choose gentle and wise words, and remember that God calls us to pursue peace.
exp.6:2:
This verse asks that the father's teachings not stay only in the mind. "Bind them upon thy fingers" means tie them to your fingers, like a reminder you can always see, and "write them upon the table of thine heart" means engrave them deep within, so that they become part of you.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son. Throughout the chapter he warns him against seduction and bad decisions. Earlier he asks him to keep his commands as the apple of the eye, that is, with the greatest care. Then he invites him to treat wisdom like a close sister, so that it will protect the young man from the forbidden woman who deceives with smooth words.

Today you can choose a Bible verse, write it in a visible place, and repeat it every day. That way, when temptation or a difficult decision comes, you will already have it in your heart.
exp.2:1:
It says that whoever keeps the teaching of wisdom will receive a long life, with good years and with peace. The sentence that explains the word for length and the phrase about these blessings being added to your life is rewritten for the words in the verse: the blessings of length of days, long life, and peace are added to your life. It does not speak only of living many years, but of living well, with tranquility.

The speaker is a wise father who instructs his son, in the style of the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon. The verses before ask not to forget the law or the commandments. The proverbs express general principles of life with God, not automatic promises for every case.

For today: spend a few minutes each day reading the Bible and put one concrete teaching into practice, such as speaking the truth or forgiving. Wise habits, repeated over time, bring peace to the heart and order to life.
exp.14:1:
This proverb compares two ways of speaking. The wise person speaks in a way that makes what they know clear and appealing, like someone who presents a gift well. By contrast, the fool pours out nonsense without thinking.

Proverbs is a collection of sayings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though some passages have other authors. Here the wise teacher advises the young. The verse before speaks of the gentle answer, and the next reminds us that God sees everything, including our words.

For today: before you respond in an argument, at home or on social media, pause briefly. Ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true, kind, and helpful. Speaking with calm and humility is a practical way to live out wisdom.
exp.1:8:
This verse promises that, if you seek God's wisdom, you will come to understand what is right, what is correct when making decisions, and what is fair and impartial. "Judgment" means good sense for deciding, and "equity" means fair and even dealing with everyone. In the end, wisdom leads you to recognize "every good path," that is, the best way to live in each situation.

It is part of the teachings of a wise father to his son in Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Before this, the text says that God gives wisdom to the upright and watches over the way of his faithful ones. Afterward, it explains that this wisdom must enter the heart to protect you. In other words, understanding what is right is a gift from God that is received by seeking it with sincerity.

Before making a difficult decision, ask God for wisdom and check whether your choice is just and honest toward others.
exp.23:3:
It says that when there is knowledge, the rooms of the house are filled with things that are valuable and good. "Knowledge" here means understanding or learning; "shall be filled" means "shall be filled up"; "rooms" are the chambers or storerooms of the house; "precious" means valuable.

These are proverbs attributed to Solomon, with advice from a teacher to someone who wants to live well. The verse before it speaks of the house being built with wisdom. Earlier, it contrasts with the wicked, whose heart plans to steal. Many understand "house" as the home and the family, and the riches as blessings in general, not only money. This is interpreted in several ways.

For today: set aside time to learn and to seek advice in whatever you are responsible for, whether your family, your work, or your finances. A home is enriched more by good decisions, patience, and understanding than by shortcuts or dishonest gain.
exp.25:16:
Meddling in a quarrel that is not your own is as reckless as grabbing a dog by the ears. The word "passeth by" refers to someone who is only passing through, with no connection to the matter. The phrase "gets himself caught up in anger" means that he flares up in temper and becomes involved. A dog seized like that can turn around and bite.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of this section of the book (Proverbs 25:1 notes that the men of Hezekiah copied these sayings). Here the teacher, using the language of practical wisdom, warns against foolish conduct. The verses nearby speak of the lazy person and of the one who harms another and then says he was only joking. All of them show a lack of good sense in everyday life.

Before you give an opinion or step into an argument that is not yours, stop and ask yourself whether it is your place. Often it helps more to listen, pray, and keep calm than to add anger to someone else's conflict.
exp.8:5:
This verse is an invitation to leave foolishness behind in order to live well. The word for the naivety of someone who neither thinks nor seeks wisdom is rendered in the verse as "foolish," and the understanding that helps us choose well is the "understanding" that the verse calls us to walk in. "Live" speaks of a full life, not merely of existing.

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a woman who prepares a banquet and calls the simple, that is, the inexperienced who can still learn. She offers bread and wine as a sign of friendship and provision. Later, the text contrasts this invitation with the attitude of the scoffer, who rejects correction.

Today we can apply it this way: if you notice a habit or a decision that is pulling you away from what is sensible, do not justify it. Ask for counsel, read the Bible with humility, and take a concrete step to change course.
exp.30:20:
She does not worry when the cold comes, even when there is snow. She has already prepared her household, and everyone has clothing that is sufficient for the cold, that is, enough warmth. Some translations speak of scarlet clothing, and the original sense is not certain. Either way, the idea is that they are well protected.

Chapter 31 gathers words that, according to the text, the mother of King Lemuel taught him. From verse 10 on, the poem describes the woman of noble character. This verse still shows her work with the spindle and the distaff, and her generosity toward the poor. Her wisdom is seen in foresight and in the daily care of her home.

For today: preparing ourselves in good time and with love for whatever may come, such as saving a little, caring for our health, or attending to the needs of our family, helps us live with less fear and with more trust in God.
exp.7:17:
This verse says that wisdom offers riches and honour to those who follow her. "Durable riches" means lasting goods, the kind that do not run out easily. Along with them comes "righteousness," that is, an upright and good life before God and others.

The speaker is wisdom, who in Proverbs 8 appears as a voice calling out to people. She says she loves those who seek her diligently. The verses that follow make clear that her fruit is worth more than gold. For that reason many understand that she is speaking mainly of riches that go beyond money, though some also see a promise of practical well-being.

For today: before pursuing success or money, first aim to act with wisdom and righteousness in your daily decisions. Ask God for direction, be honest in your work, and value character more than gains.
exp.8:7:
This verse compares two responses to correction. The "scorner" is someone mocking and proud, who laughs at advice. If you rebuke him, he will probably hate you. The wise person, by contrast, is humble and wants to learn; he will value your correction and love you for it.

Here Wisdom speaks, which in Proverbs 9 appears as a woman who invites everyone to her table. She offers life to the simple, but warns that not everyone receives teaching well. The verses that follow say that the wise person grows wiser, and that the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the LORD, that is, reverent respect toward God.

For today: before correcting someone, observe how they respond to advice. Put your energy into those who are willing to learn. And ask yourself whether you receive correction with humility or with mockery.
exp.20:4:
The thoughts of the diligent lead only to abundance, and this verse compares two kinds of people. The diligent person is careful, works steadily, and plans things well; his plans lead to plenty. The hasty person, by contrast, acts in a rush without thinking, and that leads him to want.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. It teaches general principles, not absolute promises. The verses nearby speak of righteousness, humility, and riches gained through lying or violence. Thus the text contrasts the prosperity that comes from orderly work with the rush to get rich, which usually ends badly.

Today, before making a decision about money, work, or business, take time to think, plan, and seek counsel. Ask God for wisdom, and avoid shortcuts that promise quick gains.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that respecting and honoring God ("the fear of the Lord") includes hating evil. Wisdom lists what it rejects: pride (haughtiness), arrogance (thinking oneself superior), the evil way (a crooked way of living), and the froward mouth (false or harmful speech). "Hate" here means rejecting something firmly.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented as a person who calls out to people in Proverbs 8. She has just said that she is worth more than precious jewels. Here she explains that she cannot be separated from an upright life: true wisdom is not only knowing things, but living in reverence for God and turning away from evil.

For today: review your words and your attitude this week. If you notice pride or hurtful speech, ask God to help you change. Loving God shows in what we decide to reject.
exp.30:0:
This verse presents the words of a king named Lemuel. It says they are a "prophecy," that is, a serious and weighty message, which his mother taught him. The word "prophecy" here can also be understood as "warning" or "solemn teaching."

Context: No one knows for certain who Lemuel was. Some think he was a foreign king; others think it is another name for Solomon. What is clear is that the one speaking is his mother, and that she gives him advice on ruling well and living with wisdom. The following verses show her concern for him.

For today: Value the advice of mothers, fathers, and wise people who love you. Listen with humility before making important decisions, especially if you have responsibility over others.
exp.27:27:
When the wicked gain power or influence, good people hide themselves out of fear or prudence. But when those wicked people fall or disappear, the righteous grow again in number and freedom. The word "hide" is used here for "hide themselves," and "wicked" refers to those who live without respect for God; "perish" means that they fall or die.

This text belongs to the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although this chapter was probably gathered together later (Proverbs 25:1 mentions the men of Hezekiah). These are short sayings of wisdom for everyday life. Here it speaks of how unjust leadership affects a whole people, just as verses 12 and 2 of the same chapter do.

For today: pray for those who govern and lead, and do not stay silent in the face of injustice out of fear. Through your honesty at home, at work, and in your community, you help good flourish.
exp.14:14:
This proverb compares two ways of living. The person who is weighed down, burdened by troubles, is the one described as afflicted, and their days are hard and heavy. For that person, every day feels difficult. By contrast, the one with a merry heart, that is, a cheerful spirit at peace, lives as if they were always at a celebration: a feast is a festive meal shared with many.

The book of Proverbs is largely attributed to Solomon, although it also contains other collections. Here the wise teacher instructs his reader, like a father to his son, on how to live well. The verses around it speak of the cheerful heart and of preferring little with the fear of the LORD. In this way, true joy springs from wisdom, not from riches.

Today, when anxiety weighs on you, ask God for a grateful heart. Write down three things each day for which you give thanks. This does not erase pain, but it helps you see the table God has already set.
exp.13:8:
This verse says that fools, that is, people who refuse to learn or to obey God, make a mock of sin. They take it lightly, as if it did not matter. But among the upright, meaning those who live with honesty, there is favor, which means acceptance, goodwill and blessing. The Hebrew phrase is difficult, and some translations understand it differently, for example, that sin mocks fools.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon. Here it contrasts two paths: that of the fool, who deceives himself, and that of the upright, who walks with integrity. The nearby verses speak of the same contrast.

Today we can take sin seriously, without joking about what harms others or pulls us away from God. When we go wrong, it is wise to acknowledge it with humility and ask for forgiveness.
exp.28:20:
He who indulges his servant from childhood, without setting limits, will in the end find that servant behaving as if he were a son of the household. "Indulging" here means being overly soft and lenient, and "in the end" means finally.

The key Hebrew word is rare, which is why some Bibles translate it differently. It can refer to a servant who becomes insolent or who thinks he has rights that do not belong to him.

These are proverbs of wisdom, attributed to Solomon and compiled later. The verse before it speaks of a servant who does not change through words alone. The theme is discipline and character: a lack of limits forms bad habits.

Today we can apply it this way: with children, students, or employees, affection should not cancel firmness. Correct with patience, set clear limits, and be consistent. That too is love.
exp.11:4:
This verse compares what each kind of person thinks and advises. The righteous, that is, those who seek to obey God, have thoughts that are right, meaning what is upright, honest and correct. By contrast, the wicked, those who live without taking God into account, give advice that is deceit, that is, lies and trickery.

Proverbs gathers teaching on wisdom, and this saying is traditionally attributed to Solomon. Here the wise man contrasts two paths of life. The verses nearby speak of stability: the righteous have a firm root, while the wicked lie in wait and end up falling. What a person thinks inside sets the course of his life.

For today: before following a piece of advice, ask yourself who is giving it and what they are seeking. And examine your own thoughts, asking God to help you be honest, even when no one is watching.
exp.19:6:
The explanation says the righteous person lives with integrity, that is, with consistency: what they believe, what they say, and what they do go together. The word "blessed" means happy, favored. So the children of that man receive a good inheritance after him.

This is a proverb attributed to Solomon, written as wisdom for everyday life. The nearby verses speak of people who boast of being generous and of how hard it is to find someone truly faithful. This verse contrasts that with a sincere and steady life. The proverbs describe general principles, not absolute promises for every case.

Today, your children and those around you learn more from your example than from your speeches. Try to be honest in small things: keep your word, do not exaggerate, and admit your mistakes. And remember that only God makes us righteous and sustains us.
exp.3:26:
It says that we should not turn aside to the right or to the left, that is, that we should keep to the straight path without drifting off it. The "right hand" is the hand on your right side, and the "left hand" is the one on your left. At the end it asks for something concrete: to remove your foot from evil, meaning to stay away from whatever harms you.

Here a father speaks to his son, as in much of Proverbs chapters 1 through 9. It is traditionally attributed to Solomon, although the text itself does not say so in this passage. The father advises looking straight ahead, examining your own steps, and keeping an orderly life. This verse closes that teaching with a simple warning: do not wander from the path.

For today: think of a small detour that often pulls you away from what is right, such as a friendship, a habit, or an excuse. Decide today on a clear limit for that area, and ask God for help to stay firm and move forward with honesty.
exp.30:11:
It says that the woman of strength does her husband good and never evil, and that she does so always, all the days of her life. "She will do him good" is a more modern way of saying the same thing. It does not speak of perfection, but of a steady loyalty and goodwill toward him.

These words belong to Proverbs 31:10-31, a poem presented as teaching that a mother gave to King Lemuel (v. 1). It is an acrostic poem in Hebrew, shaped so it could be remembered easily. It describes the "woman of strength," or virtuous woman, and this verse explains why her husband trusts her (v. 11). Scholars debate whether it is an ideal portrait or a specific model.

For today: trust is built through good done day after day. This applies to any close relationship: today, look for one concrete act of kindness and faithfulness, without expecting recognition.
exp.30:1:
This is a repeated question, full of affection and urgency. The mother says something like: "What shall I tell you, my son? What, son of my womb, son so longed for?" The word "vows" can also be understood as "promises," or prayers she made to God for him. The Hebrew text is brief and is translated in different ways.

The speaker is the mother of King Lemuel, and she gives him advice before he rules. We do not know with certainty who Lemuel was; some think he is another name for Solomon, but this has not been proven. She begins with tenderness because what follows is a serious warning about immorality and wine.

For today: if you love someone, speak to them with kindness and with clarity. Correcting out of love is a way of caring.
exp.4:15:
The verse says that the "fountains" and "rivers of waters" would be spread out "por de fuera," that is, toward the street and the squares, so that everyone could use them. The wording is old, but the picture is simple: water flowing out of control into the open. Many scholars read it as a question, while the 1909 version presents it as a statement.

Here a wise father is instructing his son. The water represents intimate life and marital faithfulness. For that reason the preceding verse invites a man to drink from his own cistern, and the following one asks that this fountain be only for you, not for strangers. Some interpreters see here a warning against unfaithfulness; others, an image of wasting what is valuable.

Today, guard the most intimate part of your life and give it faithfully to the one God gave you, without wasting it outside.
exp.2:10:
This verse asks the son not to reject the "chastening" of God, meaning his discipline or instruction. The word "despise" means to scorn or push aside. Being "weary" of his correction means growing tired of it, bothered by it, or resentful of it. And "correction" is when God points out what is wrong so that he can guide us.

Here a wise father, traditionally associated with Solomon, instructs his son. It comes after speaking of honoring God with what one has, and the following verse gives the reason: God corrects the one he loves, as a father corrects a beloved son. Correction, then, is a sign of affection.

For today: when a correction hurts, whether it comes as advice, as a consequence, or through reading the Bible, do not shut yourself off or grow weary of it. Ask yourself with humility: "What is God trying to teach me through this?"
exp.14:30:
The explanation says that the person who pays attention to correction that helps them live well will end up living among wise people. The word "ear" here refers to the ear itself, meaning the person who truly listens. "Reproof of life" is the correction that gives life, not the kind that destroys. "Abideth" means dwells or remains there.

This proverb belongs to the collection attributed to Solomon, where a father or teacher of wisdom instructs young people. The verses nearby speak of discipline, understanding, and humility, which comes before honor. So the text teaches that receiving counsel is part of the path of wisdom and the fear of the LORD.

Today you can apply it this way: when someone you trust points out a mistake, do not defend yourself right away. Listen calmly, pray, and ask yourself what you can learn. That humility will help you grow and remain among wise people.
exp.0:3:
The explanation says that Proverbs gives shrewdness to the simple, that is, the ability to think with good judgment and know what to do. The "simple" are people without experience, who are easily led astray. To young people it offers knowledge (understanding) and discretion (good judgment, knowing how to act with prudence).

The book begins by presenting itself as the proverbs of Solomon (1:1), although some scholars think other people also helped in gathering them. Here the purpose of the book is explained: to shape character and give direction to life. It is addressed especially to those who are just starting out and can still be taught.

Today: if you are young, or lack experience in something, do not rush ahead or hold onto your own opinion alone. Seek wise counsel, read the Bible regularly, and ask mature people of faith before you decide.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that wisdom does not come only from human intelligence, but that God himself is the one who gives it. "The Lord" is the name of God. "His mouth" speaks of his word. From it come knowledge (knowing things) and understanding (knowing how to grasp them and use them well).

In Proverbs 2, a father speaks to his son and asks him to receive his words. The verses before this one encourage him to search for wisdom with the same eagerness with which people search for silver or a hidden treasure. This verse gives the reason: it is worth seeking, because God gives it. The verses that follow say that he watches over those who live uprightly.

For today: before making an important decision, ask God for wisdom in prayer and look for his guidance in the Bible. Do this consistently, not only when you have a problem, and be humble enough to learn from others.
exp.3:15:
They say the wicked cannot sleep peacefully unless they have first done something wrong. They even lose sleep if they have not managed to make someone stumble or fall. It is a way of showing that doing evil has become a need for them, almost an addiction.

Here a wise father is speaking, teaching his son. Before and after this verse he warns him to stay away from the path of the wicked. He describes them plainly so that his son will not feel drawn to their company. Then he contrasts their way with the way of the righteous, which is like the light of dawn.

Today we can be careful about who we spend time with and what influences we allow to shape us. If a group takes pleasure in harming others, it is better to keep our distance. Let us ask God that our hearts may rest in doing good.
exp.22:11:
This verse calls us to give our full effort to learning. "Apply your heart" means devoting the mind, the desires and the will to teaching, or instruction. "Turn your ears" toward the words of wisdom means listening closely and with a willingness to obey.

It is in Proverbs, a book of wise counsel. Much of it is traditionally attributed to Solomon, and this section is connected to the words of the wise. Here a teacher speaks, like a father advising his son. Before this, the text speaks of being just and not taking advantage of the fatherless; after it, of correcting the young. In this way, wisdom includes learning, being just, and accepting correction.

For today: set aside a fixed moment each day to read the Bible and listen with humility, ready to change in whatever God shows you.
exp.26:15:
This verse speaks of the quarrelsome woman, the one who is always arguing. It says that whoever tries to control her is like someone trying to catch the wind, or like someone trying to grip oil in the right hand: it slips away and cannot be held. Today we would say that "trying to hold her back" means "trying to restrain her" or "trying to hide her."

The verse before it compares the quarrelsome woman to a constant dripping on a rainy day. Proverbs gathers sayings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, that use images from everyday life. Some interpreters understand the proverb as a warning: constant conflict is impossible to control. Others read it as a satire on stubbornness in general.

Although the text mentions a woman, the principle applies to everyone: continual fighting wears down any home or friendship. Instead of trying to control others by force, let us seek to speak calmly, to listen, and to ask God for patience and peace.
exp.26:18:
As water reflects a face back to whoever looks into it, the verse says, so a person's heart reflects who that person is inside. Others read it as saying that all human hearts resemble one another. The sentence is difficult and is interpreted in more than one way.

It is a proverb of Solomon, later gathered by the scribes of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). These are short sayings of wisdom for everyday life. Here, among verses about friendship, work, and desires, the topic is knowing oneself and knowing others.

For today: look at yourself honestly. What you do and say reflects your heart, and that humility helps you understand and treat others better.
exp.22:19:
This verse advises against joining with those who drink wine to excess or those who eat meat without restraint. The words "winebibbers" and "eaters of flesh" do not refer to someone who enjoys a meal or a drink now and then, but to those who live given over to excess. Being "among" them means keeping their company and sharing their way of life.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, as in much of the book of Proverbs. The verses that follow explain the reason: excess leads to poverty and ruin. The father wants his son to guard his heart and his future. Some think the reference to eaters of flesh points to gluttony; others, to wild and unrestrained feasting.

For today: ask yourself which friendships or surroundings push you to overindulge, whether in drink, food, or spending. You can remain kind to everyone, but choose carefully who you spend most of your time with, and ask God for self-control.
exp.0:14:
A father speaks to his son and asks him not to walk alongside certain people. The way of life is pictured as a road, and "walk" and "path" describe the manner in which a person lives. Keeping your foot away from their path means staying completely clear of them, not just watching them from a distance. "They" are the sinners who invite him in the verses before.

The one speaking is a wise father who instructs his son, as in the whole opening of Proverbs. These men propose that he join them with the promise of easy riches, plunder, and a shared purse. Behind that offer lies violence, since the verse that follows says they rush to shed blood. The father warns him before he falls.

For today: think about which friendships or proposals invite you to make money or gain acceptance dishonestly. Even when they sound attractive, say no in time, and look for companions who help you live with integrity.
exp.17:5:
The explanation says that the foolish person, the one who does not think and does not fear God, always speaks in a way that provokes quarrels. The verse speaks of "contention," which means dispute or fight. The phrase "calleth for strokes" means that his mouth invites blows, as if he were looking for them.

The book of Proverbs gathers sayings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of them to Solomon. Here the wise teacher instructs his reader, like a father to his son. The neighboring verses contrast wise words, which are like deep waters, with those of the fool, which ruin himself and harm others. The theme is the power of words.

For today: before you respond in a discussion, at home, at work, or online, pause and ask yourself whether what you are about to say seeks peace or only feeds the quarrel. Sometimes silence or a gentle answer is the wisest course.
exp.9:11:
This verse compares two attitudes. Hatred stirs up quarrels, meaning it provokes disputes and arguments. By contrast, love covers all sins: it does not ignore or approve of wrongs, but forgives them instead of spreading them around.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and this one is attributed to Solomon. It speaks often about how we use our words: the gossip and the fool cause harm, while the righteous and the prudent bring life. Love that covers wrongs fits that theme. Some understand it as forgiveness, others as discretion. The New Testament quotes it in 1 Peter 4:8.

For today: when someone wrongs you, before repeating it to others or holding a grudge, consider whether you can forgive and speak with respect. If the matter is serious, talk with the person directly, seeking peace.
exp.20:23:
The explanation says that the person who acts with overflowing pride and fury is known by names such as "proud," "arrogant," and "scoffer." A scoffer is someone who mocks others with contempt. Wrath describes a harsh, hot anger. The phrase "proud wrath" means that he acts with arrogance and rage, with no respect for anyone.

These are sayings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, that teach what the good life and the foolish life are like. The verses nearby speak of guarding the mouth, of laziness, and of generosity. This proverb shows that pride and mockery become the mark of a person.

For today: before you answer with mockery or anger, pause and ask God for humility. Try to speak with respect, even when you disagree, and your reputation will be one of peace and not of pride.
exp.8:9:
This verse says that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of true wisdom. "Fear" here is not a paralyzing dread, but deep respect, reverence, and a desire to please God. "Knowledge" means understanding, and "the holy" refers to those who belong to God. Knowing Him leads to good understanding.

The speaker in this chapter is Wisdom, personified as a woman who invites everyone into her house and to her table. Before this, the text contrasts the scoffer, who mocks and rejects correction, with the wise person, who receives it and grows. This verse explains where that humble attitude comes from: from honoring God.

For today: before making an important decision, ask yourself whether you are honoring God with it. Pray, seek out His Word, and humbly accept correction from someone who cares for you.
exp.13:14:
The simple person, that is, naive and inexperienced, swallows whatever he is told without examining it. The prudent person, by contrast, the careful and wise one, thinks before acting and considers where his steps are leading him.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom that tradition attributes in large part to Solomon, though it also contains other collections. Here a teacher of wisdom instructs young people. The neighboring verses contrast the wise with the foolish: one fears evil and turns away, the other rushes ahead and trusts too much. This verse fits into that teaching about prudence.

Today, before sharing a piece of news, accepting an offer, or following advice, take a moment to verify, ask questions, and pray. Believing is not always wrong, but prudence watches your steps.
exp.20:11:
The verse says that the righteous person carefully observes the house of the wicked, that is, their life and their family, and sees how the wicked are brought down by their own wickedness. The word "overthroweth" means ruined, cast down. Here there is a difficulty: some understand "the righteous man" to be an upright person who reflects on the end of the wicked; others think it refers to God, the Righteous One, who watches and overthrows the wicked. Both readings are possible.

This is in the book of Proverbs, which gathers the wisdom of Solomon and other wise teachers to teach people how to live well. The verses around it contrast the wicked person, who desires evil and has no compassion for his neighbor, with the wise person, who learns when he is corrected. The message is that wickedness has consequences.

For today: instead of envying those who prosper by cheating, learn from what you observe. Choose to live with honesty, knowing that evil ends up destroying the one who practices it.
exp.1:7:
He watches over the "paths of judgment," that is, the ways of justice and of doing what is right. He also protects and keeps safe the way of his "saints," who are those who belong to him and seek to live for him. The word "preserves" means to keep, to take care so that nothing is lost.

These words are part of a father's teaching to his son in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. He invites the reader to seek wisdom with all their heart. In the verses nearby he explains that God gives wisdom to the upright and is a shield for those who walk with integrity. So the verse shows that God cares for the one who desires to walk well.

For today: when you have to make difficult decisions, ask God for direction and walk with honesty. You can trust that he watches over your path, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.5:23:
The commandments and the teaching of parents serve to protect us from the evil woman, that is, from the unfaithful or immoral woman. "The flattery of the tongue" means smooth, flattering words full of praise and charm. "The strange woman" is the woman who belongs to another man, the one who is not your own wife, and who seduces with her words.

The one speaking is a wise father, in the book of Proverbs, who is instructing his son. Earlier he has said that his teachings are like a lamp that guides, watches over, and accompanies day and night. Now he explains one of their functions: to warn against the seduction of adultery, which promises pleasure but brings ruin, as the verses that follow say.

For today: do not trust your willpower in the moment of temptation. Fill your mind with the Word of God ahead of time, and stay away from conversations or messages that flatter you and lead you to betray your commitments.
exp.26:17:
It says that whoever tends a fig tree will get to eat its figs, and that whoever faithfully serves his master will be honored. "Keepeth" here means to look after, to tend with care. "Honoured" means that he will be valued and rewarded.

This verse is in a collection of proverbs that tradition attributes to Solomon, although the book also mentions other compilers. They are sayings of wisdom for daily life. It uses two images common in the ancient world: the cultivation of a tree and service to a master. Both show that constant and patient work brings good results.

For today: do your work well and faithfully look after what has been entrusted to you, whether it is a job, a studies, or a family. You may not see the fruit right away, but daily faithfulness usually brings reward and a good name over time.
exp.0:26:
This verse describes how the consequences of ignoring wisdom arrive. What is feared comes suddenly, like a storm that sweeps everything away, a whirlwind that tears through everything in its path. Disaster is a catastrophe, and distress and anguish speak of deep pain and of a tightness felt in the heart.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented as a woman who calls out in the streets (Proverbs 1:20-33). She offered counsel and correction, but people rejected them. That is why she warns that when the disaster comes, it will already be too late. The mocking laughter she describes is not human cruelty; it is a strong image meant to show how serious it is to despise a warning.

For today: do not wait for the storm to arrive before you listen. Accepting wise counsel in time, even when it is uncomfortable, can spare you a great deal of pain. Today you can ask God for the humility to receive correction.
exp.17:16:
What it says: The one who presents his case first usually sounds convinced and in the right. But when the other person arrives and examines him with questions, details come to light that were missing. The word "searcheth" means to investigate thoroughly, like measuring how deep the water is.

Context: This is a proverb from the wisdom tradition of Israel, which the Bible largely attributes to Solomon, although the book gathers several collections. Here the subject is lawsuits and disputes, as in the verses that follow. The verses before it praise the one who listens and seeks wisdom, and that helps us understand the advice.

For today: Before judging a conflict, listen to both sides. And when you tell your own version, do it with humility, willing to have others ask you questions and to acknowledge what you had not seen.
exp.25:13:
It says that a door turns on its hinges (the "hinges" that the verse calls the pivots), but it does not leave its place. In the same way the lazy person turns over and over in bed: he moves a lot, but he goes nowhere. It is a picture with humor.

The one speaking is a teacher of wisdom, a father who teaches his children. This section of Proverbs is attributed to Solomon and was copied by the men of Hezekiah (25:1). The verses around it make fun of the lazy person: he invents excuses, such as there being a lion in the street, and he is so unwilling to work that he cannot even bring food to his mouth.

For today: if you notice that you turn over and over without doing what you should, choose one small task and begin now. Ask God for strength, and arrange your day so that you act, not just turn over.
exp.11:12:
This verse says that the wicked person is caught as in a trap by the lies and evil words that come out of his mouth. The "impious" person is someone who lives without respect for God. "Prevarication" means deceit, falsehood, or wrongdoing in speech. By contrast, the just person, that is, the one who lives uprightly, will come out well from distress or "trouble."

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition attributes largely to Solomon, although it contains other collections as well. Here the teacher speaks like a father giving advice. The neighboring verses speak of how our words and actions bring consequences: what we sow with our mouths and our hands, we reap.

For today: before speaking, think about whether what you are about to say is true. A lie seems to help for a moment, but then it traps us. Speaking honestly, even when it costs us, gives us peace and trust.
exp.4:13:
This verse says that the person laments: "I was almost in all evil in the midst of the congregation and assembly." The word "almost" means that he came very close to total ruin. The words "assembly" and "congregation" refer to the people gathered together, the people of God, who witnessed his shame.

It is a man who, at the end of his life, acknowledges his mistake. Solomon, as a father, warns his son about the strange woman and adultery (Prov 5:1-13). This man pictures the cries of someone who ignored the advice and now suffers the public consequences of his sin.

For today: listen in time to those who counsel you wisely, whether in your family or in your church. Accepting an uncomfortable correction today can spare you pain and shame tomorrow. Pride and rebellion cost dearly; humility protects.
exp.2:6:
It says that we should not consider ourselves wise on our own. Instead of relying only on what we think, we are invited to fear the Lord, which means to respect him and take him seriously with reverence, and to depart from evil, that is, to stay away from what harms us. The old wording of the verse uses forms that are no longer common, but the call is the same: to turn away from evil.

The book of Proverbs presents wisdom in the form of advice from a father to his son. Here the teacher follows his own call to trust God with all the heart. The verses that follow say that this attitude will bring health and strength, expressed with images that speak of the whole body.

For today: before an important decision, pause, pray, and ask for advice from wise people and from God's Word. Recognize that you can be wrong, and let God correct your course.
exp.10:22:
What it says: The righteous only long for what is good, that is, they want good for themselves and for others. But what the wicked hope for ends in wrath, an expression understood here as anger, punishment or judgment. In other words, their hope leads them to frustration and to the displeasure of God.

Context: This proverb belongs to the wisdom attributed to Solomon, a father instructing his son on how to live well. The verses nearby contrast the evil man, who will not go unpunished, with generosity that brings blessing. Thus the desire of the righteous shows itself in the way they give and serve.

For today: Examine what you truly desire. Before seeking something, ask yourself whether it will do good to others and whether it pleases God. Today, do one concrete act of generosity or help.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that a wise person can be given instruction, and by receiving it will grow even wiser. The same is true of the just person, that is, the one who lives in an upright way: if he is taught, he will increase in what he knows. The verse's phrase "increase in learning" means growing or gaining more knowledge.

Proverbs 9 presents Wisdom as a woman who invites everyone to her table. Before this verse, it is noted that correcting a scoffer brings trouble, because he does not accept correction. Afterward, it is said that the fear of the LORD, that is, respecting God with reverence, is the beginning of wisdom.

For today: ask yourself whether you receive correction and advice well. This week, ask someone you trust to tell you where you could improve, listen without getting defensive, and thank God for that help.
exp.24:9:
This verse warns that if you tell others a secret that was not yours to reveal, the one who hears it could bring shame upon you. "Put to shame" means to make someone look bad and take away their good name. "Infamy" is a bad reputation, and "turn away" means to be restored or set right. In other words, the damage to your reputation could no longer be corrected.

Proverbs 25 gathers sayings attributed to Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah copied, according to verse 1. It is wisdom from a father or teacher advising young people. Here it speaks of conflicts with another person: it is best to resolve them in private and not spread other people's secrets, because a careless tongue can destroy your own credibility.

For today: when you have a problem with someone, speak with that person first, directly and calmly. Avoid bringing the matter up on social media or among friends, because a word said too much cannot be taken back afterward.
exp.23:26:
It says first to prepare well the work of the field, that is, what provides livelihood. The word "prepare" means to get ready or set in order; "work without" is the labor done outside, such as planting and tending the ground; "field" is the land a person owns. Only after securing that, the proverb says, should one "build thine house," which can be understood as constructing a dwelling or also as establishing a home.

It is a proverb within the wisdom collections attributed to the sages of Israel. Its purpose is to teach order and prudence. The nearby verses speak of uprightness, honesty, and not taking revenge, so this verse adds another trait of the wise person: planning with patience and not rushing. Some read it as economic advice; others, as a broader principle of priorities.

For today: before taking on a large expense, such as a house or a loan, secure your source of income and your stability. Put the basics first and then the rest.
exp.16:27:
Even a fool, when he keeps quiet, is considered wise, and the person who keeps his lips shut is regarded as a person of understanding. The word "fool" refers to someone without good judgment. The phrase "is considered wise" means that people regard him as wise. "Understanding" means intelligent and prudent.

This is a proverb within the collection attributed to Solomon. It offers practical wisdom for everyday life, not the speech of any particular person. The verse before it speaks of holding back one's words, and this verse reinforces that idea: speaking less often protects one's reputation. It does not say that the fool becomes wise by staying silent, but that he appears wise.

For today: before giving your opinion in a discussion, at work, or on social media, pause. Listen first, and speak only if you have something useful or kind to offer. Knowing when to stay quiet prevents many mistakes.
exp.29:13:
