This verse describes a kind of people whose cruelty is so fierce that their teeth seem like swords and their back teeth like knives. Their aim is to devour the poor and the needy, that is, to abuse them and take advantage of their weakness. "Generation" here means a class or type of people. "Needy" refers to those who lack what is necessary.

These words are part of the sayings of Agur, son of Jakeh (Proverbs 30:1). He lists several kinds of people who concern him: the proud, those who think they are pure when they are not, and those who oppress. Then he goes on to the leech and to things that are never satisfied. In this way he shows that greed has no bottom.

For today: check whether, in your work or your business, you take advantage of someone in a weaker position. And better still, look for a concrete way to help a person in need, with justice and generosity.
exp.25:18:
This verse speaks of someone who harms a friend with deception or blows and then defends himself by saying, "I was only joking." The phrase "does harm" means to hurt someone, and "was joking" means he was playing or fooling around.

The context is the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon and which offers wise counsel for everyday life. In this part, a person who toys with conflict and lies is compared to someone who shoots burning arrows without thinking about the consequences. The verses that follow describe how gossip and quarrelsome people keep fights alive.

For today: before making a joke, ask yourself whether it truly makes the other person laugh. If someone has been hurt, ask for forgiveness without excuses and without saying "it was only a joke." Love takes care of a friend's feelings.
exp.25:1:
It says that just as a sparrow that flutters about or a swallow that flies does not settle anywhere, a curse spoken without a just cause does not reach its target. To wander means to go back and forth from one place to another, and a curse is a word spoken to wish or bring harm on someone.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, and here a teacher instructs young people with images from nature. It comes after verses about the fool, and the contrast is clear: honor does not suit the fool, but an unjust curse also fails to achieve its effect. Some understand that God does not allow it to prosper, and others see it only as a general observation.

If someone speaks ill of you without reason, do not live in fear. Examine your heart with humility, trust in God, and do not repay evil with evil.
exp.16:20:
This verse says that having a foolish son brings sorrow. The word "begetteth" means "has a son" or "fathers." "Fool" refers to people who lack wisdom, who despise good advice, and who live foolishly. For that reason, the father of such a person finds no joy, only sorrow.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed in large part to Solomon. It is the wisdom of a father teaching his son. Here the "fool" is not someone with little intelligence, but someone who rejects God and correction. The verses nearby speak of a corrupt heart, a harmful tongue, and a sorrowful spirit, and they show how decisions affect the joy of the family.

For today: if you are a father or mother, teach with patience and pray for your children. If you are a son or daughter, remember that the way you live brings joy or sorrow to your family. Seek the wisdom of God.
exp.9:13:
The explanation says that wise people store up knowledge, that is, they guard it and do not let it go carelessly. By contrast, what the foolish person says brings near ruin. "Calamity" means disaster or harm. His careless words soon bring trouble both on himself and on others.

This verse is part of the proverbs of Solomon, according to the heading of the book (Proverbs 10:1). These are short sayings that teach us to live with common sense and the fear of God. Here two kinds of people are contrasted, which is very typical of this chapter. The nearby verses also speak of the value of prudent words and the harm of foolish words. Some understand that "lay up" includes knowing when to keep silent, while others take it to mean continuing to learn.

Today, before replying in anger or talking too much, pause. Ask God for wisdom and listen first. That can prevent many conflicts.
exp.16:8:
He who covers over another's offense, that is, forgives it and does not go around spreading it, seeks to cultivate affection and friendship. But the one who brings the matter up again and again, who keeps returning to the issue, ends up separating friends. Here, an offense or wrong committed against someone is what the verse calls a transgression.

The book of Proverbs is attributed largely to Solomon, although scholars debate how it was compiled. It offers words of wisdom for everyday life. This verse appears among sayings about words, bribes, and correction, and it shows that what we say can either unite or divide.

If someone offended you and has repented, do not make it a topic of conversation or remind them of it in every argument. Truly forgiving includes not telling the matter to others. This does not mean tolerating abuse or staying silent about serious harm that needs help or justice.
exp.14:3:
This verse compares wholesome words to a tree of life: they bring freshness, nourishment and encouragement to the one who receives them. A "wholesome tongue" is a way of speaking that heals, calms and builds up. "Perverseness" is wickedness or falsehood in speech, and it leaves a person wounded inside and without strength.

Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of them to Solomon. Here it speaks to anyone who wants to live well before God. The nearby verses contrast the wise and the foolish, and they remind us that the LORD sees everything. Our words therefore matter to Him too.

Before you respond in an argument or comment on someone else, stop and ask yourself whether your words will lift up or hurt. Today you can choose to sincerely encourage a person in your family or at work, and to avoid sarcasm, mockery and lies.
exp.26:9:
The explanation says not to abandon your friend or your father's friend, meaning to take care of loyal friendships and family ties. It says that a near neighbor helps more than a brother who lives far away.

The Book of Proverbs is largely attributed to Solomon, and these chapters were collected later. A wise person speaks here, advising like a father to his son. Before that, it speaks of the friend who gives advice with affection. The line about the brother's house can be understood in several ways: perhaps not going to burden him with your problems, or that in a crisis the person who is close by helps more.

Today, cultivate good relationships with those who live near you. Greet them, help them, and be faithful, so that there is mutual support when a need arises.
exp.23:16:
This verse asks us not to rejoice when our enemy falls into trouble. The words "rejoice not" mean "do not be glad" or "do not take pleasure in it." And "stumbleth" means that he fails or takes a wrong step. God does not want the heart to fill with gladness at another person's misfortune, even when that person has done us harm.

Proverbs are teachings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, and this section presents sayings of the wise to give counsel. Earlier it speaks of the righteous who falls and rises again, and of the wicked who falls into evil. Later it says that the Lord sees the heart and can be displeased. That shows that God cares about our inner attitude, not only our actions.

Today, if someone who offended you suffers a setback, avoid mocking or secretly celebrating. Better to keep silent, pray for that person and, if you can, help them.
exp.19:23:
It says that God directs the steps of each person. The name for God in this verse is "the Lord." "Path" is the course of one's life. The closing question shows that no one fully understands their own journey, because God works beyond what we can see.

This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, though not all scholars agree on every saying. These are teachings of wisdom for daily life. Here, among warnings against revenge and deceit in business, the verse reminds us that God governs life, so there is no need to take justice into our own hands or cheat to get ahead.

Today, when you do not understand why your life has taken a certain direction, trust God. Do what is right, plan wisely, and be honest, and leave in his hands what you do not control. His guidance does not depend on your understanding everything.
exp.20:20:
This verse says that whoever truly pursues righteousness and kindness toward others finds something very valuable. The verse uses the word "followeth," meaning to go after something with effort and determination. "Mercy" means compassion and generous treatment of others. "Findeth" means will find. The promise is life, righteousness, and honour, that is, a full life, a good standing before God, and a respected name.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition attributes largely to Solomon. This saying is part of a collection of short pieces of advice, without a continuous thread. The verses nearby speak of prudence, of the foolishness that squanders everything, and of wisdom being worth more than strength. Proverbs describe how things usually go; they are not automatic promises.

Today we can choose one concrete act of justice or compassion each day, such as paying what is fair, forgiving, or helping someone in need. In this way we gradually form a character that God honours.
exp.10:19:
It says that God finds repugnant people with a crooked heart, that is, those who inwardly think and plan evil, even though outwardly they appear to be good. On the other hand, he takes delight in those who are "upright in their way," that is, those who live with integrity, without duplicity. "Abomination" means something that God detests. "Upright" here does not speak of people without faults, but of people who are righteous and sincere. "Delight" means that he is pleased with them.

This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon in this section. It is wisdom in the form of a contrast: the wicked person against the upright one. The surrounding verses speak of how wickedness does not yield lasting fruit and how righteousness leads to life. These are general principles about how life tends to be under God's care, not mechanical promises.

For today: God looks at the heart. This week, examine your motives and seek to make what you do in front of others match what you think in private. Ask God to help you be sincere.
exp.26:26:
The explanation says that goats give not only meat or wool, but also plenty of milk. That milk was enough to feed the one who tends the flock, his whole household, and also the maidens, that is, the women who worked in the house. The words that were quoted from the source, which mean food and what is needed to live, simply describe the food and provision the verse speaks of.

These verses close the book of Proverbs, which tradition attributes to Solomon and to other wise men who were gathered together later. Here the teacher advises the shepherd: know your livestock well and take care of it, because your provision will come from it. The verses before speak of lambs, young goats and pasture, and show how God provides through diligent work.

For today: value what God has already given you, whether it is work, studies or a small business, and care for it with steadiness. That is often where your provision lies, and you can also share it with your family and with others.
exp.27:26:
He who gives to the poor will not go lacking, but he who shuts his eyes to their need will receive many curses. "Shutting one's eyes" means pretending not to see the person who is suffering. "Curses" here is understood as reproach, rejection, or painful consequences; it is not a magical punishment.

It is a proverb of Solomon, a teaching of wisdom to guide everyday life. The verses around it speak of trusting God and not in oneself. Giving to the poor shows that trust: we believe God takes care of us. The proverbs describe general tendencies, not automatic promises in every case.

Today, truly look at the person in need close to you: a neighbor, a relative, someone in your church. Give something concrete, even if it is small, with joy and without showing off.
exp.9:16:
This proverb says that whoever accepts and keeps instruction walks on the path that leads to life, that is, to a good and full life. By contrast, whoever refuses correction goes astray, which means he makes a mistake and wanders off course. Also, the word "abandons" here means to give up on or to look down on. It can also be understood that this error drags others along, although the Hebrew text allows several readings.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, and in this chapter the sayings are brief and contrast the wise person with the fool. The verses around it speak of the life of the righteous, the harm of lying, and care in speech. Here the teaching is that listening to the one who corrects us is part of the wise path.

Today, the next time someone points out a mistake of yours with good intentions, do not answer right away in defensiveness. Listen, think about whether there is truth in what they say, and ask God for humility to change.
exp.6:9:
It says that suddenly a woman appears who approaches the young man walking along the street. She is dressed like a prostitute, that is, in clothing that draws attention and reveals her intentions. He also describes her as "crafty of heart," meaning she has a scheming mind, one that knows how to hide her true plans and deceive.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son. Throughout chapter 7 he tells this scene to warn him about the danger of unfaithfulness and of temptations that seem attractive but lead to ruin. The young man, lacking good judgment, walks in the dark near her house.

For today: temptations almost never show up with their real face. Be careful about the places and times you walk by, and ask God for wisdom to flee in time.
exp.13:13:
He who turns away from good judgment, or from God, will end up filled with the consequences of his own ways. The word for "filled" here means fully satisfied, having received everything he sowed. The good man, by contrast, will be content with the fruit of his path. Some translators understand that his contentment comes from his own conduct, and others that it comes from God.

This is a proverb, largely attributed to Solomon, that teaches wisdom through contrasts. The verses nearby warn that a path can seem right and still end badly, and that the wise person thinks carefully about his steps. Here it is shown that every path has its outcome.

Today, before making a decision, ask yourself: "Where does this path end?" Ask God for direction and choose what is right, even if it takes time to bear fruit.
exp.11:1:
The explanation says that a good person receives the approval and kindness of God, but that God will declare guilty the one who plans evil. "Will receive favor" means that the good person will receive God's pleasure. "Will condemn" means that God himself will judge. "Evil devices" refers to the crooked plans and intentions of the heart, not only to actions.

This is a proverb from Hebrew wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, that teaches young people how to live. It comes right after a passage about accepting correction, and before a statement that wickedness does not bring stability. The whole passage contrasts two paths: that of the wise person and that of the wicked. It is a general principle, not a promise that always comes true immediately.

Today we can examine not only what we do, but what we plan and think. Ask God to cleanse your intentions, and seek to be good at heart, trusting that He sees what no one else sees.
exp.3:8:
It says that wisdom, if we value it, will place on our head an ornament of grace, that is, something that makes us look good and pleasant. It also says that it will deliver to us a crown of glory. The word "give" in the verse is a gift we receive from her, and "deliver" means it is placed into your hands. It is an image: wisdom honors us the way a person is honored when they receive a crown.

Here a father speaks to his son, in the style of Proverbs, which tradition attributes to Solomon. He urges him to seek wisdom before anything else. The verses before it speak of embracing her and exalting her, and the verses after it speak of listening so as to live many years on upright paths.

For today: before deciding something important, take a moment to ask God for direction and to listen to wise counsel. Whoever practices this consistently gradually forms a character that others respect.
exp.24:18:
It says that trusting someone who is disloyal when you are in trouble is as painful and useless as chewing with a broken tooth or walking on a foot that slips. A "traitor" is someone who betrays, breaks their word, or acts with deceit. When we most need support, that person fails us and does us harm.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed mainly to Solomon, and this chapter, according to its heading, includes sayings that the men of Hezekiah copied. Here the theme is relationships: earlier it speaks of false testimony against a neighbor, and afterward of how to treat the afflicted and one's enemies. The wise person wants to teach us to discern whom we can truly trust with our lives.

For today: be wise in choosing whom you trust in difficult moments, and seek to be someone faithful and dependable to others.
exp.2:12:
It says that the person who finds wisdom and gains understanding is happy and blessed. "Blessed" means happy, favored by God. "Finds" is the word for coming across something, and "gains" refers to reaching or winning it. Wisdom is knowing how to live well, and understanding is grasping things and telling them apart.

The speaker is a father (tradition attributes this to Solomon) who is giving advice to his son. Just before this, he asks him not to reject God's correction, because God corrects the one he loves. Then he compares wisdom with silver and gold, to show that it is worth far more. In this way, correction and wisdom go hand in hand.

For today: when you receive difficult advice or correction, do not harden yourself. Receive it with humility and ask God for wisdom, since it enriches your life more than money does.
exp.17:14:
The person of understanding does not settle for what they already know: their heart, that is, their mind and will, acquires wisdom. And the wise keep their ear attentive so they can keep seeking knowledge. The wise learn all the time, and they do it by listening.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although the book brings together several collections. Here the counsel is connected with the preceding verse, which calls foolish the one who answers before listening. The wise person, by contrast, listens first, and that is why they grow.

Today you can put this into practice this way: in your next difficult conversation, listen fully before giving your opinion. Ask a question, and ask God for humility to learn from what you hear.
exp.13:22:
It says that all hard work brings some benefit, even if it is small, but being content with words alone leads to poverty. The word "labour" is hard work or effort. The word "profit" is gain or benefit. The phrase "the talk of the lips" refers to talking a lot, making promises, or showing off without doing anything.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon, though the book gathers wisdom from several voices. It speaks like a teacher advising his people. Around it are counsels about showing mercy to the poor, truthfulness, and honesty. Here the person who acts is set against the person who only talks.

For today: if you have a goal or an unkept promise, take one concrete step today. Begin working on it, instead of only talking about it. God values diligence and a word that is kept.
exp.9:17:
This verse speaks of two mistakes made with the tongue. The first is hiding resentment behind friendly words: whoever does this has lying lips, meaning they speak falsely. The second is spreading a slander, which means spreading gossip or accusations to harm another person's name. The Bible calls the one who does this a fool, that is, someone without wisdom.

These are sayings of wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, directed above all at young people learning how to live well. In this chapter the righteous are contrasted with the wicked, and it often speaks of the power of words. The following verse warns that talking too much makes sin easier.

For today: if someone has hurt you, do not pretend all is well while you keep resentment inside, and do not relieve it by speaking badly of that person. Speak honestly and respectfully with the right person, or hand that pain over to God and be silent.
exp.6:6:
This verse says that the one speaking noticed a group of naive people, or "simple" ones, and among the young men he discovered one who was "a young man void of understanding." The "simple ones" are those who are easily led along, without thinking about where their path is taking them. "Young man" simply means a youth. "Void of understanding" means he lacked wisdom and good judgment.

The one speaking is a wise father, teaching his son. From his window he observes a scene in the street and recounts it as an example. It is a warning against the forbidden woman and her smooth, deceptive words. Many understand Solomon to be the author, although the text itself does not state this here.

For today: a lack of wisdom usually does not show up all at once, but in small, careless decisions. Ask God for discernment, listen to wise counsel, and stay away in time from places and situations where you know you could fall.
exp.11:7:
This proverb says that a person is recognized and praised for their wisdom, that is, for their good judgment and sensible way of living. On the other hand, whoever has a twisted or crooked heart (someone who deliberately turns away from what is good) will end up being despised. Despised here means held in contempt, looked down on with scorn.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, aimed at forming character. Here the author repeatedly contrasts the righteous with the wicked. The verses around it speak of words that wound or deliver, and of the house of the righteous that stands firm. This verse adds that wisdom brings genuine respect, and that inner wickedness eventually reveals itself.

For today: take more care of your character than of your image. Seek counsel, act with honesty, and think before you speak. Over time, that builds a good reputation without your having to pretend.
exp.28:15:
It says that when the wicked increase, transgression also increases, along with rebellion and sin. But the righteous, those who live uprightly, will see the fall of the wicked.

This is a proverb from Hebrew wisdom literature, traditionally attributed to Solomon, although the book also gathers other sayings. It sits among verses about good government, the discipline of children, and the need for God's guidance. It seems to show that when wickedness grows in a society, sin multiplies, but God's justice ultimately prevails.

Today it encourages us not to despair when evil seems to abound. We can keep living with integrity at home, at work, and in the community, trusting that God has the final word.
exp.7:15:
This verse says that princes rule and that rulers or judges govern and administer justice on the earth thanks to wisdom. The phrase "rule" here means to command or direct, and the words about judging the earth mean that they exercise authority through fair decisions. The idea is that good government depends on wisdom.

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a person who calls out to people in Proverbs 8. She explains her worth: she has counsel, understanding, and strength. The verses that follow show that she loves those who seek her and gives lasting riches and justice. Many understand this to be a poetic device; others see in her a foreshadowing of Christ, and this is debated.

For today: if you have some responsibility over others, at home, at work, or in the church, ask God for wisdom before you decide. Listen to counsel, seek justice, and do not look only at what is convenient for you.
exp.24:17:
The explanation says that a person who falsely accuses their neighbor is like a weapon that wounds: a hammer that strikes, a knife that cuts, and an arrow that pierces. "Bearing false witness" means lying about someone, especially when it is stated as if it were true. The three images show that a lie is not a simple mistake but causes real harm.

This is a proverb of Solomon, preserved in the time of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). It is a wise saying from a father or teacher who teaches how to live well with others. The verses nearby speak of moderation, respect for one's neighbor, and misplaced trust.

For today: before you comment on something about someone, whether in person or on social media, ask yourself whether it is true, whether you know it for certain, and whether it helps. If you are not sure, it is better to keep silent.
exp.1:0:
It says that a father speaks to his son and asks him to receive his words and keep his teachings deep within himself. The phrases "if thou wilt receive" and "and hide" are the wording of the verse itself, so they are not explained here; this sentence simply opens a statement that continues in the verses that follow.

The speaker is a wise father, and in Proverbs he is traditionally associated with Solomon, although the text itself does not say so here. He teaches his son with affection and shows that wisdom does not come on its own: it must be received, treasured, and sought with attention. The verses that follow speak of listening, inclining the heart, and crying out for understanding.

For today: it is not enough to hear good advice or to read the Bible. Choose a short passage this week, read it each day, meditate on it, and ask God to help you put it into practice.
exp.21:23:
This verse advises against becoming a close friend of someone who gets angry easily. "Mixing yourself in" here means getting involved with or joining up with such a person. The angry person is one who quickly fills with rage, and the man of temper is someone who lives irritated and often lashes out.

These words are part of the Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, which teach practical wisdom for everyday life. Just before this, the text speaks of justice toward the poor, and then it explains the reason: a person can pick up the ways of another and fall into a trap. It is the advice of a teacher who wants to shape someone well.

For today: think about your closest friendships and ask yourself which habits you are copying. You can treat everyone with respect, but choose as your constant companions people who help you become patient and respond with calm.
exp.29:31:
If someone has fallen into shame or failure, it was often because they thought more highly of themselves than they should, out of pride. And if a person has plotted something wrong in their mind, they should stop themselves in time. The verse's call to put a hand over the mouth means keeping quiet and not going any further.

Chapter 30 begins with the words of Agur, son of Jakeh, a wise man about whom we know very little. Before that, it speaks of animals and of a king, which inspire respect. Then it uses the example of churning milk and blowing the nose: forcing things brings consequences. In the same way, pride and anger, when they are fed, produce trouble.

For today: if you notice a proud, vengeful, or angry thought, stop and keep silent before you speak or act. Ask God for humility and calm, and wait until you can think clearly.
exp.24:2:
This verse compares three things that cannot be fully reached: the height of the heavens, the depth of the earth, and the heart of kings. It says they cannot be searched out, that is, that they cannot be fully examined or measured. The thoughts and intentions of a king are beyond the reach of ordinary people.

The book of Proverbs attributes this section to Solomon, and says that men of King Hezekiah copied it centuries later. The verse before it says that God is honored by keeping matters hidden, and that a king is honored by searching them out. Here the limit of that search is shown: there are things a person cannot fully see. Some read this as a warning about prudence before authority.

For today: accept that you cannot know everything or understand the heart of every person. Be humble, do not judge motives you cannot see, and trust God, who does know every heart.
exp.0:9:
It says that if people who live in sin try to deceive you or lure you into doing wrong, you should not give in or agree. "Deceive" here carries the sense of drawing someone in with flattery or persuading them with bad intentions. The phrase "consent thou not" is an old way of saying "do not go along with it" or "do not let yourself be carried away."

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son, as the earlier verses show, where he also mentions the teaching of the mother. The verses that follow show what the deception is: an invitation to join a violent gang that robs and harms innocent people. The father warns him before the temptation arrives.

For today: decide ahead of time what you will not do, even when your friends or companions pressure you. If someone invites you into something dishonest, learn to say "no" calmly and firmly, and walk away.
exp.20:14:
It brings joy to the righteous person to do what is right and just. But for those who practice wickedness, ruin and downfall are waiting. "Doing judgment" means acting with justice and uprightness. "Downfall" is a word for destruction or a fall. "Wickedness" is evil or injustice.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the title of the book, within a collection of sayings of wisdom. There is no narrator in a scene; it is teaching for daily life. The nearby verses speak of helping the poor, of bribes, and of paths that lead to ruin. In this way, the proverb contrasts two paths: justice brings joy, and wickedness ends badly.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we enjoy doing what is right, even when it costs us. For example, being honest at work, paying what is fair, or standing up for someone treated unjustly. God can form in us that delight in what is good.
exp.12:12:
It says that whoever despises the word, that is, the instruction or teaching given to them, will have to pay the consequences. "Shall be destroyed" means that such a person will suffer harm because of their own attitude. On the other hand, whoever "feareth the commandment," meaning takes it seriously and respects it, "shall be rewarded," that is, will receive good fruit.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom, and this saying is largely attributed to Solomon. The verses around it speak of riches, of hope, and of the teaching of the wise as a fountain of life. Many understand that "the word" refers to God's instruction, though it can also include good counsel in general.

For today: when someone corrects you, or when the Bible confronts you, do not ignore it right away. Listen with humility, pray, and take one concrete step of obedience this week.
exp.0:20:
This verse shows wisdom calling out loudly in the busiest places. The "chief places of concourse" are the spots where many people gather, such as markets and main streets. "The openings of the gates" were the places where business was done and legal matters were settled in the city.

The speaker is wisdom, pictured as a woman who raises her voice, as a poet does in the book of Proverbs. She comes right after the warning against greed that traps the soul. She does not hide: she offers her counsel openly, and in the verses that follow she calls the simple to turn back and promises to pour out her spirit and make her words known.

Today, God's wisdom is not reserved for a few. We can hear it in his Word, in sound advice, and in everyday situations. Before deciding something important, stop for a moment and ask yourself what wise counsel you are ignoring.
exp.0:15:
The explanation says that wicked people are in a great hurry to do evil. They do not hesitate or stop; their feet "run" toward violence. Words like "shed blood" mean killing or fatally wounding others. The phrase "make haste" means being in a hurry, eager to act.

Here a wise father speaks to his son. Sinners have just invited him to join their gang, promising easy gain: "let us all have one purse." The father warns that this road ends badly. The next verse shows that those men, without realizing it, set a trap for themselves.

For today: when someone invites you to something harmful, do not let hurry or group pressure carry you along. Stop and think about where that path leads. Choose friends who draw you closer to God and to what is good.
exp.28:22:
It says that pride eventually brings a person down, while someone who is humble in heart receives respect and dignity.

The verse's word "pride" stands for the arrogance that puffs a person up. The idea that brings them low means being knocked down or humbled. The verse's phrase "honour shall uphold" means that honor sustains and accompanies the humble person.

This proverb belongs to the sayings attributed to Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah copied, according to Proverbs 25:1. These are wise counsels for daily life. The verses nearby speak of anger, sin, going along with wrongdoing, and fear of people. Together they show that the inner character sets the direction of our life.

For today: when you are wrong, admit it without excuses and ask for forgiveness. Listening to advice without becoming defensive is a simple way to practice humility, and God honors that heart.
exp.24:22:
It says that just as the north wind drives away rain, an angry face silences the one who speaks badly of others. The phrase "backbiting tongue" refers to the one who slanders or gossips in secret.

Some translations understand the Hebrew the other way around: the north wind brings rain, and a gossiping tongue brings angry faces.

It is a proverb of Solomon, later copied out by the men of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). It offers wisdom for everyday life. It comes after the command to love your enemy and before the passage about quarrels at home, so it is about how our words and reactions affect our relationships.

For today: do not give gossip room. When someone starts speaking badly about another person, calmly show that you do not want to listen, and take care that your own tongue does not cause anger.
exp.17:13:
It says that a person's spirit can help them endure an illness of the body. But when the one who is wounded is the spirit itself, that is, when there is anguish, sadness, or discouragement within, who will be able to sustain it? Here "spirit" refers to the inner self, the inner life of the person. "Will sustain" means that it will bear up under it or carry it.

This verse is part of the book of Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings that tradition largely attributes to Solomon. It is not a scene with a particular speaker, but advice for life. The verses nearby speak of pride, of listening before speaking, and of seeking wisdom. Scholars do not agree on a single thread that ties them together.

For today: take care of your heart and do not carry it alone. If you are distressed, pray, talk with someone you trust, and seek help, including professional help if needed.
exp.26:8:
Just as a scented oil and a fragrant aroma lift the spirits, so does a friend who gives honest advice. "Ointment" is a fragrant oil, and "hearty" means "from the heart," with true affection. Some translations understand the second part differently, but the general idea is that sincere friendship is sweet and brings joy to life.

This is a book of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon. The proverbs in this chapter were gathered in the time of King Hezekiah, according to Proverbs 25:1. The nearby sayings speak of the value of friendship, of neighbors, and of loyalty. Here the wise man compares simple pleasures with the joy of having a true friend.

Today, value the one who tells you the truth with kindness. And be that kind of friend yourself: before giving advice, listen, speak with gentleness, and seek the good of the other person.
exp.0:17:
The explanation says that wicked people who prepare ambushes to kill others are actually setting them up for themselves. "Ambushes" are hidden traps or snares, and "snare" is a trap meant to catch. "Their own blood" and "their own lives" refer to their own lives. Without realizing it, they fall into the very trap they set.

It is a wise father speaking to his son (Proverbs 1:8-19). He warns him not to join a gang of young men who invite him to steal and do harm with the promise of easy riches. The verse before says that the bird sees the net and avoids it, but these men, without seeing the danger, rush toward it. The verses that follow connect this to greed.

For today: be wary of quick gains that harm others. Greed promises profit, but it ends up trapping the one who follows it. Choose honest friendships and decisions, even when they seem slower.
exp.9:31:
This proverb compares two ways of speaking. "The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable" means that the upright person knows which words are fitting, helpful, and good. The word "acceptable" can refer to what pleases God and also to what is fitting for others. By contrast, "the mouth of the wicked" speaks crooked things, that is, things twisted, deceitful, or harmful.

The book of Proverbs gathers the wisdom of Israel, and this chapter attributes it to Solomon. The verses before this one speak of the mouth of the righteous producing wisdom and of the perverse tongue that will be cut off. Here the author closes the chapter by repeating the idea: what a person says shows what is in their heart.

For today: before you speak, especially when you are upset, ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true, fitting, and edifying. Ask God to help you speak with kindness.
exp.13:5:
It says that the scoffer, that is, the mocking person who thinks himself superior and looks down on what is right, seeks wisdom but does not find it. By contrast, the person who has understanding finds it with ease. Here "easy" means that wisdom is within reach of whoever is humble and attentive.

The book of Proverbs gathers the teachings of wise men, and tradition links much of it to Solomon. It speaks like a father or teacher warning the young. The nearby verses contrast the truthful witness with the false one, and the prudent person with the fool. The underlying idea is that the attitude of the heart determines whether one learns or not.

For today: if you want to grow in wisdom, begin with humility. Listen to advice, accept correction, and avoid mocking what you do not understand. Ask God for a teachable heart.
exp.7:30:
She says that Wisdom rejoices in the habitable part of the earth, and that what she delights in most is being with human beings. "Rejoicing" is the word the verse uses for "rejoicing" or "delighting," and "habitable part of his earth" refers to the world where people live.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented as a person who was beside God when he created everything. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, though others understand her only as a poetic figure of God's wisdom. She speaks to invite the sons of men to listen to her, as the next verse shows.

Today we can remember that God is not distant: his wisdom delights in our daily life. Before deciding something at home or at work, pause briefly and ask God for his counsel.
exp.8:15:
It says the foolish woman calls to everyone who is "simple," that is, naive, without experience, and easy to persuade. She also calls to those who lack good sense, that is, those who have no good judgment. She says to them: "Come here." The final phrase, "saith," introduces what she is going to say in the following verse.

In Proverbs 9, Wisdom and Folly, presented as two women, invite people to a feast. Wisdom invites to life. Here Folly speaks, and she copies the same words that Wisdom used in verse 4. She sits in a visible place to attract those who are walking the right path. Her invitation seems innocent, but it ends in death.

Today, not every attractive invitation is good, even when it sounds kind or uses words similar to God's. Before accepting something, ask yourself where it leads. Ask God for discernment and seek wise counsel.
exp.13:20:
This verse says that it is sin to despise another person, and that the one who shows compassion to those in need is happy and blessed. "Sinneth" means that he does wrong before God. "Neighbour" is any person close to us. "Happy" means joyful, blessed by God.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although some proverbs have other origins. Just before this, the text describes how people often reject the poor and seek out the rich. This verse corrects that custom: God does not measure people by their money, but values mercy.

For today: think of someone you tend to overlook because of their humble condition. Today greet them with respect and, if you can, help them with something concrete, such as food, time, or a kind word.
exp.24:19:
Singing cheerful songs to someone who is sad is as out of place as taking a coat off a person when it is cold. It is also like pouring vinegar on soda. The Hebrew word here probably refers to a kind of soda or natron; when mixed with vinegar, it foams up and is ruined.

These proverbs are attributed to Solomon, and chapter 25 says that the men of Hezekiah copied them. They are wise sayings, not a speech with a single theme. Here it is taught that speaking well also requires timing and sensitivity.

Today, when someone is suffering, do not be quick to cheer them up with happy phrases or to fix their pain. First accompany them, listen to them and, if needed, weep with them. Then, with tenderness, the time for words of hope will come.
exp.13:32:
It says that wisdom rests quietly in the heart of the person who is sensible. "Sensible" is the word for the wise person, and the people who do not want to learn are the ones who lack understanding. The second part can be understood in two ways: that wisdom shows itself even among those who lack understanding, or, as some other versions translate it, that they do not show it.

This book gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, to guide people in everyday life. Here, among verses about treating the poor well and seeking justice, it reminds us that true wisdom is seen in how we live.

Today, you do not need to boast about what you know. Cultivate a quiet and attentive heart, and let your fair and kind treatment of others speak for you.
exp.18:6:
This proverb says that poverty brings loneliness. Even the poor man's relatives turn away from him (here "hate" means to despise or to keep away), and his friends leave even faster. The last sentence is difficult: the Hebrew is obscure and is translated in several ways. Perhaps it speaks of the poor man who goes after words of help and does not find them.

The speaker is a teacher of wisdom, whom tradition links with Solomon. He does not command us to abandon the poor; he describes with sadness what he sees. The verses nearby speak of self-interested friendships: many seek the one who gives.

For today: do not measure people by what they can do for you. Think of someone who is going through hardship and is alone. Call him, visit him, or help him this week. In this way you reflect the love of God, who does not abandon the one in need.
exp.29:29:
This verse describes the lion as the strongest of all the beasts, one that does not turn back from anyone. It is the first of four examples of a stately bearing or majestic walk. The phrase about not turning back here is simply the verse's own wording, so it needs no separate explanation. The lion advances with confidence and without fear.

Chapter 30 presents these as the words of Agur, son of Jakeh. Exactly who he was is not known with certainty. Agur observes nature to draw lessons, and here he uses animals to illustrate noble bearing. The next verse moves to a king whom no one dares to challenge, so the image points to firm and dignified authority.

For today: true firmness is not pride or harshness. It is seen in someone who walks with conviction and does not back down under pressure when they know what is right. Ask God for courage to remain faithful, but also for humility, because the same passage warns against exalting oneself.
exp.20:3:
It says that a haughty look, a proud heart, and "the shining" of the wicked are sin. "Haughtiness of eyes" means looking at others with contempt. "Shining" can be understood as their lamp, their success, or even the way they work; translators do not agree. The central idea is that pride stains everything the wicked person does.

It is a proverb, traditionally attributed to Solomon, that offers brief wisdom for daily life. It comes after "the LORD weighs the hearts" and after God's preference for justice over sacrifice. God looks at the inner attitude, not only at outward appearances or achievements.

For today: before boasting of an achievement, examine your heart. Give thanks to God, acknowledge that you received everything from Him, and treat others with humility and respect.
exp.29:7:
This verse is part of a prayer in which a man asks God for two things. First, that He keep falsehood and lying words far from him. Then, that God give him neither poverty nor riches, but only the food he needs. "The bread I need" means the bread that I require, that is, what is just enough to live.

The one speaking is Agur, son of Jakeh, the author of this chapter. He says he asked God for two things before he dies. The verses that follow explain his reason: with too much he could forget God and feel self-sufficient, and with too little he could be tempted to steal and dishonor the name of God.

For today: before wanting more money, we can ask God for contentment and honesty. It is worth asking ourselves whether what we have brings us closer to God or pulls us away from Him, and being thankful for how sufficiently He provides for us each day.
exp.20:7:
It says that the life of a wicked person is "crooked," that is, full of twists, traps and deceit. It is also "strange," that is, far from what God considers right. By contrast, the person of honest heart, the one who is "pure," does works that are "upright," straight and without duplicity.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, addressed to those who want to live well before God. Here, the verses nearby speak of gain through lying and of people who reject justice. The proverb contrasts two paths: that of deceit and that of integrity. It is a general principle about how things usually go, not a promise for every case.

Today you can examine your small decisions: what you say at work, how you handle money, what you promise. Ask God for a pure heart and choose today one honest action, even if it costs you.
exp.12:4:
A righteous person hates false words, that is, lying. The wicked, who live turned away from God, end up being disagreeable and having a bad name. The word "hates" here means rejecting something firmly, and "shame" means they lose their good reputation.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, and it serves to teach young people to live uprightly. The verses nearby speak of care in what we say, of laziness and diligence, and of the paths that lead to life or to ruin. Lying fits that theme: what comes out of our mouth reveals and shapes our character.

For today: try to tell the truth even when it would be convenient to stay silent or exaggerate. Avoid small lies, such as false excuses or gossip, and ask God for a heart that loves what is true.
exp.29:12:
It says there is a kind of people, a "generation," who look down on others with pride. "Lofty eyes" are eyes that think themselves superior, and "raised eyelids" describes someone who looks upward with contempt, as if they feel above everyone else.

This verse comes from the words of Agur, son of Jakeh, at the beginning of Proverbs 30. He describes four kinds of people who harm others: those who dishonor their parents, those who think themselves clean when they are not, the proud, and those who exploit the poor. Here he is not speaking of an era, but of a way of being that keeps repeating. Some scholars see a general warning, others a criticism of specific people of his time.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we look at others with superiority. Ask God for a humble heart, one that listens, values everyone, and does not think itself better than anyone else.
exp.11:26:
The lazy man does not make use even of what he has already caught: he does not even roast the game he hunted. "Indolent" means lazy or slothful, and "precious wealth" means valuable riches. The word that is hard in the Hebrew is understood by some as "roast" and by others as "to lift up the prey"; the general idea is clear: diligence is a treasure.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, addressed to the one who seeks to live uprightly. Here it contrasts the lazy man with the diligent one, just as the chapter contrasts the righteous with the wicked. The verses that follow join faithful effort with the path of life.

Today: do not leave unfinished what you have already begun. Choose one pending task, at work, at home, or in your spiritual life, and finish it today, doing it with gratitude to God.
exp.18:19:
This verse invites us to listen to good advice and to accept being corrected by someone. "Counsel" is wise guidance, and "correction" is a call to change our ways. "Latter end" speaks of the final stage of life. The idea is that whoever learns now will become wise over the years.

It is part of the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although not every proverb has a certain author. It speaks like a teacher of wisdom instructing a young person. Just before, it speaks of discipline for children and the danger of anger; after, it says that human plans are many, but the Lord's purposes endure.

For today: think of a recent correction that made you uncomfortable. Before defending yourself, ask yourself with humility: "What can I learn from this?" Then take one concrete step to change.
exp.3:21:
The explanation says that the father's words, that is, his wise teaching, are life to those who find them, and health for their whole body. Some of the wording is old-fashioned: "find" means to discover or come upon, and "flesh" here refers to the whole person, the entire body. The word translated as "health" can be understood as wellbeing or healing.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, in the style of the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Before this, he asks for attention and for the son to keep his words in his heart. Then he tells him to guard his heart and his mouth. Some understand "health" in a literal sense, others as general wellbeing; the text does not specify.

For today: spend a few minutes each day reading a passage of Scripture and repeat it during the day. In this way you keep it in your heart and let it guide your decisions, your words and your rest.
exp.3:20:
It says the father's words must not be lost from sight. "Let them not depart from thine eyes" means keeping them always present, and "keep them in the midst of thine heart" means holding them in the innermost part of a person. The "words" are the teachings mentioned earlier. The old accent mark on the "a" is written differently today.

A wise father speaks to his son, in the style of the book of Proverbs, which tradition associates with Solomon. Earlier he warns that the way of the wicked is dark and makes people stumble. Now he asks his son not to let his teaching slip away, because those words give life and health, and for that reason he later tells him to guard his heart.

For today: choose one teaching from the Bible, write it in a visible place, and review it each morning. In this way it will move from your eyes to your heart and guide your decisions.
exp.15:5:
It says that sin is corrected or covered through mercy and truth, and that the fear of the Lord, that is, a reverent respect toward God, makes people turn away from evil. "Mercy" is kindness and compassion; "truth" is faithfulness and uprightness. Some understand it to speak of God's mercy and faithfulness that forgive; others, of the conduct we should show toward one another.

This is a proverb attributed to Solomon, within a series of wise sayings about God, pride, and justice. Earlier, it speaks of God's sovereignty and of rejecting the proud. Afterward, of the ways that please God. The verse shows the way out: kindness together with truth, and reverence for God.

For today: when someone fails, try to correct them with both love and honesty. And ask God for a heart that fears him, so that you avoid evil from within.
exp.29:16:
The explanation says that the eye, that is, the person who mocks his father and despises his mother's teaching, will meet a terrible end. The ravens will pick out the eye in the valley or dry riverbed, and the young eagles will devour it. Mocking means making fun of someone with contempt. A dry riverbed is the channel where a stream once flowed.

This chapter contains the words of Agur, son of Jakeh, about whom we know very little. He speaks in images from nature and in lists of things. Here he uses a strong, almost harsh image to show that despising one's parents is a serious matter. It is the language of warning, not a literal description of what always happens.

For today: honor your parents with respect, even if you do not agree with them. Listen to their advice, be thankful for the good they taught you, and avoid speaking about them with mockery or contempt.
exp.30:21:
It says that this woman makes her own tapestries, that is, embroidered quilts or covers for her house. Furthermore, her clothing is fine linen, a delicate and good-quality cloth, and purple, an expensive dye that was associated with wealth and dignity. Her clothing shows the fruit of her labor and her good taste.

These are words of the mother of King Lemuel, who teaches him what a virtuous woman is like (Proverbs 31:1, 10-31). The preceding verses speak of her care for her family and for the poor. For this reason, her good clothing does not seem like vanity, but the result of her effort and order. Some scholars see in this poem an ideal portrait, not a mandatory list for every woman.

For today: care diligently for what God has entrusted to you, your home, your work, and your generosity. Seek to ensure that your order and your effort honor God and bless others, without seeking empty appearance.
exp.15:15:
This proverb says that getting wisdom is better than having fine gold, and that gaining understanding is worth more than silver. To "get" means to acquire or obtain through effort. "Precious" means of great value. Wisdom is knowing how to live well, and understanding is grasping and discerning things clearly.

Proverbs are sayings of instruction, attributed in large part to Solomon, that teach for daily life. Here, among verses about kings and about pride, the proverb reminds us that whoever lives with wisdom avoids evil and downfall. The text says no more; the link with the nearby verses is one possible reading.

For today: before spending time and energy only on earning money, set aside a moment each day to seek wisdom, by reading the Bible, praying, and listening to advice from mature people.
exp.15:8:
This verse says that we people make plans and think about where our lives are going, but it is God who directs our steps. "Directeth" means to guide, to set straight. "Heart" refers to the mind and the will, not only to the emotions.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom attributed in large part to Solomon, though the book has several authors and compilers. Here a teacher of wisdom instructs his people. The verses around it speak of pleasing God, of justice, and of rulers. In this way it shows that planning is good, but God has the final word.

For today: make your plans with effort and wisdom, but place them in prayer and stay willing to change course. If a door closes, trust that God may be guiding you down another path.
exp.14:12:
What it says: This proverb explains that what we feel inside shows on the outside. A joyful heart shows in the face, and the person looks kind and pleasant. On the other hand, when the heart suffers, the spirit is broken. The phrase "is broken" means it gives way and falls apart.

Context: It is part of the book of Proverbs, a collection of teachings on wisdom, largely attributed to Solomon. It is not a conversation, but advice for living well before God. The nearby verses speak of the human heart, of wisdom, and of the lives of the troubled and the content. It is a text that observes how life works, not a promise that the believer will never suffer.

For today: Take care of your heart with healthy habits: give thanks to God, spend time with people who encourage you, and share your burdens with someone you trust. If you are going through pain, do not pretend to be cheerful; bring it to God honestly.
exp.30:14:
She rises while it is still night, before dawn, to prepare food for her household and to give out a portion of food to her servant girls, that is, the share of food or daily task that belongs to each of them.

These words are part of the closing poem of Proverbs, which describes the woman of strength. According to the text, they are teachings that the mother of King Lemuel gave to her son. The poem paints a picture of a life of hard work, good order, and care for the home. Some read it as an ideal portrait rather than a duty required of every woman.

For today: care for your own with responsibility and generosity, including in the small and hidden things. You can plan your day ahead, serve with joy, and treat fairly those who work with you or help you.
exp.4:12:
This verse is part of the lament of someone who ruined his life. He says he did not listen to those who taught and instructed him, his teachers and counselors, and did not give them his attention or want to obey them.

The words "the last days" are not in this verse, and "in the midst of the assembly" is not either, so I have translated the passage without them.

The speaker is the young man who, in the verses before, fell into immorality with another man's wife. The wise father warns him in Proverbs 5 how his lament will sound if he keeps on that path. In the end he admits that he despised correction and that his failure was exposed before everyone.

For today: learn to listen before you stumble. Seek out people who are wise and faithful, such as a pastor, your parents, or a mature friend, and receive their counsel with humility, even when it hurts. Being corrected in time costs far less than grieving afterward.
exp.8:10:
The explanation says that whoever listens to wisdom will receive a longer and fuller life. "Your days will be multiplied" and "the years of your life will be added" repeat the same idea in different words, as Hebrew poetry often does. The word "me" refers to wisdom.

In this chapter, wisdom appears as a woman who invites people to her banquet and speaks to the simple. The verses before say that the fear of the LORD, that is, reverence and trust toward God, is the beginning of wisdom. Proverbs usually speaks of general principles, not absolute promises: the wise life tends to avoid many harms. Some also understand a life with more meaning, not only more years.

Today, we can learn to ask for advice, to accept correction, and to make decisions with calm and respect for God. In this way we care for our own life and the lives of others.
exp.7:13:
It says that wisdom has good counsel and "ser," that is, firm and solid knowledge; some understand it as "practical wisdom" or "success." It also says that she is intelligence or understanding, and that strength belongs to her, that is, power and firmness to act well.

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a person who calls out to people in Proverbs 8. She has just said that she hates evil, pride, and lying. So here she shows that her counsel and her strength are not selfish but serve justice. In the verses that follow she says that righteous rulers depend on her. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, although this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: before making an important decision, ask God for wisdom and seek sound counsel. Remember that true strength is not about imposing yourself, but about acting with humility, truth, and justice.
exp.5:4:
It says that someone who has gotten into a dangerous commitment must get out of it quickly, like a young deer that escapes the hunter or a bird that gets away from the trap.

Here a wise father speaks to his son. The verses before this one speak of someone who became bound by the debt or the guarantee of another person. He is told to act fast, to humble himself, and not to sleep until the matter is resolved. Then comes the example of the ant, which works without anyone forcing it to.

For today: if you have tied yourself to a reckless promise or debt, do not put it off. Speak with humility, seek a settlement, and learn to think before you commit.
exp.26:13:
It says that if someone praises his friend in a loud voice and very early in the morning, that praise will be taken as a curse. The word "blesseth" here means speaking well of someone, praising them. "Rising early in the morning" means getting up very early. "It shall be counted" means it will be considered or taken into account.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom attributed largely to Solomon. This chapter belongs to a collection that, according to the book itself, was copied by the men of Hezekiah. The proverb is part of a series of practical counsel about daily life. Its exact meaning is interpreted in several ways: it may speak of excessive praise that proves annoying, or of self-interested flattery that arouses suspicion.

For today: when you want to encourage or congratulate someone, do it with sincerity, prudence, and good timing. A loud or out-of-place compliment can make someone uncomfortable. Sometimes a simple, sincere detail is worth more than many words.
exp.21:18:
This verse says that the teacher shares his teachings with a clear purpose: that the reader's trust may be placed in the Lord (Jehová, the name God is called here). The phrase "I have made known to thee this day, even to thee" means "I have made these things known to you today, to you in particular." The word "these" refers to the words of wisdom mentioned before.

Here a teacher of wisdom speaks, like a father instructing his son. This section begins the collection called "the words of the wise." Scholars debate how much it relates to other ancient texts, but the purpose here is spiritual: good teaching should lead to trusting God.

For today: when you read the Bible or receive good advice, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to trusting God. Choose one wise piece of counsel, put it into practice this week, and entrust it to Him in prayer.
exp.13:18:
This proverb says that, sooner or later, the wicked will have to acknowledge the good. "Bow down" is an image of reverence or submission, like someone who asks for help or admits defeat. "The gates" were the public place where matters were handled and decisions were made in the city. The "wicked" are those who live without respect for God.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the book's title, and it is part of a series of contrasts between wise and foolish people. Just before, it speaks of the one who gets angry quickly and of those who inherit foolishness. Afterward, it speaks of how the poor are treated. It is not clear when this bowing will happen: it may be in this life or at God's judgment. Interpreters understand it in both ways.

For today: do not be discouraged when doing what is right seems to get no results. Keep being honest and kind, and leave to God the moment when justice becomes visible.
exp.30:17:
She sees and knows that her work is bearing good fruit. Her business and earnings are profitable, and her lamp does not go out at night. That she keeps her lamp lit through the night can be understood in two ways: either she worked late into the hours, or her household was well supplied and had light and security. Many scholars see here an image of prosperity and steadiness.

Chapter 31 records the words that King Lemuel's mother taught him (v. 1). It is a poem about the woman of noble character. The verses nearby show her as wise, hardworking, and generous. It is not a rule for every age, but a portrait of wisdom and the fear of God in everyday life.

For today: do your work with steadiness and integrity, and check whether it is bearing good fruit. But also take care of your rest, and use what you earn to bless others.
exp.22:34:
It describes a drunk person who, after being struck or beaten, claims they felt no pain. The alcohol has numbed the body and the mind. And on waking, instead of learning the lesson, they want to drink again. The quoted phrases "they have stricken me," "they have beaten me," and "I will seek it yet again" are the verse's own wording, so the explanation simply keeps those words.

It is part of a wise father's teaching to his son in Proverbs. From verse 29 on it describes the harms of wine: woe, quarrels, wounds for no reason. The verse before speaks of confused visions and of feeling dizzy as if on a ship. Here the bondage of the vice is shown: the person no longer reacts to the harm and only desires more.

For today: if something harms you and you still go back to it, whether alcohol or another habit, do not hide it. Ask God and trustworthy people for help, and take one concrete step today.
exp.16:0:
It says that it is better to eat little and simply, like a piece of dry bread, but to live in peace, than to have a house full of food and celebration where there are always fights.

The words "dry morsel," "strife," "sacrifices," and "feasts" do not appear in the verse you are reading, so the explanation of them is omitted here. The meaning of the verse is that a plain, simple meal shared in peace is better than a home overflowing with abundance but filled with quarrels.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and this one is attributed to Solomon. Its purpose is to teach people how to live well before God. Here it compares two things people value: wealth and the calm of the home. The next verse speaks of other family relationships and says that God tests hearts.

For today: do not sacrifice the peace of your home to have more things or more success. Take care of how you treat one another in your family, lower your voice when you disagree, and ask for forgiveness quickly.
exp.12:9:
This verse says that pride always ends up causing quarrels and conflict. By contrast, wisdom is found in those who allow themselves to be advised. "Pride" is the word for the sin of arrogance; the verse's own wording shows that pride brings forth or produces strife, and "well advised" refers to people who receive counsel and listen with humility.

These words are part of the Proverbs of Solomon, according to tradition. They are teachings from a master of wisdom addressed to his listeners, especially the young. Nearby verses speak of people who refuse correction, of the light of the righteous, and of hope. In this way, the verse shows that a heart that will not listen damages relationships.

Today, before arguing, ask yourself: am I defending my pride, or seeking what is right? Try to ask a wise person for their opinion and listen without becoming defensive. This can prevent many quarrels in the family, at work, or in the church.
exp.4:14:
It says to drink water from your own cistern, that is, from the reservoir you yourself have, and from the running waters of your own well, that is, from the stream that flows out of your own spring. Running waters are waters that flow with force and in abundance. It is a simple image: enjoy what is yours.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, in a long piece of advice about avoiding adultery. The verses before it show the lament of someone who ignored the teaching and suffered the consequences. Almost all interpreters understand the water as an image of love and faithfulness within marriage, though some also see a broader application to being content with what one has.

For today: care for and nourish your relationship with your partner through time, attention and gratitude, instead of seeking satisfaction elsewhere. If you are single, learn to be faithful and thankful for what God has given you.
exp.2:24:
This verse promises that whoever lives with wisdom does not need to live in fear. "Sudden fear" is an unexpected fright, a calamity that arrives all at once. "The desolation of the wicked" is the destruction that falls on those who live without God.

Here a wise father is speaking to his son, as in much of Proverbs 3. He encourages him to keep the commandments and to trust God. The next verse explains the reason for that calm: the LORD is his confidence. It does not promise a life without problems, but security in the midst of them.

For today: when bad news comes or a sudden fear rises, stop and pray simply, "Lord, you are my confidence." Then calmly do what is your responsibility, without letting fear make the decisions for you.
exp.11:22:
The explanation says that the prudent person does not go around showing off what they know, but keeps it with discretion. The heart of fools, that is, of those who act without judgment, lets their foolishness pour out loudly.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. The verses nearby speak of the contrast between the righteous and the wicked, true words and lying words, diligent work and laziness. Here the theme is the use of words: knowing when to keep silent is also wisdom. It does not say that knowledge must always be hidden, but that the wise person does not use it to boast.

Today we can practice humility in how we speak. Before giving our opinion or showing off what we know, let us ask ourselves whether it will help someone or only feed our pride. Let us ask God for prudence.
exp.10:15:
The explanation says that the woman who is "gracious," meaning kind, good-natured, and of noble character, will receive honor and respect. The "strong men" will have riches. In the original language, that word usually means violent or ruthless people, which is why many Bibles translate it that way. Some understand it only as powerful people.

These are proverbs of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, to teach how to live well. Here two paths are compared: the honor that comes from good character and the wealth that is gained by force. The verses that follow speak of mercy and of justice that bear lasting fruit.

For today: take care of your character more than your influence. Kindness and respect give you an honor that money cannot buy. Treat others with gentleness, even when you have power.
exp.9:12:
This proverb says that wisdom shows in the words of a prudent person. On the other hand, the one who lacks understanding (that is, good judgment) will receive a rod on the back, which was a punishment or physical correction. "Void of understanding" means that he lacks common sense.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and tradition largely attributes them to Solomon. This chapter repeatedly contrasts the righteous with the wicked and the wise with the foolish, especially in how they use their mouths. The nearby verses speak of the mouth as a source of life or of violence.

For today: before you speak, consider whether your words build up or wound. And if someone corrects you, listen with humility. Learning in time spares you harder blows later.
exp.16:11:
This proverb compares two dangerous encounters. The first is a she-bear, and the second is a person who is foolish, who acts without sound judgment. It says it is better to come upon a bear that has been robbed of her cubs, one of the most fearsome animals, than to meet a fool who is caught up in his foolishness. In other words, a stubborn fool who is confident in his mistake can cause enormous harm.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, though not every proverb is necessarily his. Here the wise teacher addresses a young listener, using an exaggerated image to give a warning. The verses nearby speak of the fool who does not learn from correction, of the rebel, and of the one who repays good with evil. The theme is the danger of stubborn foolishness.

Today it invites us not to argue uselessly with someone who shuts themselves off from all reason, and to ask God to keep us from stubbornness. We can set limits calmly, asking for wisdom to know when to speak and when to be silent.
exp.18:20:
Many plans and ideas arise in a person's mind, the explanation says, but what ultimately comes to pass is what God has determined. "Heart" here means the mind and the desires. The "counsel of the Lord" is his purpose or plan. "Shall stand" means it remains firm and is not overturned.

Proverbs is a collection of sayings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, though the book had several compilers. Here the wise teacher is speaking about listening to counsel and accepting correction. This verse reminds us that our plans are limited, and that true wisdom submits itself to God.

For today: make your plans with effort and order, but bring them before God in prayer, with humility. If something does not turn out as you expected, do not despair; trust that God may be guiding your path toward something better.
exp.21:21:
It says we should not take advantage of the poor just because they are weak and cannot defend themselves. The word "rob" here can include taking something from them through deceit or abuse. The word "oppress" means to crush or mistreat. "In the gate" refers to the place where judges gathered and cases were decided, so the verse also speaks of not bending justice against the afflicted, that is, the one who suffers.

These words are part of the "sayings of the wise," a collection of advice in Proverbs. The speaker is a teacher of wisdom, traditionally associated with Solomon, although this section has its own introduction. The verses that follow give the reason: God himself defends the cause of the poor.

Today we can apply this by being honest at work, in prices and in dealings, especially with those who have few resources. Nor should we stay silent before an injustice that someone weaker is suffering.
exp.10:23:
This verse says that some people give generously and yet end up receiving more. Others, on the other hand, hold back more than they should and end up in poverty. The word for "scattereth" means giving or sharing freely. For "withholdeth," the verse speaks of those who are tight-fisted, holding on very closely to what they have. The phrase "more than is meet" refers to holding back what should be given or used with fairness.

These words are part of the proverbs attributed to Solomon, which offer wisdom for everyday life. Here generosity is set in contrast with greed. The verses that follow reinforce this: whoever blesses others will be blessed. It is a general principle of wisdom, not a promise that giving will always bring material wealth.

For today: practice generosity with trust in God. You can begin with something concrete, such as helping a neighbor in need or supporting your church, without expecting anything in return.
exp.25:4:
This verse says that sometimes you should answer a fool according to his foolishness. The reason is that, if no one corrects him, he will think he is wise. A "fool" is a stubborn person who rejects correction. "According to his folly" means in a way that shows how absurd what he says is. "In his own conceit" means "in his own opinion."

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom from Solomon and other sages to teach how to live with prudence. This verse seems to contradict the previous one, which says "do not answer a fool." Many understand that the two complement each other: there are times to keep silent and times to respond. Others see different ways of responding. The text does not fully clarify this.

Today, ask God for discernment. If a person insists on an error and could harm others, respond with calm and firmness. If he only seeks to argue, it is better to keep silent.
exp.11:17:
This verse compares two kinds of words. Some people speak in a way that wounds, like someone thrusting a sword with every sentence. By contrast, the words of the wise bring healing, like a medicine that soothes and restores.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here it is not a character speaking within a scene; it is a teacher giving counsel. The verses nearby speak of the anger of the fool, of truth, and of lying. In this way, the proverb shows that words can either harm or help, depending on the heart of the one who speaks them.

Before you respond in a discussion, pause and ask yourself: "Does this wound, or does it help to heal?" Try to speak the truth with calm and respect, seeking to encourage and correct without humiliating.
exp.11:14:
This verse says that the fool believes his way of living is right, because everything seems fine to him according to his own opinion. The wise person, on the other hand, is the one who listens to counsel and follows it. The word "fool" refers to someone who rejects instruction, and the phrase "right in his own eyes" describes a person who considers himself correct.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and this section is attributed mainly to Solomon. Here the teacher, like a father instructing his son, contrasts people by the way they speak and act. The verses nearby speak of words, anger, and truth, and this one shows that wisdom begins with having a heart willing to learn.

For today: before making an important decision, ask the opinion of someone wise and faithful, and pray for humility. Listen sincerely, even when the counsel is not what you wanted to hear, and compare it with what the Bible teaches.
exp.16:14:
This proverb says that God deeply dislikes injustice. Declaring someone innocent when they are guilty, or declaring someone guilty when they are innocent, is something God finds detestable, meaning something that repels Him. The phrase in the original meaning "both alike" says the two wrongs are equally offensive to God. "Wicked" is one who lives without respect for God, and "just" is one who acts with uprightness.

The book of Proverbs is largely attributed to Solomon, though this chapter does not explicitly say who wrote it. These are short sayings of wisdom for everyday life. Here the theme is justice in judgments, something very close to the warnings about conflict, revenge, and relationships found in the verses around it.
