Today we can apply this by looking for the facts before forming an opinion about someone or repeating gossip, and by being fair even when that costs us something or favors someone we dislike.
exp.5:28:
Proverbs 6:29 says that whoever sleeps with his neighbor's wife will not go unpunished. The verse's wording about going in to her and touching her refers to that same intimate union, and "innocent" here means he will not get away free, that is, he will suffer the consequences.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, as in this whole section of Proverbs. Earlier he gave two images: no one carries fire in his chest without being burned, and no one walks on hot coals without hurting his feet. Then he compares this sin with theft: a thief stealing out of hunger is understood, but he still has to pay back a great deal. Adultery is more serious, since it has no excuse.

For today: do not play with temptation. Set limits early, guard your friendships and conversations, and flee from situations that could lead you to harm a marriage, yours or someone else's.
exp.27:4:
Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the Lord understand all things. This verse says that wicked people do not grasp what is right and just, while those who seek the Lord, the God of the Old Testament, understand all things. This does not mean they know everything. It means they grasp what truly matters for living righteously.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom teachings, and this section is attributed to Solomon, although chapters 25 through 29 were gathered together later, according to the book itself. The verses nearby contrast the one who keeps God's law with the one who abandons it, and the upright poor man with the wicked rich man.

For today: if you want to discern well in difficult decisions, do not rely on your own judgment alone. Seek God through prayer and Bible reading, and let Him shape your heart.
exp.15:4:
God detests pride. "Abomination" describes something that is utterly detestable to him, and "proud in heart" refers to someone who feels superior on the inside. "Will not go unpunished" means the person will not be treated as free of guilt. The phrase about the hand is hard to translate. Some understand it as "though hand join in hand," and others understand it differently, so the exact sense is uncertain. Even so, the central message is clear: the proud person will not escape God's judgment.

This is a proverb of wisdom, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon. It is a teaching meant to guide the reader toward living well. The verses around it speak of committing our works to God and living in the fear of him. Pride appears as the opposite of that trust.

Today we can examine our hearts and hand over our plans to God. When you achieve something, give thanks to him and acknowledge those who helped you. In this way success will not fill you with arrogance.
exp.24:21:
This verse says that if you give food and drink to someone who hates you, you are heaping "coals" upon his head, and God himself will reward you. "Heap" means to gather together or pile up. "Lord" is the name of God.

The speaker is the wise man of Proverbs, who here teaches how to treat an enemy. Interpreters explain the burning coals in several ways. The most common view is that kindness brings shame and repentance in the other person, like a burning in the conscience. Paul quotes this text in Romans 12:20, calling us to overcome evil with good.

For today: do one concrete act of kindness toward someone who treats you badly, such as helping them or answering them with gentleness. Do not do it to humiliate them, but with a good heart, and leave the result in God's hands.
exp.8:2:
She has sent out her servant girls to invite people to come, and she herself calls out loudly from the highest places in the city. "Servant girls" means her female attendants or messengers. "Called out" means she shouted or called with force, so that everyone could hear.

In Proverbs 9, wisdom is presented as a woman who prepares a great feast. The author of the book speaks, personifying wisdom. Her invitation is public, open, and visible, not hidden. Later in the same chapter, foolishness also appears as a woman who invites, and so the reader must choose whom to listen to.

For today: God's wisdom is not hidden; it seeks us out and invites us. We can set aside a fixed time each day to read the Bible and pray, accepting that invitation with humility.
exp.0:32:
He says that whoever listens to wisdom will live in safety and peace, without fear that something bad will happen to them. The phrase "dwell safely" means living secure, without anguish. "Shall be quiet" means at peace, calm. The phrase "from fear of evil" speaks of not living frightened by misfortune.

The speaker is Wisdom, who in Proverbs 1 appears as a voice calling out in the streets. She warns the foolish who reject her counsel that they will suffer the consequences of their own choices. This verse is the contrast: a promise for the one who does listen. The proverbs describe what usually happens; they do not guarantee that there will never be problems. Some scholars see this as inner peace rather than the absence of difficulties.

For today: before deciding something important, stop and listen to wise counsel, whether that is the Bible, prayer, or mature people. That habit brings peace to the heart.
exp.20:29:
It says that no human wisdom, no understanding, and no plan or counsel can overcome God. The name of God appears in the original wording, and the word for "against" means "in opposition to him." Human resources have value, but they cannot stand against what God wants.

The book of Proverbs gathers sayings of wisdom, and this verse is attributed to Solomon. Just before it, the passage speaks of the wicked person who hardens himself and of the upright person who thinks carefully about his way. Then it says the horse is made ready for battle, but the victory belongs to God. The whole passage teaches us to plan with care, without forgetting that God is the one who decides the outcome.

For today: make your plans with effort and good judgment, but place them in prayer and submit yourself to God. If one of your plans clashes with his will, have the humility to change direction. Trusting him brings peace, because your future does not depend only on your own intelligence.
exp.26:4:
It says that an open correction, given frankly, is worth more than a love that is kept in secret and never shown. "Open rebuke" is a clear correction, made face to face. "Secret love" is an affection that exists but is not expressed or shown through actions. The proverb teaches that love which stays silent when it should speak is of little use.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book, addressed to the one who seeks wisdom. Before this, it speaks of anger and envy, which damage relationships. Afterward it says that the wounds of one who loves are faithful, that is, a true friend can hurt us with the truth. Many understand the contrast to be between honesty and false kindness.

For today: if you love someone and see that they are going down the wrong path, do not stay silent out of fear. Speak with humility, with care, and in private. And when someone who cares for you corrects you, receive it as a sign of love.
exp.14:2:
God sees everything that happens, in every place. "Jehovah" is the name of God in the Old Testament. Those who live in evil, and those who seek what is right, are both within his sight. Nobody is left outside his view.

Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed in large part to Solomon. Here the theme is words: a gentle answer calms anger, and the mouth of the fool speaks nonsense. This verse reminds us that God also hears and sees how we speak and act. His watchfulness is not only vigilance; it can also be understood as care and justice.

Today, before you answer in anger or talk too much, remember that God sees you. That can help you choose kind and honest words, and it also brings comfort: God sees what no one else notices.
exp.10:17:
This verse compares two kinds of people. "Deceptive work" means a deceitful labor, something that looks like it will bear fruit but does not. "Reward" is a payment or wage, and "sure" means certain, something that will not fail. So the wicked person gains something that vanishes, but the one who sows righteousness receives a reward that can be trusted.

These words are part of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon, although the book gathers sayings from several different collections. They are teachings of wisdom meant to guide everyday life. In this chapter the righteous life is contrasted with the wicked life, and the verses nearby speak of mercy, justice, and life versus death.

For today: when it is tempting to cheat to get ahead, remember that what is gained through deceit does not last. Choose to be honest in your work, your accounts, and your words, even when it costs you. It is like sowing: the fruit of righteousness takes time, but it is certain, and God sees it.
exp.10:11:
This verse contrasts two kinds of people. The one who lacks understanding, that is, who has no good sense, despises his neighbor: he looks down on him or treats him as if he were worth little. The wise person, the one who thinks before acting, holds his peace and does not answer with mockery or contempt.

The book of Proverbs is attributed in large part to Solomon, although it also contains other collections of wisdom. Here the sage teaches about how our words affect the whole community. The nearby verses speak of the city, of the mouth of the wicked that overturns it, and of the gossip who uncovers secrets. Thus prudent silence protects life together.

Today, before you criticize or mock someone, pause for a moment. Keeping quiet does not mean approving of everything, but choosing wisely when to speak. Very often, holding your tongue prevents wounds and cares for relationships.
exp.19:16:
It says that what is gained through deceit seems sweet at first, but in the end it turns out bitter. "Bread of deceit" is the food or benefit obtained by fraud. "Gravel" refers to small stones or grit: instead of soft bread, the mouth is left filled with stones, that is, pain, harm, and regret.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the title of the book (Proverbs 1:1), though some scholars think there may be other contributors in certain sections. Here a wise father teaches a young man through contrasts. The nearby verses speak of wise words, of reckless commitments, and of gossip. All of them are about how to use the mouth and life well.

For today: before taking advantage of a doubtful gain, such as a lie to earn money, a job, or an excuse, ask yourself what the final taste will be. Honesty may cost something at first, but it leaves peace and a clear conscience.
exp.6:15:
She says she has decked her bed with coverings and hangings. "Coverings" are the cloths and draperies that dress up a bed. Embroidered work is the kind stitched with thread, and the fine linen that came from Egypt is the finest cloth of that time. So she boasts of a luxurious bed, made to impress and to draw him in.

The woman speaking in Proverbs 7 is a married woman who goes out to seek a young man who lacks judgment. Earlier she tells him she has already fulfilled her vows and offerings, so that she will seem religious and trustworthy. Now she uses comfort and luxury as bait. The wise father tells this scene to warn his son about the deception and the danger of adultery.

For today: sin almost always comes with an attractive presentation and persuasive words. Before giving in, ask yourself where that road really leads, and flee while there is still time.
exp.22:32:
It says that whoever gets drunk will see strange and confusing things, and his heart will say twisted or wicked things. The phrase "strange women" can be understood in two ways: other men's wives, or strange things and distorted images caused by alcohol. Scholars interpret it in both ways. Perverse things are words and thoughts that are twisted, outside what is right.

It is part of the wise sayings in Proverbs, where a father or teacher warns his son. Just before, it describes wine that looks attractive but bites like a serpent. After that, it shows dizziness and addiction. The aim is for the young man to see the end before he starts.

For today: alcohol lowers your defenses and loosens the tongue. If you know that something makes you think and speak badly, set clear limits on it or stay away from it. Ask a trusted person for help, and ask God, before the habit takes control of you.
exp.4:22:
The explanation says that the person who will not accept correction will end up dying, and will be lost because of his great foolishness. "Going astray" here means wandering off, leaving the right path. "Foolishness" is a lack of wisdom, failing to think soundly. The verse speaks of someone who rejects guidance and sinks because of his own decisions.

Proverbs 5 is the advice of a wise father to his son. He warns him against adultery and sexual immorality. The verses before it say that God sees all our ways, and that the sin of the wicked catches him like cords. This verse closes the warning: the one who does not listen destroys himself. "Death" can be understood as ruin or as physical death; interpreters see it in both ways.

Today, let someone you trust correct you. If a brother, a relative, or a pastor points out a mistake, do not defend yourself right away. Pray, listen, and examine whether they are right. Humble correction can save you from great harm.
exp.19:3:
The explanation says that the sluggard does not plow his land because of the winter cold. To plow means to prepare the ground for sowing. Because he did not sow on time, when the harvest comes, he goes out to beg for food and finds nothing.

Proverbs gathers practical wisdom attributed largely to Solomon. This chapter contrasts prudence with foolishness. Earlier it speaks of avoiding strife and the anger of a king; afterward, of deep counsel and true integrity. This proverb shows another form of foolishness: making excuses to avoid work.

For today: do not wait for perfect conditions to do what you need to do. If something is uncomfortable, such as studying, saving, or starting a difficult job, take one small step today. What you sow now, even if it costs you, prepares your harvest.
exp.7:20:
This verse says that wisdom wants to give an inheritance to those who love her. To "cause to inherit" means to leave something as an heritage, and the phrase "the being" refers to something real and lasting, not passing. "Fill" means to make full. So wisdom promises to fill the treasures of her friends with true riches.

The speaker is Wisdom, who in Proverbs 8 appears as a figure who calls everyone to listen to her. She has just said that her fruit is worth more than gold, and that she guides along paths of justice. Then she speaks of her existence from before creation. Some Christians see in this an image of Christ, while others understand it only as God's wisdom personified. Scholars debate which meaning is the main one.

For today: God does not promise to fill us with money, but with a firm life that has meaning. Today you can seek his wisdom by praying, reading the Bible, and asking for counsel before deciding. In this way your decisions become an investment that lasts.
exp.17:22:
This proverb describes a common reality: the poor person has to speak with pleas, asking humbly, because they depend on others. The rich, on the other hand, often answer harshly, with rough or brusque words. The word "pleas" is what the poor offer, and "harsh answers" are replies that are curt and unkind.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom attributed largely to Solomon. Here the sage does not approve of this behavior; he only observes it, like someone describing how the world works. The verses nearby speak of the power of words, and this one shows how social position can harden the way people treat each other. Other proverbs clearly warn against despising the poor.

Today we can examine how we speak when we have the advantage: as bosses, parents, customers, or people with more resources. Even when we have power, we can answer with patience and respect, remembering that every person has dignity before God.
exp.18:24:
It says that when the scorner (the mocker, who laughs at wisdom) is punished, the simple (the naive person, who does not yet have good judgment) learns and becomes wary, that is, prudent. And correcting the person of understanding (the sensible person) is enough to increase his knowledge. "Knowledge" here means knowing or discernment, not modern science.

These are wise teachings from the book of Proverbs, attributed largely to Solomon, though the book gathers several collections. A wise father instructs his son. The nearby verses speak of the fear of the Lord, of laziness, and of respect for parents. The point is that each person learns in a different way.

For today: receive correction with humility, and learn from the mistakes of others without waiting to make your own. Ask God for a heart willing to listen.
exp.16:12:
This proverb says that whoever repays someone who has done them good with evil will not see evil depart from their household. "Repaying evil for good" means paying back with harm or ingratitude the person who helped us. The word "household" can refer to the family and to the whole atmosphere of the home.

The Book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition attributes largely to Solomon, although not all scholars agree on every section. Here the teacher warns about the consequences of wrongdoing. The verses nearby speak of the rebellious person, the fool, and the one who stirs up quarrels. The proverb shows a general rule of life, not a promise that comes true in exactly the same way in every case.

For today: think of someone who helped you, such as a relative, a boss, or a friend. Avoid answering them with contempt, gossip, or ingratitude. Instead, give thanks and return the good, and in this way you care for the peace of your home.
exp.5:22:
This verse compares God's teaching to a lamp. A "lamp" is a light carried in the hand to see where one is walking. The commandment gives light, the teaching illuminates, and the corrections, that is, the reproofs, are a path that leads to life. Being corrected hurts, but it protects.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as in much of Proverbs. He wants the young man to keep in his heart what he has been taught, because that guidance will watch over him every day. The following verses give a concrete example: this light will protect him from unfaithfulness and from seductive words.

For today: when someone corrects you with good intention, do not react defensively. Ask yourself humbly what light may be in that correction, and ask God to help you apply it.
exp.26:2:
It says that a stone and sand are burdens that are hard to carry, but putting up with the anger of a foolish person is even heavier. A fool is someone who does not listen to advice or think about the consequences. Uncontrolled anger is what is meant here, and the rage of a fool wears out and weighs down those around them.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book, and it belongs to the wisdom passed down for living well. Earlier it speaks of humility: not boasting about the future or about oneself. Later it speaks of anger and envy as destructive forces. Proverbs are usually general observations, not promises or absolute rules.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our anger becomes a burden for others. Before responding in rage, pause, breathe, and pray. If you are dealing with someone who is very angry, set limits calmly and seek help if needed.
exp.14:18:
It says the life of the lazy person is filled with obstacles, as if he were walking through a hedge of thorns that wounds him and holds him back. By contrast, the path of the upright, that is, of those who are honest and obedient to God, is like a highway: a raised, firm, and clear road.

It is a proverb from Israel's wisdom tradition, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Here a wise teacher speaks like a father instructing his children. This chapter continually contrasts the wise with the foolish. Before this, it speaks of anger and peace, and after, of the wise son. The point is that our daily decisions determine whether life feels complicated or clearer. Proverbs give general principles, not absolute promises.

For today: do not put off what you know you should do, such as a job, a debt, or an unfinished conversation. Take one small, honest step today, and you will see how the road clears.
exp.30:15:
She examined a field carefully and bought it, the explanation says. Then, with the fruit of her own labor, she planted a vineyard. The words "bought it" and "planted" show that she thought first and acted afterward.

These words are part of a poem describing the virtuous or capable woman (Proverbs 31:10-31). It is presented as teaching that the mother of King Lemuel gave him (31:1). The poem is an ideal portrait of practical wisdom, not a list of mandatory tasks. Several scholars point out that the Hebrew text is organized as an acrostic, that is, following the alphabet.

For today: before investing time, money, or effort, evaluate well and plan calmly. Then use what you have earned through your work to plant something that bears lasting fruit, whether for your family or for others.
exp.25:14:
It says the lazy person buries his hand in his bosom, that is, he hides it inside his clothing, and then he is so weary of bringing it out that he does not even lift it to carry food to his mouth. The words "bosom" here refer to the fold of the clothing over the chest, and bringing it back means returning it.

This is a proverb of Solomon, written with humor and exaggeration so that the reader sees himself in it. Earlier, the lazy man made up absurd excuses, such as there being a lion in the street, and he kept turning in bed like a door on its hinges. Afterward, he believes himself wiser than seven counselors. Laziness becomes stubborn.

For today: think of a task you have been putting off. Do it now, even if it is only a small step, and ask God for strength so that you do not grow used to making excuses.
exp.23:8:
The plans and thoughts of the fool are sin, that is, they are not neutral before God. It also says that the scorner, meaning the mocker who laughs at what is good and looks down on others, is repugnant to people. The word "abomination" means something detestable.

It is part of the proverbs attributed to the wise (Proverbs 24:23 refers to them this way). These are counsels of wisdom for daily life. The nearby verses speak of people who plan evil and of the wisdom that the foolish person does not reach. Afterward, the text speaks of not being lazy and of helping those who are in danger.

For today: examine not only what you do, but what you think and plan. Ask God to cleanse your mind. And avoid mocking others, because mockery hurts and drives people away. Better to use your words to encourage, to correct with respect, and to help.
exp.28:21:
This verse says that the person who gets angry easily stirs up quarrels and arguments. And the one who lets fury take over ends up committing many mistakes and wrongs. An angry person is someone prone to anger; quarrels are fights or disputes; a furious person is one whose anger has run out of control.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, attributed in large part to Solomon, although this chapter relates to the proverbs that the men of Hezekiah copied (Proverbs 25:1). Here the wise teacher counsels his readers, especially the young, with short sayings. The verses nearby speak of hasty words, of pride and of humility, and all of them show how an uncontrolled temper damages relationships.

Today, when you feel anger rising, pause before you respond. Breathe, stay silent for a moment, and pray for calm. Then speak gently. In this way you avoid quarrels and wounds that are hard to heal later.
exp.22:20:
The explanation says that whoever gives himself over to drinking and eating in excess will end up poor. "Glutton" refers to someone who eats with greed. The verse's "drowsiness" points to the laziness and dullness that come from such excess. "Rags" are tattered clothing, that is, the clothes of a poor person.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, as in the whole book of Proverbs (traditionally associated with Solomon and other wise men). That is why just before this he says: "Do not be among those who drink too much wine." He warns that bad company and excess ruin a life, and then he invites his son to honor his parents and to buy truth and wisdom.

For today: review your habits with food, drink, and rest. Set a concrete limit for yourself, such as not overspending on outings or avoiding places where you always end up overindulging. Choose friends who help you live with self-control.
exp.7:8:
The explanation says that the words of wisdom are upright and clear to the one who understands, and sound to those who have already found knowledge. The word "upright" here means "right" or "good," and "á" is the old form of "a."

The one speaking is Wisdom, who in Proverbs 8 appears as a figure calling out to people in the streets. She has just said that her mouth speaks truth and that nothing in it is crooked. She then invites people to prefer her teaching over silver and gold. Some understand this as a poetic personification; others see in her a foreshadowing of Christ, but the text itself does not say so here.

For today: when a teaching from the Bible seems hard or uncomfortable, do not set it aside right away. Ask God for a heart willing to understand, because wisdom appears more upright and clear when a person receives it with humility and begins putting it into practice.
exp.0:16:
It is pointless to spread a net in plain view of a bird, because it sees the net and turns away. The saying shows that even a bird knows to escape an obvious trap.

The one speaking is a father giving advice to his son. He warns him against certain men who invite him to commit violence to make easy money. The verses that follow say that these men fall into their own trap. Some understand that the son should be as wise as the bird. Others see an irony: the wicked, blinded by greed, are less wise than a bird.

For today: when an offer of quick profit carries clear signs of harm or injustice, do not pretend you did not see them. Listen to wise counsel and walk away in time.
exp.30:26:
She watches closely over how her household runs. The verse's wording "looketh well to" means to observe and pay careful attention to what is happening at home. The "ways of her household" are the daily activities and needs of her family. "Eateth not the bread of idleness" means she does not live off the work of others, but contributes through her own effort.

These words are part of the closing poem of Proverbs, which describes the woman of strength and virtue. Tradition holds that these are teachings that the mother of King Lemuel gave to her son (Proverbs 31:1). It is a poem that praises practical wisdom, hard work, and character. The text does not say that her worth depends only on what she does at home; her faith and her kindness are mentioned as well.

For today: whether you are a man or a woman, we should look carefully at what goes on in our home and take responsibility for it. Today you can ask yourself what your family needs and do something concrete about it, with gratitude and without laziness.
exp.30:24:
She is said to be "clothed" with strength and honor, meaning that her character is like her clothing: everyone can see it. "In time to come" refers to the future, and "shall rejoice" speaks of facing it with joy and without fear. Some understand that she laughs at the hard days ahead, because she is prepared.

These words are part of a poem about the virtuous woman. According to chapter 31, they are teachings that the mother of King Lemuel gave to him (verse 1). The poem is an acrostic, that is, it follows the order of the Hebrew alphabet. It presents the example of a wise, hardworking, and respected life. Many see it as an ideal portrait, not a mandatory list.

Today we can care for our character with the same dedication we give to our clothing: being honest, working with steadiness, and trusting God. In this way we can look toward the future with greater peace.
exp.0:25:
It says that Wisdom responds with mockery and laughter when disaster comes upon those who rejected her. The word "calamity" is replaced here by the verse's own wording: the phrase "your calamity" refers to the disaster itself. Then "your fear" refers to what those people feared would happen to them.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented as a woman who calls out in the streets (Proverbs 1:20-33). She offered advice and correction, but the people refused to listen. Many understand this "laughing" as strong language meant to show the seriousness of the consequences, not human cruelty. Others see it as a picture of foolishness turning back against itself.

For today: let us not harden our hearts against correction. If a wise person, the Bible, or our conscience warns us, let us listen in time, before the consequences arrive.
exp.14:10:
This verse says that God knows even the most hidden and mysterious places. The word "hell" here translates the Hebrew Sheol, which refers to the place of the dead, and "destruction" is Abaddon, meaning ruin or the place of destruction. If God sees all of that, how much more does He see what is in the hearts of people.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon. The verses nearby speak of correction, of the way of the wicked, and of the heart. The one who teaches wants to show that we cannot hide anything before God, not even our intentions. For this reason it is good to receive correction with humility.

For today: when we pray, let us not try to appear other than we are. We can tell God honestly what we feel and think, including our doubts or mistakes. He already knows them, and He invites us to draw near to be corrected and healed.
exp.6:14:
She says to the young man that she went out on purpose to look for him. "Therefore" means "for this reason," and "diligently" means with effort and care. She makes him believe that he is special and that she had been searching for him, until she "found" him.

The speaker is the seductive woman of Proverbs 7, a married woman who goes out into the street at night. She has just kissed the shameless young man and mentions her peace offerings, so that she will seem religious. Her flattery is part of a trap. The wise father uses this scene to warn his son about the deceptions of temptation.

For today: be wary of very flattering words that push you toward hasty decisions. When something sounds too perfect or pressures you to abandon your principles, stop, pray, and seek counsel from wise people before acting.
exp.2:13:
This verse says that wisdom is worth more than money.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, as in much of the book of Proverbs. Earlier he spoke of the correction of God, which comes from love, like a father's. Then he calls happy the one who finds wisdom. He wants the young man to value what truly lasts more than money.

For today: before making an important decision about work, money, or relationships, stop to pray and ask God for direction. Also seek the advice of mature people in the faith, and read the Bible. That daily search for wisdom pays off more than any quick gain.
exp.23:21:
The explanation says that the ruin of rebels comes suddenly, without warning. The word for "destruction" in the older wording simply means calamity or disaster, and the verse above uses "calamity" for that idea. The word "both" probably refers to God and the king, whose punishments no one can measure. Some readers understand it this way; others are not sure.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, within the sayings of the wise in Proverbs. Earlier he told the son to fear the Lord and the king, and not to join with those who rebel. This verse gives the reason: whoever rises against lawful authority can fall suddenly.

Today, before you join a group or a cause, ask yourself where it will take you. Seek the company of people who are steadfast and who honor God, and respect authority, while still obeying God first.
exp.22:6:
This verse says that what a person thinks in the deepest part of themselves reveals who they really are. It speaks of a host who invites you to eat and drink, but does so without sincerity: his kind words do not match what he feels. The word "soul" here refers to a person's inner self, and "heart" to their true intentions.

The speaker is a wise man, probably a father instructing his son, as in much of the book of Proverbs. He warns against accepting the hospitality of someone stingy or self-interested, someone whose generosity is put on. Some translators understand the verse this way; others read it more generally, but the context supports this reading.

For today: don't be won over just by kind words or gestures; watch people's attitudes with patience. And guard your own thoughts, because God looks at the heart.
exp.9:24:
It says the wicked person is like a whirlwind: it arrives with force, makes noise and seems powerful, but it passes quickly and nothing of it remains. The righteous person, by contrast, is a foundation that lasts forever, meaning he has firm footing and the storms do not move him. The wicked person and the one without regard for God or others refer to someone who lives with no respect for God or for other people.

This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, attributed largely to Solomon. It is wisdom expressed as contrast, very common in this chapter: the righteous set against the wicked. The verses nearby speak of what each one receives in the end, and of how the fear of the LORD sustains life. It is not a promise that the righteous will never suffer, but that his foundation is secure.

For today: do not lose heart if you see someone dishonest doing well for a while. Better to build your life on honesty and trust in God, because that is what holds when the storms come.
exp.27:3:
This verse says that those who abandon God's law end up praising the wicked, while those who obey it stand against them. "Contend" means to oppose, argue with, or resist. "Wicked" refers to people who live without reverence for God.

These are proverbs attributed to Solomon, with wisdom for everyday life. The verses around it speak of corrupt leaders, the oppression of the poor, and the difference between the evil person and the one who seeks the LORD. Here it is shown that one's attitude toward the law reveals where the heart is. Some understand "law" as the Torah, and others, more broadly, as God's instruction.

Today, do not applaud or excuse what is wrong merely for convenience or out of fear of looking bad. Ask God for the courage to speak the truth with firmness, but also with humility and love.
exp.2:4:
This verse invites us to trust God with complete sincerity. "Trust" is what the verse calls us to do, and to "lean" means to rest your full weight on something. The word "understanding" here refers to your own reasoning or judgment. In other words: trust God with your whole being, and do not rely only on what you yourself think.

Proverbs gathers the wisdom of Israel, and tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon. In this chapter, a wise father speaks to his son. Earlier he asked him to keep mercy and truth in his heart. Now he tells him to acknowledge God in every path and not to consider himself wise in his own eyes. Trusting is part of living in the fear of the Lord.

For today: before an important decision, pray and seek God's guidance in his Word. Ask advice from wise people. Use your mind, but do not make it your only support.
exp.24:8:
When you have a disagreement with someone, settle it directly with that person, one on one. Do not tell a secret to a third party. The "cause" is the matter or the quarrel; the "neighbour" is the one next to you; "discover" means to reveal or make known.

These are proverbs of wisdom, attributed to Solomon and gathered by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). The context speaks of not rushing to take disputes before the courts. If you talk too much, you may be left ashamed, and gossip will harm you. Some understand "the secret" as the confidence of the other person; others understand it as the information at stake in the conflict.

Today: if someone has offended you, raise it with them first, calmly and in private, before telling others or posting it online. In this way you protect trust and make room for reconciliation.
exp.8:3:
The explanation says that Wisdom makes an open invitation: "Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither." The "simple" person is someone inexperienced, who does not yet have sound judgment and is easily led astray. "Wanteth understanding" means they lack good sense. "Mingled her wine" means she mixed it, probably with water or spices, to have it ready to serve.

In Proverbs 9, Wisdom appears as a woman who prepares a feast in her house. She sends out her maidens and calls from the highest places of the city, so that everyone can hear. She is the one speaking, and her invitation stands in contrast to that of the foolish woman, who later in the chapter also calls to the simple, but toward death.

For today: do not be ashamed of not knowing. If you recognize that you lack wisdom, draw near to God and to his Word with humility. He invites precisely those who are willing to learn.
exp.29:15:
It says there are four things that are never satisfied: the grave (death, which always receives more), the barren womb (the deep longing to have children), the earth that always asks for more water, and the fire that consumes everything and never says "enough", that is, "it is already enough".

Agur, son of Jakeh, speaks in a collection of numerical sayings. It comes after mention of the leech, which always cries "Give, give". Agur uses images from everyday life to show that there are desires that seem to have no bottom. Some think it also warns against human greed, although the text does not say so directly.

For today: the desire to have more can grow without restraint. Today you can practice contentment. Give thanks for what you already have and ask God for wisdom to know when to say "Enough".
exp.19:26:
The explanation says that the spirit or soul of a human being is like a lamp that God lights. The word for lamp here can also be rendered as candle. Here "soul" can also be understood as spirit or breath of life. That inner light searches the most hidden parts of the person; the phrase for the innermost part of the person is an older way of speaking of the deepest self, the inner being.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon. It stands among sayings about kings, justice, and conduct. Some understand that God uses conscience to reveal us to ourselves; others, that God himself examines our inner being with that lamp. Both ideas fit.

For today: When you feel unease in your conscience, do not ignore it right away. Stop, pray with sincerity, and ask God to show you what is in your heart. Then humbly correct what he points out to you.
exp.30:12:
She seeks out wool and flax, which are materials for making cloth and clothing. And she does it "willingly," that is, with pleasure and a ready heart. "Worketh with her hands" means she works with her own hands, spinning and weaving. She does not work under compulsion, but with eagerness and dedication.

Proverbs 31 records the words that the mother of King Lemuel taught him (31:1). It is a poem about the virtuous woman, and it is presented as a portrait of practical wisdom. The verses before it speak of her husband's trust, and the verses that follow compare her to a merchant ship that brings food from afar. Many understand that the poem describes an ideal of character rather than an obligatory task.

For today: do your work, whether at home, at your job, or in your studies, with a good disposition, as something that serves others and honors God. Ask Him to help you work with joy and not merely out of obligation.
exp.28:12:
This verse says that a poor man and a moneylender who charges unfair interest meet one another in life. A moneylender is someone who lends money to make a profit, often in an unjust way. The phrase "the Lord lighteneth both their eyes" means that God gives life and the light of the sun to both of them; it can also be understood as God giving both of them understanding.

This is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book, and it speaks with the voice of a wise teacher to someone who wants to learn. The verses nearby deal with righteous and wicked rulers. Some understand the message to be that God sees both and sustains both, and so the rich person should not think himself superior or crush the poor. Others read it as a call for both to acknowledge God.

For today: treat with respect both the one who is in need and the one who has power over you. If you lend or collect debts, do so with justice, remembering that God sees everyone.
exp.9:26:
The explanation says that respecting and honoring God, what the Bible calls "the fear of the Lord," lengthens life, while the life of the wicked, that is, of those who live without caring about God and do evil, is shortened. The phrase "prolongeth days" means that it adds years. "Shall be shortened" means that they will be reduced.

This verse is found in the Proverbs of Solomon, short sayings of wisdom meant to teach people how to live well. They are general principles, not automatic promises, because the Bible also shows righteous people who die young. Here the steady life of the righteous, who stand firm forever, is contrasted with the wicked, who pass away like a whirlwind. It speaks of a stable life in contrast with a life without direction.

For today: living with respect for God includes wise decisions, such as avoiding excess and harmful quarrels, and caring for what He has given us. Today you can begin the day by asking God for guidance in every decision.
exp.12:0:
This proverb compares two kinds of people. The wise son receives his father's advice, that is, he listens to it and takes it seriously. The scorner is someone who mocks and thinks himself superior, and for that reason he pays no attention when he is corrected. Corrections, or calls to attention, are the words that point out what needs to change.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, and many of its sayings are written as a father's teaching to his son. Tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon, although not all scholars agree on every section. The verses that follow speak about words and their consequences, so the background theme is the attitude of the heart: listening or shutting oneself off.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we allow to correct us. This week, when someone you trust points something out to you, try to listen without defending yourself right away, and ask God for humility to learn.
exp.14:13:
This verse contrasts two kinds of people. The heart that has understanding, that is, the person with good judgment and humility, always seeks wisdom and wants to learn more. The fool's mouth, on the other hand, feeds on foolishness: the fool takes in nonsense and repeats it in his own words.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here the teacher speaks like a father to his children. The verse before this one speaks of the scoffer, who does not tolerate correction and does not keep company with the wise. This saying continues the idea: whoever has understanding desires to learn, and whoever does not is satisfied with what is empty.

Today we can ask ourselves what we feed on each day. If we read the Bible, listen to good advice, and accept correction, we grow. If we only consume gossip and mockery, that will come out of our mouths.
exp.7:2:
This verse says that wisdom stands by the gates of the city, right where people come and go, and from there she calls out loudly. "The place of the gates" is the entrance of the city. "Calls out" means she speaks loudly so that everyone can hear her.

In the context, the one speaking is wisdom, presented as a woman who speaks in the first person. In ancient times, the city gates were the place of gathering, of trade, and of legal decisions. So she does not hide herself: her message is public and addressed to everyone, even the simple and the foolish, as the verses that follow say.

For today: God's wisdom is not reserved for a few. If you are about to make a decision, stop for a moment, pray, and seek counsel in the Bible and from mature people in the faith. Listen to that voice before you act.
exp.19:27:
This proverb says that a king is protected by mercy and truth, that is, by kindness and sincerity. And that his throne stays firm through mercy, which means treating others with compassion and not with harshness. The word "upholden" means held up or kept steady.

It is a proverb from the wisdom of Solomon, according to the title of the book; some scholars think it was gathered by several hands. The nearby verses speak of a king who punishes the wicked with justice. This verse balances that idea: authority is held up not only by firmness, but also by love and honesty.

For today: if you have authority, whether in your home, your work, or your church, seek to be sincere and compassionate. Correcting with truth and with tenderness earns more trust than ruling with fear.
exp.18:26:
This verse tells the son to stop listening to teaching that leads him away from words of wisdom.

The book of Proverbs presents a teacher, often a father, speaking to his son to shape him in wisdom. The nearby verses speak of correction, of children who dishonor their parents, and of scoffers who bring judgment on themselves. Here the teacher warns that listening to wrong voices has consequences. Some scholars interpret the phrase in different ways, but the general meaning is clear.

Today we can examine which voices we listen to: social media, friendships, programs, or books. If something gradually pulls us away from the truth and from the love of God, it is wise to keep our distance and seek sound counsel.
exp.2:31:
This verse says that God deeply rejects the wicked, that is, the crooked person who lives in deceit and wrongdoing. "Abominated" means that such a person is repugnant to God and rejected by him. By contrast, "his secret is with the righteous" means that God has intimacy and trust with those who live with honesty, and he makes his ways known to them.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, within the book of Proverbs, which is traditionally attributed to Solomon. Earlier he advises not to envy the violent or imitate their ways. This verse gives the reason: the one who seems to prosper in wrongdoing does not have God's friendship, and the verses that follow contrast his house with the house of the just.

For today: when you feel envy toward someone who succeeds through trickery, remember that what is most valuable is closeness to God. Choose today to be honest in one specific matter, even though it costs you.
exp.25:0:
This proverb compares honor given to a fool with things that are out of place: snow in the middle of summer, or rain at harvest time. The word "harvest" in the verse above is the time of reaping. The proverb says that honor does not fit a fool, that is, someone who rejects wisdom and acts without judgment.

It is part of the proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah copied, according to Proverbs 25:1. It is wisdom in the form of short sayings to teach the young. What follows speaks of the curse without cause and the rod for the fool, and it reinforces the idea that everything has its place and its consequence.

For today: before praising someone or placing them in a position of authority, look at their character and not only at their fame, their money, or their charm. Give honor with prudence.
exp.25:27:
The explanation says that the lying tongue "afflicts" those it hates; that is, it wounds and destroys the people it despises. And the flattering mouth, which uses pleasant but false words, "makes a slippery path," meaning it prepares a fall and brings ruin. There is a question about the first part: some understand that the liar hates his victims, and others understand that the lie itself does harm to those who suffer it.

It is part of the proverbs of Solomon, later gathered by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). These are wise sayings meant to shape character. The verses before it speak of a hatred hidden behind kind words, which in the end comes to light, and of the one who digs a pit and falls into it.

Today, be wary of excessive flattery, especially when it seeks to gain something from you. And examine your own words: let your praise be sincere and your tongue build up, not deceive.
exp.27:0:
The person who is wicked lives in fear, running away even though no one is chasing. By contrast, the one who lives in righteousness feels secure and brave, like a young lion, that is, a lion that is young and strong. The word "wicked" refers to someone who lives without reverence for God. "Righteous" describes the person who strives to live uprightly before God and others.

This is a proverb, traditionally attributed to Solomon, although this chapter belongs to a section said to have been copied by men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). It is brief wisdom, not an absolute promise. The verses that follow speak of governments and of abuses, so the idea also applies to public life: guilt weighs heavily, and integrity gives firmness.

For today: if something troubles you because of a lie or an injustice, make it right with honesty and ask for forgiveness. A clear conscience gives a peace that nothing else can give you.
exp.10:13:
Where there is no wise guidance, a people falls, but with many advisers there is safety. This verse says that a nation or community stumbles when it lacks good direction, but finds security when it has many counselors.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, attributed largely to Solomon. Here the speaker is not a prophet announcing something, but a teacher giving practical advice. The verses around it speak of prudence, of keeping confidences, and of not acting rashly. This verse shows that wisdom is also something we share with one another.

For today: before an important decision, seek the counsel of wise and trustworthy people, such as mature family members, a pastor, or an honest friend. Listen to them with humility, even when they do not tell you what you want to hear.
exp.23:29:
This verse tells how the author walked past the land of a lazy man and past the vineyard of someone who lacks understanding, meaning a person who does not use good judgment. A "heritage" is a property or land that is received as an inheritance. "Walked past" means simply passed by.

The speaker is a wise man, traditionally associated with Solomon, although this section of Proverbs (verse 23 onward) introduces itself with the words "these also are sayings of the wise." He describes what he saw in order to teach through a real example. The verses before it speak of being fair to your neighbor, and the verses after it show the field full of thorns and the wall fallen down.

For today: neglected things fall apart little by little. Today you can review which responsibility you have left half-done, such as your work, your health, or your family, and take one small, steady step to look after it.
exp.14:31:
This verse says that whoever brushes off discipline is harming himself. The word "soul" here refers to one's own life or person. To "despise" means not giving something its proper value. By contrast, whoever listens to correction shows that he has understanding, that is, good judgment for living.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though the book has several authors. Here a teacher of wisdom speaks, like a father to his son. The neighboring verses speak of receiving correction and of humility, and the next one says that the fear of the LORD teaches wisdom.

Today, when someone corrects you with good intent, do not respond right away on the defensive. Breathe, listen, ask yourself what you can learn and, if it is fair, change. That is how we grow.
exp.28:10:
The explanation says that the fool lets out everything he feels without any restraint: his anger, his words, his rage. The wise man, by contrast, keeps it in and stays calm, that is, he holds his feelings back and waits. The phrase can be understood as the wise man waiting and controlling himself until the storm passes, or as keeping calm until the end. Translations vary a little at this point.

This is a proverb attributed to Solomon, part of a collection of sayings of wisdom. The verses nearby speak of conflict: arguing with a fool brings no peace, and violent people hate those who are upright. This proverb shows the difference between someone who is carried away by his impulses and someone who governs his character.

Before you respond in anger, pause. Breathe, pray, and wait for your emotions to settle. You can feel anger without letting it decide your words or your actions.
exp.19:25:
It says that a wise king separates the wicked from the rest of the people, like someone winnowing grain to remove the chaff. Then he brings the wheel over them: that is, he applies punishment to them. The image may be the wheel of a cart that threshes and crushes the grain, although some scholars understand it in another way.

It is a proverb of Solomon, a saying of wisdom addressed to the one who governs and to the one who listens. It speaks of how a good ruler defends justice and protects the people. The neighboring verses mention that God guides the steps of a person and that the king is upheld by mercy and truth. Thus human justice must be joined to kindness.

For today: if you have some authority, in the home, at work, or in the church, seek to correct what is wrong with firmness, but also with justice and compassion, without abusing your position.
exp.29:20:
Verse 21 says that for three things the earth is shaken, and for four it cannot bear up under them. "Is shaken" means it is upset or thrown into turmoil. "Cannot bear" means it cannot endure them. It is a way of introducing a list of things that cause great disorder.

Agur, son of Jakeh, speaks here, and we know very little about him. In this chapter he gathers numerical sayings to observe life with wisdom. The verses that follow name those things. All of them show people who receive power, food, or position without having the character to handle them. Some details, such as the one about the woman who is hated, are interpreted in several different ways.

For today: when you receive more authority, success, or possessions, ask God for humility and gratitude. Let your character grow at the same pace as your blessings, so that they help others and do not harm them.
exp.28:14:
The rod and the reproof bring wisdom, the explanation says. The rod was a shepherd's or teacher's staff, a symbol of discipline and guidance. "Left to himself" describes the boy who is allowed to do as he pleases, without limits. "Bringeth his mother to shame" means he will bring grief and disgrace. There is wisdom where there is guidance; there is shame where it is missing.

It is a proverb of Solomon, a wise man who teaches in short sayings. It speaks out of the family life of his time, when parents raised their children. The nearby verses speak of justice and of wickedness growing unchecked, so the theme is that order and correction protect. Some understand "rod" literally and others as discipline in general.

For today: correct with firmness and love, without humiliating or mistreating. Set clear limits, explain the reason, and be consistent, so that your children grow up wise and secure.
exp.0:13:
It says that sinners invite the young man to join them. "Cast in thy lot among us" means "take part with us, share the same risk, and share the outcome." "Let us all have one purse" means that everything stolen would be put into one common bag, to be divided among all of them equally.

Here the wicked are speaking, the ones who in the verses before urge the son to lie in wait for the innocent and take his goods. It is part of a wise father's warning to his son. This invitation sounds appealing: easy money, companionship, and belonging. But the father answers right away: "walk not thou in the way with them," because that way ends in violence.

For today: be wary of any proposal that promises quick gain and friendship in exchange for doing harm. Before you join a group or a business, ask yourself: "Is this just? Who does it hurt?" Ask God for wisdom to say no.
exp.15:22:
This verse says that the wise person first thinks with the heart, that is, with their mind, desires, and decisions, and so speaks with care. "Careful" means cautious and sensible; that is why the wise person weighs their words before speaking. Here "teaching" means instruction, and "adds" means that the wise person's speech makes learning grow. What the wise person says helps others learn.

These words are part of the book of Proverbs, a collection of sayings about wisdom. Tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon, although some passages have other authors. The verses nearby speak of gentle words that heal and teach. The message is that inner wisdom shows in the way a person speaks.

For today: before you answer in a discussion or give advice, pause and pray. Ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true, kind, and helpful. In this way your words can build up others.
exp.5:26:
It says that no one can carry fire against their chest without their clothes catching fire. It is a rhetorical question: the obvious answer is "no." So, playing with sexual temptation brings certain harm.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, in the style of Proverbs, which is largely attributed to Solomon. He wants to warn him against adultery. Earlier he spoke of the woman who seduces with her eyes, and then he uses another image: walking on hot coals. All of them show that sin has consequences.

For today: do not get close to what you know can make you fall. Set clear limits from early on, such as guarding what you look at, whom you speak with alone, and which relationships you nurture. It is easier to avoid the fire than to put out a blaze.
exp.29:30:
This verse completes the list of four things that walk in majestic bearing. It mentions the greyhound, which is probably a swift and muscular hunting dog, although the exact meaning of the Hebrew term is uncertain; some translate it as "rooster." It also names the male goat, which walks at the front of the flock, and a king against whom no one dares to rise up.

The speaker is Agur, in the section of Proverbs 30, where he observes creation to draw out lessons. Here he admires creatures that move with dignity and confidence. The verses that follow warn against pride and provocation, which suggests a contrast between true authority and arrogance.

For today: true firmness does not need arrogance. Seek to have your confidence come from acting with uprightness and calm, not from boasting or provoking others.
exp.6:0:
He says that a father is speaking to his son and asks him to pay attention to his words. The word "keep" in the verse above refers to his words or teachings, and "lay up" means holding them carefully, like a treasure that should not be lost or handled carelessly. His "commandments" are his instructions for living well.

The speaker is a teacher of wisdom, presented as a father, and tradition connects him with Solomon, although this is debated. In Proverbs 7 the teaching prepares a serious warning against seduction and unfaithfulness. The verses that follow say that obedience gives life and that the words should be engraved on the heart.

For today: choose one wise teaching from the Bible and keep it on purpose. You might memorize a verse this week, repeat it when temptation comes, and ask God to help you obey it.
exp.20:6:
This proverb says that the violence and theft of the wicked will turn back against them and drag them down to ruin. The word "robbery" in the verse means taking something from others by force or through abuse. The phrase "do judgment" means acting with justice and doing what is right. The reason for their downfall is clear: they refused to do it.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon, though the book gathers wisdom from several voices. A wise teacher speaks to his hearers to warn them. In the verses nearby, it contrasts honest effort with gains won by lying, and the crooked path of the wicked with the upright work of the pure.

For today: do not get rich at the expense of others, whether through small deceptions or great abuses. Even when it seems to work, such gain is not secure. Practice justice, even when it costs you, and trust that God cares for those who act with uprightness.
exp.11:16:
This proverb says that whoever speaks the truth brings righteousness into view, that is, helps things be seen as they really are. By contrast, a false witness produces only deceit.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom from Solomon and other wise teachers to guide everyday life. Here the setting seems to be that of the courts and of life in community, where one person's testimony could decide another person's fate. The verses nearby contrast the fool, who always thinks he is right, with the wise person, who listens and watches over his words.

For today: before you say something about someone, ask yourself whether it is true and whether you are saying it to do what is right. Be honest even when it costs you, because your words can either protect or harm.
exp.20:24:
It says that the lazy person destroys himself. He wants many things, but he does not want to work to get them, and that desire without effort ends up killing him. The word "slothful" in the verse means someone who avoids work, sluggish. It can refer to a slow ruin: poverty, hunger, or frustration.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, although the authorship of each section is debated. It is a teacher's advice to his listeners about how to live well. The verses around it contrast the one who craves everything all day with the righteous person who gives and does not hold everything back. Thus, laziness appears as a selfish desire that is never satisfied.

Today we can ask ourselves: what dream do I have that I have only wished for? Choose a small, concrete step, such as studying, saving, or looking for work, and do it this week, asking God for strength to persevere.
exp.25:17:
The verse describes a madman who throws fire, arrows, and things that bring death. Arrows are the weapons in the verse itself. It is a strong picture of someone who does harm without thinking about the consequences.

This sentence begins a comparison that is completed in the next verse: this is how it is with the one who hurts his friend and then says, "I was only joking." The book of Proverbs gathers the teaching of wise men, and this section is attributed to Solomon, copied by men of King Hezekiah. Here the teacher warns the learner about the danger of mockery and hurtful words.

For today: before making a joke or a sarcastic remark, ask yourself whether it could hurt someone. If you have already hurt a person, do not excuse yourself with "it was just a joke"; ask for forgiveness sincerely.
exp.12:22:
The explanation says that the cultivated land of the poor can produce much food. A fallow field is the land that is left to rest or prepared for sowing. But that yield can be lost "for want of judgment," that is, through injustice, abuse, or poor management. The Hebrew text is difficult, and some understand it this way: the poor person produces quite a lot, but someone stronger takes it from him without justice.

These words are part of Proverbs, a collection of wisdom that tradition attributes largely to Solomon, although the book mentions other authors. Here a wise teacher observes everyday life. Before and after, he speaks of the righteous and the wicked, of inheritance, and of discipline. He shows that justice and good judgment protect what God gives.

For today: take wise care of what God entrusts to you, and never take advantage of the weakest. If you work with little, plan and save. If you have power, act with justice.
exp.25:25:
This verse says that a person can hide their hatred behind a false attitude, such as kindness or pleasant words. But that wickedness does not stay hidden forever. Deceit is pretense, and the "whole congregation" refers to the assembly or community of the people. His malice will come to light before everyone.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, attributed largely to Solomon, although scholars debate how they were gathered. Here the wise teacher warns about the one who speaks sweetly but keeps a grudge. The verses that follow show that whoever plots evil ends up falling into his own trap.

For today: do not be deceived only by pleasant words; also observe people's actions and character. And examine your own heart: if you hold resentment, do not disguise it with smiles. Bring it to God and seek reconciliation with sincerity.
exp.12:2:
This verse says that whoever takes care of what they say takes care of themselves. Guarding your mouth means thinking before you speak and knowing when to stay silent. In this verse, the word "life" means one's whole life or the whole person. "Destruction" means ruin or disaster. Someone who talks too much, without restraint, puts themselves at serious risk.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition credits much of it to Solomon. Here a teacher speaks, like a father instructing his son. The verses around it speak of listening to advice, of the fruit that words produce, and of rejecting lies. Everything comes together in one idea: our words have consequences.

Before you answer in anger, gossip, or make a hasty promise, pause briefly and pray. Ask yourself: Is it true? Is it necessary? Is it kind? Keeping silent at the right time can save a friendship, a job, or your peace.
exp.28:4:
The explanation says that someone who flatters their neighbor, that is, who praises them with false or exaggerated words to gain some advantage, is laying a net before their feet. "Flattering" means praising in a self-interested way. "Neighbor" means the person next to us or someone like us. The net is a trap that catches. It can be understood that the trap is meant for the one being flattered, who trusts and stumbles, although some think it also catches the flatterer himself.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, and this chapter was copied in the time of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). Here the wise man warns a young listener, in the style of a father who teaches. The verses nearby speak of kings, of justice and of traps, and this proverb shows that words too can be dangerous.

For today: try to speak with truth and with love, and be careful with anyone who only tells you what you want to hear. Be thankful for the friend who corrects you with respect.
exp.7:14:
The explanation says that kings reign through wisdom, and that princes or rulers set down what is just by means of it. The phrase about setting down justice means that they establish right laws and decisions. The word "princes" here refers to rulers or authorities in general, not only to the sons of kings.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented in Proverbs 8 as a person who calls everyone to listen to her. She has just said that she hates pride and the evil way, and that counsel and strength are found in her. Leaders who govern well need that wisdom. Some see in this verse a reference to Christ, but this point is interpreted in several ways.

For today: if you have any responsibility, at home, at work, or in the church, ask God for wisdom before you decide. Seek decisions that are just, not merely convenient.
exp.17:19:
This verse says that each person receives the consequences of what they speak. The words of their mouth and the products of their lips refer to their words. "Shall be satisfied" means they will be full, like someone who eats until they are filled. Just as food fills the stomach, words bring results that a person ends up "eating" for themselves, whether good or bad.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though some sections come from other authors. Here the teacher speaks like a father instructing his child. The nearby verses speak of conflicts between brothers and of the power of the tongue. Verse 21 reinforces this: the tongue brings life or death.

Today, before you speak, think about what harvest you want. Words of encouragement, truth, and peace produce good relationships; harsh or false words tend to turn back against us. Ask God to watch over your mouth.
exp.22:27:
This verse says that the immoral woman acts like a thief who stays hidden, waiting for her chance. The word "lieth in wait" means to watch closely in order to catch someone. The people described as "transgressors" are those who betray what is right and turn away from faithfulness. In this way, she causes more and more men to leave the straight path.

The one speaking is a wise father teaching his son. He has just said to him: "My son, give me your heart." He warns that immorality is a deep trap, and then he will go on to warn about drinking wine to excess. These are two dangers that promise pleasure but end in pain.

For today: guard what feeds your heart, and stay away from tempting situations before they catch you. Ask God for wisdom, and seek out friends who will help you remain faithful.
exp.5:9:
This verse shows what the lazy person says to keep resting: "A little more sleep, another little nap, and I fold my arms to rest." "Nap" means drifting into a half-sleep, and "folding the hands" means sitting still without working. Each excuse seems small and harmless.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son in Proverbs. Earlier he held up the ant as an example, which works without anyone forcing it. Then he asks the lazy person when he will get up. He goes on to warn that poverty will come suddenly, like an armed robber. He does not condemn rest itself, but the laziness that disguises itself as "just a little while."

For today: notice which important task you keep putting off with a "later." Do it today, even if it is only a small first step, and ask God for the strength to be consistent.
exp.22:22:
This verse invites you to buy the truth and not sell it. Along with it, it mentions wisdom, instruction, and understanding, which are also worth the cost. "Buy" means that truth has a price: time, effort, and sometimes giving things up. "Instruction" is the teaching or correction that shapes us.

Proverbs presents a wise father speaking to his son. Just before this, it warns against overindulging in food and drink, and it calls for honoring parents. Afterward, it speaks of the joy of a father whose son is righteous and wise. In this way, truth is seen as an inheritance that is received, treasured, and passed on. Many understand "do not sell it" to mean not trading it away for comfort or gain.

For today: set aside a fixed time each week to study the Bible and to listen to wise counsel, even when it is hard. And do not give up what is true to please others.
exp.13:17:
This verse compares two paths. The "simple" are naive people, who believe everything and do not think before they act. "Inherit folly" means they will receive, as an inheritance or as a result, their own lack of judgment. The "prudent" are those who think and weigh the consequences. They are "crowned with knowledge": their wisdom will be their adornment and their honor, like a crown.

It is part of the book of Proverbs, which tradition attributes in large part to Solomon, although the book gathers several collections. These are brief teachings meant to shape character, especially that of the young. The nearby verses contrast the wise person who turns away from evil with the foolish one who rushes ahead and gets angry quickly.

Today we can pause before deciding: ask questions, seek advice, and pray. In this way prudence becomes a habit that protects us and shapes us.
exp.10:26:
This verse says that whoever gets up early and seeks good with real effort will find favor, that is, acceptance and goodwill. On the other hand, whoever goes about looking for evil will have that evil come back upon them. Here "diligently seeketh" means to pursue something with earnest effort and eagerness. The verse's own phrase "it shall come unto him" carries the same sense as the explanation's point that the evil itself will reach the person.

These are sayings of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. They are not automatic promises, but general observations about how life tends to work. The verses before this one speak of generosity and of not hoarding grain; this one reinforces the idea that what we pursue shapes our path.

For today: ask yourself what you seek first each morning. You might begin the day thinking about how to help or encourage someone, and ask God to direct your steps toward good.
exp.23:20:
It says I should respect God and also civil authority. "Fear" here means to honor with reverence. "Given to change" refers to people who are unstable, who change their opinions and loyalties according to what suits them. "Do not meddle" means not to mix yourself in with them or join them. Some translators understand it as those who seek to overturn the order or rebel.

It is spoken by a teacher of wisdom, like a father to his son. It comes from a section of advice that warns against the wicked. The following verses say that ruin can come suddenly to those who rebel.

Today, try to surround yourself with people who are steadfast and honest. Respect God and those in authority, and do not let yourself be swept along by those who switch sides according to their convenience.
exp.19:28:
It says that each stage of life has its own honor. Young men are distinguished by their strength, their energy, and their ability to work. Old men are adorned by their old age, that is, their years, their experience, and their gray heads. The word "beauty" in the verse as quoted in the King James Version here means something that gives dignity or splendor, not physical attractiveness.

This verse belongs to the Proverbs of Solomon, brief sayings of wisdom meant to guide everyday life. Here there is no speaker in a particular situation; it is a wise observation. The verses nearby speak of the human heart that God examines, of the just king, and of correction that heals. Some think there is no clear thread connecting them, since the book often gathers loose sayings.

Today we can stop envying the stage of life that others are in. If you are young, use your strength wisely and serve. If you already have years, share gladly what you have learned, and let the rest of us value that riches.
exp.1:9:
It says that something truly changes when wisdom does not stay only in the head but enters the heart, that is, the deepest part of a person. It also says that knowledge, which here means understanding, becomes pleasant to the soul, meaning agreeable and desirable.

The speaker is a father instructing his son, as in the whole opening of Proverbs. The verses before explain that God gives wisdom and watches over those who walk uprightly. This verse opens the promise that follows: wisdom will keep the young man from the evil way and from bad companions.

For today: it is not enough to know what the Bible says; ask God that these truths move you and that you come to love them. Read one passage each day and ask yourself what concrete decision it calls you to make.
exp.23:6:
It says wisdom is "high," meaning out of reach, for the fool. He does not understand it and cannot attain it. So in the gate he does not open his mouth. The city gate was the place where the elders judged cases and gave counsel. There the fool has nothing of value to say.

The book of Proverbs gathers the teachings of wise men, and this chapter is attributed to the wise (verse 23 presents it that way). The nearby verses praise the strength of wisdom and the value of many counselors. This verse shows the contrast: the person who refuses to learn falls silent exactly when sound judgment is most needed.

For today: before you give your opinion in the family, at work, or in church, listen and learn. Seek the counsel of wise people, and speak when you have something good and well-considered to contribute.
exp.2:16:
It says that the ways of wisdom are pleasant and full of joy, and that all its paths lead to peace. "Pleasant" means enjoyable, the kind of thing that brings delight. "Paths" are roads or smaller trails. "Her" refers to wisdom, which the book presents as a person.

Proverbs is a collection of teachings about wisdom, and this part is traditionally attributed to Solomon, who speaks like a father to his son. Just before this, he has said that wisdom is worth more than jewels. He wants to encourage the young man to seek it, showing that living wisely is not a burden but a good way of life. It is a general principle, not a promise that there will never be difficulties.

Today we can remember that obeying God and deciding with care brings a deep peace. Before a hard decision, stop to pray and ask God for direction, and seek counsel in his Word.
exp.19:7:
This proverb says that a king who sits on his throne to judge, with only his attentive gaze, separates and drives away evil. "Scatters" means to disperse or make disappear, the way the wind clears away fog. "Throne of judgment" refers to the place where the king heard cases and decided them with justice.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom, and this saying is attributed to Solomon. Here it shows how a just and wise ruler, who watches carefully, uncovers wickedness and restrains those who act unjustly. The verses nearby speak of truth, integrity, and purity of heart. Some understand that it also points to God as the perfect Judge, although the text speaks directly of a human king.

For today: if you have authority, in your home, your work, or your church, be attentive and just, and do not let evil pass unchecked. And remember that none of us sees everything clearly, so ask God for wisdom.
exp.26:22:
This verse says we should pay close attention to the condition of our sheep and give our whole heart to caring for the flocks. "Be diligent" means to look carefully, without neglecting anything. "State" refers to the condition of the animals.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, which were gathered together later, in the time of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). The speaker gives counsel of wisdom to a people who lived from the land. The verses that follow explain the reason: wealth and power do not last forever, but careful and constant work provides for us.

Today we can apply it this way: take careful attention to what God has entrusted to you, whether your work, your family, or your health. Do not let things fall apart through neglect. Ask yourself: "What should I check today with more care and responsibility?"
exp.1:1:
