It says we should pay attention to wisdom and turn the heart toward understanding. Listening carefully, not in a distracted way, is what it means to give your ear close attention. The word for "incline" points to leaning toward something, and the second part, "apply thine heart," describes the mind and heart working together. Here the ear and the heart work together: we listen, and we also want what we hear.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, in the style of the book of Proverbs, traditionally associated with Solomon. This verse is part of a long conditional sentence (verses 1 to 5) that begins with "if." First a person receives the teaching, then seeks it eagerly, and in the end comes to understand the fear of the Lord.

For today: before you open the Bible or listen to wise advice, set your phone aside and ask God for a willing heart. Listening well is the first step toward growing in wisdom.
exp.11:19:
This proverb compares two kinds of heart. "Deceit" is a lie or a hidden trap. Those who "imagine evil" are the ones who plan harm against others. That kind of heart holds traps. By contrast, those who are counselors of peace, meaning those who seek peace and good for others, have joy within.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, though not every proverb has a certain author. Here the teacher speaks like a father giving advice. The verses around it contrast the tongue that wounds with the tongue that heals, and the truth that endures with the lie that does not last long. This verse shows that what we say comes from what we think.

Today, before you speak or act, examine your intentions. If you notice a desire to deceive or to hurt someone, ask God for a clean heart. Choosing to seek the good of others brings a quiet joy.
exp.15:18:
It says that it is better to be humble and to stay with ordinary, simple people, even if one has little, than to share in plunder with proud people. The phrase "humble spirit" means being gentle and not showing off. The "spoil" refers to gains taken in war or by force. The "proud" are the arrogant.

These words come from the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, as the advice of a wise father to his children. Just before this, it warns that pride goes before a fall. So the proverb shows that wealth shared with the proud has a dangerous end, while humility is a safe path.

Today we can ask ourselves who we associate with and what gains we accept. If a business or a group requires pride, deceit, or abuse of others, it is better to stay with little and with a clear conscience, beside people who are simple and honest.
exp.11:15:
The explanation says that the fool shows his anger right away, in the very moment he is offended. By contrast, the one who "covers shame" is prudent. "Covering" here does not mean pretending or being false. It means keeping the offense hidden, not reacting at once, and not giving the insult power over you. "Prudent" means wise and sensible.

This is a proverb attributed to Solomon, within a book of wisdom meant to shape character. It contrasts the fool with the wise person, as the verses around it do, which speak of counsel, of true words, and of the tongue that heals. The theme is self-control in speech.

Today, when someone hurts you with a word, do not answer on the spot. Breathe, pray, and wait a little before you respond. This is not keeping silent about the truth or putting up with abuse, but choosing calmly when and how to speak.
exp.10:24:
It says that the generous person ("liberal" here is not political, but means open-handed) will be prospered and will come to be well nourished, like a well-fed animal. And whoever satisfies others, that is, whoever gives food or drink to others and refreshes them, will also receive the same in their own life.

It is a proverb of wisdom traditionally attributed to Solomon, addressed to anyone who seeks to live well. The nearby verses contrast the one who scatters and yet gains more with the stingy person who ends up in poverty, and the one who hoards grain with the one who sells it and is blessed. It is a general rule of life, not an automatic promise in every case.

Today we can practice generosity without expecting anything in return: sharing time, food or help with someone who needs it this week. God often enriches the heart of the one who gives, though the blessing does not always come in the form of money.
exp.23:11:
This verse says that saying "we knew nothing" is no excuse. God knows the deepest parts of the heart, that is, our true intentions. The phrase "weighs the hearts" means that He judges exactly what is within us. The phrase "watches over your soul" means that He keeps watch over you and cares for your life. In the end, God will repay each person according to what they have done.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son in the book of Proverbs. The verses just before this one speak of helping those who are in danger of an unjust death. If someone pretends not to notice so as to avoid helping, this proverb reminds them that God sees their heart.

For today: do not look the other way in the face of injustice or a need close to you. Ask yourself what you can do, even if it is little, and do it sincerely before God.
exp.28:7:
The explanation says that scornful and insolent people "ensnare" the city, meaning they wrap it in trouble, the way someone sets a trap or starts a fire (the Hebrew word can also be understood as "kindle"). By contrast, wise people "turn away wrath": they calm tempers and keep anger from growing. "Scornful men" are those who mock everything and look down on what is right.

This is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed in large part to Solomon. These are brief teachings from a wisdom teacher meant to shape character. Here, among verses that speak of the righteous and the wicked, the fool and the wise, it shows how the attitudes of a few people affect an entire community.

For today: before responding with mockery or anger in a discussion, at home, at work, or online, pause and choose words that calm. A humble heart can keep a conflict from growing large.
exp.27:1:
It says that when a land turns away from God and justice, it has many rulers who change again and again. By contrast, under a person of understanding and wisdom, stability is kept. "Princes" are rulers or leaders, and "without change" means without sudden shifts, firm.

This proverb comes from a collection attributed to Solomon, which according to Proverbs 25:1 was copied out by the men of Hezekiah. The nearby verses contrast the wicked, who flee full of fear, with the righteous, who live with confidence. The Hebrew text of this verse is difficult, and some understand it as a reference to a long and stable life of the nation or of its order.

Today it reminds us that wisdom and integrity sustain families, churches, and communities. We can ask God for wisdom, pray for our leaders, and be people of integrity wherever we live.
exp.0:31:
It says that the complacency of the simple will lead them to death, and that the prosperity of fools will ruin them. "Simple" here refers to those who lack wisdom and do not want to learn it. "Fools" are those who reject correction. The word "turning away" refers to a false rest, a carefree life that springs from indifference rather than from true peace.

The speaker is Wisdom, who in Proverbs 1 appears as a voice calling out to people in the streets. She warns those who would not take her counsel or accept her rebuke. She tells them they will reap the consequences of their own choices. By contrast, the following verse promises security to whoever listens to her.

For today: do not confuse a comfortable life with a healthy one. When everything is going well, it is a good time to seek counsel, accept correction, and review your decisions with humility.
exp.14:17:
The explanation says that the person who is quick-tempered, who gets angry easily, stirs up quarrels and arguments. On the other hand, the one who is slow to anger, that is, the one who has patience, calms the disputes.

The verse is in the book of Proverbs, which gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here a teacher of wisdom speaks, like a father advising his children. The verses around it speak of peace in the home, of love and the fear of God, and show that a wise life seeks harmony.

For today: when someone provokes you, take a deep breath and wait before you respond. A calm answer can put out an argument that, with shouting, would grow much bigger.
exp.19:29:
It says that blows and wounds that leave a mark serve to cleanse and correct evil. The "wounds" (open sores) reach to the deepest part of a person, "the belly," which in biblical language means the inner self, the heart and the conscience. Other versions translate: "the blows that wound cleanse away evil." The text is brief and can be understood in several ways.

It is a proverb of Solomon, a wise father teaching his son. It comes after verses about the king who rules with mercy and truth. It may refer to correction and just punishment, which help stop evil and transform the heart.

For today: do not flee from correction. If someone who loves you points out a mistake, or if a painful consequence confronts you, receive it with humility. God can use it to heal the deepest part of your heart and help you grow.
exp.30:27:
It says that this woman's children stand up to honor her and call her "blessed," meaning happy or favored. Her husband also praises her with words. The old-fashioned forms are rewritten here as "arise up" and "call her": the verse above reads "arise up" and "call her blessed."

These words close the poem about the virtuous woman, which runs from Proverbs 31:10 to 31. The chapter begins as teaching that a mother gave to King Lemuel (verse 1). Scholars are not certain who Lemuel was. The poem shows that her work, her wisdom and her kindness bear fruit in the family, and that this fruit is recognized with gratitude.

For today: don't wait for someone to die or leave before you thank them. Today, seek out a person in your family who serves faithfully and tell them, in concrete words, what good you have seen in them and why you are grateful.
exp.7:21:
The explanation says that Wisdom, who here speaks as if she were a person, existed before God made his works. The King James wording "possessed me" means that God had her with him, as something belonging to him from the beginning. The phrase "in the beginning of his way" refers to the start of his manner of acting or creating. "Of old" means from very distant times. Some translations say "created me," because the Hebrew verb can be understood in several ways.

In Proverbs 8 Wisdom speaks, presented as a voice calling people to listen to her. It shows that wisdom is not a passing idea but something that was present from before creation. Many Christians see here a foreshadowing of Christ, but scholars debate whether this is only a poetic personification or something more.

For today: if God's wisdom is so ancient and firm, it is worth seeking it before deciding. Before acting, pause, pray, and consult the Bible.
exp.20:17:
This proverb says that the wicked person becomes the ransom for the righteous, and the treacherous one (the person who betrays or acts with deceit) takes the place of the upright. A ransom is the price paid to set someone free. The idea seems to be that the harm prepared for the righteous ends up falling on the wicked.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the section (Proverbs 10:1). Here the teacher of wisdom instructs his readers about how God's justice works. Interpreters understand it in several ways: some see a reversal of positions, like Haman and Mordecai in Esther; others see it as a general principle, not a rule without exceptions.

For today: do not lose heart or seek revenge when you are treated unjustly. Keep doing what is right, and trust that God is a just judge who knows how and when to set things right.
exp.24:24:
This verse compares two things: cold water and good news. When someone is very thirsty, a drink of fresh water restores them. In the same way, receiving good news from a distant place refreshes the heart. "Soul" here means the whole person, with their desires and needs.

It is a proverb of Solomon, which the men of King Hezekiah copied and gathered, according to Proverbs 25:1. It was written to give practical wisdom through images from everyday life. In those times news could take weeks to arrive, so hearing from a loved one was a great relief. The verses around it speak of other everyday matters.

Today we can be that "cold water" for others. Write to or call someone who is far away or discouraged, and share a kind word, a message of hope, or a prayer. A simple message can refresh the one who needs it.
exp.6:10:
She is loud and restless, without any self-control. She is stubborn and defiant, hard to correct. And "her feet abide not in her house" means she does not stay at home; she is always out in the streets, looking for something.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son. He tells what he saw from his window: a young man without understanding who approaches that woman's corner at nightfall. She is an example of seduction that leads to ruin. The father describes her behavior so that the son will recognize the danger before he falls.

Today we can learn to watch our steps. If a place or a friendship feeds temptation, it is better to avoid it from the start. And let us seek to make our home a place of peace, rest, and the presence of God, so that we do not go looking outside for what only He can fill.
exp.19:11:
This verse says that God is the one who made both the ear that hears and the eye that sees. The phrase "the Lord hath made even both of them" means that both are his handiwork, and "the Lord" is the name of God in this older translation.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom from Solomon and other wise men of Israel, and this section is a collection of short sayings. The verses around it speak of honesty, work, and fair dealing. For that reason, some understand that God, in giving us our senses, also expects us to use them responsibly. Others read it simply as a praise of the Creator. The text does not settle the question, so both readings are possible.

Today we can use what we see and hear with gratitude and attention: listening patiently to others and looking honestly at our own actions, knowing that God gave us these gifts.
exp.6:12:
She grabs the young man, kisses him, and, with no shame at all, speaks to him boldly.

Here the wise father speaks, teaching his son. He describes a scene he witnessed, to warn him about the danger of the unfaithful woman. She has just been described as restless and fond of the streets. Now her speech begins, full of religious and sweet-sounding words, which in the verses that follow she will use to deceive the young man and justify what she is doing.

For today: do not trust only what is attractive or what sounds pious and flattering. Before you act, ask yourself whether this brings you closer to God and to faithfulness, or pulls you away. Fleeing temptation in time is wisdom, not weakness.
exp.21:25:
This verse advises against being one of those who "strike hands," that is, those who seal a deal by shaking hands in order to become guarantors. "Being sureties for debts" means answering with our own goods for what another person owes. The warning is not to commit ourselves to paying someone else's debt.

The book of Proverbs gathers practical wisdom, attributed in large part to Solomon, though this section is presented as the teaching of the wise. It is addressed to a young person so that he may live with prudence. The next verse shows the danger: if the debtor does not pay, the guarantor may lose even his bed. For the Israelites, this could mean economic and family ruin.

For today: before signing as a guarantor or lending your name to a loan, ask yourself whether you could pay that debt on your own. Helping is good, but it can be done through a gift you can truly afford to give, without putting your family at risk.
exp.10:3:
This verse says that money is of no use on the day God judges. "The day of wrath" refers to the moment of God's judgment. "Righteousness" means living uprightly and honestly before God. Only that righteous life delivers from death, that is, it rescues from ruin and condemnation.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings, and many are attributed to Solomon. Here the wise teacher instructs his reader through contrasts: the proud fall, the humble receive wisdom; the upright advance securely, the wicked stumble. Some understand "death" as an untimely death; others, as the final judgment. Both readings fit.

For today: do not place your security in what you have in the bank. Care more about your honesty, your humility, and your relationship with God, because that is what truly sustains you in the hardest moments.
exp.29:1:
Agur says that he feels more "brutish" than anyone, that is, dull or poorly taught. He adds that he does not have the understanding of a man, meaning he does not consider himself to possess the wisdom one would expect of a person. It is a very humble way of speaking.

The one speaking is Agur, son of Jakeh. We know very little about him, and scholars discuss who he was and where he came from. His humility prepares what follows: he acknowledges that he does not know the knowledge of the Holy One and asks who governs the heavens, the winds, and the earth. Some think he speaks with irony; others, that he says it sincerely. In both cases, he points to the greatness of God.

For today: before believing that we know everything, it is wise to approach God with humility. Recognizing our limits opens us to learn from Him and from His Word.
exp.28:0:
The person who is corrected again and again, yet becomes stubborn and refuses to listen, will one day fall suddenly, with no way to recover. To be stiff-necked means to be stubborn, like someone who stiffens the neck so as not to lower the head. The word that describes being broken down means destroyed or shattered. Without remedy speaks of there being no cure or way out.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and this chapter is attributed to Solomon, although some scholars think it was compiled later. The tone is that of a teacher who warns, like a father speaking to his children. The verses that follow speak of rulers who are just and unjust, and of the wisdom that brings joy to parents.

For today: when someone you trust points out a mistake, before defending yourself, stop and consider it calmly. Ask God for a humble heart. Listening in time can spare you painful falls.
exp.18:25:
This proverb says that whoever takes what belongs to his father and drives his mother out of the house, or mistreats her until she runs away, is a son who brings shame and disgrace. The verb it uses for "drive out" means making someone leave out of fear or mistreatment. The one who brings shame is the one who causes shame, and the one who dishonors is the one who takes away the honor of his family.

The book of Proverbs collects teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although this chapter does not say so directly. Here a wise father speaks to his son. The verses nearby speak of laziness, correction and mockery, and show that foolishness shows in how we treat others, beginning with our family. Honoring one's parents is also found in the Ten Commandments.

For today: care for your parents with respect, patience and concrete help, especially when they grow old. Visit them, listen to them, and never take advantage of them.
exp.29:18:
The explanation says there are four mysterious things: how an eagle flies through the air, how a serpent moves over a rock, how a ship sails through the middle of the sea, and how a man behaves with a young woman. In every case, the "trail" is the path or track, and these four leave no visible mark.

Agur, son of Jakeh, speaks in this chapter with humility and admits that he does not understand everything. The first three images come from nature; the fourth refers to the mystery of love or courtship. Some believe the following verse suggests a sense of deceit or concealment, and others see only wonder. It is not entirely certain.

For today: recognize that not everything can be explained or controlled. Admire the mystery of life, and in your relationships act with honesty, without hiding what you do.
exp.15:16:
This verse says that upright people, those who live with integrity, have a path or way of life that consists in turning away from evil. "Path" speaks of the way a person lives day by day. And whoever keeps their way, that is, whoever watches over it with care, is protecting their own soul, which means their whole life.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though the book has several sections. Here the teacher speaks like a father to his children. The verses nearby speak of wisdom and humility, and this one reinforces the idea: living wisely includes avoiding evil carefully, so as not to fall into the pride that comes afterward.

For today: think of a situation that tends to make you stumble, such as certain conversations, websites, or companions, and decide to step away from it with one concrete action. Ask God for help to keep that care.
exp.10:28:
This verse says that whoever causes trouble, quarrels, or disorder in their own family will not keep anything of value: they will "inherit the wind," that is, something empty that cannot be grasped. To "trouble" means to disturb, unsettle, or harm. It also says that the fool, the one who refuses to think wisely, will end up serving the person who is wise of heart.

It is a proverb, attributed in large part to Solomon. These sayings teach through contrasts: the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the foolish. Some think that troubling one's house refers to greed or injustice within the home; others take it to mean quarreling in general. In either case, the point is that foolishness has a price.

Today, take care of the peace of your home. Before you shout, criticize, or neglect your loved ones for your own interests, think about what you are truly building. Ask God for wisdom and seek to be a peacemaker.
exp.28:5:
This verse says that the sin of a wicked man is like a trap for himself. The word "transgression" means disobeying or bending what is right, and "snare" is a trap for catching animals. By contrast, the righteous person lives in freedom and can sing and rejoice.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, which according to Proverbs 25:1 were copied out by the men of Hezekiah. They are sayings of wisdom meant to teach people how to live well. The verses around it speak of flattery, injustice, and caring for the poor. All of them show that evil deceives and traps, while righteousness gives stability.

For today: when you feel tempted to lie, take advantage of others, or bend things just "a little," remember that sin often traps the one who practices it. Choose honesty, even when it costs you, and over time you will have peace and real reasons to rejoice.
exp.12:16:
This proverb compares two kinds of messengers. The wicked messenger is the one who cannot be trusted: he changes the words, lies, or fails to carry out his task, and so he falls into mischief, meaning he ends up in trouble. The faithful messenger, on the other hand, brings a true message and carries out his task, and so he brings health: his words help to heal and to resolve matters.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and this one is attributed largely to Solomon. In these verses the wise person is contrasted with the fool, and the one who accepts correction with the one who despises it. Here it is applied to someone who carries words from one place to another.

For today: be a trustworthy person in what you say and in what you are entrusted with. Pass on the truth with love, adding nothing and hiding nothing. Your faithfulness can bring relief to others.
exp.5:24:
This verse warns us not to let a desire for the beauty of another person's wife grow in the heart. "Lust" is to desire something strongly when it is not rightfully ours. "Take" here means to catch, as when someone is held captive. The "eyelids" refer to the flirtatious glances with which someone tries to draw another in.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son in Proverbs. He has just said that the commandments are like a light that guards against the seductive woman. What follows shows the consequences: ruin, loss, and burning, like someone playing with fire. The guarding begins in the heart, not only in outward actions.

For today: be careful about what you feed with your mind and your gaze. If you feel attraction toward someone who is not your spouse, do not cultivate it. Step away quickly, pray, and set clear boundaries.
exp.4:19:
This verse is a question a father asks his son: "Why be blinded by another woman?" The phrases "another's" and "stranger" refer to a woman who is not your wife. The phrase "walk blind" speaks of losing good judgment, and "embrace the bosom" means seeking intimacy outside of marriage.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son in Proverbs 5. Just before, he invites him to rejoice in the wife of his youth. Afterward, he reminds him that God sees all the paths of a man. The question shows that unfaithfulness makes no sense: it exchanges something good and blessed for something that blinds and traps.

For today: guard your heart in your marriage. Be thankful to your spouse, give them your time, and avoid situations or conversations that lead you to look elsewhere. Faithfulness is cultivated every day.
exp.25:9:
The verse says that someone great and authoritative, one who "formed all things," that is, made or produced everything, also gives pay to both the fool and the transgressors. The word "fool" means someone lacking good judgment. Here there is a real difficulty: the Hebrew of this verse is very obscure, and translations differ widely. Some read it this way: the employer who hires anyone at all, fool or wicked person, wounds everyone. For that reason it is wise to hold this reading with humility.

It is a proverb of Solomon, within a series of sayings about the fool (Prov. 26:1-12). The neighboring verses warn against giving honor to the fool. It probably teaches that giving power or reward to people without judgment brings harm.

For today: before entrusting a position or responsibility to someone, look at their character and wisdom, not only at their desire to have it.
exp.29:23:
The verse says there are four creatures that are very small on the earth, yet so wise that they surpass those who think themselves wise. The phrase about the smallest refers to what is weakest or most insignificant. It is the introduction to a list that follows with ants, rock badgers, and other animals.

These words are part of the sayings of Agur, son of Jakeh. About who he was, the Bible says very little, and it is best not to invent more. Agur observes nature to teach practical wisdom. Note that in other verses some translators render the word for the small animal as "coneys," meaning rock-dwelling animals, but this is one possible interpretation.

For today: do not lose heart if you are small or do not have much power. Wisdom is learned by observing with humility: planning ahead, working with steadiness, and seeking a safe place. God can teach you even through the simplest things.
exp.14:26:
He who is greedy for gain brings trouble on his own household, the explanation says, the one who always wants to win more. But the one who turns away from bribes or gifts meant to buy favors will have a long and secure life. The word "troubleth" means to stir up unrest and conflict. "Shall live" can be understood as living in peace and well-being.

This is a proverb of Solomon, a teacher of wisdom who instructs his son through contrasts. In this chapter, God tears down the house of the proud and protects the widow. In the same way, the house of the greedy is set against the life of the honest. Some think the word about gifts refers to bribes in the courts, but it can also cover any unjust gain.

For today: before accepting a deal, a favor, or money of doubtful origin, ask yourself whether it will cost you the peace of your home. A clean and quiet income is worth more than a gain that divides your family.
exp.25:22:
It says that lips that speak with a lot of fire and affection, but hide a wicked heart, are like a thin layer of silver dross laid over a clay pot. A "potsherd" is a broken piece of a clay pot, and "dross" is the waste that comes off when metal is melted down. It shines on the outside, but it is worth nothing.

The verse's wording about "burning lips" can be read as speech that is intense and passionate. Some translators understand "burning lips" as words of exaggerated affection.

The book of Proverbs gathers the wisdom of Solomon and other wise people of Israel, to teach people how to live with prudence. This verse comes among warnings about gossip and deceit. The verses that follow explain that a person who hates can disguise it with kind words.

For today: do not be won over just by pretty words. Watch conduct and character over time. And examine your own heart, so that what you say on the outside is sincere on the inside.
exp.18:14:
Slothfulness, it says, casts a person into a deep sleep, like someone who dozes off and lets life pass by. And the idle soul, that is, the careless one with no interest in fulfilling their duties, will suffer hunger, meaning they will go hungry. Here "fall into sleep" does not speak only of sleeping, but of an attitude of inactivity.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom; tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though not everything can be known with certainty. Its purpose is to teach how to live with prudence. The verses nearby speak of family, of foolishness, and of the consequences of heeding or despising good paths. This proverb shows that neglect has a price.

For today: do not leave for later what you can do today. Choose one pending task, at work, in study, or at home, and do it today with steadiness, trusting that God blesses diligent effort.
exp.17:17:
It says that casting lots can end a dispute and separate two powerful people who are at odds. "Lot" was like throwing stones or sticks to decide a matter.

This proverb is part of the wisdom attributed to Solomon. It comes after verses about the one who seems right until the other side arrives, and before others about how hard it is to reconcile offended brothers. It shows that when no one gives way, a method accepted by everyone was needed to decide. Scholars do not agree on whether it approves this practice or only describes it.

Today, when an argument gets stuck, look for a fair path that everyone agrees to: prayer, wise counsel, a mediator, or a clear agreement, before the conflict separates people further.
exp.2:2:
This verse asks that mercy and truth never leave you. "Not forsake" means they should never abandon you. Being bound "about your neck" speaks of wearing them like a necklace, visible to everyone. "Write them upon the table of your heart" means engraving them deeply, so that they become part of who you are.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs. Just before this, he asked the son to keep his commandments, and then he promises that whoever lives this way will find favor with God and with people. Many understand mercy here as faithful and loyal kindness.

Today we can ask ourselves: am I kind and honest at the same time? Choose one situation this week, at home or at work, where you can be sincere without losing compassion, and practice it consistently.
exp.29:17:
He says there are things the author cannot fully grasp, and he counts them like this: "three... yea, four." It is a common way of speaking in Proverbs to show a list that keeps growing. "Are hidden from me" means they seem mysterious to him, hard to understand completely.

What follows in verses 19 and 20 are the things that leave him amazed.

The speaker is Agur, son of Jakeh, who appears in this chapter as a humble man who acknowledges his limits. Before this verse he spoke of things that are never satisfied, and of rebellion against parents. Now he changes tone and confesses wonder before mysteries. Some understand that the fourth example speaks of the mystery of human love; others see a moral warning. Scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: accept that you do not understand everything. A humble attitude before God and before life keeps you teachable and grateful.
exp.9:27:
This verse compares two kinds of hope. The "righteous" are people who seek to live according to God. The "wicked" are those who live without taking him into account. The hope of the righteous ends in gladness, that is, in joy. The hope of the wicked will perish, meaning it will come to an end and will not be fulfilled.

Proverbs is a collection of wise sayings. Tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon, although some scholars think it was gathered by several authors. Here the wise man speaks like a teacher advising his listeners. The verses nearby speak of the fear of the Lord, which gives life, and of the steadfastness of the righteous. It is a general observation, not a promise for every case.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our hope. If we base it on God and on living with integrity, we will have a hope that does not crumble with the changes of life.
exp.12:18:
It says that when someone achieves what they long for, their soul rejoices and feels satisfied. But for fools, that is, those who reject wisdom and do not want to be corrected, turning away from evil is "abomination" (something that repels them). They prefer to stay in wrongdoing rather than change.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the title of the book, aimed at teaching wisdom to young people. The verses around it speak of accepting advice and correction, and of the company we keep and how it shapes us. Some think the verse contrasts the sweetness of a good desire fulfilled with the bitterness the fool feels in giving up his wickedness; others see it as a warning that the fool cannot enjoy what is good because he loves what is evil.

Today, examine what you desire and what it costs you to let go. Ask God for a heart that longs for what is good, and give yourself the opportunity to leave a harmful habit behind with the help of wise people.
exp.24:0:
This verse introduces a new section of the book. It says that what follows (chapters 25 to 29) are proverbs of Solomon, but that they were copied out by the men of King Hezekiah. The word "copied out" can be understood as gathering together, transcribing, or arranging.

The book does not say who is speaking here; it seems to be a note from the editor. Hezekiah reigned about 270 years after Solomon. His men, probably scribes or advisers, gathered and preserved these sayings. The text does not explain in detail how they did it, but it shows that wisdom was cared for and passed on with effort.

For today: wisdom does not keep itself; someone cares for it and passes it on to others. We can be thankful for those who taught us the Bible, and seek the habit of reading it, writing down what we learn, and sharing it with our family or our friends.
exp.10:20:
Though the explanation says that even if the wicked join together and give each other a hand to support one another, they will not escape punishment. By contrast, the children and descendants of the righteous will come out safe. The word "seed" in the verse means offspring, so this phrase refers to the descendants of the righteous. The expression "hand join in hand" is hard to pin down: some understand it as an alliance or pact among the wicked, others as a united effort to escape.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, which teaches wisdom by way of contrast between the righteous and the wicked. The verses nearby speak of righteousness that leads to life and of evil that leads to death. Proverbs express general principles, not automatic promises for every case.

For today: do not let yourself be persuaded by the force of the majority, nor by "arrangements" between people who cheat. Choose today to be honest, even when it seems that others are coming out ahead. God sees, and his justice is more certain than any human alliance.
exp.6:22:
It says that a young man is led along without realizing the danger, just as a bird rushes toward the trap without knowing it will cost it its life. The word for the bird's trap is a snare, a device for catching birds. The word for the arrow is the dart. The "liver" is mentioned as a vital organ; the image speaks of a deadly wound. The blow comes through until it is already too late.

The speaker is a wise father, who is teaching his son in the book of Proverbs. He has just described a seductive woman who persuades an inexperienced young man with smooth words. The father uses strong images (the ox, the fool, the bird) to warn him that sin attracts with sweetness but ends in ruin.

For today: do not trust what only sounds good or looks appealing. Before making a tempting decision, think about where it leads in the end, and seek counsel from wise people and from God in prayer.
exp.9:0:
It says that a wise son brings joy to his father, and that a foolish son brings sorrow to his mother. "Proverbs" are short sayings of wisdom. A "fool" is someone who acts without good judgment and refuses correction. "Joy" and "sorrow" show how the choices of children affect the heart of the family.

The title attributes this group of proverbs to Solomon, king of Israel, known for his wisdom. Here begins a collection of short sayings, without a continuous narrative thread. The verses that follow speak of wealth gained wrongly, righteousness, and God's care for the righteous. The teaching of a father who wants to form the next generation is reflected here. Father and mother are mentioned together; this is not a rigid rule, but a way of speaking about the whole family.

Today: think about how your decisions, big or small, touch those who love you. Seek counsel, listen to correction, and ask God for wisdom to live in a way that honors your family.
exp.12:14:
The explanation says that a person with good understanding, that is, with good judgment and wisdom, gains the favor and goodwill of others. By contrast, the way of transgressors is hard. Those who break faith, act with deceit, or despise what is right are the ones meant by transgressors. The way of such people is "hard": difficult, rough, full of stumbling.

The book of Proverbs is a collection of teachings on wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon. Here the counsel is given as a contrast between the wise person and the foolish one. The nearby verses speak of obeying instruction and of the life that this produces. Some understand "favour" as the favor of God and others as the esteem of people; both senses fit.

Today we can ask God for discernment and act with honesty and humility, even when that is harder. Listening to advice and keeping your word builds trust around you.
exp.26:24:
It says that nature follows its cycle: the grass sprouts (the tender pasture), the green herb appears, and then the hay that grows in the mountains is cut down. The word "gathered" in the verse above means "cut down" or "harvested."

The book of Proverbs collects practical wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon and other wise men. Here the teacher advises someone who has livestock to look after them carefully, because wealth does not last forever. The verses that follow show that God provides through the pasture, and the pasture through the animals: clothing, income, and food for the family.

For today: God sustains your life with simple, steady provisions, but he expects you to be diligent. Take responsible care of your work, your money, and your resources, without assuming they will last forever, and give thanks for what God gives you each day.
exp.15:13:
This proverb says that a king's anger can bring death, because a king had the power to punish and even to take a life. But the wise person knows this and seeks to calm that anger or avoid it. "Messenger of death" is a way of saying that his rage announces a serious danger.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition connects it with Solomon, though it also contains other authors. The verses nearby speak of righteous kings who love what is right and of their favor, which gives life. Here the teaching is about prudence before someone who has authority.

Today we can apply it this way: when a boss, an authority, or someone with power is upset, it is wise to respond with humility, calm, and sensible words, without provoking the conflict further. This does not mean approving of what is wrong, but acting with wisdom.
exp.12:17:
This proverb says that whoever ignores advice will end up in need and shame. By contrast, whoever heeds correction, that is, whoever receives it and takes it seriously, will be honored. "Refuseth" means to reject or give little value to something. "Regardeth" means to keep something in mind and act on it.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, though this verse does not say who is speaking. It is a wise father or teacher giving instruction. The nearby verses contrast the wise with the foolish, and those who listen with those who shut themselves off. It is a general rule of life, not a promise that is always fulfilled immediately.

For today: the next time someone corrects you, do not defend yourself right away. Listen calmly, pray, and think about what you can learn. Seek out a wise and sincere person who can advise you.
exp.6:11:
This verse continues to describe the woman who goes out to meet the young man. It says that at times she is outside, at other times in the streets, and that she lies in wait at every corner. "Lying in wait" means watching secretly, waiting for the right moment to catch someone. The open squares of the city, where people gathered, are the places where she moves about freely.

The one speaking throughout the chapter is a wise father instructing his son. With the image of this crafty and restless woman, he warns him about seduction and adultery. She does not stay at home, and her movements show that she deliberately seeks out victims. It is a scene that teaches by contrast: what seems attractive may hide a trap.

For today: do not trust your willpower in the moment of temptation. Stay away in advance from the places, conversations, and screens that put you at risk, and ask God for wisdom to flee in time.
exp.16:6:
It says that refined, lofty speech does not suit a fool, because his life does not back it up. Speech that is very polished and pompous is a kind of fancy talk, and if that already clashes in a fool, it is far worse for a prince, a leader, to speak with lies on his lips.

These sayings belong to the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, a king who taught practical wisdom. Here words and character are compared: just before, there is mention of mocking the poor and of honor within the family, and just after, of friendship and words that cause harm. Some scholars understand the "fool" and the "prince" as examples of what does not go together with what is said.

For today: whoever has influence, at home, at work, or in church, should make sure their words are true. A good speech does not replace honesty.
exp.7:26:
It says that Wisdom was present when God made the heavens, and when he marked out with a compass the horizon, that is, the circular line where the sky seems to meet the sea. "Upon the face of the depth" refers to the surface of the deep waters. "Set a compass" is like drawing a circle with a tool, with order and measure.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented as a person, in Proverbs 8. She calls people to listen to her and explains that she existed before creation. Many Christians see here a shadow of Christ, the Wisdom of God, though others read it only as a poetic way of speaking of divine wisdom. Its purpose is to show that living wisely means living in line with God's design.

For today: if God ordered the universe with such wisdom, you can trust him with your decisions. Before deciding something important, ask him for guidance in prayer.
exp.0:19:
This verse presents wisdom as if she were a person speaking aloud. "Crieth" means she cries out or calls with force. "Without" means out in the street, in the open air, and "streets" are the public places where people gather. Wisdom does not hide; she speaks where everyone can hear her.

The book of Proverbs uses here a poetic device called personification. The one speaking is wisdom, not a historical figure. Just before, the text showed the end of those who pursue greed and fall into their own traps. Now wisdom offers another way and calls people to listen before it is too late.

For today: good guidance is not reserved for a few. Today you can seek it in the Bible, in prayer, and in the counsel of sensible people. Ask yourself: am I listening, or am I ignoring that voice?
exp.24:20:
It says that if someone who hates you or treats you as an enemy goes hungry, you should give him bread, and if he is thirsty, water. That is, help him in his basic need. The word translated "hates" in the source means to hate or wish harm.

It is a proverb attributed to Solomon, copied in the time of King Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). These are wise sayings for living well. The verse that follows speaks of heaping burning coals on the enemy's head; scholars understand this in several ways, such as stirring up shame that leads to repentance. Paul quotes this teaching in Romans 12:20, urging us to overcome evil with good.

Today we can respond with a concrete act of kindness toward someone who has hurt us: a meal, a help, a kind word. This does not mean approving of the harm, but refusing to repay evil with evil and leaving justice in God's hands.
exp.19:15:
It says that if someone has become a guarantor, that is, has stood surety for a stranger's debt, the lender may keep his garment as security. To stand surety is to answer for another person's debt, and a pledge is something left behind to secure a payment. Some understand "the stranger" as a foreign woman, and others as a stranger in general. The central meaning is the same either way.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, in the tone of counsel from a father to a son. The warning against committing oneself to the debts of people one does not know well is repeated in Proverbs. Here it seems to describe, with irony, that someone who acted without thinking must face the consequences.

Today: before you sign as a guarantor or lend your name for someone you barely know, consider whether you could pay that debt. Helping is good, but do it with prudence.
exp.6:20:
The explanation says that the strange woman convinced the young man with very smooth and pleasing words. Her words "caused him to yield," meaning she overcame him or made him give in. "Forced him" means she dragged him along or pressed him. "The flattering of her lips" speaks of sweet, flattering talk. She did not use force, but the seduction of her words.

Here a wise father speaks, teaching his son. He has just described the scene of a young man without sense who meets a married woman. She gives him excuses and promises pleasure while her husband is away on a trip. The father wants his son to see how deception comes step by step, and not to be carried along by it.

For today: do not trust only how pleasant something sounds. Sweet words can hide harmful paths. Before giving in, compare what you hear with the truth of God and ask for wise counsel.
exp.5:14:
This verse says that the ruin of that person will come all at once, without warning.

Here a wise father is instructing his son, in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. He has just described a wicked man who deceives with his gestures, thinks evil all the time, and stirs up quarrels. "Therefore" shows a consequence: whoever sows division does not escape forever. Right after this comes the list of things that God hates.

For today: do not be fooled if someone seems to get their way while lying or dividing others. Try to be someone who builds peace, speaks the truth, and corrects their wrong path in time, before it is too late.
exp.0:28:
This verse gives the reason for what was said before: people face consequences because they rejected wisdom. "Hated" means that they looked down on it and turned away from it. "Did not choose the fear of the Lord" means that they did not pick reverence for God, trusting Him and obeying Him, and instead chose to live without Him.

Here Wisdom speaks, who in Proverbs 1 appears as a person calling out in the streets. She had invited people to listen, but she was ignored. That is why, when calamity comes, it is already too late for those who insisted on their own way. It is a serious warning, not a wish to punish.

For today: let us not wait for a crisis to seek God. Today we can choose to listen to His Word, accept sound counsel, and correct what is not right. That daily decision protects us.
exp.11:18:
It says that what is spoken with truth lasts forever, but a lie lasts only a moment. "Lip" and "tongue" stand for the person who speaks. "Shall be established" means it stays firm and does not fall. "For a moment" means the lie lasts only a short time, because sooner or later it comes to light.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon, though it also contains other voices. Here the wise person compares the one who tells the truth with the one who deceives. The verses around it speak of words that wound like a sword and words that heal like medicine. The point is that our words have real consequences.

For today: before you exaggerate, hide something, or tell a "small" lie to get out of a tight spot, remember that the truth, though it may cost you, gives a firm foundation. Decide to be honest today, even when it is uncomfortable, and ask God for the courage to do it with kindness.
exp.24:25:
It says that when a righteous person gives way, goes wrong, or is overcome before a wicked person, it is like a well of clean water that has been muddied. "Troubled" means stirred up and dirty; "corrupt spring" is a spring of water that has been spoiled. The "wicked" are those who live without regard for God.

This proverb belongs to the sayings of Solomon that the men of Hezekiah copied (Proverbs 25:1). They are brief sayings with images from daily life. Here water, so precious, serves as the comparison. Earlier the text spoke of cold water for the thirsty; now muddied water shows the loss when a righteous person fails. Scholars debate whether the "falling down" refers to sinning, to yielding out of fear, or to being defeated; the text does not specify.

For today: our conduct influences others, who drink from our example. When you feel pressure to give way on what is right, ask God for firmness. If you fall, return to Him soon: the spring can be cleansed.
exp.26:19:
It says that the grave and destruction are never full: there is always room for more dead. In Hebrew, "destruction" is Abaddon, a name for the place of ruin. In the same way, the eyes of a person are never content: they see something and always want more. The word "satisfied" means to be full and content.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, which were copied out by the men of Hezekiah, according to Proverbs 25:1. It is wisdom for daily life. Before this it speaks of the human heart, and after it speaks of how praise tests us. The common theme is that we should know our desires and our hearts.

For today: when you feel you need something more to be happy, stop and give thanks for what you already have. Ask God for a contented heart, and do not let what your eyes see or social media rule your desires.
exp.21:0:
It says that having a good name is worth more than having a lot of money. "Good reputation" is an honorable standing, and "good favor" is the goodwill and esteem of others, earned through good character. According to the proverb, that outweighs silver and gold.

This verse is in the book of Proverbs, a collection of wise sayings. This section is attributed to Solomon, though scholars debate how the book came together. Its purpose is to teach how to live wisely. The next verse says that God made both the rich and the poor, which suggests that a person's worth does not depend on their money.

Today we can take care of our word and our everyday dealings. Keeping our promises, being honest at work, and treating everyone with respect builds a reputation that money cannot buy. Before a difficult decision, ask yourself: "Will this protect my good name?"
exp.20:9:
This verse says that the wicked person has a heart that desires evil. "Soul" here refers to the deepest part of a person: their desires and their will. The "wicked" person is one who lives without reverence for God. And "his neighbour finds no favour in his eyes" means that he has no compassion or goodwill even toward those who are close to him; he does not look on them with favour.

This is part of the book of Proverbs, a collection of wisdom teachings attributed largely to Solomon. The wise teacher contrasts the crooked path of the wicked with the upright life of the pure. Here he shows that wickedness is not only an isolated act, but a desire that is born within and harms others.

Today we can examine our desires, not just our actions. If we notice envy, resentment or indifference toward someone, we can ask God for a compassionate heart and look for a concrete way to do that person good this week.
exp.15:26:
The explanation says that the wicked person, that is, the one who has chosen evil, does not only do it without thinking: he digs at it, like someone working hard to open a pit. His words are like "a burning fire": they burn, they harm, and they can start a blaze. Here "ungodly" is translated from a Hebrew word that speaks of someone without moral worth, sometimes called a worthless person.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book, within a collection of wise sayings. Its purpose is to teach us to recognize the one who causes harm. The verses nearby speak of quarrels, gossip, and those who deceive their neighbor, so the emphasis is on the harm done with words.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself whether your words build up or burn. Avoid gossip and mockery, and stay away from anyone who pushes you to speak badly of others.
exp.27:5:
It says that a poor person who lives with honesty and uprightness is better off than someone who is rich but lives in a crooked way. The word "uprightness" means being whole, consistent, and sincere. "Perverse in his ways" speaks of corrupt or deceitful conduct. The verse does not condemn wealth or praise poverty; it compares the value of an honest life with the value of wealth gained through a dishonest life.

It is a proverb from the wisdom tradition of Israel, traditionally attributed to Solomon in this section. The verses nearby contrast those who keep God's law with those who abandon it. In this way, the proverb teaches that what matters most before God is character, not money or position.

Today it invites us not to measure our success only by what we have. If the temptation arises to gain more through lies or cheating, let us remember that a clear conscience is worth more. Today you can choose to be honest in a small situation, even when it costs you.
exp.13:19:
It says that the poor man is rejected even by his own friend, or is a nuisance to him, while the rich man is surrounded by many who claim to love him. The word "hated" here means that he is shunned or pushed away, and the old-style spelling "á" is simply the older form of "to." It is an observation about how people often treat others according to their money.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the title of the book (Proverbs 10:1), within a collection of short sayings about everyday life. It does not approve of this behavior, only describes it. The verses that follow make the point clear: the one who looks down on his neighbor sins, and the one who shows mercy to the poor is blessed.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we value people for what they have or for who they are. One concrete step: seek out a friend who is going through financial hardship, visit or call him, and offer your company and, if you can, some simple help.
exp.25:2:
This verse compares three animals with the tools used to control them. The whip is used to move the horse forward, the halter (a rope or strap placed on the head) serves to guide the donkey, and the rod is for the back of the fool. In this book, the "fool" is not someone with little intelligence, but someone who rejects wisdom and refuses to be corrected.

Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and this chapter is attributed largely to Solomon. Here the teacher speaks with irony: just as an animal needs force to obey, the stubborn fool does not learn from gentle words. The verses around it speak of how to deal with him.

For today: if someone insists on not listening to advice, do not lose your peace trying to convince them by force. Ask God for wisdom to know when to speak, when to be silent, and when to let life teach. And examine your own heart: are you willing to be corrected?
exp.22:1:
It says that if a person is a heavy eater or has a strong appetite, he should put a knife to his throat. This is an exaggerated way of speaking: it is not about harming oneself, but about restraining oneself firmly. Here "appetite" means strong desire for food.

The speaker is a teacher of wisdom, who in Proverbs advises a young man. He is at the table of a ruler or an important person. The verses that follow say that this meal may be "deceptive bread": an invitation that may hide other intentions. Some understand it as a warning against being seduced by power and luxury.

For today: when you are invited to a place where there is abundance or influential people, keep self-control. Do not let the desire to eat, to impress, or to gain favors control you. Think before you act, and be grateful without being anxious.
exp.3:1:
He says that the one speaking offers good and valuable teaching, and asks that his instruction not be abandoned. The phrase "I give you" means "I give to you," and to "forsake" means to abandon or set aside. The "law" here is the instruction or guide for living, not only external rules.

In this chapter a father, traditionally understood as Solomon, instructs his children. Soon he recalls that he too was a son and that his own father taught him. This shows a chain of teaching that passes from generation to generation, with affection and the desire that they live well.

For today: think of a wise piece of advice you received from your parents, grandparents, or teachers in the faith. Choose one and put it into practice this week. If you are a parent, teach with patience and by your example, not only with words.
exp.9:6:
What it says: The memory of a righteous person, that is, someone who lives uprightly and honors God, leaves good fruit and is a reason for blessing. But the name of the wicked will rot, a way of saying that it becomes corrupted, fades away, and is left to be forgotten or to shame.

Context: These are proverbs of Solomon, according to the heading of chapter 10. They are short sayings of wisdom that contrast two paths of life: that of the righteous and that of the wicked. The nearby verses speak of blessing, of words, of integrity, and of their consequences.

For today: Live with an eye to the mark you will leave. More than fame or money, aim to be remembered for your honesty, your kindness, and your faithfulness to God. Today you can start with a small decision: keep your word and treat someone well.
exp.2:34:
It says that those who live with wisdom will receive honor as an inheritance, something that is given to them and remains. By contrast, fools, who despise God's guidance, will carry dishonor, that is, shame and disgrace. The idea of "carrying" here suggests they will bear it on themselves or receive it as the result of their way of life. Some translations understand it as folly "lifting" them up to display them in shame, and this is interpreted in several ways.

The speaker is a wise father instructing his son, in the style of the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. In this chapter he asks his son to trust in God and not lean on his own understanding. The verses before this one contrast the wicked with the righteous, and the scorner with the humble, and this verse closes that contrast.

For today: choose humility and God's wisdom, even when they bring no immediate applause. Before deciding something important, pray and seek counsel in the Bible. In this way you are not chasing fame; you are trusting that God knows how to honor in his own time.
exp.13:6:
This verse advises staying away from a foolish person. "Go from the presence of" means to step away from their company, and "the lips of knowledge" refers to sound, wholesome wisdom spoken with understanding. The phrases "when thou perceivest not" can be read as "when you do not notice" or "when you do not find." In the Bible, the fool is not someone who lacks education, but someone who scorns wisdom and God.

It is a proverb of Solomon, given as advice from a father to his son. It comes after verses about truth and lies, and before others about the prudent and the fool. It seeks to teach the reader to tell apart the one who speaks with wisdom from the one who does not. Some understand it as advice about prudence, not contempt for the person.

Today we can be careful about who we spend our time with and whom we take advice from. If a conversation only leads to mockery, gossip, or bad decisions, it is wise to withdraw with respect and seek counsel from prudent people and from the Word of God.
exp.0:21:
The explanation says that Wisdom asks a sad but firm question: how long will people keep loving certain harmful attitudes? The "simple ones" are the naive, who let themselves be led along without thinking. The "scorners" are those who mock what is right. The "fools" are the foolish, who do not want to be corrected. "Knowledge" here means knowing and understanding God, not just academic study.

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a woman who calls out in the squares and at the city gates, that is, where everyone passes by and can hear her. She does not hide. Her question is not only a scolding but an invitation to turn back, as the verses that follow show.

For today: do not get used to ignoring good advice. Think of a correction you have been avoiding, perhaps from the Bible or from someone wise, and take a humble step today to listen to it.
exp.16:19:
This proverb says that a person with a crooked heart, that is, one who thinks and desires wicked things, will not find good in life. A word that appears in the verse is "froward," which describes someone who turns away from what is right. The phrase about using the tongue refers to a person who uses words to tangle things up, deceive others, or stir up trouble. That person will end up falling into the harm they cause.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, though some later editors are also mentioned. Here the wise teacher instructs a young listener, using contrasts between what is upright and what is twisted. The verses nearby speak of foolishness, quarrels, and the sorrow a foolish son brings. The whole passage shows how the heart and the words are bound together.

Today we can care for the heart and the tongue together. Before you speak, ask yourself: does this build up or does it tangle things? Ask God for a sincere heart, and your words will be cleaner.
exp.21:2:
The explanation says that the prudent person sees the danger coming and steps aside or protects himself. By contrast, the "simple," that is, the naive or thoughtless, keep going straight ahead without thinking and end up suffering the harm.

This verse is part of Proverbs, a collection of wisdom teachings that tradition largely attributes to Solomon. Here the teacher speaks like a father instructing his children. The verses nearby speak of good reputation, humility, the fear of the LORD, and the dangers of the path of the wicked. Thus, prudence appears as part of living wisely before God.

Today we can apply it this way: when you notice a sign of risk, such as a debt that keeps growing, a friendship that drags you into wrongdoing, or a harmful habit, do not ignore it. Pray, seek counsel, and change course in time.
exp.30:6:
Those who are very poor, sad, or close to death, it says, may drink wine or beer to forget their need and their misery for a while. The needy one is the person who lacks what they need. The one who is faint is someone without strength. The bitter of soul speaks of a heart full of pain.

The one speaking is the mother of King Lemuel, who gives him this advice. Before that, she warns that a ruler must not drink, so that he does not forget the law or twist justice. Many read this verse as a contrast: alcohol is not for judges, even though it may ease the suffering of someone who hurts. Others read it with irony or as a limited concession. The Bible does not present it as a solution to sadness.

Today we can offer real comfort to those who suffer: companionship, food, help, and fair defense. Our task is not only to calm pain, but also to speak up for those who have no voice, as the text goes on to say.
exp.7:35:
He who sins against wisdom harms his own soul. The explanation says that whoever goes against wisdom cheats and robs himself, losing the good he could have received. "His own soul" refers to his whole life. And whoever hates wisdom is, in fact, choosing the road that leads to death, even if he does not notice it.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented in Proverbs as a person who calls everyone to listen to her. Earlier, she said that the one who listens to her each day is blessed, and that whoever finds her finds life and the favor of God. This verse shows the opposite side: rejecting her has serious consequences.

Today we can seek God's wisdom every day by reading the Bible and praying before we decide. When we ignore good advice, we are not only disobeying; we are harming ourselves.
exp.25:11:
Does this verse ask whether we have seen someone who thinks he is wise on his own account? The answer is surprising: there is more hope for a fool, meaning someone without good sense, than for that person. "Wise in his own conceit" means that he considers himself wise, though perhaps he is not.

Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and this saying appears in a section about the fool and the lazy person. It is attributed to Solomon, and the wise men of Israel preserved it to instruct the young. Here a warning is given that pride is a serious obstacle: whoever believes he already knows everything does not listen or change. Some see it as a contrast with the fool who at least might still learn.

For today: practice humility. Ask for advice, accept correction, and ask yourself honestly: "What if I am wrong?" God gives wisdom to whoever recognizes that he needs it.
exp.4:16:
This verse says that the love and intimacy of marriage should belong only to the husband and wife, not be shared with other people. Strangers are people outside the marriage. The words "only thine own" refer to the water and springs mentioned in the verses before it.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son in Proverbs 5. He warns him against the woman of another man and against unfaithfulness. He uses the image of water, which is very precious in dry lands: the cistern and the well stand for what a person has at home and must take care of. Interpreters differ on verse 16. Some read it as a question or as a warning, and others see an image of faithfulness.

Today, this invites us to guard faithfulness and to nurture affection in marriage: giving time, attention, and tenderness to our partner, and setting clear boundaries that protect that trust.
exp.5:34:
He says that the offended husband will not accept any payment or compensation. Here "redemption" means a ransom or a payment to repair the harm. "Respect" means to take into account or to accept. Although the offender "gives many gifts," that is, offers him many presents, the husband will not calm down or forgive.

It is part of a wise father's teaching to his son in Proverbs 6:20-35. He warns him against adultery. The verses before this one say that a thief may return what he stole, but the adulterer cannot make up for his wrong with money. The aim is to warn about the consequences, not to approve of revenge.

For today: there are harms that no gift or quick apology can repair. Guard your faithfulness and your decisions before you hurt others. If you have already failed, seek God's forgiveness with humility, and do not expect everything to be repaired right away.
exp.20:21:
A wise person can accomplish what seems impossible: capture a city defended by powerful people and overcome the strength that the city relied on. The word "captured" in this verse is not needed here, and "tore down" means pulled down. The idea is that wisdom is worth more than brute force.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, although no one knows with certainty who wrote each saying. It belongs to a collection of short sayings, with no specific story behind it. The nearby verses speak of wisdom, justice, pride, and control over words. For this reason many read it as a comparison: good judgment surpasses power.

For today: before facing a big problem, do not rush to use force, anger, or pressure. Pray, ask for advice, think calmly, and look for a sensible plan. God gives wisdom to those who ask for it (James 1:5).
exp.28:1:
It says that when the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice. On the other hand, when the wicked rule, the people mourn. The wicked is the one who lives without respect for God or for others, and the people mourn, that is, they suffer and cry out in grief.

This is a proverb from the wisdom tradition of Israel, attributed in large part to Solomon, although the book also had other compilers. Its purpose is to teach how to live well. The verses nearby speak of pride that ends in ruin, of the wise son, and of a king who gives stability through justice. The common theme is that the decisions of those who hold authority affect everyone.

Today we can pray for our leaders and choose carefully whom we support, looking at their honesty and not only at their promises. And if you have any authority, in your home, your work, or your church, use it with justice and service.
exp.23:5:
This verse says that to fight a war you need cleverness, that is, strategy and intelligence, and not only strength. The word "safety" here does not speak of sickness, but of victory, rescue, or a good outcome. Thus success depends on having many counselors.

We are in the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although this section is presented as "the words of the wise." The verses around it praise wisdom and knowledge as a greater force than mere power. Afterward, the text shows the fool, who does not know how to speak when wisdom is needed.

For today: before making an important decision, such as a change of job, a business, or a family matter, seek the opinion of wise and honest people. Listen even to those who think differently, and pray asking God for direction.
exp.21:9:
This proverb says that if the scoffer is driven away, the conflict comes to an end. The "scorner" is the one who mocks everything and rejects correction. The constant fighting is quarreling, the dispute is the argument, and the shame is the dishonor or insult. Wherever someone keeps provoking, the arguments disappear.

This book is one of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here a teacher speaks who gives advice from experience. Before and after this verse, it speaks of sowing and reaping, of generosity, and of sincere words. Throughout, it contrasts the upright character with the crooked one.

Today, if a person constantly divides people and mocks everyone, sometimes it is necessary to put distance between yourself and them, firmly and without hatred. Protecting the peace of the family, the church, or the workplace is also wisdom.
exp.28:25:
Many people go looking for the favor of rulers or important people, hoping they will be given justice or advantages. But true justice, the final verdict on each person, comes from God (Jehovah). The word "ruler" here means a governor or someone with authority.

This verse is among the Proverbs of Solomon, which were gathered and copied by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). They are wise sayings for everyday life. The verse before it speaks of the fear of man that traps like a snare, and of trusting in Jehovah, who keeps a person safe. This proverb continues that thought: do not depend on powerful people.

Today we can respect those in authority and ask for help when needed, but without living to please others or making improper concessions. If you face an injustice, act with honesty and trust that God sees everything and has the last word.
exp.10:4:
The righteousness of the upright guides his way, that is, it makes his path clearer and safer. But the one who lives in wickedness stumbles because of his own wickedness. "Upright" here does not mean without mistakes, but honest and sincere in heart. "Wicked" is the one who lives without reverence for God.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, largely attributed to Solomon, which gives wisdom in the form of short sayings. The verses around it repeat the same idea: integrity guides and protects, while wickedness traps and destroys. It speaks of a general principle of life, not a promise that is fulfilled the same way in every case.

Today, when you have to decide something, choose the honest path even when it seems slower or harder. Over time, living with integrity gives you direction and peace, and trusting in God helps you persevere.
exp.11:3:
The explanation says that a wife of noble and strong character is like a crown to her husband: she brings him honor and respect before others. By contrast, the wife who shames him slowly weakens him from within, like rot that eats away at bones. Rot is a decay that gnaws at wood or bone little by little. A virtuous woman is one of good character, strong and trustworthy.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom that tradition largely attributes to Solomon. Here the contrast between the righteous and the wicked continues: a person is not established through wrongdoing, but the righteous have firm roots. This proverb shows that the character of those closest to us deeply affects our lives and our home.

Today it applies to every marriage, and also to any close relationship: cultivate a whole character and be a source of support and honor for the one you love. Words of encouragement, faithfulness and respect build up; constant criticism and contempt wear down little by little.
exp.12:3:
It says that the lazy person longs for many things but gets nothing, because he makes no effort. The diligent, that is, those who are hardworking and steady, will be "made fat," an old way of saying they will be satisfied and will prosper. The word "soul" here refers to the person, with his desires and needs.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, and tradition connects it largely with Solomon, though it also contains other collections. Here a wise teacher instructs his listeners, especially the young. The nearby verses speak of guarding one's words and walking the straight path, and this one reminds us that a wise life also includes responsible work.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there something good that I desire and have not yet started to do? Choose a small step, such as studying, saving, or finishing a pending task, and do it today, trusting that God blesses honest effort.
exp.2:26:
This verse says that we should not withhold or delay good from those who are owed it, when it is in our hands to do it. "Withhold" means to keep back or refuse. "Them to whom it is due" are the people who have a right to receive that good: it may be a debt, a fair wage, or help that is owed to them. The phrase "when it is in the power of thine hand" means "when you are able to do it."

The book of Proverbs gathers the wisdom that a father passes on to his son, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Before this, the text speaks of trusting God and not fearing. Afterward, it asks us not to postpone help to our neighbor or to harm them. Thus, trust in God is shown in a just and generous life toward others.

For today: if you must pay a wage, a bill, or return a favor, do it on time. If you can help someone today, do not leave it for tomorrow.
exp.25:24:
It says we should not simply trust someone who speaks with sweet and kind words, because their heart may be full of malice. The phrase about "abominations" is dropped.

These are proverbs of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, meant to teach people to live with prudence. The nearby verses speak of people who pretend affection while hiding hatred. They compare such words to a shiny glaze over a clay pot: it looks attractive, but it covers something of no value. The text adds that deception sooner or later comes to light.

For today: do not let yourself be carried away only by pleasant words. Observe a person's conduct over time. Be kind, but prudent, and ask God for discernment without becoming distrustful of everyone.
exp.29:11:
This verse speaks of a group of people who believe they are clean, pure, and without blame, yet in reality they have not been washed from their wickedness. "Filthiness" means dirt, in this case sin. "In their own eyes" means that they see themselves as good, by their own judgment. They appear good on the outside or in their own estimation, but inside they remain stained.

These words are found in Proverbs 30, which bears the name of Agur, son of Jakeh. Very little is known for certain about him. Here he lists several kinds of people who show wickedness: those who curse their parents, those who think they are clean, the proud, and those who oppress the poor. The verse works as a warning about self-deception.

For today: do not measure yourself only by your own opinion. Ask God to examine your heart, as Psalm 139:23-24 says, and be willing to acknowledge your faults and ask forgiveness.
exp.19:24:
It is a trap for a person to rush into calling something "holy," that is, set apart for God, and only afterward start to think about whether they can really keep what they promised. "Snare" in the verse is a trap; to "devour" here means to take lightly or act rashly; "enquiry" means investigating or examining; the "vows" are promises made to God.

This is a proverb of Solomon, according to the book's title, and it is part of a sage's teaching to someone who seeks to live uprightly. It comes after speaking about honesty in business and about God guiding our steps. That fits the theme: being sincere before God and before people.
