Some connect it with Ecclesiastes 5:4-5, though that is an interpretation.

For today: before promising something to God, or to the church, think it over calmly and in prayer. It is better to promise less and keep your word than to promise much out of emotion and find yourself trapped.
exp.17:8:
The explanation says that whoever works with laziness or carelessness is a "brother" to the one who destroys and wastes. "Negligent" is the careless one, the person who does not put in effort. "Wastrel" is the one who squanders and ruins what he has. In other words, leaving things half-done or poorly done ends in harm similar to that of the one who wastes.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, which teaches in short sayings to shape character. Here, among warnings about foolish and gossiping words, it shows that deeds too can destroy. The next verse speaks of security in the name of the LORD, not in our own strength or riches.

Today: do not underestimate small carelessness. Choose a task you tend to leave unfinished, such as a job, a bill, or a promise, and do it with care, as for God.
exp.21:16:
It speaks of paying attention with humility. "Bow down thine ear" is like leaning in to listen closely. "Hear the words of the wise" means learning from people who have lived with wisdom. "Apply thine heart" means taking it seriously, not only with the mind but with your whole will. "Unto my knowledge" is the teaching that follows.

Here a new section of the book begins, where a teacher speaks like a father to his son. Many scholars see here an introduction to the "sayings of the wise," and some compare them with Egyptian wisdom texts, though this is debated. The verses that follow explain the purpose: that we trust in Jehovah.

Today we can choose a wise voice, such as the Bible, a pastor, or a mature family member, and listen to it without becoming defensive. Learning begins with a heart that is ready.
exp.8:13:
She says that the foolish woman sits on a seat at the door of her house, in a high place of the city. The word "sitteth" is an old form of "sits." It is a visible place, from where everyone can see her.

Here the author of Proverbs presents two calls: that of Wisdom (Proverbs 9:1-6) and that of the foolish woman, Folly. She imitates Wisdom, who also calls from on high (9:3). She occupies a prominent spot to attract the innocent who pass by. Scholars see here a warning about temptations that present themselves as very attractive.

Today, what looks easy and appealing is not always good. Before accepting an invitation, an idea, or an offer, stop and ask: where will this lead me? Ask God for wisdom, and consult his Word.
exp.20:0:
This verse compares the king's heart to channels or irrigation ditches that carry water wherever it is directed. It says that God guides the will of the king the way a farmer guides water. To "turn" means to direct or steer toward one side, and "wherever he will" means wherever God desires.

Proverbs is a book of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, that gives short counsel for living well. Here the wise writer reminds us that no ruler is outside God's control. The verses that follow add that a person may think himself upright, but God examines the heart, and that justice pleases Him more than sacrifices.

For today: if you are worried about those in authority or about other people's decisions, pray for them and trust that God is at work even where we cannot see it. And seek to practice justice in the matters that are yours to handle.
exp.29:22:
The explanation says that the earth trembles, or cannot bear, to see a woman who is unloved get married, and a servant take over her mistress's possessions. A woman who is unloved means a woman who has been rejected or is little loved. Here, to inherit means to take the place of the mistress and receive what belongs to her. Some understand that the unloved woman has a bitter character; others, that she is simply despised. The text does not fully clarify this.

These words belong to the sayings of Agur, in Proverbs 30. He lists things that turn the order of life upside down: a servant who rules, a fool who is full, a bitter woman who gains a position, a servant who replaces her mistress. The point seems to be that power or prosperity without a healthy character produces disorder.

For today: when you receive a promotion, money, or influence, cultivate humility, gratitude, and self-control. Ask God to let your character grow at the same pace as your opportunities.
exp.26:20:
This verse compares two tests. The crucible is the vessel in which silver is melted, and the furnace (or hearth) is the oven where gold is refined. The fire shows how pure each piece is. In the same way, the proverb says, a person is tested by what is said in his praise: how he reacts to being praised reveals his character. Another possible reading understands that a person is tested by what others say about him.

The Book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed mainly to Solomon, though this chapter was copied by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). The verses nearby speak of the human heart, of desires that are never satisfied, and of folly that does not change. Here another way of knowing ourselves is offered.

Today, notice how you feel when you are praised: do you swell with pride, or do you give thanks with humility? Ask God for a simple heart.
exp.28:11:
It says that if a ruler or leader gives ear to lies, the people who work for him end up being wicked. "Lord" here means the one who gives orders, "ministers" are his servants or helpers, and "wicked" means people with no respect for God or for justice.

It is a proverb of Solomon, part of Israel's wisdom, offering counsel drawn from experience. The verses nearby speak of justice, of the fool who cannot control himself, and of the king who judges with truth. Here it is shown that the character of the one who leads shapes everyone around him. If he rewards flatterers and accepts deceit, those who serve under him learn to lie to please him.

If you have authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, see to it that people tell you the truth, even when it hurts. Be grateful to whoever corrects you, and do not reward flattery. In this way you guard your own character and that of those who follow you.
exp.23:4:
This verse says that a wise person has true strength, and that someone who has knowledge has a power that keeps growing. The phrase about "strong" as in great and steady strength explains the idea of a firm, substantial power. A learned person is someone who knows and has been taught. The idea is that wisdom and knowledge give a strength that goes beyond physical muscle.

Proverbs is a collection of teachings about wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon. In this section, the verses before it compare wisdom to the foundations of a house. The verses that follow connect it with war and with good counselors. It teaches that thinking well and listening are worth more than raw force.

For today: before making a difficult decision, stop to ask for advice and to learn, instead of acting on impulse. Ask God for wisdom, as James 1:5 teaches, and seek mature people who will speak to you honestly.
exp.18:16:
What it says: The one who generously helps a poor person is like someone who lends to God himself. The verse says God does not forget that kindness and will repay it in his own way. "Lends" means to give or let something go with the expectation of its return, and "pays" is the reward.

Context: Proverbs gathers practical wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, to teach people how to live uprightly. The verses nearby speak of laziness, obedience, and discipline. This proverb adds that compassion is also part of a wise life. It does not say how or when God will repay; many understand that the reward is not always money.

For today: This week, help someone in need with something concrete: share a meal, pay for a bus fare, or give your time. Do it without expecting applause or gain, trusting that God sees what you do in secret.
exp.7:31:
The explanation says that children should listen closely, and that those who follow the ways of wisdom are happy and blessed. The word "hearken" means "listen to me." "Blessed" means "happy" or "blessed." "Keep" means "obey" or "follow," that is, they live according to those ways.

The one speaking is Wisdom, presented as a person who calls out to people. Earlier she said she was with God when everything was set in order and that she delights in the children of men. Many Christians see here an early pointing toward Christ, though not all agree on this. Now she invites people to obey, because her way leads to a good life.

For today: before making an important decision, stop and listen to God's counsel in his Word and in prayer. Then take one concrete step of obedience, even if it is small.
exp.10:0:
The explanation says that false weights are hateful to God, meaning the rigged scale that cheats the buyer. In contrast, he takes delight in the honest weight, that is, the exact and fair weight. The word "abomination" refers to something that stirs up strong rejection. "Delight" shows that God approves of honesty in business.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here a wise teacher instructs his people. In that time silver and goods were weighed on scales, and it was easy to cheat. The verses that follow contrast pride with humility and integrity with wickedness.

Today, God cares about honesty in everyday life: charging what is fair, paying on time, giving good service, and not cheating in accounts or in work hours, even when no one is watching us.
exp.6:26:
It says that the house of the seductive woman is like a road that leads straight to the grave. "Grave" is the tomb, and the phrase about the chambers of death refers to the deepest places of death, where one goes down step by step. The sentence about the old form of a letter is removed because it explains a word that does not appear in the verse. The verse shows that the end of that road is not pleasure, but ruin.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, in a warning discourse. Earlier he said that many have fallen, even strong men. He closes with this vivid image so that the young man will not be carried away by temptation. Many see here a warning against adultery; others also apply it to foolishness in general.

For today: before entering a tempting situation, ask yourself where it really leads. If the end is harm, step away from the very beginning. Avoid places, conversations, or habits that weaken your heart, and ask God for wisdom to choose in time.
exp.27:13:
He is happy and blessed who lives with a healthy fear, that is, with reverence for God and care not to sin. "Blessed" here means happy and favored. On the other hand, the one who "hardens his heart," meaning who becomes stubborn and refuses to listen or be corrected, will end up falling into evil.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom, and this part is attributed to Solomon, although chapter 25 indicates that his sayings were copied by men of Hezekiah. The verse before this one speaks of confessing sin and turning away from it. This verse contrasts the one who stays attentive and humble with the one who closes himself to correction.

For today: do not get used to what pulls you away from God. When a trusted person or your own conscience points something out to you, listen with humility. Ask God for a soft heart, and acknowledge your mistakes in time.
exp.19:8:
This verse asks a question that no one can answer honestly: who can claim that they have cleaned their own heart and no longer have sin? The expected answer is "no one." "I am clean of my sin" sounds like someone who believes they are perfect on their own.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. Before it, the text speaks of the upright person and the king who judges with righteousness; afterward, of false weights and of the deeds of the young. In the middle, this verse reminds us that human righteousness has limits, because all of us need humility before God.

Today, instead of boasting about how good we are or comparing ourselves with others, we can pray sincerely: "Examine my heart, O God." Recognizing our need for forgiveness brings us closer to Him and makes us more patient with others.
exp.7:1:
This verse describes wisdom as a person who takes her stand in the most visible places: on the high hills, beside the road, and at the places where the paths meet. Hills and high ground are the places that catch the eye, and the crossroads are where many paths come together.

Here the writer of Proverbs presents wisdom as a woman who asks whether she is not calling out. She does not hide. She places herself where people pass by and where they must decide which way to go. Many see here a contrast with the deceptive invitation of folly, which appears later.

For today: God's wisdom is within reach in our everyday decisions. Before choosing a path, stop to pray, open the Bible, and listen to the counsel of wise people.
exp.25:3:
This verse advises not to answer a foolish person using their own methods: insults, mockery, anger, or absurd arguments. "According to his folly" means "in his own way, in his own style." If you do so, you end up becoming like him.

These words belong to the proverbs of Solomon, collected in Proverbs 25 through 29. In chapter 26 there is much talk of the fool, that is, the one who rejects wisdom and correction. The following verse seems to say the opposite ("Answer a fool..."), and for that reason many understand it this way: sometimes it is better to keep silent so as not to lower yourself, and other times a firm answer is needed so that the fool does not think himself wise. Discernment is required.

Today, when someone argues with mockery or foolishness, in person or online, before responding, ask God for wisdom and ask yourself: does this build up, or does it just drag me down to his level?
exp.11:9:
The explanation says that the righteous person cares for the well-being of their animals: they look after them, give them food and water, and attend to their health. By contrast, even what the wicked consider mercy (their "tender mercies," that is, their deepest feelings) ends up being cruelty. Here "beast" means a domestic or working animal, and "regardeth" means "takes care of" or "knows the needs of."

This proverb belongs to the collection attributed to Solomon, a teacher of wisdom who instructs his people in how to live well. The verses around it speak of work, honor, and common sense. Here it shows that a person's character is revealed in how they treat those who depend on them, even animals.

For today: notice how you treat those who cannot defend themselves or make demands of you, such as a pet, a working animal, or someone who depends on you. Caring for them with patience and kindness is a practical way of living out righteousness.
exp.25:10:
It says that the fool repeats his foolishness like a dog that returns to eat what it has vomited. The image is strong and unpleasant on purpose. A "fool" is not someone with little intelligence, but someone who despises wisdom and does not want to be corrected. The word "returneth" means "returns."

Proverbs gathers wise sayings that tradition attributes largely to Solomon. This chapter speaks about how to deal with fools, the lazy person, and the gossip. The proverb shows that the fool does not learn from his mistakes or from their consequences. The verse that follows adds that there is even less hope for the person who thinks he is wise.

For today: when you fall into an error, do not repeat it. Ask yourself what caused it, ask forgiveness if you did harm, and seek counsel and concrete changes, such as staying away from what makes you stumble. God gives grace to begin again.
exp.18:18:
The verse says that a person of great anger will have to bear the consequences of their character. And if they also become violent, or if someone tries to rescue them from their consequences, the problems only multiply. Some translations render the second part differently: "if you deliver him, you will have to do it again." The Hebrew text allows both readings.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon, that teaches his son how fools and wise people live. It comes after speaking of discipline for children without reaching fury, and before calling the reader to listen to counsel. Everything points to the same lesson: self-control protects life.

Today, when you feel anger rising, stop before you speak or act: breathe, step away for a moment, and pray. It is better to wait than to carry the consequences of a sudden outburst afterward.
exp.2:8:
It tells us to honor God with what we have. "Substance" means goods or riches. "Firstfruits" are the first and best of the harvest. "Increase" is what we produce or earn. In other words, we give to God first, not what is left over.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, within a book of wisdom traditionally attributed to Solomon. Earlier, he asked the reader to trust in God and not in their own opinion. Then he promises abundance, with barns full and presses overflowing. It was a promise within Israel's covenant; the wise understood it as a general principle, not an automatic guarantee of wealth.

Today, we can set aside the first part of our income for God, the church, and those in need, before spending on other things. It is a practical way of saying: "Lord, everything comes from you."
exp.25:6:
It says the legs of the lame hang limp and are of no use for walking. In the same way, a wise saying in the mouth of a fool is of no use, because he neither lives it nor understands it. Some versions translate that the legs "hang" loose; the Hebrew text is brief and is interpreted in several ways, but the general idea is the same: something good that does not work.

The book of Proverbs gathers the wisdom attributed largely to Solomon. In this group of verses (26:1-12), the author describes what the fool is like: someone who despises correction. He compares the way such a person uses wise sayings to useless or dangerous things, to warn us that repeating correct words is not enough.

For today: the point is not to quote the Bible skillfully, but to live it. Before advising others with a verse, ask yourself whether you practice it yourself. Let your life support your words.
exp.23:17:
This verse gives the reason for the warning just before it: one should not rejoice when an enemy falls, because the Lord sees it and is displeased. The words "lest he see it" mean "lest the Lord see it." The phrase "lest he turn away his wrath from him" means that God might stop being angry with that enemy, and that would not be what you desire.

These words are in a collection of wise sayings, which teach people to live uprightly. The author, who is not identified with certainty here, warns against revenge and against taking pleasure in another's misfortune. God looks at the heart, not only at actions. Some understand that God might stop punishing the enemy; others understand that he would look more closely at your wrong attitude.

Today, when someone who has harmed you fails, resist the secret satisfaction. Instead, ask God to give you a humble heart, and leave justice in his hands.
exp.22:16:
This verse says not to let your heart envy sinners. Instead, we should stay steadfast in the fear of the Lord every day. "Rather" means "instead," and "stay steadfast" means to keep standing firm without giving up. "Fear of the Lord" is a deep respect and reverent love toward God.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son, as in much of the book of Proverbs. He wants to see him live uprightly and would rejoice in it. The verses that follow give the reason: there is an end, that is, a future, and the hope of the one who trusts in God will not be cut off.

Today, when you see someone doing well even though they live without honoring God, do not compare yourself or grow bitter. When you feel that temptation, thank God for something specific and decide to obey him that day, trusting that his way has a good ending.
exp.7:16:
She says that Wisdom loves those who love her, and that those who seek her earnestly find her. Seeking her early means looking for her eagerly and making her a priority.

In Proverbs 8 the speaker is Wisdom, presented as a person who calls out to everyone to listen. Earlier it says that kings and rulers depend on her to act justly. Afterward it promises lasting riches and righteousness, more precious than gold. Many Christians also see here a reflection of Christ, but the text itself speaks of the wisdom of God.

For today: set aside a few minutes at the start of the day to read the Bible and ask God for direction. Seek his wisdom before the rush of the day, and trust that he responds to those who seek him sincerely.
exp.7:7:
This verse says that everything wisdom speaks is just and right. In other words, there is no lie or trickery in her words.

In Proverbs 8, the one speaking is wisdom, presented as a woman who calls out in the streets and the squares so that people will listen to her. Many Christians also see here a sign pointing to Christ, although this is understood in different ways. She invites everyone and says that her teaching is worth more than silver and gold.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our words are straight. Before speaking, it is good to think: Is this true? Is it fair? Am I trying to deceive or manipulate? We can also measure the advice we receive against the Word of God, which does not deceive.
exp.17:15:
The explanation says that a gift opens doors for the one who gives it. The phrase "makes room for him" means it gives him space and opportunities, and it can bring him before important people (the great ones). The proverb describes what usually happens in life, without saying whether this is right or wrong.

It is a proverb of Solomon, part of a collection of short sayings about everyday life. The verses around it speak of encouragement, wisdom, and judgment. Some interpreters see it as a neutral observation about generosity; others see it as a warning about bribery, something the Bible condemns in other passages (Exodus 23:8).

For today: practice sincere generosity, without seeking favors in return. A kind and honest gesture can open doors and create friendships. But do not use gifts to bend justice or to gain unfair advantages.
exp.22:15:
What it says: The speaker says that his "reins", that is, the deepest part of his being and his feelings, will rejoice when his son's lips speak "right things". This means words that are just, honest, and in line with what God approves.

Context: In Proverbs 23, a wise father speaks to his son. He has just said that correction is part of loving him, and that his heart rejoices when the son is wise. Here he adds that he cares not only about what the young man thinks, but also about what he says. He will then encourage him not to envy sinners and to fear the LORD.

For today: Let us take care with our words, because they reveal the heart and also affect those who love us. Today you can choose to speak with truth and respect at home, at work, and online, and so bring joy to others and please God.
exp.12:24:
The righteous person has enough to be satisfied, while the wicked person is always going hungry and in need. "Satisfying his soul" means being fully content, not just having a full stomach. "Belly" here stands for the appetite, the person's desire.

This is a proverb of Solomon, according to the heading of the book, and it closes chapter 13. It is a teaching of wisdom that describes what usually happens, not an automatic promise in every case. Other passages in the Bible acknowledge that sometimes the righteous go without. Here the contentment of the one who lives uprightly is contrasted with the constant dissatisfaction of the one who lives without God.

For today: learn to value what you have and to live with integrity. The person who seeks first to do what is right often finds peace and sufficiency, while greed is never satisfied. Thank God for your provision today.
exp.3:12:
It says we should hold fast to the instruction we have received and not let it go. The word "instruction" here can also be understood as discipline, teaching, or correction. "Keep her" means to care for it and protect it as something precious. The text states that this instruction is our life: it is not an ornament, but what sustains us.

The one speaking is a father passing on to his son what he learned from his own father. He reminds him that he has already guided him along straight paths, and he promises that wisdom will give him firmness as he walks. Right after, he warns him against the way of the wicked, so that he does not turn aside.

For today: choose one good teaching you have received, from the Bible or from a wise person, and decide to put it into practice this week. Review it each day so you do not forget it.
exp.23:7:
It says that whoever spends their time planning to do evil ends up with a reputation as a mischievous person. The word "shall be called" means that others will know him that way. "Deviseth to do evil" means he plans or schemes to do harm. Hidden plans end up shaping one's reputation.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and many are attributed to Solomon, although this section (chapters 22 to 24) is connected with the sayings of the wise. The nearby verses speak of wisdom, good counselors, and the foolish. Here the wise person is contrasted with the one who devotes his mind to wickedness. The next verse says that the thought of the foolish is sin.

For today: take care with what you think and plan, because that shapes your character. When the idea comes to you of taking revenge or of taking advantage of someone, do not feed it. Ask God to renew your mind and seek wise counsel.
exp.3:4:
This verse encourages us to get wisdom and understanding, and not to forget the words that the father is teaching. "Get" here means to obtain or acquire through effort. "Understanding" here means comprehension, the ability to grasp things well. "The words of my mouth" are the words and teachings the father speaks. "Neither decline" means to turn away from them.

In this passage, Solomon is the one speaking, as a father instructing his children. He recalls that he himself was taught by his own father, David, when he was a boy. In this way we see a chain of teaching that passes from generation to generation. His desire is that his children live well, guided by wisdom.

For today: wisdom does not come on its own; it takes effort. You could set aside a few minutes each day to read a passage of the Bible and think about how to put it into practice. You can also listen to the advice of older people you trust, and not forget it when the time comes to make a decision.
exp.28:9:
The violent, who do not respect life, hate the person of integrity, the one who lives with honesty. The upright, on the other hand, seek his good. "Contentment" means well-being or satisfaction, and the verse is understood to mean they seek his wellbeing or his good.

It is a proverb of wisdom, attributed to Solomon and compiled by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). The teacher contrasts two paths: that of the foolish and violent, and that of the wise and just. The neighboring verses speak of scoffers, fools and corrupt rulers, and show how wickedness reacts to integrity.

For today: if someone rejects your honesty, do not be surprised or harden yourself. Seek to surround yourself with upright people and, at the same time, be the one who seeks the good of those who live with integrity.
exp.29:3:
This verse asks a series of questions about who has power over the heavens and creation: who has gone up into heaven and come down, who holds the wind in his fists, who wrapped the waters in a garment, and who set the ends of the earth in place. At the end it asks for the name of that being and the name of his son.

Agur, who presents himself as humble and without wisdom of his own, speaks here. With these questions he acknowledges that God is infinitely greater than human beings. Some believers see in "his son" an early sign of Jesus; others think it is a poetic question without a human answer. Its exact meaning is debated.

For today: when you feel small or without answers, remember that God sustains all things. Draw near to Him with humility and trust His word, which is sure.
exp.30:5:
It says to give strong drink to someone who is about to die or is fainting, and wine to those whose souls are bitter with grief. "Strong drink" here means an intoxicating beverage, and "ready to perish" means someone who is about to die. "Of heavy hearts" means of very sad heart.

The one speaking is the mother of King Lemuel, who gives him advice (Proverbs 31:1). First she warns that a ruler must not drink to the point of drunkenness, because he might forget the law and pervert justice. Then she says that such drink can bring relief to someone who suffers without remedy. Many read it as a comfort for extreme pain, not as permission to get drunk. Some see an ironic tone, but there is no certainty.

Today we can learn to comfort with tenderness those who suffer, and at the same time use our position to defend the weak, with a clear mind and without excess.
exp.29:26:
It says that the locusts have no king to command them, yet they all go forth together, in good order, like an army arranged in ranks.

These words come from Proverbs 30, attributed to Agur, son of Jakeh, who presents himself as a humble man. Here he lists four small creatures that are wise: ants, rock badgers, locusts, and lizards. His point is that wisdom does not depend on strength or power. Some understand it to teach voluntary cooperation.

For today: you do not need someone watching over you to do your part. In the family, the church, or the workplace, unity and order arise from personal responsibility and a commitment to work together.
exp.23:31:
The speaker says the wise man did not pass by what he saw. He looked at the abandoned field with attention, took it to heart, that is, he thought about it seriously, and from what he observed he drew a lesson.

The speaker is the wise man who writes in this section of Proverbs. He tells what he saw as he passed by the land of a lazy person, full of thorns and with its fence fallen down. Then he explains what he learned: laziness, little by little, brings poverty. In this way he teaches his readers to learn from what they observe.

For today: do not just stand there looking at other people's neglect; think about what it teaches you. Ask yourself which area of your life, such as your work, your studies, or your spiritual life, needs constant attention, and take one small step today.
exp.23:2:
It says that a house is built with wisdom, that is, with good judgment for living according to God. And it affirms that it is established, that is, kept firm and secure, through prudence, which is knowing how to think before acting. The word "house" can mean the building, but also the family and everything a person builds up in life.

The context is the sayings of the wise in Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon and other sages. The verses before it warn against envying the wicked, who build their lives on theft and evil. This verse shows the contrast: what endures is built with wisdom. The verses that follow say that knowledge fills the house with precious and pleasant things.

For today: before important decisions about money, family, or work, pray, seek wise counsel, and think about the consequences. In this way your home rises on firm foundations, not on shortcuts.
exp.9:9:
He who winks with the eye causes sorrow, that is, whoever makes signs with malice, to deceive, to mock, or to hide a bad intention, ends up causing pain to others and to himself. And "the prating fool," that is, the foolish one who talks without thinking, will receive the consequences. "Causeth" means that he brings about or provokes.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, according to the heading of the book. They are advice from a teacher of wisdom. The nearby verses contrast the wise one, who listens, with the fool who talks too much, and the upright with the one who twists his way. Some scholars think the wink speaks of deceit; others, of mockery.

Today we can guard honesty, not only with our words but also with our gestures. Let us avoid hints, cutting sarcasm, or messages with a double meaning. Let us speak plainly, with respect and truth, and ask God for mastery over what we say.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that God gives firm and true wisdom to upright people, that is, to those who seek to live with honesty. It also says that God is a shield, a protection, for those who walk with integrity. The phrase "he layeth up" means that he gives or keeps that wisdom stored up for them, and "sound wisdom" means wisdom that is secure, useful, and does not fail.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, according to the book of Proverbs, and encourages him to seek wisdom as one seeks a treasure. Earlier he already said that wisdom comes from the mouth of God. Afterward he says that God watches over the way of his faithful ones.

For today: when you have to make a decision, ask God for wisdom and choose to do what is right, even when it costs you. Trust that he guides you and cares for you as you walk in honesty.
exp.28:26:
This verse says that righteous people feel revulsion toward the person who is unjust, and that wicked people feel revulsion toward the one who lives uprightly. "Abomination" means something deeply detestable. The unjust person is one who is dishonest and wicked, and the ungodly person is one who lives without reverence for God. The phrase about upright walking refers to the person who lives with honesty.

It is the last proverb of the book, among the sayings attributed to Solomon and gathered later, according to Proverbs 25:1. Here no character speaks in a scene; instead, the wisdom of a teacher instructs his people. Earlier, the book spoke of trusting God rather than fearing people. This closing verse shows that following God creates a real division between two ways of living.

For today: if your honest life makes others uncomfortable or provokes rejection, do not be discouraged. Keep doing what is right with humility and without pride, trusting God more than the approval of people.
exp.28:8:
This verse says that if a wise person argues or gets into a dispute with a fool, they will find no peace. Whether the fool gets angry or mocks, the argument does not end well. The word "contend" means to argue or fight, and "rest" means peace or calm.

It is a proverb from Israel's wisdom tradition, traditionally attributed to Solomon (although this chapter also mentions that it was collected by the men of Hezekiah). Here the "fool" is not someone with little intelligence, but someone who rejects correction. The verses nearby speak of calming anger and of the fool losing control, while the wise person keeps self-control.

For today: not every argument is worth having. If someone only wants to shout or mock, you can speak calmly, say what needs to be said, and step away, instead of spending your peace on a fight that never ends.
exp.30:25:
She speaks with wisdom, that is, with good judgment and prudence. In addition, "the law of kindness" means that what she teaches and says is guided by goodness, compassion, and gentle treatment of others. "Kindness" here is mercy toward other people.

These words are part of the final poem in Proverbs, which describes the woman of noble character. The chapter says these are words his mother taught King Lemuel. The poem is a portrait of practical wisdom in daily life: work, managing the household, and also the way one speaks. Some read it as an ideal and not as a required checklist.

For today: before answering in a difficult conversation, pause and ask yourself whether what you are about to say is true and also kind. Practice correcting with firmness, but without humiliating anyone.
exp.14:5:
This verse says that in the home of the righteous person there is abundance of goods, or stored treasure. By contrast, the gains of the wicked bring trouble, that is, problems, unrest and disorder. "Yet" means "but," and "wicked" refers to someone who lives without respecting God.

It is a proverb of Solomon, according to the title of the book, given as a father's teaching to his son. The verses around it speak of accepting correction, of speaking with wisdom, and of pleasing God. Proverbs describe what usually happens, not a promise for every case. Other texts, such as Psalm 73, acknowledge that sometimes the wicked prosper.

For today: do not measure your success only by how much you earn, but by how you earn it. Seek honest income and live with integrity, because what is well obtained brings peace and can be shared with a clear conscience.
exp.14:22:
This proverb says that a person is filled with joy when they can give a good answer. It also says that a word spoken at the right moment is something very valuable.

This verse is part of the book of Proverbs, which tradition largely attributes to Solomon, although some sections have other authors. It is wisdom in the form of short sayings. The nearby verses speak of seeking counsel and living with understanding. Here the point is that speaking well is not only having something to say, but saying it with wisdom and good timing.

Today we can learn to think before we speak. Before answering in an argument or giving advice, it is good to ask ourselves whether this is the right moment and whether what we will say will build up. Sometimes the wisest thing is to wait a little before speaking.
exp.26:11:
This verse compares two kinds of people. The prudent person is the one who pays attention to what is happening and recognizes danger in time; for this reason he hides himself, meaning he withdraws and protects himself. The simple are the naive, those who do not think about the consequences; they pass on without caution, and they are punished, that is, they suffer the penalty or the harm.

It is a proverb of Solomon, given as the counsel of a wise father to his son. In the chapter, the father asks for wisdom, loyal friendship, and good judgment in decisions. This same proverb appears almost word for word in Proverbs 22:3, which shows how much prudence mattered.

For today: do not ignore warning signs. If you see that a friendship, a business deal, a debt, or a habit is leading you toward trouble, stop and change course before you suffer the consequences. Ask God for wisdom and listen to the advice of mature people.
exp.21:12:
This proverb describes a lazy man who makes up an excuse to avoid going out to work. He claims there is a lion outside and that he will be killed in the middle of the street. "Lazy" here means the sluggard, the one who avoids effort. The exaggeration shows that the fear is not real but a pretext.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, to shape character. Here it is not God who speaks, but a wise person who mocks absurd excuses with irony. A lion in the middle of the city would be very unusual, and that is why it sounds ridiculous. The verses around it speak of integrity, correction, and the danger of foolishness, and this saying fits as a portrait of a foolish attitude. A similar idea is repeated in Proverbs 26:13.

Today we can ask ourselves what "lions" we invent to postpone what we know we should do. Let us distinguish between a real risk and an excuse. Choose one pending task, take the first step today, and pray, asking God for courage and perseverance.
exp.9:23:
This proverb says that the fears of the wicked will come upon them, and that the desires of the righteous will be granted. "Wicked" refers to someone who lives without reverence for God. The phrase "will come upon him" means it will reach him. The phrase "will be granted" means they will receive it.

It is part of the proverbs of Solomon, a collection of short sayings of wisdom. Here two ways of life are contrasted, that of the wicked and that of the righteous, as in the verses around it. It is a general principle, not a promise for every case: the Bible itself recognizes that there are sometimes exceptions, as in Job and in some psalms. The desires of the righteous are understood as desires shaped by God.

For today: ask yourself what you fear most and what you most desire. If you place your life in God's hands and seek to do what is right, your desires will grow healthier and your heart will have more peace.
exp.30:13:
It says this woman is like a merchant's ship: she brings her food from faraway places. The image shows a resourceful woman who works hard to get the best for her household.

Chapter 31 ends with a poem about the virtuous woman. The opening verses say these are words that King Lemuel's mother taught him. It is an alphabetic Hebrew poem, presenting wisdom lived out in everyday life. Trade is mentioned, but we do not know in detail how she traveled; the image is poetic, not a historical report.

For today: caring for your own requires planning and effort, whether you are a man or a woman. Think of a need in your family and look for a wise and honest way to meet it, even if it takes a little more work.
exp.0:7:
This verse invites the son to listen carefully to his father's teaching and not to reject his mother's guidance. "Instruction" here means teaching, and "guidance" refers to the direction given for living well. "Despise" means to take something lightly or set it aside.

At this point, the speaker is a teacher of wisdom, traditionally identified with Solomon, who addresses a young man as if he were his son. Earlier he spoke of the fear of the LORD as the beginning of wisdom. Now he shows that this wisdom is first learned at home. The verses that follow say this teaching will be like an ornament and warn against bad companions.

Today we can value the advice of those who have raised us or guided us with love. They will not always be fully right, but listening with humility protects us from mistakes and helps us grow.
exp.1:19:
This verse says that wisdom has a purpose: that you walk in the way of good people and keep to the paths of the righteous. "Paths" are roads or trails, and "keep" here means staying on them, not wandering off.

In Proverbs 2, a father speaks to his son and explains that seeking wisdom will protect him from evil and from bad companions, such as the strange woman mentioned earlier. The verses before it describe a way that ends in death; this verse offers the opposite. The next one speaks of the upright remaining in the land and the wicked being cut off.

For today: think about who you walk with. Seek out friends and examples who encourage you to live with honesty and faith, and stay firm in those habits every day, even when others go astray.
exp.14:4:
The explanation says that the foolish person does not value or take seriously the guidance given by his father, but whoever keeps correction, that is, whoever receives it and puts it into practice, becomes wise, that is, sensible and prudent. The word "despiseth" means that he gives it little importance, and the phrase "becomes" points to the idea that this happens gradually.

This verse is in the book of Proverbs, a collection of sayings about wisdom. Many of them are attributed to Solomon, and here the voice is that of a teacher of wisdom advising young people. The verses around it contrast the wise with the fool and the righteous with the wicked. The father's counsel represents the teaching passed down within the family.

For today: learn to receive correction without becoming defensive. The next time someone you trust points out a mistake, thank them, pray about it, and make one concrete change.
exp.12:10:
What it says: This verse says that money that comes from vanity, that is, from what is empty, false or easy, gets used up over time. By contrast, the one who gathers little by little, working with his own hands, will see what he has grow. The phrase "shall be diminished" means it will shrink away, and "gathereth" means gathers or collects.

Context: It is a proverb of wisdom within the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon in this section. No character speaks in a scene; it is a teacher giving advice to someone who wants to live well. Around it, the righteous and the wicked are contrasted, as are the proud and the prudent. Some versions translate "by vanity" as "gotten by fraud" or "with haste"; that is why it is understood in several ways, but the central idea is similar.

For today: Be wary of quick and easy gains. It is better to save steadily, work honestly, and manage with patience what God has given you.
exp.29:5:
This verse asks us not to add anything to God's words. "Lest he reprove thee" means "so that he does not correct you." And "thou be found a liar" means that he exposes you as someone who speaks falsehoods in God's name.

The one speaking is Agur, son of Jakeh, the author of chapter 30. Before this, he acknowledges through questions that God is great and mysterious, and that we are limited. He then affirms that God's word is pure and protects those who trust in him. That is why he warns against mixing human ideas with what God has said.

Today we can read the Bible with humility: not using phrases like "God said" to support our own opinions, and distinguishing between what Scripture teaches and what we ourselves think.
exp.30:4:
It says that a king should not drink to excess, because alcohol clouds the mind. If he becomes drunk, he may forget the law and bend justice against the afflicted, that is, the poor, the weak, and the needy. The word "pervert" means to twist or turn aside, and what is just is the right judgment.

The one speaking is the mother of King Lemuel, who passes on a teaching to him. We do not know for certain who Lemuel was; some think he was a foreign king, and others think the name is symbolic or alludes to Solomon. She warns him that his office requires a clear mind to care for those who have no voice.

For today: if you have authority, whether in the home, at work, or in the church, guard your mind and your habits. Avoid whatever takes away good judgment, so that you can decide with justice and protect the most vulnerable.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that the words of the strange woman are sweet and smooth, like honey and oil. A "strange woman" means a woman who is not one's wife; in context, someone who seduces. Her lips "drop" like honey, meaning her speech flows out smoothly. Her mouth is "smoother than oil," and here it refers to her speech, which sounds gentle and flattering.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son, as in much of Proverbs. Earlier he asked his son to listen to his wisdom so that he would keep good judgment. Now he warns that the temptation appears attractive, but the next verse shows that it ends in bitterness and harm.

For today: do not let yourself be guided only by what sounds sweet or flattering. Before accepting a tempting proposal, think about where it leads, and seek wise counsel and faithfulness in your relationships.
exp.13:16:
He who is quick to anger acts foolishly, and a man of wicked devices is hated. The one who is quick to anger does foolish things, and the person who plans harm or schemes with cunning ends up being rejected by others.

This proverb is in the collection that tradition attributes to Solomon. It is a teaching of wisdom, like a father advising his children. The verses nearby compare the fool, who rushes in and trusts himself too much, with the wise person, who takes care and turns away from evil. Hasty anger and calculated wickedness are two paths of foolishness.

For today: before you respond in anger, pause. Breathe, pray briefly, and wait a few minutes before you speak or write. This way you avoid words you would later regret.
exp.15:30:
It says that old age is like a crown of honor, that is, something worthy of respect and beauty. But it sets a condition: that crown is found on the path of righteousness. Gray hair alone does not guarantee honor; honor comes when a life has been lived doing what is right.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon, although scholars debate how it was compiled. This verse contrasts with the wicked man of the preceding verses, who deceives and leads others into evil. Thus the proverb shows two paths: one that ends in dishonor and another that leads to a respectable old age.

For today: do not wait until you are old to care for your character. The small decisions of honesty, patience, and faithfulness that you make now are shaping the life others will respect later. And if you are already old, it is never too late to walk in righteousness.
exp.14:28:
This verse says that God is far from the wicked, that is, from the evil people who live without wanting to obey him, but that he listens closely to the prayer of the righteous, that is, of those who try to live uprightly.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, attributed in large part to Solomon. Here the path of the righteous is contrasted with that of the wicked, as in the nearby verses: the greedy person harms his household, and the righteous person thinks before he speaks. Being "far" does not mean that God cannot see the wicked, but that there is no fellowship with him while he persists in his wrongdoing.

For today: if you want your prayer to be sincere, draw near to God with humility, acknowledge your mistakes, and seek to live honestly. He invites everyone to return to him.
exp.18:11:
This proverb compares a king to two images. His anger is like the roar of a young lion: a loud sound that warns of danger. His favor, on the other hand, is like dew on the grass: something gentle that refreshes and gives life.

These words are part of the proverbs of Solomon, a teacher of wisdom who instructs with short sayings. In that time, the king held great power, and his mood could bring punishment or blessing. The verses nearby speak of controlling anger and of foolishness, so the theme is how to act wisely before authority.

Today, we can treat with respect and prudence those who have authority over us, such as a boss or a teacher. And if we hold authority, it is good for our treatment of others to be more like dew than like a roar.
exp.19:19:
This proverb says that whoever curses their father or their mother, that is, whoever insults them or treats them with contempt, will see their lamp go out in the midst of a very deep darkness. The lamp represents a person's life, prosperity, and hope. The ending, the final outcome, is what the proverb warns about, and the darkness it describes is very deep and complete.

It is a proverb of Israel's wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon. It belongs to a series of short sayings about everyday life. In the law of Moses, dishonoring one's parents was a serious matter (Exodus 20:12; 21:17). The proverb warns that this path ends badly, though it is not a promise that works out the same way in every case.

For today: honor your parents with respectful words, even if they have failed or do not agree with you. If there are wounds, seek to speak truthfully, without mockery or contempt.
exp.10:14:
He who puts up security for a stranger, that is, who promises to pay the debt of someone he does not know, will end up suffering greatly. But the one who refuses to make such guarantees lives in peace. Being "surety" here means standing as guarantor, and avoiding such commitments means not taking them on.

The book of Proverbs gathers wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, aimed mainly at young people learning to live with prudence. This verse is among sayings about discretion, good counsel, and kindness. Proverbs warns several times against vouching for others carelessly. It does not forbid helping, but teaches not to take risks without thinking.

Before you sign as a guarantor or lend your name for someone, think about whether you could pay that debt without harming your family. Helping is good, but do it with prudence, praying and asking for advice. Sometimes it is wiser to give limited help than to take on someone else's debt.
exp.1:13:
They say there are people who feel pleasure when they do wrong. Not only do they do it, but they enjoy it. Where the text speaks of those who take delight, the sense is that they find amusement and joy in it. The phrase about twisted and harmful conduct refers to behavior that is crooked and damaging, when wickedness becomes a habit.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as in the whole opening of Proverbs. He explains that wisdom which comes from God will protect him from bad companions. This verse describes the wicked men from whom wisdom wants to keep him, so that he does not let himself be influenced by them.

For today: be careful with whom you spend time and what you find entertaining. If something gives you delight while it harms others or pulls you away from God, stop. Ask God to teach you to take joy in what is good, and to choose friends who encourage you to walk straight.
exp.6:18:
She tells the young man there is no danger of being discovered: her husband is not at home, for he has gone on a long journey. The word "gone" here is an older form that means "has left." Their word for "a" is an old spelling, so I've left it out.

The speaker is the seductive woman of Proverbs 7. A wise father warns his son about her. She uses flattery, perfume, and promises to trap him. She mentions the journey to take away his fear and his conscience. Yet the verses that follow show that the husband will return on a set date. She assumes no one will know, but the truth will come to light.

For today: when someone tells you "no one will ever find out," be suspicious. Sin is often sold with the idea that it is hidden, but God sees everything. Flee from temptation in time, and seek to be faithful even when you are alone.
exp.8:14:
This verse says that the foolish woman sits at the doorway of her house to call out to those who pass by, to those who are going along calmly, doing what is right on their way.

The writer of Proverbs, traditionally Solomon, presents two women who represent two invitations: Wisdom and Folly. Here he speaks of Folly, who imitates the call of Wisdom, but offers something deceptive: forbidden and secret pleasures. She does not seek out the lost, but interrupts those who are already going well.

Today, temptations often appear just when we are moving forward uprightly, and they look attractive and easy. It is wise to stop, ask where they really lead, and follow the path God points out, even when it seems less eye-catching.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that good judgment and understanding act like guards who watch over you. "Discretion" is the ability to decide wisely, and "understanding" is the insight to tell good from evil. The words "preserve" and "keep" mean that they protect you from danger.

The one speaking is a wise father teaching his son (Proverbs 2:1). He explains that if he receives wisdom and seeks it with his whole heart, wisdom will protect him. The verses that follow say what it will rescue him from: evil paths and people who speak deceit and prefer darkness.

For today: before making an important decision, such as a business deal, a friendship, or a relationship, stop to pray, seek guidance from the Bible, and ask advice from mature, trustworthy people. That prudence can spare you harm that would later be hard to repair.
exp.28:18:
What it says: This proverb says that a certain servant cannot be corrected by words alone. A servant is someone who works under another person's authority. The word "answer" means to respond or to pay heed. The servant understands what is said to him, but does not obey it. The problem is not a lack of understanding, but a lack of willingness.

Context: It is part of the proverbs of Solomon, gathered by the men of Hezekiah (Proverbs 25:1). It speaks in a tone of wisdom for everyday life. The nearby verses deal with discipline, guidance, and the shaping of character. It shows that instruction needs a response from the heart.

For today: If someone understands what is right but does not change, perhaps what is needed is wise and firm consequences, not more lectures. And if you are the one listening, ask yourself: do I not only understand, but also respond with humble obedience?
exp.16:7:
The verse says that a bribe seems like a precious stone to the one who gives or receives it. It thinks that wherever it is used, it will open doors and bring success. The ones who own it are those who possess it.

The book of Proverbs is attributed largely to Solomon, who gives counsel about wisdom. Here it describes what people believe, not necessarily what it approves. Some read it as an ironic warning, since the Law condemns bribery (Exodus 23:8). The nearby verses speak of lying, friendship, and correction.

Today: do not seek advantages through bribes or unfair favors, even when they seem to work. Instead, act with honesty, even if you advance more slowly, because God sees and values what is right.
exp.27:8:
This verse says that if a person refuses to listen to God's law, that is, his teaching and his commands, even his prayer is repugnant to God. "Turns away his ear" speaks of a decision not to pay attention.

Proverbs gathers wise sayings, most of them attributed to Solomon, although it is believed they were collected over time. Here the wise teacher contrasts the prudent son who keeps the law with the one who rebels, keeps company with gluttons, or grows rich by oppressing the poor. Prayer is not presented as a shortcut for ignoring obedience.

For today: if you want God to hear your prayers, listen to his Word as well. Read the Bible with a willingness to obey, not only to ask. God does not reject the one who repents, but the one who prays while deliberately hardening his heart.
exp.6:23:
The explanation says that the teacher calls his children to listen to him with attention. "Hearken" is "listen," and "attend" is "pay attention." The words "the words of my mouth" mean "the words I am telling you." It is a serious warning after describing how a young man falls into deception.

The one speaking is a wise father instructing his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs. He has just described a young man who follows a seductive woman without realizing the danger, like an animal going to the slaughter. Now he moves from the story to the teaching: he wants his listeners to learn before they fall.

For today: listen to wise counsel in time, before temptation clouds our judgment. We can seek out mature people and the Word of God, and decide ahead of time which places and companions to avoid.
exp.0:27:
It says that a time will come when people will cry out for help, but will receive no answer. "They shall seek me early" means seeking eagerly, from the start, searching with urgency. "They shall not find me" means they will not be able to find her, even though they look for her.

The speaker is Wisdom, presented as a woman who calls to everyone in the street (vv. 20-21). She had offered advice and correction, but the people ignored her. So, when disaster arrives, she warns that it will already be too late. It is strong language, typical of Hebrew poetry, to show that rejecting wisdom brings serious consequences. The following verses explain the reason.

Today, let us not wait until we are in crisis to seek God and his guidance. If he speaks to us now through his Word or through wise counsel, let us listen with humility. Other parts of the Bible show that God receives the one who turns to him sincerely (Isaiah 55:6).
exp.21:19:
The writer asks: "Have I not written to you three times in counsels and knowledge?" It is a rhetorical question meant to remind the reader that they have already received teaching. "Knowledge" here means wise understanding, not modern science. The phrase "three times" is difficult: some translate it as "thirty sayings" (as several modern versions do), since the Hebrew allows that reading, and many connect it with the thirty sayings that follow. Others think it means "on repeated occasions." There is no single certain explanation.

Here a teacher of wisdom speaks, like a father to his son, introducing a collection of practical teachings. He wants the young man to keep these words in his heart, trust in God, and be able to give true answers to anyone who asks him.

Today, it is not enough to hear good advice just once. Choose one teaching from the Bible, repeat it, meditate on it, and apply it this week.
exp.4:10:
It says that, at the end of life, the person will groan or lament in pain, when their flesh and their body are spent. "The last times" means the final stage of life. "Spent" means worn down or weakened until exhausted.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, as in the whole chapter. He warns him against the adulterous woman, that is, unfaithfulness. Earlier he said that this path takes away honor, years, and the fruit of one's labor. Then comes the lament of the one who admits he did not want to listen to advice. Some understand the "wasting away" as physical harm or illness, others as the general wearing down of life; the text allows both ideas.

For today: the decisions we make now leave marks on the future. Before acting, ask yourself how you will feel many years from now. Listen to wise and faithful people, and accept their correction in time, before the cost becomes greater.
exp.21:10:
This proverb says that the one who values a pure heart, meaning sincere and without deceit, and who also speaks with kind and gracious words, can come to win the friendship of a king. "Pureness of heart" refers to inner purity and honesty. "The grace of his lips" speaks of pleasant and wise speech.

It is part of the book of Proverbs, to which tradition attributes much of the material, traditionally linked to Solomon, though this section (verse 22:17 onward has a different tone) is presented as wisdom for everyday life. The nearby verses speak of generosity, of driving away the one who stirs up quarrels, and of God watching over those who act in truth. Some understand the king as an image of anyone who holds authority.

For today: take care of your inner life and of the way you speak. Honest dealing and kind words open doors of trust, even with important people, though they do not always guarantee results.
exp.5:1:
This verse says that a person becomes trapped, like an animal caught in a snare, by what they themselves promised with their words. The words "snared" and "taken" mean tied up and caught. "Words" here means what one says or expresses. The idea is repeated twice to underline it.

It is a wise father speaking to his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs. The verses before it speak of standing surety, that is, pledging to pay another person's debt, and of striking hands, which was the way a deal was sealed. The father wants to warn his son about the danger of promising without thinking, and then urges him to get out of that trouble as soon as possible.

For today: before you sign, co-sign a loan, or promise something, stop and think about whether you can truly keep it. And if you have already committed yourself to more than you can handle, act with humility and speak with the other person soon.
exp.5:31:
This verse says that whoever commits adultery with another man's wife has no common sense. "Lacks understanding" means he is missing good judgment or wisdom. And "destroys his own soul" means he harms himself from the inside, in his life and in his character.

Here a wise father is instructing his son, as throughout the book of Proverbs. He compares the adulterer to a thief. A thief driven by hunger can be understood, and yet he must still repay. The adulterer has no excuse, and his punishment is worse: disgrace and the anger of the wronged husband.

For today: guard your heart before desire leads you to decisions you cannot undo. Set clear limits in your friendships, in what you look at, and in your conversations. If you are struggling, seek help from someone mature and trustworthy. God offers forgiveness and restoration to those who repent.
exp.18:10:
A sensible person keeps their anger under control. The word "discretion" means good judgment and wise restraint. Where the verse says "deferreth his anger," it means he holds back his anger before it breaks out. And "pass over a transgression" means letting an offense go, not making much of it or answering with revenge. The verse says that this is his "glory," that is, his dignity and his worth.

Proverbs is a collection of wisdom. Tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon, though not all scholars agree on every section. Here a teacher of wisdom instructs, especially the young. Around it there are contrasts between the wise and the foolish, between the false word and the prudent one, and between the anger of a king and his favor.

Today, when someone offends you, wait before you respond. Breathe, pray, and ask yourself whether it is worth answering. Many small offenses can be let go with calm, and that patience protects your relationships and your peace.
exp.15:1:
This verse says that people tend to see their own conduct as right and pure. We almost always find good reasons for what we do. But God does not stop at appearances or at our explanations: he "weigheth the spirits," that is, he examines the deepest motives of the heart as though weighing them on a scale. "In his own eyes" means how he sees himself.

This text is in the book of Proverbs, which tradition attributes largely to Solomon, though not all scholars agree on every detail. These are teachings of wisdom to guide daily life. The verses nearby speak of planning and of trusting God, so this one reminds us that our plans need humility.

Today, before justifying yourself, ask God: "Why did I really do this?" Ask him to examine your motives and to correct you with love.
exp.16:18:
He who loves strife loves transgression, since a quarrel almost always brings offense and harm. The verse calls that sin "transgression," meaning a fault, a wrongdoing, or rebellion. The second part speaks of someone who "exalteth his gate," that is, who makes the door of his house very high or showy. It probably refers to pride or ostentation, and for that reason such a person seeks "destruction," that is, ruin. Some think it may also refer to a mouth that speaks with arrogance; the text allows both readings.

It is a proverb from the book of Proverbs, attributed in large part to Solomon, which offers brief wisdom for daily life. Here it stands among sayings about friendship, reckless commitments, and the perverse heart. It contrasts the person who builds relationships with the one who breaks them through pride and conflict.

For today: before entering an argument, ask yourself whether you are seeking truth and peace or simply trying to win and look impressive. Choose humility and, when you can, end the quarrel with a kind word.
exp.27:20:
It is not good to show favoritism, that is, to treat some people better than others because of their position, their money, or how much we like them. "Showing favoritism" means that eye-to-eye sense: leaning toward someone without justice. The proverb notes that a person can bend justice even for something very small, "a piece of bread."

It is a proverb of wisdom attributed to Solomon, according to the book, though this section was gathered together later. It stands among warnings about honest work, greed, and truth. It teaches that the desire for gain, even a small gain, can corrupt judgment.

Today we can examine whether we favor someone out of convenience: at work, in the church, or in the family. We can choose to treat everyone with justice, even when no one is watching and it does not benefit us.
exp.25:12:
This verse shows a lazy man who invents an excuse to avoid going out to work. He says there is a lion on the road and another in the streets. The point is that, in his view, going out would be too dangerous. The "streets" were the squares or open spaces of the city.

The book of Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and here the speaker is the wise teacher who instructs. He is not describing a real danger but mocking, with humor, exaggerated excuses. The verses that follow compare the lazy man to a door that turns on its hinges without moving forward: a lot of motion in bed, but no progress. It is a portrait of laziness.

For today: when you notice yourself making dramatic excuses to avoid a task, ask yourself honestly whether the obstacle is real or is only fear or comfort. Take the first small, concrete step today.
exp.27:22:
He who corrects a person sincerely will, in time, receive more respect than he who praises them with flattering words. To correct means to point out a mistake. To flatter means to praise someone, saying what pleases them even when it is not true. To find favor means to be well regarded or to gain goodwill and respect.

This verse is among the proverbs of Solomon, later gathered by the men of Hezekiah. They are words of wisdom for everyday life. Just before it, the text speaks of not showing partiality for convenience or letting oneself be bought, and afterward, of dishonesty. So honest truth spoken with courage is set in contrast with self-serving flattery.

Today, if you see a friend or family member going down the wrong path, tell them with respect, calmness, and love, even when it is uncomfortable. And avoid flattering people just to be liked. In the long run, kind honesty builds trust.
exp.22:12:
The verse says that a parent should not refuse to correct their child. "Child" is the young boy or youth, and "withhold" means to hold back or to refuse to do something. The "rod" was the common tool of discipline in that time. The idea is that firm correction will not destroy the child. Here "hell" translates the Hebrew word Sheol, which refers to the grave or the place of the dead.

It is a teacher of wisdom speaking to his son, within a series of practical advice for living well. Before this, he warns against taking advantage of orphans, and afterward he encourages the pursuit of wisdom. Interpreters debate whether the rod should be understood literally or as a symbol of authority and guidance.

Correcting with love and clear limits, without being carried away by anger, is a way of caring for the future of children. Avoiding all correction is not love; wise discipline seeks the good of the child and never harm.
exp.18:12:
This verse uses two images of suffering in the home. A foolish son, that is, one who acts without good sense and rejects correction, is a calamity or ruin to his father. And contentions, meaning constant quarrels and arguments, are compared to a continual dropping, that drip that never stops and wears down the one who hears it.

These words are a proverb of wisdom, attributed in the book to Solomon. The verses nearby speak of self-control, of the anger of kings, and of laziness. Here the wise teacher shows, with examples from everyday life, how certain attitudes damage peace in the family. The text speaks of a wife, but the principle of constant complaint applies to anyone.

For today: take care of the atmosphere in your home. Correct with patience, learn to listen, and when there are differences, speak with calm and truth, without repeating the reproach again and again. Ask God for wisdom to be a source of peace and not of wearing down.
exp.10:5:
It says that an honest and upright life protects people, while those who live in wrongdoing end up trapped by their own mistakes. The word "righteousness" in the verse means living with integrity and doing what is right before God and other people. The "upright" are those who walk the straight path. The word "shall be taken" means caught, like an animal in a net.

It is a proverb of wisdom, traditionally attributed to Solomon, directed above all at young people who are learning to live well. The verses around it repeat the same idea: riches do not save, but righteousness does. It is a general principle of life, not a promise that comes true automatically in every case. Other passages, such as Job, show that righteous people also suffer.

For today: when a dishonest shortcut tempts you, remember that wrongdoing often traps the one who practices it. Choose today to be honest in something small, trusting that God watches over the path of the one who walks uprightly.
exp.22:25:
Here the speaker asks his son to give him his heart, that is, his will, his affections, and his deepest decisions. He also asks that his eyes take careful notice of the ways he teaches. "Ways" are the ways of living.

The book of Proverbs presents a wise father instructing his son. Earlier it speaks of the joy of parents when the son is wise. Afterward it warns against the seduction of the immoral woman. Some also see here the voice of Wisdom, or even of God as Father; the text does not make this clear, and it can be read in either way.

For today: before making an important decision, ask yourself to whom you are giving your heart. Spend time in God's Word and in wise counsel, and let them guide what you look at and what you choose.
exp.13:28:
Here is what it says: The one who is slow to anger is the person who is patient before getting upset, and the Bible says that person has great understanding. By contrast, the one who is short-tempered is the person who has little patience and flares up quickly. That kind of person makes folly bigger, that is, increases their foolishness, because when they explode in anger they reveal and add to their madness.

Context: Proverbs gathers teachings of wisdom, and tradition attributes much of the book to Solomon. Here a teacher of wisdom speaks, like a father instructing his children. The nearby verses speak of the fear of the Lord, of a calm heart, and of compassion, and they show that a wise life shows in one's character.

For today: When something bothers you, before you respond, take a breath, stay silent for a few seconds, and pray. That pause can prevent words you later regret and helps you respond with calm and good judgment.
exp.4:21:
He says that the wicked will be caught by his own wrongdoing. His sins are like ropes or snares that bind him and keep him from moving freely. The person who lives without respect for God is called the ungodly one. The twisted or unjust acts are the wrongdoings. Held fast means bound or caught.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. He warns against unfaithfulness and immorality. The previous verse reminds us that God sees all the paths of a person, and the next one shows the end of whoever rejects correction: he loses his way through his foolishness.

For today: small sins that are repeated can become habits that enslave. Do not wait until you feel trapped. Seek God today and a trusted person, confess what binds you, and accept correction in time.
exp.29:6:
The explanation says that the speaker makes a prayer to God: he asks for two things and begs that they not be refused to him while he lives. He is making a sincere and urgent request.

The speaker is Agur, son of Jakeh, according to the opening of the chapter. We know almost nothing else about him. He begins by acknowledging that God's word is trustworthy and that nothing should be added to it. The two things he asks for follow right away: to keep falsehood far away from him, and to have neither extreme poverty nor extreme wealth, so that he will not forget God or fall into theft.

Today we can learn to pray with few words and with clarity, asking for what truly matters: honesty and a heart that depends on God. Before asking for much, it is good to ask ourselves what we really need in order to remain faithful to Him.
exp.23:0:
This verse advises not to envy wicked people, that is, not to look with longing at what they seem to have. Nor should we want to be associated with them. The word "envy" here means desiring their success or their way of life.

The book of Proverbs attributes much of its content to Solomon, although this section (chapters 22 to 24) is presented as "the words of the wise." It is wise counsel, like a father's advice to his son. The reason is explained in the following verse: the wicked plan harm and speak with malice. Their apparent success is not a good model.

For today: if you see that someone is doing well even though they act with deceit, do not envy or imitate them. Choose friends who encourage you to live with honesty, and trust that what is right has a more lasting value.
exp.20:19:
In the house of the wise person, the verse says, there is a treasure that is desirable and plentiful. "Desirable" means it is worth wanting, and "rich" means full and abundant. The fool, that is, the person who does not think ahead or control himself, will squander it, which is to say he will spend it all and waste it.

Proverbs gathers practical wisdom, and tradition attributes much of it to Solomon. Here the teacher compares two ways of living. The verses nearby speak of justice, conflicts, and decisions. Some think the "treasure" means material goods; others think it also includes the good life that wisdom leaves behind.

Today, wisdom shows up in simple things: spending with a plan, saving a little, and not living on impulse alone. Before a big purchase, wait a day and pray. Take care of what God has entrusted to you.
exp.2:7:
It says that trusting God, acknowledging him in everything, and turning away from evil brings something good for the body and for the whole of life. The phrase that would correspond to "it will be healing" means that it will bring health or relief. The word for the navel here stands for the body in general, and the word for marrow refers to the substance inside the bones that gives them life and strength. The small word spelled with an accent mark before "your" is simply old spelling.

It is a wise father speaking to his son in the book of Proverbs, traditionally attributed to Solomon. He wants the young man to live with humility and not to think himself wise in his own eyes. The verse is a proverb, that is, a general principle of wisdom, not a promise that sickness will never come. Some understand it as physical health, others as the well-being of the whole person.

Today you can practice this by letting go of worry and pride: before deciding something important, pray and ask God for direction, and seek wise counsel. A life at peace with him often brings rest to the heart and the body.
exp.11:0:
It says that whoever enjoys being corrected is in fact someone who loves to learn and grow in wisdom. On the other hand, whoever hates being rebuked is "ignorant," a strong word that here describes someone stubborn who refuses to learn. "Correction" is the discipline that guides us, and "rebuke" is the call to pay attention.

This verse is in Proverbs, attributed largely to Solomon, where a wisdom teacher instructs the young. There is no earlier narrative context. What follows contrasts the good person, who receives the favor of the LORD, with the wicked, who does not stand firm, while the root of the righteous remains steady.

For today: the next time someone points out a mistake to you, take a breath before defending yourself. Ask yourself humbly, "What can I learn from this?" And ask God for a heart willing to be taught.
exp.5:27:
