This verse asks a question that everyone would answer the same way: no one can walk on hot coals without burning their feet. The obvious answer is "no," and that is the lesson.

It is part of a wise father's instructions to his son. In the verses before and after, he compares adultery to playing with fire. He says that whoever goes in to his neighbor's wife will not go unpunished or escape the consequences. The passage does not aim to frighten, but to protect.

For today: some decisions seem small, but they have real consequences. If you know that a certain friendship, habit, or place is pulling you toward something that would damage your marriage, your conscience, or your family, step away in time. It is wiser to avoid the fire than to wait until you are burned.
exp.6:25:
She has brought down many wounded, and many strong men have been slain by her. The explanation says that the seductive woman described in this chapter has thrown down a great number of people, leaving them wounded. Even the strongest and most capable were killed because of her. The words "á" and "oidme" are old forms: today we would say "a" and "escúchenme."

The phrase "brought down the wounded" suggests people who were knocked to the ground as victims, not people who merely stumbled.

It is a wise father, in the manner of Solomon, who is speaking and instructing his children. He warns them against unfaithfulness and seduction. He gives as an example a woman who attracts with smooth words but leads to ruin. The verse is a warning: no one is strong enough to let their guard down. Many scholars also see here an image of temptation in general.

For today: do not think you are immune. Avoid the places, conversations, and situations that feed a temptation, and surround yourself with sincere people who help you stay firm.
exp.14:9:
It says that for someone who has strayed from the good path, being corrected is very hard and painful to bear. A rebuke is a call to attention or a reproach, and "painful" here means heavy and grievous. Furthermore, whoever hates correction and always rejects it comes to a bad end; the word for "dies" speaks of a ruin that can reach as far as death.

This is a proverb of wisdom, attributed largely to Solomon, directed above all at young people and at the whole people. In its context, God rejects the way of the wicked and loves those who pursue righteousness. The verse shows that a stubborn heart cannot even tolerate being corrected, and the next verse says that the scoffer does not love the one who reproves him.

Today, the next time someone corrects you with respect, do not react defensively right away. Listen, pray, and ask yourself whether there is truth in what they are saying. Correcting yourself in time prevents greater harm.
exp.20:1:
This proverb says that every person thinks their own way of living is right. The word "opinion" in the older text means "eyes" or "appearance": what a person sees and believes. But the Lord "pondereth the hearts," that is, He examines the intentions and the deepest motives, like someone placing something on a scale.

It is part of Proverbs, wisdom attributed largely to Solomon, although some scholars think the book gathers several collections. It speaks like a teacher advising his people. The verse before it says that God guides the heart of the king, and the verse after it says that God values justice more than sacrifices. So the theme is that God looks at what is inside, not only at outward appearances.

For today: before defending a decision, sincerely ask God, "What motives are there in my heart?" Also, listen to the advice of wise people, because sometimes we do not see our own mistakes.
exp.5:20:
The verse says we should always keep our parents' teachings in our hearts. To bind them on the heart and tie them about the neck is a picture: let those words be as close to us as something we wear and never take off.

Here a wise father speaks to his son, within the counsel of the book of Proverbs, which is traditionally associated with Solomon. Earlier he warned against lying and against quarrels among brothers. Now he asks the son to keep his father's commandment and his mother's teaching, because they are a guide and a protection in daily life.

Today we can choose one piece of good advice we have received, from the Bible or from someone who loves us, and go over it each morning. That way we carry it in our hearts, and it guides us when we have to make decisions.

sum.10: Proverbs 11 contrasts the righteous person with the wicked. Honesty, humility, careful speech, and generosity bring life, protection, and blessing. Pride, deceit, gossip, and trusting in riches lead to downfall. God values integrity and rejects wickedness.
sum.21: Proverbs 22 teaches that a good name is worth more than wealth, and that God made both the rich and the poor. It advises being prudent, humble, generous, and hardworking, raising children well, avoiding quick-tempered people, and not taking on debts for others. It also commands not to exploit the poor, because God defends their cause.
sum.9: Proverbs 10 contrasts the righteous person with the wicked. The righteous are wise, hardworking, honest, and careful with their words, and God sustains and blesses them. The wicked, who are lazy, deceitful, or foolish, come to a bad end. The chapter also teaches that love covers over wrongs and that talking too much brings trouble.
sum.2: A father asks his son not to forget his teachings, to trust God with all his heart and not lean on his own understanding, and to honor Him with what he has. He says that wisdom is worth more than gold and brings life and peace. He also encourages the son to be generous toward his neighbor and not to envy the unjust.
sum.5: Proverbs 6 warns against putting up security for someone else's debt without thinking it through. It warns against laziness, and it uses the ant as an example of diligent work. It also warns against wickedness, lying, and the quarrels that God hates. It advises keeping the teaching of your parents as a light on your path. Finally, it warns that adultery brings shame and ruin.
sum.16: Proverbs 17 teaches that peace, loyalty, and wise words are worth more than wealth or quarrels. God tests hearts, and the chapter warns against mocking the poor, injustice, bribery, and arguments that get out of control. It also shows that a cheerful heart does good, and that even a fool seems wise if he keeps quiet.
sum.6: A father asks his son to hold on to his teachings and to love wisdom, so that they will keep him safe from the seductive woman. He tells how he once saw a young man with no sense fall for her flattery, like an ox walking to the slaughterhouse. He ends with a warning that this path leads to death.
sum.7: In Proverbs 8, wisdom speaks like a person calling out to everyone in the streets and at the city gates. She offers truth, justice, and riches better than gold, and she says she was with God from before creation. She invites people to listen, because whoever finds her finds life and God's favor.
sum.3: A father urges his children to listen to his teaching and to pursue wisdom above all else, recalling what his own father taught him. He warns them to stay away from the path of the wicked, because the way of the righteous shines brighter and brighter, like the light of day. He asks them to guard their hearts, watch their words, and walk straight without turning aside.
sum.4: A father asks his son to listen to his wisdom and stay away from the adulterous woman, whose words are sweet but whose end is bitter and leads to death. He encourages him to be faithful to the wife of his youth and to enjoy her love. He reminds him that God sees all his ways, and that the fool dies for refusing correction.
sum.22: Proverbs 23 advises against craving wealth or the food of someone who has bad intentions, and it urges respect for boundaries and for the rights of orphans. It encourages seeking wisdom, disciplining children, honoring parents, and continuing in the fear of Jehovah. It warns against gluttony, sexual immorality, and wine, which ends in pain and enslavement.
sum.27: Proverbs 28 contrasts the righteous person, who lives with courage and integrity, with the wicked person, who flees even when no one is chasing them. It teaches that God blesses honesty, humility, the confession of sin, and generosity toward the poor. It also warns against oppression, greed, get-rich-quick wealth, and an unjust ruler.
sum.18: Proverbs 19 teaches that an honest life is worth more than wealth, even when a person is poor, than lies and foolishness. It warns against false testimony, laziness, and anger, and encourages people to listen to advice and to respect their parents. It says that the fear of the LORD gives life, and that his plans prevail.
sum.14: Proverbs 15 contrasts the wise and the foolish, especially in how they speak and how they receive correction. It teaches that a gentle answer calms anger, that God sees everything and hears the prayer of the upright, and that a little with the fear of God and love is better than wealth with conflict. It ends by saying that humility comes before honor.
sum.15: Proverbs 16 teaches that people make their plans, but God directs their steps, so it is wise to commit our work to him. It warns that pride leads to a fall and praises humility, justice, and wisdom, which are worth more than gold. It also speaks of governing one's character and of watching over words that are gentle and honest.
sum.30: Proverbs 31 records what the mother of King Lemuel taught him: that he should not spend his strength on excess or on wine, but should defend the mute, the poor, and the needy with justice. It then describes the strong woman, who is hardworking, generous, and wise, and it concludes that the woman who fears Jehovah is worthy of praise.
sum.19: Proverbs 20 offers advice for living wisely: avoiding excessive wine, laziness, quarrels, gossip, and cheating in business. It teaches that God detests dishonest weights, that no one can claim to be completely free of sin, and that it is good to honor one's parents. It also says that God directs our steps, and that we should not take revenge but wait on Him.
sum.12: Proverbs 13 contrasts the wise person with the fool. The wise person listens to advice, watches what they say, works hard, rejects lies, and keeps company with wise people, and so receives life, honor, and good things. The fool despises correction, is lazy and proud, and ends up in poverty, conflict, and ruin.
sum.28: Proverbs 29 contrasts the life of the righteous with that of the wicked. It warns that whoever rejects correction will be destroyed, that good government brings joy and justice to the poor, and that discipline produces wisdom. It also teaches that pride brings humiliation, and that whoever trusts in the LORD is secure.
sum.29: Agur humbly admits that he has no wisdom of his own, and he affirms that every word of God is pure and that God protects those who trust in him. He asks not to be either poor or rich, so that he will not forget God or fall into stealing. He then warns against pride, greed, and disrespect toward parents, and he teaches through examples of small animals that are nonetheless wise.
sum.17: Proverbs 18 shows the power of words. The fool speaks without listening and gets tangled up in his own mouth, while the tongue can bring life or death. It also teaches that the name of the LORD is a safe refuge, more than riches, and that humility and true friendship are worth a great deal.
sum.24: This chapter gathers proverbs of Solomon that were copied out in the time of Hezekiah. It teaches humility before rulers, wisdom in speaking and in settling disputes, and the value of right words and of a faithful messenger. It also calls for self-restraint, for rejecting false testimony, for doing good to an enemy, and for mastering one's own spirit.
sum.20: Proverbs 21 teaches that God governs even the heart of the king and examines the intentions of everyone. He prefers justice and mercy to empty sacrifices, and it warns against pride, lying, laziness, greed, and quarrels at home. In the end it says that no plan can defeat God, because salvation comes from Him.
sum.1: A father asks his son to receive and keep his words, and to seek wisdom the way someone searches for silver or hidden treasure. God gives that wisdom, watches over the upright, and protects them from the wrong path and from the seductive stranger. The upright will remain in the land, but the wicked will be cut off from it.
sum.0: Proverbs 1 says its purpose is to give wisdom, discretion, and good judgment, and that the beginning of knowledge is the fear of the LORD. A father warns his son not to join with violent people who seek unjust gain, because those paths lead to destruction. Wisdom calls out in the public squares, and whoever rejects her will face the consequences, but whoever listens to her will live in peace.
sum.8: Wisdom has prepared her house and her feast, and she calls to the simple to leave their foolishness, to live, and to walk in the way of understanding. She teaches that the wise person accepts correction and grows, that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and that each person bears the consequences of their own choices. By contrast, the foolish woman also calls out, but her allure hides death.
sum.26: Proverbs 27 gives practical advice for living: do not boast about tomorrow or about yourself, and value the friend who corrects you honestly. It also warns against anger, envy, and foolishness, and reminds us that riches do not last forever. For this reason it encourages careful attention to the flock and to one's work.
sum.11: Proverbs 12 contrasts the righteous with the wicked, and the wise with the foolish. It teaches that those who accept correction, speak the truth, work hard, and give advice kindly live better lives. By contrast, lying, laziness, and wickedness lead to deception and ruin. It says that there is life on the path of righteousness.
sum.25: Proverbs 26 describes the fool, to whom honor does not fit, and warns that his words and errands cause harm. It also portrays the lazy person, who makes up excuses and thinks himself wise. Finally, it warns about the gossip, the deceiver, and the one who speaks falsely, for they end up trapped by their own wrongdoing.
sum.13: Proverbs 14 compares the wise person with the fool. The wise person fears God, thinks before acting, controls their anger, and shows compassion to the poor. The fool mocks sin, deceives themselves, and is driven by envy and anger. It says that righteousness exalts a nation.
sum.23: Proverbs 24 advises not to envy wicked people and to seek wisdom, which builds up a household and strengthens a person. It calls us to rescue someone who is in danger, not to rejoice when an enemy falls, and to be fair without showing favoritism. It ends with the example of the lazy person's field, which becomes overgrown with thorns, and warns that laziness brings poverty.
